title: Bysa - Bring Your Smart Agent
pitch: Have you read a lengthy article and wish to ask about certain points but there is nowhere to ask? Now, you can, with WebMCP. Just bring your own agent and let them "see" the same website with you.
about_excerpt:
Have you read a lengthy article and wish to ask about certain points but there is nowhere to ask? Now, you can, with WebMCP. Just bring your own agent and let them "see" the same website with you.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 WebMCP tool that allows users to ask their agents to summarize an article 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP tool that allows users to ask their agents to summarize an article 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP tool that allows users to ask their agents to summarize an article 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I was on a learning website and I ran out of credits to ask their bespoke AI assistant. At that time, I wished I could bring my ow agent and ask it about points that I didn't understand. When I learned of WebMCP, I knew it would be perfect for my use case. Instead of depending on other developers' implementation of AI agents, I will let my carefully personalized agent be my reading, learning and researching partner. 

 What it does 

 The website exposes several tools that the agents can use: 

 
 Get the content of the current article the user is reading 
 List all articles available on the website 
 Save the summary of an article to localStorage . 
 

 Now, users can ask the agent about concepts in the article they are reading or in other articles. They can ask the agent to summarize an article and this summary will be saved to a flyout that can be toggled with a button. Next time, when the user visits the same article again, the Summary button will be there for you! Of course, they can ask the agent to delete the summary. 

 How we built it 

 The website is nothing more than a basic React app, something that you will build whenever you learn a new frontend framework. The meaty part is the use of WebMCP imperative API to register tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Nothing significant that I can remember. Implementing WebMCP turns out to be a small project. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I think I have empowered readers to get answers for things they don't understand about a third-party website. And I would be amused if I can have a summary of a verbose article I am reading using my own agent without leaving the website. 

 What we learned 

 The most obvious use cases for WebMCP is ecommerce - you can use it to enhance storefront, booking platforms etc. However, you can also use it to create delightful experience for a humble website, even when you think it has no use for WebMCP. 

 What's next for Bysa - Bring Your Smart Agent 

 Fine-tune the existing tool to enhance the human and agent's experience. Keep the tools working seamlessly while watching the WebMCP standards evolve.

title: ToolMint
pitch: ToolMint lets non-technical site owners make their website agent-ready, by showing it how to do a job one time.
about_excerpt: ToolMint lets non-technical site owners make their website agent-ready, by showing it how to do a job one time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We provided small and medium businesses assistance with various no-code tools, such as site creators, form builders, and tools for automating processes over the years. What makes these tools work is simple: users don’t need to write detailed technical specifications. They show or explain the tool what they want, or build it visually(drag n drop editors), and the tool handles the technical work. That’s how a shop owner can create a booking form without needing to call a developer. When we explored WebMCP, we noticed a clear gap. Making a website agent-ready required writing tool definitions in code. But avoiding code is exactly why people choose no-code tools in the first place. This meant that many of the businesses that could benefit most from agents were also the least likely to adopt them. We started thinking about what a no-code approach to WebMCP might look like and built a workflow that feels familiar.A website owner records themselves performing an action on their site. ToolMint’s SDK converts that recording into a draft WebMCP action, along with a clear, human-readable description of what the tool does, what inputs it requires, and what action it performs - all in simple, non technical terms.The owner reviews and approves the draft. Once published, the action becomes available for visitors to use through their agents. What it does ToolMint lets a site owner perform a task once, like booking an appointment. It records the workflow and turns it into an approved WebMCP tool that agents can use. How we built it ToolMint runs as a single Node.js service on Render. It serves the demo website, SDK and a control-plane API , with SQLite storing approved tools and their versions. It has four main parts: Recorder (part of sdk) — Runs inside the website and observes the task performed by the owner. It captures meaningful form changes, actions, page outcomes and the structure of related same-origin network requests. Compiler — Converts the recording into a versioned capability. It identifies the successful workflow, determines possible agent inputs, builds a replay recipe, and creates success and failure checks from what actually happened on the page. SDK — Loads approved capabilities for the current website and user surface, then registers them as native WebMCP tools. Tools can be updated or revoked without changing the website’s application code. Runtime — Executes a tool inside the live authenticated page. It validates inputs, resolves the correct record, follows the recorded steps, respects confirmation policy, and verifies that the expected page state and network operation occurred. Individual tool calls do not pass through the ToolMint backend. OpenAI helps improve names, descriptions and input recommendations. It does not generate selectors, execution steps, permissions or success proofs. Those come from observed evidence, are reviewed by the owner, and are compiled deterministically before publishing. Challenges we ran into Knowing whether the task really worked was harder than replaying the clicks. A success message was not enough. Every write capability needs evidence that the page actually changed, together with the expected network response when available. If ToolMint cannot produce a reliable proof, it will not publish the capability. People make mistakes while recording. Our first version treated the entire recording as one script, so a typo followed by a retry became part of the generated tool. We had to split recordings into attempts, compile only the path through the final success, and preserve earlier failures as known failure conditions. Deciding what should become an agent input. Real pages contain many fields that have nothing to do with the task. ToolMint considers what the owner changed, what appeared during the workflow and what the success proof depends on. The owner makes the final decision, but cannot remove an input required to verify the result. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built the complete record-to-tool loop. A site owner can perform a real task, review the inferred inputs and policy, publish it, and see a new native WebMCP tool become available without writing a handler or building another API. The generated tools work across user sessions. A workflow recorded with one customer’s vehicles can be invoked with another customer’s vehicles because account-specific choices are rebuilt from the current authenticated page. The tools verify their own results. A write is not reported as successful just because the final button was clicked. ToolMint checks the observed page state and related network response before returning success. We kept AI assistance within clear boundaries. OpenAI can improve names, descriptions and recommendations, but it cannot invent selectors, execution steps, permissions or proofs. The final capability is compiled deterministically from recorded evidence and approved by the owner. What we learned A recorded workflow is evidence, not a finished tool. Raw clicks include mistakes, temporary state and values that only belong to the person recording. They need to be interpreted before they can become a reusable capability. Reliable agent tools need clear success conditions. Executing the final action is not enough. The tool must know what changed and whether it changed for the right record. What's next for ToolMint Tell the owner when a tool breaks. We already record every execution; right now that data stays in the browser. Sending it back gives us health status, drift detection at registration, and a reason to pause a capability automatically. Wider Capture - autocomplete widgets and shadow-DOM component libraries are all invisible to the recorder today. title: Visually
pitch: The browser-first design studio where people and agents create on the same editable canvas.
about_excerpt: The browser-first design studio where people and agents create on the same editable canvas. Like Comment Story Updates From templates to timeline, Visually keeps the complete workflow in one responsive studio. Visually — design together with WebMCP. Human direct manipulation stays visible, editable, and undoable after every agent action. 17 typed WebMCP tools let agents create, revise, audit, and inspect the same live canvas. Browser-local rendering, export, ML, and media pipelines keep creative work on-device. Inspiration Most creative tools still treat an AI agent as an outside observer. Visually explores a more useful model: a professional design editor whose real product actions are available to people and agents on the same editable canvas. What it does Visually is a responsive, local-first visual design studio built around Konva. A person can start from 18 polished templates and edit text, shapes, images, drawings, tables, layers, media, effects, animations, timing, and multiple square, portrait, landscape, print, or custom-size pages. Its WebMCP layer registers 17 typed product-native tools. In the fastest judge path, one brief becomes five coordinated assets—Instagram post, Instagram story, YouTube thumbnail, poster, and landscape banner. An agent can then propagate semantic copy, color-token, and typography changes across all five pages and run a read-only audit for overflow, contrast, safe-area crossings, missing image alt text, and brand consistency. Every call emits a sanitized receipt with affected pages and elements. The full run is undoable in one click, but that undo disables itself after a later human edit so it cannot silently overwrite the person's work. The result is not “AI beside a design app.” It is one shared creative surface: the agent accelerates setup and repetitive changes; the human retains judgment, direct manipulation, and final control. How we used WebMCP Visually feature-detects document.modelContext and progressively registers JSON-schema tools through registerTool . The tools call the same Zustand actions used by the visible React UI, so mutations immediately appear on the Konva canvas, enter the same transaction-aware history, persist locally, and remain directly editable. Read tools are annotated read-only; schemas bound sizes, types, and input lengths; project replacement and deletion require explicit confirm: true . A legacy navigator.modelContext fallback supports earlier browser builds, while the editor continues to work normally when WebMCP is unavailable. This is more reliable than screen-coordinate automation: agents query semantic state, act on stable element IDs, receive structured results, and share the human's real document instead of maintaining a parallel representation. How we built it The application uses React 19, Vite, TypeScript, Konva, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Base UI, and Cloudflare Workers. The document engine, autosave, rendering, and export paths are browser-first. PNG, JPEG, WebP, SVG, PDF, printable HTML, PPTX, GIF, MP4, and WebM exports run client-side. Media conversion loads ffmpeg.wasm on demand, and background removal uses a lazy browser ML pipeline with WebGPU/WASM fallback. An optional Worker signs direct R2 transfers with progress, cancellation, and retry. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was making agent actions feel native rather than bolted on. Tool calls had to share pointer and keyboard mutation semantics, selection, grouping, page operations, undo/redo, persistence, and destructive confirmations. The second challenge was proving safety without making the flow tedious; that led to read-only annotations, bounded schemas, semantic roles, visible receipts, atomic history steps, and conflict-aware undo. We also had to keep large media pipelines responsive on mobile and robust across radically different aspect ratios. Accomplishments that we're proud of 17 typed, product-native WebMCP tools with structured receipts. One brief becomes five coordinated, fully editable campaign formats. Semantic brand updates modify copy, colors, and typography across every format in one operation. A read-only production audit checks five categories and reports affected pages. A judge-facing activity panel makes real calls inspectable and offers safe one-click undo. 18 original templates and a responsive desktop/mobile editor. Client-side image, document, animation, and video export. Destructive confirmation gates and an unsupported-browser fallback. A complete release gate: 260 frontend tests, 15 Worker tests, 26 applicable desktop/mobile Chromium tests, lint, TypeScript, backend type-checking, and production build. Frontend line coverage is 96.81%; Worker line coverage is 97.14%. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it exposes domain intent rather than a second DOM. “Create this campaign,” “apply this brand revision,” and “audit every page” are safer and more useful than asking an agent to guess coordinates. Just as importantly, agent output must remain immediately editable and reversible or the experience still feels like a handoff rather than collaboration. What's next Next we want opt-in live collaboration, richer typography flow, an attributed third-party asset catalog, reusable agent recipes, and a published reference contract for semantic canvas tools. title: Split WebMCP
pitch: Turn browsing into collaboration: Split combines dual-browser workspaces with WebMCP, letting humans and AI agents understand and act on the same shared context.
about_excerpt:
Turn browsing into collaboration: Split combines dual-browser workspaces with WebMCP, letting humans and AI agents understand and act on the same shared context.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 I originally built Split because I didn't like constantly switching between apps or browser pages when I wanted to do two things at once. The Android version of Split lets me keep two browser panes open together and organize them into different workspaces. 

 When I saw the WebMCP Challenge, I started thinking about Split differently. Instead of only asking how a person could use two browsers together, I wanted to know what would happen if an AI agent could work with that same workspace too. 

 The important part for me was that I didn't want to put a chatbot inside Split and call that AI integration. I wanted the AI to stay external and use WebMCP to understand and interact with Split through tools that the application intentionally exposes. 

 That became Split WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 Split WebMCP gives you two browser panes at the same time and four workspaces: T1, T2, T3, and T4 . 

 You can use Split normally as a human but when it is opened in a WebMCP-capable environment, an external AI agent can discover 11 WebMCP tools . 

 Those tools allow the agent to: 

 
 check the current workspace and panes 
 inspect the T1–T4 workspaces 
 switch between workspaces 
 open a resource in a selected pane 
 configure pane preferences 
 read and add notes 
 read and save bookmarks 
 create comparisons 
 

 The part I find most interesting is that the human and the agent are not working in two separate versions of Split. They work with the same application state. 

 For example, if the agent switches the workspace or adds a note through WebMCP, that change appears in Split for the human too. Agent actions are also marked with Agent provenance so it is clear where the action came from. 

 The AI itself is not built into Split. It stays external. WebMCP is what connects the agent to the application. 

 How we built it 

 The original Split Android app existed before this challenge. For the WebMCP Challenge, I built Split WebMCP as a separate web implementation . The original Android source was not copied into this project and is not included in the public repository. 

 I built the web version around shared state for the browser panes, T1–T4 workspaces, navigation, notes, bookmarks, comparisons, preferences, and activity. 

 Both normal human controls and WebMCP actions use that same state. This was important because I wanted an action performed by an agent to become a real part of the workspace instead of something happening in a separate AI demo. 

 The WebMCP tools are registered using: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 There are currently 11 registered tools . They have structured inputs and runtime validation, and the actions they perform are connected to the same state as the normal Split interface. 

 I also added URL validation, restricted URL schemes, local persistence, WebMCP feature detection, security headers, and same-origin demo pages that make the WebMCP behavior easier to test reliably. 

 I tested the finished public deployment with an external Codex browser agent. It discovered all 11 WebMCP tools and successfully called get_workspace . During integration testing I also verified actions such as switching workspaces and adding notes through WebMCP. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge was understanding what WebMCP should actually do for Split. 

 At first, it is easy to think that adding AI means putting an assistant or chatbot inside the application. But that isn't what I wanted to demonstrate. I wanted an external agent to be able to use specific parts of Split through WebMCP while I could still use the same interface normally. 

 Browser security was another challenge. Some third-party websites do not allow themselves to be embedded because of things like CSP and framing restrictions. I didn't want to bypass those protections or pretend every website could be embedded, so I added same-origin demo resources for reliable testing and kept a fallback for resources that cannot be displayed inside a pane. 

 I also had to think carefully about what an agent should be allowed to do. The WebMCP tools use defined schemas, validation, bounded inputs, and restricted URL schemes instead of giving the agent unrestricted access. 

 Another important challenge was separating my previous work from my hackathon work. Split already existed as an Android app, but Split WebMCP is the new web implementation I created for this challenge. The Android source remains separate. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm especially proud that the WebMCP integration actually works with an external agent . 

 On the public deployment, an external Codex browser agent was able to discover all 11 tools and call Split through WebMCP. 

 I'm also proud that I didn't have to turn Split into an AI chatbot to make that happen. Split still works as a normal human-controlled dual-browser workspace. WebMCP adds another way of interacting with it when a compatible agent is available. 

 The human can do something, the agent can continue from that workspace and the human can continue again from the agent's changes. 

 That is the part of Split WebMCP that I wanted to prove with this project. 

 What we learned 

 Before working on this project, I mostly thought about AI interacting with software through chat interfaces or by trying to operate the interface like a person. 

 Working with WebMCP showed me another approach. A website can expose specific tools that tell an agent what it is actually allowed to do and what inputs those actions require. 

 I also learned why shared state matters. If the AI has its own separate state, it doesn't really feel like the human and agent are working together. Connecting WebMCP actions to the same state as the human interface made the collaboration much more real. 

 I learned a lot about WebMCP tool design, browser security, validation, shared application state, and the limitations that come with embedding external web content. 

 What's next for Split WebMCP 

 I want to keep exploring what happens when the agent can understand more useful workspace context while still having clearly limited permissions. 

 I would like to improve research and comparison workflows and give agents more useful ways to help organize a browsing session without taking control away from the person using Split. 

 For me, the interesting direction is not simply putting AI inside a browser. It is finding better ways for a person and an external agent to work with the same browsing workspace together.

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Moxscore
pitch: Moxscore turns a Magic the Gathering Commander decklist into a clear health score, spotting weak mana, missing ramp, draw or interaction, so you and you agent can make smarter upgrades through webmcp
about_excerpt:
Moxscore turns a Magic the Gathering Commander decklist into a clear health score, spotting weak mana, missing ramp, draw or interaction, so you and you agent can make smarter upgrades through webmcp
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agents can ask for analysis, propose changes and reanalyze 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Moxscore logo 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Home page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 You can add your commander deck by pasting or uploading it in a textfile 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agents can ask for analysis, propose changes and reanalyze 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Moxscore logo 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Home page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 You can add your commander deck by pasting or uploading it in a textfile 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Agents can ask for analysis, propose changes and reanalyze 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Commander decklists can be hard to read at a glance. A list of 100 cards does not immediately reveal whether a deck has enough ramp, draw, interaction, lands, or a healthy mana curve. 

 I built Moxscore to turn a decklist into understandable signals and practical next steps, without handing players an unexplained, black-box verdict. My goal was to have a really useful tool that helps me tune my decks towards the bracket I aim for. 

 What it does 

 Moxscore is a browser-based Commander deck analyser. Paste a decklist, upload an export to receive: 

 
 A transparent deck health score 
 Role breakdowns for areas such as ramp, draw, interaction, lands, and mana 
 A mana-curve view 
 Combo signals and a beta Commander-bracket estimate 
 Deterministic category- and card-level tuning guidance 
 

 The core analysis runs locally in the browser, with no account required. WebMCP makes this analysis accessible to agents through clear, structured interactions as well as the normal player-facing interface. 

 How we built it 

 I designed Moxscore around a simple pipeline: ingest a Commander decklist, normalize the cards, classify cards into useful deck roles, calculate structural signals, and turn those signals into readable guidance. 

 The scoring system is heuristic and deterministic rather than AI-generated. That means players can understand what is being measured and why a recommendation appeared. I paired that analysis with a browser-first interface and WebMCP capabilities so both people and agents can work with the same deck-analysis flow. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making analysis useful without pretending it is absolute truth. Commander decks are highly contextual: a card that looks weak in isolation may be essential to a commander, theme, budget, or playgroup. 

 A real challenge was also had to handle varied decklist formats, incomplete exports, card-role ambiguity, and the challenge of translating many individual card signals into guidance that is concise and actionable. For WebMCP, we needed to make the important actions and outputs explicit enough for an agent to use reliably. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that Moxscore provides a useful first read of a 100-card deck in seconds while keeping its reasoning grounded in visible deck structure. 

 We are especially happy with: 

 
 Local, account-free core analysis 
 Transparent deterministic scoring instead of a black-box verdict 
 A practical health score, role breakdown, and mana-curve view in one place 
 Guidance that points to categories and cards, not just a number 
 A WebMCP-enabled experience that lets agents participate in deck analysis meaningfully 
 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the best agent-facing website actions are not vague commands—they need clear inputs, predictable outputs, and useful boundaries. WebMCP encouraged us to think carefully about what “analyse this deck” should mean and what structured information should come back. 

 We also learned that transparency is a feature. For a hobby as nuanced as Commander, players need guidance they can inspect, challenge, and adapt to their own table. 

 What's next for Moxscore 

 Next, we want to improve card-role classification, expand import reliability, refine the bracket estimate, and add more context-aware tuning suggestions. 

 In the product roadmap there are accounts with bracket aimed AI enhanced suggestions, pod analytics to see how 4 decks could stack up against each other Discord bot extensions to make it even more accessible. 

 I also want to deepen the WebMCP experience so agents can help players explore specific questions e.g whether a deck needs more interaction, where its curve is crowded, or which structural changes are most likely to improve consistency, or go deeper in specific meta, all while keeping the final deckbuilding decisions with the player.

pitch: WebMCP tools for safe App Store Optimization: agents research, explain, draft, and stage proposals; people retain approval.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tools for safe App Store Optimization: agents research, explain, draft, and stage proposals; people retain approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for ShipASO Inspiration App Store Optimization is a high-leverage workflow with a sharp boundary: an agent can do the research and drafting, but a person should retain the approval decision. What it does ShipASO watches app listings, keywords, and competitors. When a change matters, it prepares a proposal: title, subtitle, keywords, and promotional text at their exact character limits. On a run page, WebMCP tools let an agent read the queue, explain why a proposal exists, draft an alternative that preserves the brand, and stage it for review. The agent never gets an approval, publish, ship, or push tool. Staging changes what a person will review; it leaves the run awaiting approval. How it uses WebMCP ShipASO declares 14 page-scoped WebMCP tools. The browser reads the live tool list after registration, so the interface distinguishes a declared manifest from tools the browser actually received. Read and draft tools are available where they make sense; run-specific tools appear only on a run detail page. The boundary is also enforced on the server. Approval requires a single-use challenge issued when a run is opened and consumed with the approval update. That prevents replay and makes bulk approval follow the same per-run protection. What we learned Tool descriptions are not a security boundary. WebMCP makes the page's intended contract legible to agents, but server-side enforcement is still required for consequential actions. We deliberately built both: helpful tools for analysis and drafting, and a separate human decision point. Built with TypeScript, React, Cloudflare Workers, D1, WebMCP, App Store Connect integrations, and a standard-library Python ASO engine. title: Match Room: Football’s Shared Language
pitch: An agent-native football review room where coaches draw what they mean and ChatGPT searches a full match through native WebMCP, returning inspectable video, tracking and event evidence.
about_excerpt: An agent-native football review room where coaches draw what they mean and ChatGPT searches a full match through native WebMCP, returning inspectable video, tracking and event evidence. Like Comment Story Updates 01 -webmcp 02-space search 03-comparision 04-momentsearch 05-patternquery 06-evidenceproof Inspiration Football tactics begin spatially. A coach points to an area, draws a run, or remembers a moment when the team created space. Most analysis platforms immediately force that idea into filters, timestamps, coordinates, or database terminology. Chat interfaces have the opposite problem: they make the coach translate a visual idea into prose. I wanted to explore a different relationship between a coach and an AI agent: one where the tactical board itself becomes part of the conversation. Match Room is built around a simple division of responsibility: The coach brings judgement. The agent brings search. The pitch is their shared language. WebMCP made it possible to connect the agent directly to the live semantics of the application. The coach can draw what they mean, and the agent can read that visual state without asking them to restate coordinates or describe what is already visible. What it does Match Room is a WebMCP-native football review workspace built around a complete 44:55 first half from the SoccerTrack v2 dataset. The coach can draw a destination zone, sketch a complete route, or describe a tactical moment. ChatGPT reads the live workspace and searches 1,029 observed actions, tracking snapshots, video, and reconstructed play sequences. The agent can: Rank attacks ending inside or near a drawn zone. Search complete routes by origin, shape, destination, and entry direction. Find temporal chains such as a successful tackle followed by a shot. Open an exact observed moment and synchronize the video, pitch, clock, and timeline. Compare two attacks at their start, final pass, or outcome. Save coach-selected examples to a review tray. Search results configure the visible interface instead of returning hidden JSON. Candidate searches deliberately do not move the video or choose an answer for the coach. Only an explicit focus request seeks to the evidence. If the requested pattern did not occur, Match Room returns zero evidence. It never silently replaces the request with a more convenient event. How we built it The project combines deterministic football evidence with a live, agent-readable React workspace. SoccerTrack BAS events + GSR tracking ↓ Deterministic Python adapter ↓ Normalized evidence manifest ↓ React workspace + shared state reducer ↓ Six native WebMCP tools ↓ ChatGPT ↔ coach ↔ shared pitch Offline Python adapters normalize SoccerTrack BAS action labels and GSR tracking frames into a static evidence manifest. The browser does not need a database, API server, model inference backend, or access to the original multi-gigabyte tracking source. The interface is built with React 19 and TypeScript. An SVG tactical pitch, HTML video player, evidence cards, timeline, comparison view, and review tray all share the same reducer state. Match Room registers six semantic tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_match_room_context show_match_sequences explore_match_evidence focus_match_sequence compare_match_sequences add_sequence_to_review These tools read and mutate the same state as the human interface. The result of an agent action is therefore visible and inspectable by both the coach and the agent. The public application is deployed with OpenAI Sites. Its 1080p match video is delivered from Cloudflare R2 through a range-aware Worker, allowing the browser to request only the byte ranges needed for playback and distant seeks. The implementation is covered by unit tests, evidence validation, rendered-browser tests, and discovery and invocation tests against Chrome’s real WebMCP host. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was establishing a strict evidence boundary. SoccerTrack BAS labels determine what happened, while deterministic code calculates distances, local counts, team shape, temporal chains, and route similarity. The agent can arrange and describe those observations, but it cannot create an event or prove tactical causality. Synchronizing several representations of the same moment was also difficult. Video time, match clock, action IDs, tracking frames, tactical routes, and timeline marks all needed to remain aligned when the agent opened or compared evidence. Another important challenge was preserving human control. Early agent experiences tend to jump immediately to one result. In Match Room, searching and focusing are separate operations: search arranges candidates without moving the video, and only the coach’s explicit selection changes focus. The original tracking source was too large for a browser application. I built a deterministic preparation pipeline that preserves the complete first half while producing a compact evidence manifest. For the final 1080p video, byte-range delivery through Cloudflare R2 and a Worker made long seeks practical without downloading the whole file first. Finally, WebMCP is still an emerging browser capability. Tool registration, cleanup, JSON-serializable results, real Chrome discovery, and visible UI mutations all needed to work together rather than relying on a mocked integration. Accomplishments that we're proud of Registering six working WebMCP tools directly against the live React state. Making a drawing on the pitch a genuine search query rather than a decorative input. Indexing all 1,029 observed actions across the complete first half. Reconstructing 110 broad play sequences and 11 finishing sequences deterministically. Keeping video, tracking, event chains, pitch routes, measurements, and comparisons inspectable together. Returning no result for impossible requests instead of inventing or substituting evidence. Separating candidate search from explicit focus so the coach retains tactical control. Validating the workflow through both real Chrome WebMCP and ChatGPT Site Tools. Delivering the experience as a working public application rather than only a technical prototype. The accomplishment I value most is that WebMCP does not feel like an integration added beside the product. It changes how the product can be used: the coach and the agent genuinely operate the same workspace. What we learned An agent-native interface is not simply a conventional application with a chat box. The application must expose meaningful operations and enough live context for the agent to understand what the human is already seeing. Visible mutations are also essential for trust. Returning structured data is not enough when the user needs to evaluate the agent’s reasoning. Evidence cards, routes, timestamps, video, and measurements must all remain open to inspection. I also learned that constraints can improve the human-agent experience. Preventing search tools from seeking automatically initially felt restrictive, but it created a clearer and more respectful division between machine search and human judgement. Finally, deterministic data and generative interaction complement each other well. The agent provides flexibility in how a question is expressed, while the evidence engine keeps the answer grounded. What's next for Match Room: Football’s Shared Language The next step is to move from one public research match to user-provided matches, multiple teams, and reusable analysis workspaces. I would like to add: Secure ingestion pipelines for event, tracking, and video providers. Cross-match pattern search and opponent comparison. Larger libraries of coach-curated examples. Collaborative review rooms for analysts and coaching staff. Richer route similarity and phase-of-play models. Saved tactical concepts that remain inspectable across matches. Additional WebMCP tools as the browser standard evolves. The long-term idea is not an AI that claims to understand football better than the coach. It is an evidence workspace that helps the coach search more of the match without giving up judgement. title: Jig
pitch: A pattern that reads perfectly can still be impossible to knit. So Jig lets an agent size, chart and re-yarn a whole pattern with you, and refuses any number that will not knit.
about_excerpt: A pattern that reads perfectly can still be impossible to knit. So Jig lets an agent size, chart and re-yarn a whole pattern with you, and refuses any number that will not knit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My family's business is yarn. I grew up around patterns covered in red pen, and around customers coming back into the shop a week after buying wool to say the numbers did not work. That is the part people outside the craft do not expect. A knitting pattern can read perfectly and still be impossible to knit. The numbers all have to agree with each other. A cast on has to be a multiple of the stitch repeat plus the edge stitches. A raglan yoke can only reach a target count in whole rounds of eight increases. Shaping has to land on whole rows. Every measurement has to grow as the sizes grow. Break one of those and the pattern still reads like English, prints fine, sells fine, and then fails on somebody's needles after they have paid for the yarn and knitted half a sleeve. Designers do this work in spreadsheets today. A spreadsheet will happily give you a cast on of 87 stitches, because 87 is a number like any other. That is why tech editing is a paid profession and why publishers keep permanent errata pages. So when I read the WebMCP spec, the thing that jumped out was not that an agent could fill in my form faster. It was that the page could say no, and say why. I built Jig for myself first, and I have been grading real patterns in it since. What it does Jig is a knitting design workbench that a person and an agent use at the same time, on the same live document. Ask it for a cast on of 87 stitches on a twelve stitch cable panel. It refuses, names the rule in knitter language, gives back the offending value, and gives back 86 and 98 as the nearest counts that actually fit. The agent reads that one sentence and corrects itself, without ever being told what the repeat was. On the human side those same numbers become one click fixes in the size table. Past that, the agent can do the whole job: read the pattern, read the chart as structured rows rather than a picture, set gauge, grade a full run of sizes while you keep typing into it, swap yarn against a second website and get the answer back in whole skeins, run a tech editing audit, and export. Every call, refusal and correction lands in a transcript in plain English, with whether a person or an agent did it. Why WebMCP fits this use case Three reasons, and all three are about the constraint living in the page instead of behind a server. The rules can refuse. A tool call here is a proposal, not a command. A wrong number comes back with the rule it broke and the nearest values that satisfy it, so the caller never has to work out the arithmetic. It reads one sentence and tries again. That loop is only cheap when the rules sit next to the caller. The rules cannot be bypassed. A person typing, an agent calling a tool, a declarative form submission and the page auditing itself all enter the same propose function. The committed document type carries a private symbol brand, so building one any other way is a compile error. The document is shared rather than handed over. The designer keeps editing while a grading run is in flight, and the run picks up the edit for every size it has not reached yet. There is no session to own and nothing to merge afterwards. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before Correct a refused instruction without ever being told the rule. Ask for 87 and say nothing else. The refusal carries the rule, the offending value, and 86 and 98. A correct second call can only have come from reading that refusal, because the prompt never mentioned the repeat. That is measured against a real browser, not asserted. Edit a number while an agent's grading run is still running. The run reads through a thunk rather than a snapshot, so every size it has not computed yet picks up your keystroke, and neither of you has to wait for the other. Swap yarn across two websites and get a whole skein answer. Change yarn and gauge changes, so yardage per square inch changes, while the new skein has its own length. Two variables at once, which is the classic way to get this wrong. To the agent it is one verb. Underneath it resolves tools on the other origin, invokes them, quarantines every string that crosses the boundary, revalidates through the same gate, and answers in whole skeins per size. Watch the whole negotiation in plain English. Every call, refusal, correction and human edit becomes a sentence in the transcript with its author, so the person is never guessing what the agent just did. How I built it Two real origins, both deployed on Cloudflare Pages. The workbench, and a separate yarn shop site that lends three read only tools to the workbench and to nobody else. The workbench also runs one Pages Function so the model key stays server side and a visitor never needs an API key. Fourteen tools, and deliberately every registration path the spec offers rather than the same one fourteen times: a React hook for the main verbs, raw registration with an AbortSignal for the two tools that only exist while a chart panel is selected, raw registration with exposedTo for the tool named to another origin, and one declarative HTML form that becomes a tool with no registration code at all. The rules live in a pure engine package that cannot import React, the DOM or WebMCP, enforced by a custom lint rule. Every write from every author goes through one propose function, and the committed document type carries a private symbol brand, so building one outside the engine is a compile error rather than a code review note. Sixteen formal correctness properties run over generated inputs with fast-check, including one that proves every repair offered is itself accepted and one that proves no valid value sits between the refused number and the repair. 1,641 tests across 108 files. It also works in a browser with no flag enabled, because a polyfill host stands in and reproduces the real behaviour, refusals included. Challenges I ran into The ones that mattered all came from driving a real browser instead of trusting a test double, and every one of them is now pinned by a test that fails if the fix comes out. An AbortSignal only withdraws a tool when it is the second argument to registerTool . Put it on the descriptor and Chrome accepts it and silently ignores it. executeTool will not take a tool name, it wants the tool object from getTools . Arguments have to be a JSON string, and an object gets rejected. And a refusal's first text part has to stand alone, because some hosts collapse the whole structured result down to content[0].text , so the rule and the repairs have to be in that first part or a model reading only that part gets nothing it can act on. All four of those live in one resolver now, and my fake host reproduces the browser exactly, so a finding cannot quietly regress. My favourite catch was the smallest one. A tool description named an example panel id that did not match the seeded document, which is invisible to every unit test in the suite and obvious the moment a real model follows the description. So now a test walks every panel name any schema mentions and checks it resolves against the real document. One small thing that made a large difference: the field parameter is a closed enum rather than a free string, because a model asked to change a cast on reaches for castOnCount first, which does not exist. Naming the options in the contract removed a whole class of failed first attempts. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The refusal is the product, and it holds up under a machine. npm run verify:browser launches a real browser against the live site, drives document.modelContext with no model and no API key, and proves the loop end to end: 87 refused, the repair parsed out of the first text part alone with zero knowledge of the document, sent back, accepted, and held. Eleven checks, eleven passed. The agent eval suite scores 4 of 4 with a real model choosing real tools. I am also proud that text arriving from the other origin is wrapped in a type with no string member, so interpolating a stranger's comment into a prompt is a compile error. The demo carries a real prompt injection in a community note. The scanner flags it, the broker declines it, and the declined instruction gets written into the transcript where a person can see somebody tried. What I learned That a tool result is a piece of writing. The difference between "rejected" and "here is the rule, here is your value, here are the two that fit" is the difference between an agent giving up and an agent finishing the job, and it is one sentence of prose in a JSON field. That a draft API has to be measured, not read. The four behaviours that shaped this build the most were ones the spec does not describe, and the only way to find them was to open a browser and watch. And that constraints belong in the page. Th

title: Samu
pitch: Prove it's yours — without revealing the secrets that prove it. An agent-ready lost & found built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Prove it's yours — without revealing the secrets that prove it. An agent-ready lost & found built on WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration In Niamey, lost items live in WhatsApp groups. Someone finds a wallet, posts a photo, and then faces an impossible choice: if they publish the details that identify it, anyone can copy the post and claim it; if they don't, the real owner can never prove it's theirs. There is no verification — just trust and luck. We wanted to solve that specific tension: how do you let someone prove they own something without anyone — not even the platform, not even an AI agent — ever seeing the private details that prove it? What it does Samu (Hausa for "to find" ) is a lost-and-found where an AI agent runs the ownership interview without ever learning the answers . Whoever finds an item enters a few distinctive private details by hand. The owner describes their loss; Samu searches and opens the matching item. On the item page, the claimant answers verification questions. The server compares the answers and returns one thing : verified or not verified . Never a score, never which answers were right, never the secrets. Why WebMCP is a strong fit WebMCP tools belong to the page — an agent must be on a page to use its tools. We turned that into the whole UX: as the agent moves from search to a specific item, its toolset changes under its feet. And because verification is fundamentally a conversation ("what was inside the zipped pocket?"), an agent is a genuinely better interface than a form — while the humans and the agent share the exact same capabilities. What people and agents can now do together that was hard before: an agent can prove something about private data to a stranger's listing without either side leaking that data. How we built it Next.js (App Router) deployed on Netlify , with Netlify Functions as the backend. A deterministic verification engine : salted SHA-256 for exact/choice answers, semantic similarity (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small , with a local trigram fallback) for free-text answers, and weighted scoring: $$\text{score} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \cdot m_i}{\sum_i w_i}\times 100$$ Passing requires clearing a threshold and getting at least one decisive (weight-3) detail right, so guessing a few easy facts is never enough. Postgres via Neon in production; a zero-dependency node:sqlite store in development, seeded with real Niamey neighborhoods. How we used WebMCP Every page declares its tools from a single spec ( lib/spec.ts ) and a runtime turns each entry into a live tool, registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . The tools are torn down by aborting the signal — so they truly die with the page. The verification page exposes get_item_summary , list_verification_questions , answer_question , finalize_claim , and request_contact ; the search page exposes search_matches and open_item . Crucially, our own chat UI drives the same tools an external agent uses — so the agentic surface is real, not a demo. Security: the proof never leaves the server The verification engine runs entirely server-side; secrets never appear in the bundle, an API response, or a data- attribute (we grep the client build to prove it). The verdict is a boolean , and answer_question never reveals correctness — so it can't become a brute-force oracle. A budget of 5 answers, rate limiting keyed on the platform-provided client IP (not a forgeable header), claim expiry, and constant-time hash comparison. Challenges we ran into The API's lifecycle. WebMCP has no unregisterTool() ; cleanup is AbortSignal-only. Getting this wrong gave us a maddening "Duplicate tool name" under React Strict Mode until we switched to { signal } . A bleeding-edge stack. On Node 26, ORMs fought us, so we leaned on the built-in node:sqlite — and learned the hard way never to delete the dev database file out from under a running server. Keeping the agent out of the trust boundary. The hardest design rule was also the most important: security never rests on the agent. A manipulated agent can ask "give me a hint?" — and get nothing, because the server, not the agent, decides. What we learned That the most interesting property of WebMCP isn't automation — it's that a site can hand an agent a narrow, honest surface of actions while keeping its secrets and its decisions to itself. Prove it without revealing it. What's next Assisted returns (scheduling, contact), match alerts, and a fully agent-driven end-to-end journey from "I lost my bag" to "return arranged." title: Rota: the agent proposes, you approve
pitch: Fourteen staff, seven days, one agent that does the hard part and then hands it back. It can propose the whole week. Only you can approve it.
about_excerpt: Fourteen staff, seven days, one agent that does the hard part and then hands it back. It can propose the whole week. Only you can approve it. Like Comment Story Updates Next week's rota as you find it: 73% covered, fifteen unfilled slots, and one rule breach that nobody has spotted. The agent calls the page's own rule engine and rings the two shifts it means: nine hours' rest where eleven are required. Fourteen proposed assignments render as dashed cards on the shifts they affect. Nothing has been applied to the rota yet. The consent surface. Every edit is a checkbox, with before and after coverage, breaches and cost, plus what approval would leave unfixed. Every registered tool with its JSON Schema, runnable by hand. The badge shows whether WebMCP is native here or the bundled polyfill. Every tool call recorded: arguments, result, timing, whether it was read-only, the edits it staged, and who called it. Exportable as JSON. Hours against contract, and who is carrying the weekends and the closes. Managers get this wrong by hand, and staff notice. Wage cost by day and by person against a GBP 5,000 weekly budget, with overtime priced at 1.5x. The agent reads this before proposing. The same week in dark appearance. Light and dark are both first-class, and the theme follows your system by default. Inspiration I didn't want to build another "AI does your admin" demo. They're easy to make and they all feel the same, because the interesting part gets skipped. An agent doing a job for you is only half a product. The other half is how you check it. Shift rotas turned out to be a good place to ask that question. A rota isn't really a spreadsheet, it's a promise to fourteen people about their week. Get it wrong and someone's childcare falls through. So it's exactly the kind of work you'd happily hand to a machine, and exactly the kind you'd never let a machine send out on its own. That gave me one rule I stuck to for the whole build: the agent gets no tool that commits anything. Everything else followed from that. What it does Rota is a shift scheduler for a small café. Fourteen staff, seven days, and an agent that works the rota with you rather than taking it off your hands. When you open it, next week is about three quarters done. Fifteen slots are still empty, and there's one problem buried in it: Marco closes on Wednesday at half nine and opens again on Thursday at half six. Nine hours between shifts. The law wants eleven. Neither shift looks wrong on its own, which is why this kind of mistake survives a proofread. Ask it to finish the rota and it makes about five tool calls. It reads the gaps, runs the solver, and stages fourteen assignments that add £1,384 to the wage bill. Then it stops and tells you the fifteenth slot can't be filled at all: Liam is seventeen so the curfew rules him out, and nobody else left is a certified shift lead. Nothing on the calendar has moved. The fourteen proposals sit on top of the shifts they'd affect as dashed cards, and a drawer lists them one per line with a checkbox each. It shows you what approving would do to coverage, to your rule breaches, and to the cost. Take twelve of them and drop two if you like. Then there's publishing, which is the one action that actually tells fourteen people when they're working. I made that a declarative WebMCP form and left toolautosubmit off it. Per the spec, that means an agent can fill the form in and then has to stop. The browser puts focus on the submit button and waits for a person. So the agent writes the note to staff, picks who gets notified, ticks the confirmation box, and cannot press send. A few other things that come out of building it this way: When it can't do something it tells you why and quotes the rule. "Everyone available is over their consecutive-day limit and Tom is the only other keyholder" is useful. "I couldn't find cover" isn't. Every tool call is logged with its arguments, what came back, how long it took, and who made it. You can export the lot as JSON and answer "why is Nadia on Friday night" properly. Undo works across approvals, because every edit carries a forward and a backward patch. No signup and no API key to try it. How we built it TypeScript, React and Vite. No backend, no database, nothing phoning home. The roster never leaves your tab, which is what makes doing this client side an honest choice instead of a shortcut. Four reasons it's WebMCP and not an MCP server, roughly in the order they mattered to me: The state is in the tab. The roster, the rules and the solver all run in the browser. A server would have to mirror the manager's working state, and half of that state is a proposal nobody has agreed to yet. I didn't want the model reasoning about employment law. It never does. It calls validate_schedule and repeats what the page's own engine said. When assign_staff refuses, the refusal is a fact you can act on: "Liam Doyle is not certified as Baker." The agent needs to be able to point at things. When it says Thursday is the problem it calls highlight and puts a ring round the two shifts on your screen. Nothing running on a server can do that. Some tools should only exist sometimes. Select a shift and two more appear, scoped to it. Stage a proposal and revise_proposal shows up. Deselect and they're withdrawn. Every one of those changes fires toolchange . A static tool list on a server can't manage this, because a server has no idea what you're looking at. Under that there are three layers. The rules engine is plain TypeScript with no React and no DOM near it, because it's the part that has to be correct. Fifteen rules, split between the statutory and contractual ones and the softer ones about fairness, cost and preference. Ranking candidates works by simulating and re-validating. To score someone for a shift I copy the roster, add the assignment, and run the real validator over the copy. It's not the fastest approach, but it means the ranking can never disagree with the rules, and that was worth more to me than the speed. The solver is most-constrained-first, then two passes of local search. It's a heuristic and I'm not pretending otherwise. It won't always find the best answer, but it never returns an illegal rota and it's quick enough to run inside a tool call. Both agent modes go through getTools() and executeTool() . The in-page agent holds no references to its own tool functions on purpose, so my own UI is exercising the same path an outside agent would take. There's also a polyfill for document.modelContext , so the whole thing works in any browser today. If you open it somewhere with real WebMCP the app notices and stands aside. Challenges we ran into The demo data was the hardest part, which I did not expect. My first version of the broken week had 31 rule breaches and 65% coverage, and it just read as sloppy rather than realistic. Worse, I'd written more shifts than the staff had contracted hours to cover, so the solver couldn't finish no matter how good it was and filled nothing at all. Getting to a week that looks like a real half-finished rota, is genuinely fixable, and still leaves one slot that honestly can't be filled took several rounds of counting capacity against demand, role by role. The edit model took two attempts. Applying patches straight meant two assignments to the same shift clobbered each other, so now each patch is rebased against the roster as it stands at the moment the edit lands. And then there was the bug that nearly sank it. The "roster as proposed" value was being rebuilt every time it was read, and it's used as a state selector that compares by reference. So staging anything at all set off an infinite render loop, which tore down React and quietly unregistered all 32 tools. The app looked fine until the first time the agent tried to change something. Accomplishments that we're proud of That the constraint held. There are 36 tools and not one of them can commit, approve or publish. It would have been easy to add a commit tool for convenience halfway through and I didn't. The correctness work is tested rather than claimed. 28 checks on the engine with no browser involved, 33 in a real browser, and 35 that click through the suggested prompts the way a judge would. They assert properties I actually care about: that anyone the ranker calls eligible really is eligible when you re-validate, that the solver never increases the number of hard breaches, that the cheap objective is never more expensive than the balanced one, that absence cover never backfills with the person who's absent, and that the publish form fills but refuses to submit. And the polyfill, because it means anyone can open the URL and use every tool without an origin trial, an API key or a signup. What we learned Three things I got wrong first, all of which changed the code more than any prompt tuning did. I had tools returning JSON. title: StackKits Planner
pitch: Humans and browser agents plan self-hosted infrastructure together: module-level compute profiles, honest capacity checks, and a read-only CLI handoff.
about_excerpt: Humans and browser agents plan self-hosted infrastructure together: module-level compute profiles, honest capacity checks, and a read-only CLI handoff. Like Comment Story Updates Choose your workloads: visual use-case tiles, declared kit defaults and explicit module alternatives. Declare capacity: CPU, RAM and storage sliders with a transparent per-axis assessment. Review and copy: individual terminal commands or a complete Markdown handoff for your agent. Nothing runs in the browser. Inspiration Planning a self-hosted system should not require a browser agent to guess what a website means. StackKits already provides CUE-defined infrastructure blueprints and a standalone CLI. We built the WebMCP Planner to make those declared product facts directly usable by people and browser agents, in one visible workflow. What it does At https://stackkit.cc/planner , choose a StackKit, select compute profiles independently for its modules, and declare available CPU, RAM and storage with numeric inputs and sliders. The planner compares that capacity against declared requirements and prepares a reviewable CLI handoff. Four read-only WebMCP tools share the same implementation and planner state as the human UI: stackkits_list_catalog stackkits_get_module_profiles stackkits_assess_capacity stackkits_prepare_handoff Agent choices and results appear in the planner immediately. A small host can use a lighter module profile without forcing every module into one global tier. Missing declarations remain unverified; below-minimum capacity blocks the handoff. This is declared-capacity assessment, not a promise of host compatibility. Why WebMCP fits The useful action here is structured planning, not scraping prose or giving an agent a shell. Native document.modelContext.registerTool exposes narrow, validated operations with explicit read-only annotations. People can inspect and change the same selection an agent is working with. Without native WebMCP support, the complete human planner remains usable and explains why agent tools are unavailable. How we built it The public implementation includes JSON Schemas, generated TypeScript types, a deterministic catalog projected from the OSS CUE authority bundle, source and digest provenance, shared core logic, and a Svelte planner with a reproducible reference host. The production site is a thin host of that same component. Tool execution is local and deterministic: no model inference, provider call, or per-request server analysis. Capacity checks are simple comparisons, and bounded outputs avoid repeating the full UI explanation. Targeted local benchmarks measured sub-millisecond p95 core execution for the four tools; that excludes page loading and browser-agent transport and is not an end-to-end latency guarantee. The handoff describes init, validate, resolve, generate and plan commands. The browser executes none of them. Target-side stackkit compat remains mandatory, and apply is excluded from the executable handoff and requires a later owner decision. Challenges and lessons The most important architecture correction was separating per-module compute profiles from the kit's product selection. A uniform low or standard switch does not describe a real mixed workload. Another challenge was keeping incomplete capacity declarations honest rather than treating missing information as success. We also separated native API availability, catalog verification and registration failures in the UI. Unsupported browsers must not be made to look agent-ready, and native integration must not be replaced with a production polyfill. What is new for this challenge StackKits, its CUE definitions and standalone CLI predate this entry. The contest work adds the shared WebMCP planner, browser-tool contract, module-profile workflow, capacity UI, read-only handoff, public reference host, and focused validation and performance evidence. The public source and commit history distinguish the existing platform from this extension. Try it Open https://stackkit.cc/planner . No account is required. Choose Basement Kit to load its declared default core module. Declare 4 CPU cores, 8 GiB RAM and 32 GiB free storage, assess capacity, and prepare the CLI handoff. Copy an individual Bash/POSIX or PowerShell command, or copy the complete agent Markdown including choices, notices and provenance. Nothing is executed by copying. Add optional workloads with the visual use-case tiles and inspect their module-local profiles. Lower an axis below its declared minimum to see a blocked result, or leave it empty to see an incomplete assessment. Native WebMCP tools and the manual planner share the same implementation and visible state. The complete manual workflow also works without WebMCP support. What's next Broader declared module requirements and more agent evaluations can improve coverage without turning the browser into a second infrastructure compiler or installer.
