title: Fashion Learning Studio
pitch: A fashion eSchool where WebMCP agents guide the user's learning experience interactively using quizzes and essays.
about_excerpt: A fashion eSchool where WebMCP agents guide the user's learning experience interactively using quizzes and essays. Like Comment Story Updates Course page2 Course page Site open in Chatgpt Site home page Inspiration Fashion education is practical, visual, and highly dependent on guidance. A learner may watch a sewing demonstration and still need someone to identify the important control point, connect it to an exercise, review their understanding, and show them what to do next. Instructor-led delivery does not scale easily, especially for adult and working learners who cannot attend scheduled classes. Conventional online courses provide content, but learners must navigate long course structures and interpret practical activities largely on their own. Browser agents normally have to guess their way through changing page markup. I built Fashion Learning Studio to explore a more trustworthy collaboration: the school supplies the curriculum, demonstrations, assessments, and rules, while the learner's chosen browser agent supplies patient, contextual support. WebMCP lets the agent understand and interact with the same visible learning interface without replacing the learner or taking credit for the learner's work. What it does Fashion Learning Studio is a standalone WordPress learning experience for fashion design and sewing. It combines accessible course pages, practical video lessons, layered assessments, authentication, persistent learner progress, and five browser-native WebMCP tools. The demo includes three learning paths: Fashion Foundations : Fabric to Silhouette introduces fabric behaviour and an A-line skirt exercise. Fashion Design Studio : Concept to Collection has six ordered layers covering design signals, colour, silhouette, materials, mood-board editing, and a final rationale. Sewing Skills : Machine Control to Finishing provides 19 ordered video-led topics, practice reflections, and a final essay. The agent can inspect the signed-in learner's state, open the appropriate lesson, begin an available exercise, explain what to observe or practice, stage a proposed response in the visible form, and recommend the next step. Passed layers unlock the next task, and every learner has separate course progress. The agent cannot claim a video was watched, submit or grade an answer, or silently change progress. It stages assistance in the shared interface; the learner reviews, edits, and personally clicks Submit my answer. Without WebMCP, the school remains fully usable through its ordinary interface. What people and agents can do together A learner can ask, “What should I learn next?” Instead of guessing from the layout, the agent reads authoritative course state, opens the correct lesson, starts the available exercise, and helps stage a concise response in the visible form. The learner reviews or edits it and personally submits it. WebMCP gives the agent a reliable vocabulary for the course while preserving learner authorship and school authority. It turns static self-paced content into guided learning without requiring an instructor to repeat every basic explanation. How we built it We built the project as a lightweight WordPress plugin using PHP, the WordPress REST API, user metadata, semantic HTML, accessible CSS, and framework-free JavaScript. A companion WordPress block theme keeps the learning experience focused and responsive. After capability detection, the page registers five contextual tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): The five WebMCP tools are: get_learning_state Reads the active course, progress, current assessment, choices, and available actions. open_next_lesson Opens the learner’s available lesson visibly. start_exercise Starts the assessment after the lesson prerequisite is satisfied. review_current_answer Reviews the learner-written answer, identifies weaknesses, and displays improvement advice without submitting or saving it. get_progress_and_next_step Reports the accurate completion percentage and recommends the next action. The tools use bounded JSON Schemas, enums, length limits, additionalProperties: false, structured errors, appropriate read-only annotations, same-origin exposure, and lifecycle cleanup with AbortController. Protected REST routes require an authenticated WordPress session and valid REST nonce. WordPress remains authoritative for state transitions, grading, and persistence. The design uses progressive enhancement: the human interface remains primary and WebMCP adds collaboration only when supported. Assessment and progress are deterministic. No external AI API or API key is required by the website; the learner's browser agent supplies the intelligence and invokes the site’s structured tools. Codex helped refine the product scope, translate the educational workflow into tool contracts, implement and review the plugin, improve the learner experience, define security and confirmation boundaries, create deterministic tests, and diagnose hosting and browser-support issues. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was understanding that WebMCP is not an embedded chatbot. It is a browser-native bridge through which an agent discovers capabilities supplied by the current page. That changed the design from “add an AI teacher” to “make the school understandable and operable by the learner's chosen agent.” The hardest product decision was where autonomy should stop. Automatically submitting an educational answer might look impressive, but it would undermine learner agency and academic integrity. We separated assistance from commitment: the agent explains and stages work, but only the learner can submit, grade, or save it. Browser support is still experimental, so we needed a complete standard interface and graceful fallback. We also had to create a public demonstration without exposing learner records, proprietary course data, or private video configuration. Hosting anti-bot protection challenged some automated requests. This revealed a broader deployment issue: agent-ready applications need authentication and hosting security that recognise legitimate, user-authorised agent activity without weakening protection. Accomplishments that we're proud of Built a coherent fashion-learning experience rather than a tool-registration proof of concept. Connected five task-specific WebMCP tools to authenticated learning state. Connected agent assistance to visible lessons, exercises, feedback, and progress. Preserved learner authorship through a clear human-confirmation boundary. Created three course structures, including layered design work and 19 video topics. Kept video configuration and learner information outside the public release. Built deterministic assessment without paid model calls from the website. Preserved full functionality when WebMCP is unavailable. Added structured evaluation journeys and deterministic client and server tests. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it communicates application intent and trust boundaries, not merely when it replaces clicks. Tool names, schemas, allowed actions, state responses, and visible effects must agree. We learned to distinguish between reading information, changing the visible interface, staging a proposed change, and performing a confirmed consequential action. In education, preserving a meaningful learner action can be more valuable than maximising automation. The website must remain authoritative for authentication, access, assessment, progress, and completion. The agent provides explanation and assistance but does not replace the school's rules or the learner's responsibility. Agent-ready education can reduce the instructor bottleneck. Educators encode the course sequence, demonstrations, rubrics, common mistakes, and escalation rules once, while agents help individual learners move through that trusted structure at their own pace. What's next for Fashion Learning Studio Next, we will integrate this interaction model into the full Unikon eSchool LMS, where it can work with real courses, sections, lessons, quizzes, projects, submissions, portfolios, progress records, and certificates. We plan to expose tools dynamically according to the learner's page and state, evaluate tool selection with more natural requests, add instructor-authored rubrics and feedback, and provide accessible transcripts and captions. We also plan to add personalised study timetables, evidence-based participation tracking, missed-session catch-up plans, and escalation to a human instructor. Future activities could accept photographs, pattern files, and CAD exercises so an agent guides the process while an instructor evaluates fit, construction quality, and final competence. Our long-term vision is an agent-guided, instructor-supervised mobile fashion school that serves learners continuously without requiring an instructor to repeat every basic lesson. title: HABITAT/NULL
pitch: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time.
about_excerpt: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Design future living spaces through natural conversation. A user-created future floor plan, edited through WebMCP. Export the current floor plan exactly as it appears. Inspect, propose, validate, and apply floor-plan changes. Inspiration When I first used a computer as a child, there was something I wanted even more than a game: software that would let me design my own floor plans. I dreamed of moving walls, expanding rooms, and placing devices that did not yet exist—as naturally as drawing ideas on paper. Today, many floor-planning tools are available. However, I wondered whether designing a home could become more accessible and imaginative if people could simply describe what they wanted instead of learning specialized controls. That idea inspired me to build HABITAT//NULL, a future floor-plan simulator powered by WebMCP. What It Does HABITAT//NULL is a floor-plan simulator where users and AI collaboratively imagine future living spaces. Users can describe changes in natural language, such as: “Make the kitchen larger.” “Split this room at a 60/40 ratio.” “Turn this area into a parking space.” Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the current floor plan, propose a change, validate it, and apply it to the design. The project is not limited to conventional furniture. It is also designed to let users invent and place their own futuristic tools, devices, and living systems. Completed floor plans can be saved as PNG or PDF files exactly as they appear on the screen. Rather than simply optimizing existing homes, HABITAT//NULL aims to turn imagined ways of living—things that do not yet exist—into visible spaces. How I Built It The floor plan is managed as structured data representing rooms, walls, openings, furniture, and equipment. The visual floor plan is generated from this underlying data. I created WebMCP tools that allow AI to inspect the current layout, propose modifications, validate the result, and apply an approved proposal. This allows the AI to understand and manipulate the structure of the floor plan instead of relying on screen coordinates or button positions. Changes are first created as proposals rather than being applied immediately. After the proposal has been reviewed, the exact change can be committed to the current floor plan. The visual design combines understated science fiction with the nostalgic feeling of a hand-drawn architectural plan. I wanted the interface to suggest a quiet, deteriorated future where advanced equipment still survives among worn materials and old records. Challenges The most difficult challenge was translating ambiguous natural-language requests into precise floor-plan operations. For example, “Make the kitchen larger” raises several questions: Which wall should move? How much space should be taken from the neighboring room? What should happen to doors, furniture, and connected spaces? Changing a room’s size requires more than updating its dimensions. The relationships among walls, openings, routes, and placed objects must remain consistent. Another challenge was making the entire workflow possible through WebMCP. Creating a proposal was not enough—the AI also needed to inspect, validate, and apply the change without requiring unnecessary manual interaction. It was also important to avoid adding too many unrelated features. I continually returned to the project’s essential experience: letting users reshape a floor plan through conversation. What I Learned This project taught me that WebMCP is more than a way to automate browser interactions. It can become a structured communication layer between an AI agent and a web application. When the AI understands the meaning of rooms, walls, and openings—not just their appearance on the screen—users can express their intentions naturally without learning specialized software controls. I also learned that giving an AI freedom is not enough to create a trustworthy experience. Users need to see proposed changes, verify the results, and clearly understand what will be applied. A proposal-and-approval workflow makes collaboration with AI both safer and easier to understand. What’s Next Next, I want to give users more freedom to create and place their own furniture, machines, and imagined future systems. I would also like to support multi-story buildings and unconventional environments such as fantasy homes, spacecraft, and underground shelters. My goal is to develop HABITAT//NULL into more than a tool for selecting or editing existing floor plans. I want it to become a place where users and AI can invent new ways of living together. title: Draw_generatoe (Codex draws on canvas)
pitch: An tldraw canvas where agents using WebMCP tools : draw, create diagrams, and create visual directly in the tldraw web.
about_excerpt: An tldraw canvas where agents using WebMCP tools : draw, create diagrams, and create visual directly in the tldraw web. Like 2 Comment Story Updates 1 banner GIF demo What it does Draw_generatoe lets Codex control a live tldraw canvas through WebMCP. Users can ask it to create pages, draw scenes, add shapes and text, search and decribe youtube embed url in canvas ,Mermaid js ,finds non CC wikipedia commons image , arrange objects, and refine designs through natural-language instructions. For example, Codex can create a welcome screen, draw a car on a road, notice misaligned text, and correct the layout without replacing the user’s existing work. Inspiration The idea was inspired by OpenAI’s YouTube video, Math Problems with GPT-4o featuring Imran Khan from Khan Academy , published on May 13, 2024. Watching someone interact naturally with AI , made me wonder: what if we could do the same thing on a visual canvas? The original repository had been on my computer since 2025 . With the arrival of WebMCP, I returned to it and added tools that let Codex place, resize, move, and arrange canvas objects. The goal was simple: describe a scene in plain language and watch Codex draw it directly on the canvas. How we built it We built the interface with React, Vite, and tldraw. The application exposes structured WebMCP tools that Codex can use to inspect pages and create, move, resize, align, layer, and draw canvas objects. Codex inspects the current canvas, preserves populated pages, performs bounded mutations, fits the result into view, and visually checks the finished composition. We packaged the client application and deployed it publicly through ChatGPT Sites. Tool vocabulary Domain Tools Discovery list_tools describe_tools Canvas reading review count inspect_pages inspect_embeds Pages and camera create_page zoom_out Shape creation create pen createHtmlPreview create_mermaid_diagram Shape editing update label delete clear Layout and positioning move place align distribute stack arrange_grid Transform and layers rotate resize bringToFront sendToBack External inspiration getInspiration Open-license images search_commons_images add_commons_image This reflects all 29 tools currently listed in repo tool.txt https://github.com/mayank-devac/draw_generetoe Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was translating creative language into exact canvas coordinates, sizes, and layer ordering. Text and shapes can have different measured bounds, so something that looks centered mathematically may still appear misaligned. We also had to preserve existing pages, manage overlapping objects, verify WebMCP tool schemas, handle tldraw licensing for the deployed domain, and ensure that public client-side configuration did not expose real secrets. Accomplishments that we're proud of We created a working bridge between natural language and a live visual canvas. Codex can produce complete multi-object scenes, native shape-based layouts, hand-drawn decorations, mermaid js ... We are especially proud that it can inspect its own result, identify visual problems such as incorrect layering or alignment, and improve the canvas while leaving unrelated work untouched. What we learned We learned that reliable AI drawing requires more than generating shapes. The agent needs structured tools, clear object identities, page awareness, predictable coordinate systems, and visual verification after every meaningful change. We also learned that small corrective tools—move, align, resize, reorder, and inspect—are just as important as the initial creation tools. title: StoryRoom
pitch: The agent-native filmmaking studio where AI proposes and the director decides via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The agent-native filmmaking studio where AI proposes and the director decides via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Accepted Scene Written By AI Revision Review Diff Modal Chrome DevTools console showing Landing Page Inspiration Screenwriting is not a single-document problem. A single scene depends on what happened three scenes ago - who locked the safe, what the character emotionally knows at this moment, what the director's aesthetic rules demand about silence versus dialogue. When I tried using AI chatbots as a writing co-creator, I kept hitting the same wall: I had to manually copy-paste context, re-explain character histories every session, and hope the AI didn't contradict something established six scenes back. The real problem wasn't the AI's intelligence. The AI was operating blind - it had no structured access to the live workspace state. The moment I read about WebMCP — the idea that an agent could register structured tools directly on document.modelContext and read real browser application state - I immediately thought about filmmaking. A screenplay is exactly the kind of complex, multi-dimensional, stateful problem where a workspace-native agent thrives and a generic chatbot fails. So I asked: what if the AI director's assistant lived inside the studio? What it does StoryRoom is an agent-native filmmaking workspace where human directors and autonomous AI agents collaborate in real-time on live screenplays through the native WebMCP browser standard. The AI agent operates entirely inside the application through 8 registered WebMCP tools on document.modelContext : get_story_context - reads the full narrative: genre, logline, characters, locations, and the director's 8 codified creative rules get_current_scene - fetches the live screenplay text, slugline, characters present, and version history for any scene get_character - loads a full character dossier: psychological traits, emotional arc, and cross-scene appearance index check_continuity - audits the multi-scene timeline, prop tracking, and character knowledge for contradictions analyze_scene - evaluates dramatic pacing and dialogue against the Director's Memory rules propose_rewrite - generates a pending staged revision with justification notes — the live screenplay is never touched apply_revision - commits an approved revision to the screenplay, guarded by a strict Human-In-The-Loop security gate The centerpiece is the Human-In-The-Loop guarantee : the agent can never silently overwrite creative work. Every proposed rewrite is delivered as a side-by-side visual diff (red = removed, green = added). The director must explicitly click Accept Revision before any change reaches the script. How we built it StoryRoom is engineered in 5 architectural layers: 1. Presentation Layer React 18 + Vite + TailwindCSS cinematic workspace with a Screenplay Editor (industry-standard formatting), Character Manager, Locations Panel, Director's Memory rules editor, and a Revision Review modal. 2. WebMCP Tool Registry All 8 tools are registered on document.modelContext with strict JSON Schema definitions and input validation. They are also mirrored on navigator.modelContext and window._STORYROOM_WEBMCP_ so judges can verify every tool directly in Chrome DevTools ( F12 ). 3. WebMCP State Bridge WebMCPProvider synchronizes the tool registry with the live React ProjectStore using mutable refs - ensuring every tool call reads genuine, real-time application state rather than stale closures. 4. Dual-Mode AI Intelligence Layer Primary : Google Gemini 1.5 Flash via REST API, with an automatic model cascade (tries gemini-1.5-flash → gemini-2.0-flash-exp → gemini-1.5-pro ) so the app never hard-crashes on model deprecation Fallback : A deterministic offline simulation engine that produces high-quality, scene-aware responses with zero API key - so the full 9-step demo scenario runs for any judge, anywhere, at any time 5. Human-In-The-Loop Security Gate apply_revision checks revision status before executing. Any direct commit attempt on a pending revision is hard-blocked at the tool layer: { "success": false, "error": "HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED" } The director reviews a visual diff and clicks Accept - only then does the tool commit Version 3 to the live screenplay. Challenges we ran into 1. WebMCP state synchronization with async React rendering The hardest engineering problem. React re-renders asynchronously; the WebMCP tool registry registers once at mount. Getting check_continuity to always read the current screenplay state — not a stale snapshot from when the tool was first registered — required storing all reactive state in mutable refs inside the provider, rather than capturing values in closure scope. A subtle but critical distinction. 2. Designing the Human-In-The-Loop gate to feel like a creative decision The HITL gate had to be firm enough to be a real security guarantee, but natural enough that reviewing a diff feels like a directorial choice, not a bureaucratic approval form. Getting the visual diff presentation and the modal flow right required multiple iterations. 3. Gemini model deprecation mid-development The originally pinned model name ( gemini-2.0-flash ) returned 404 from the API partway through development. This could have broken the live demo. I responded by implementing an automatic model cascade that silently tries the next available production model before falling back to the offline simulation engine - so the app is resilient to future deprecations too. 4. Making the offline demo indistinguishable from the live AI path The deterministic fallback engine needed to produce screenplay analysis that felt genuinely thoughtful - not canned. I built scene-aware demo responses that reference real props, characters, and Director's Memory rule numbers so the 9-step walkthrough demonstrates the full product experience even without a Gemini API key configured. Accomplishments that we're proud of The Human-In-The-Loop security guarantee is real and enforced at the tool layer - not just a UI convention. apply_revision genuinely rejects unauthorized commits with a structured error response. All 8 WebMCP tools are verifiable in Chrome DevTools in under 30 seconds. Any judge can open F12 , run window._STORYROOM_WEBMCP_.tools , and see the full registry. They can call any tool directly from the console. The 9-step deterministic demo works completely offline. Zero API keys, zero setup, zero loading screens - the entire WebMCP collaboration workflow runs in one click for any evaluator. The continuity auditing is genuinely useful. The check_continuity tool catches a real planted narrative contradiction (a prop locked in a safe in Scene 4 being examined without an unlocking action in Scene 7) - the kind of error that slips through human review but a structured agent catches immediately. Building a product that feels premium, not like a proof of concept. From the cinematic design language to the visual diff review to the Director's Memory rules system, StoryRoom feels like a tool a real filmmaker would want to use. What we learned WebMCP's document.modelContext is genuinely powerful for domain-specific applications. The moment you give an agent structured, typed access to live application state instead of raw text, the quality of its reasoning improves dramatically - because hallucination requires filling in gaps, and structured tools leave fewer gaps. The Human-In-The-Loop pattern is not a limitation on AI capability - it is a trust feature. Agents that can be overruled are agents that can be trusted with higher-stakes tasks. The HITL gate is what makes directors willing to let the AI touch their screenplay at all. Deterministic fallback engines are engineering discipline, not a shortcut. A project that only works when the right API key is configured is a fragile demo. Building a high-quality offline simulation layer means the product experience is always fully evaluable. State synchronization between a reactive UI and a browser-standard tool registry is a genuinely new design problem that WebMCP introduces. The mutable ref pattern we developed is something future WebMCP + React projects will likely need too. What's next for StoryRoom Multi-agent collaboration : Allow two external agents to work on different scenes simultaneously, with the director moderating conflicts between competing proposed rewrites through a merge review interface export_final_draft WebMCP tool : Let the agent package the approved screenplay into a properly formatted Final Draft (.fdx) or PDF with one tool call after director sign-off Voice direction : Let directors leave audio notes on scenes that the agent transcribes, interprets as creative directives, and uses to inform future analyze_scene evaluations Production breakdown integration : Add get_budget_impact and check_location_availability tools so the agent can flag rewrites that introduce expensive new locations or VFX requirements before the director approves them Pers

title: Olos-AI Mini Budget Planner
pitch: A simple local-first budget tracker where people use a clear visual interface and agents use structured WebMCP tools against the same deterministic financial logic.
about_excerpt: A simple local-first budget tracker where people use a clear visual interface and agents use structured WebMCP tools against the same deterministic financial logic. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted a personal budget tracker because I'm generally hopeless (like most people) at controlling my spending and having something like this app allows me to be accounting for each and every dollar I spend, yes there are hundreds of them in the app store but I don't think people need to spend more money for a subscription and lose their privacy for a basic tracker. I used AI to assist in the development and writing to assist with expressing the story clearly Personal budgeting should be simple: record money coming in or going out, then immediately understand what remains. Many budgeting products instead introduce subscriptions, user accounts, bank connections, advertising, telemetry, and increasingly complex dashboards. Olos-AI Mini Budget Planner was built as a deliberately small alternative. Its normal experience remains a fast, visual, local-first budget tracker. The WebMCP Challenge presented a different question: can this existing application become agent-native without embedding a chatbot, adding an LLM dependency, or surrendering its financial rules to an AI model? What it does The planner records income, expenses, bills, savings, recurring commitments, revolving credit, Pay Later balances, and estimated fixed loans. It shows actual and projected monthly cashflow while keeping available cash, available credit, and loan liabilities clearly separate. People use the normal responsive interface. Compatible agents receive eleven structured WebMCP tools for reading budget information and performing explicit, validated actions. An agent can: Read the monthly budget summary List upcoming commitments Search recent activity Inspect credit and loan balances Read calendar projections Record a confirmed transaction Create or record a recurring item Record a credit payment Correct an existing transaction Delete an identified transaction with deliberate confirmation Agent-created changes appear immediately in the same interface the person uses. How we built it The application uses FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and PWA APIs. The WebMCP layer is a thin adapter. Each tool is registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) with a strict JSON schema, clear description, bounded inputs, and appropriate read-only or mutating behaviour. Tool callbacks call the same FastAPI endpoints used by the visual interface. All validation, recurrence handling, credit balances, fixed-loan calculations, and no-double-counting rules remain in the existing deterministic application logic. Financial calculations are not duplicated in prompts or delegated to an LLM. Why WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, an agent must interpret labels, click controls, and infer meaning from page layout. With WebMCP, the application directly explains what actions are available and the exact structure each action requires. A person can say, “Record an $87.40 grocery expense paid with my credit card,” and the agent can submit one validated transaction using typed fields for amount, date, category, payment method, and facility ID. The result then appears in Recent Activity and updates the monthly figures. The application itself does not contain an AI assistant and does not send financial data to a third-party AI service. WebMCP lets the browser and a compatible agent collaborate with the application at its boundary. Challenges The most important challenge was preserving one financial authority. It would have been easy to create simplified financial behaviour inside the WebMCP callbacks. Instead, the tools reuse the same tested API and domain rules as the human interface. The hosted demonstration also required a strict privacy boundary. The public Render deployment uses synthetic data and isolated disposable browser sessions. It has no connection to anyone’s personal local database. Accomplishments Eleven meaningful WebMCP tools rather than a ceremonial integration Exact decimal-string money inputs Structured separation of cash, credit availability, and loan liabilities Immediate visual refresh after agent mutations Idempotent recurring-payment recording Protection against double-counting credit and loan repayments A useful application that remains fully functional without an agent Disposable, session-isolated public demonstration data What we learned Agent-native does not have to mean “put a chatbot in every application.” A deterministic web application can preserve its normal human interface while exposing a second, structured interface designed for agents. That approach makes agent interaction more accurate while keeping the application’s own rules authoritative. What’s next The immediate goal is to keep the project small, understandable, and dependable. Future work would focus on wider WebMCP browser compatibility and further usability testing, without turning the application into banking software or a financial-advice platform.  Inspiration 

 I had the idea for Nambut long before this hackathon. I wanted to build a personal card that gave users more freedom to design and express themselves. However, after seeing similar ideas like Linktree, I put the project aside because I wasn't sure if it would solve a real problem. 

 When I discovered WebMCP and saw how AI agents could directly interact with tools provided by a website, I became interested in the idea again. I decided to bring Nambut back and explore how AI could help users create and customize their cards. 

 The name Nambut is a play on the Thai word "นามบัตร" (Nam-bat), which means a business card or a card containing your personal information. 

 What it does 

 Nambut is a flexible personal card builder where users can create, customize, and share their own cards. 

 Users can freely arrange elements, customize colors, rotate elements, apply effects such as glass blur and shadows, and choose from templates. 

 With WebMCP, AI agents can also interact directly with the editor using tools such as add_element , move_element , and delete_element . 

 How we built it 

 Nambut is a web-based visual editor with WebMCP integrated into its core functionality. 

 We exposed the editor's main actions as structured tools so that AI agents can understand and interact with the application directly, while keeping the normal UI available for human users. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I had never built an application like this before, and this was also my first time seriously working with AI agents. 

 I had to learn how AI agents work and how to expose the tools I built in a way that an AI could understand and use correctly. 

 Learning about WebMCP and this new way of connecting AI with web applications was challenging, but it also gave me a lot more motivation to learn and build. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud that I was able to bring an idea I had been thinking about for a long time back to life. 

 More importantly, I managed to finish it within the hackathon deadline and turn it into something that actually works. 

 What we learned 

 This project gave me my first real experience with AI agents and taught me that websites can provide AI with structured capabilities instead of simply being interfaces that AI has to navigate. 

 It also showed me how new technologies like WebMCP can change the way we think about building web applications. 

 What's next for Nambut 

 If Nambut proves that there is real potential, I want to add more tools and significantly improve the UX/UI. 

 I also want to make Nambut a way for more people to discover WebMCP and experience how AI can be used more effectively when it can directly interact with the tools of an application.

title: Nightwatch
pitch: An incident console where the AI agent's tools mount as the incident gets worse and unregister when it is over. Escalation has to be argued for. The human on call holds the keys.
about_excerpt: An incident console where the AI agent's tools mount as the incident gets worse and unregister when it is over. Escalation has to be argued for. The human on call holds the keys. Like Comment Story Updates Console at green with the alert firing and charts spiked The escalation panel, "AGENT IS REQUESTING SEVERITY YELLOW" with its reason The approval card, frozen rollback call with Approve and Deny Charts curving back under the SLO after the approval Blue severity, the tray with destructive tools gone and 10 / 10 on the strip Inspiration Incident response is the job everyone wants to hand to an AI agent, and the job nobody actually dares to. It is three in the morning, the checkout service is failing, and the person on call is half awake. An agent could read the logs, compare the last deploy, and find the cause in seconds. But the fixes are dangerous. Rolling back the wrong thing or draining the wrong region at 3am makes a bad night much worse. So today you get two options, both bad. Give the agent standing access to the dangerous actions and carry that risk permanently, or give it nothing and do all the work yourself. WebMCP suggests a third option, because in WebMCP the tool surface belongs to the page, and the page can change it while the agent is mid conversation. That turns "what is this agent allowed to do" from a config file into live application state. We wanted to see what happens if an agent's permissions follow the incident instead of being fixed in advance, with a human deciding every step of the way. What it does Nightwatch is an incident console for a small group of production services. The left side is what the on call engineer sees: an alert, service health, live p99 and error rate charts against their SLO lines, and a timeline. The right side is what the agent sees: every tool it is currently allowed to call, and it changes with severity. At green, the agent gets four read only tools. It can see the service list, check health, read the console state, and ask for more access. Logs, deploy history, and anything that touches production do not exist for it yet. Not disabled. Not registered. At yellow, four investigation tools mount: the alert, logs, the last deploy's config diff, and the dependency graph. Still read only. At red, the tools that change production mount: rollback_deploy, drain_region, page_owner, and set_maintenance_mode. Every one of them freezes mid call on an approval card in the page until the human clicks Approve or Deny. The agent cannot click it. At blue, those four are unregistered and two postmortem tools take their place, so nobody can roll something back by accident an hour after it is over. Severity is human only. The agent has a request_escalation tool, but it never changes anything. It records the agent's evidence and lights up the button that only the person can press. In a typical run the agent is asked to look into checkout at green. It checks health, sees the breach, realises it has no logs, and asks for yellow with the numbers to justify it: 14.2% error rate against a 0.5% budget, 1840ms p99 against 300ms. You grant yellow. It reads the deploy diff and finds that the 03:04 deploy set the database connection pool to 4 instead of 400. You tell it to fix that. It asks for red, because the rollback tool does not exist yet. You grant red. It calls rollback, the approval card appears, and the whole call is held until you click. Deny it and it reports the system is still failing and stops. Approve it and the charts curve back under the SLO. Then you press blue, the four dangerous tools vanish, and the browser's own count drops from 14 to 10. Ask for the rollback again and the agent tells you the capability is gone and asks for red back. How we built it How we built it One HTML file, vanilla JavaScript, no build step, no backend. There are 14 tools, each declaring which severities it exists at. They are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool with a navigator.modelContext fallback, since the API moved to Document in the July draft and Chrome 150 deprecates the old location. The interesting part is the sync layer. It keeps one AbortController per tool. On every severity change it registers what has become permitted and aborts the signal for anything that has not. AbortSignal is the only unregistration path the spec has allowed since unregisterTool was removed on 23 April 2026. After each sync the page calls getTools() and shows the browser's count next to its own, so the tool surface is proved on screen rather than claimed. Read tools carry readOnlyHint. Destructive tools carry destructiveHint and block on a promise that only a DOM click resolves. We verified in ChatGPT's browser that a tool call can be held open for well over a minute waiting on that click without the agent timing out. The charts are a small simulation that follows checkout-api's live numbers: fast to spike, slow to recover, noisy while breaching. That is why the recovery after a rollback is a curve and not a step. The estate itself is synthetic. That is deliberate. Anyone opening the link at any hour gets the same incident, the same root cause, and the same fix. Wired to live telemetry there would be nothing wrong to investigate most of the time. What is not simulated is the WebMCP layer, and that is the part being demonstrated. Challenges we ran into We assumed ChatGPT's browser could unregister tools and built the first demo around it. Rather than trust that assumption we wrote probe.html, a page that walks the real modelContext object and reports what is actually there. It found five methods and no removal method at all. Re-registering an existing name threw. So we rebuilt around sealing: tools stayed registered and the page refused calls that were out of severity. It worked, and the reconciliation strip showed the gap honestly: 10 permitted, 4 sealed, 14 registered. Then we found that unregisterTool had not been left unimplemented, it had been replaced. Registration accepts an options object with an AbortSignal. We extended the probe, aborted a live signal, and getTools() confirmed the tool was gone. The seal came out and real unmounting went in. The probe stayed in the repo as the evidence trail. The second real challenge was narrative rather than technical. Our first version only started the incident when the human pressed yellow, which made the whole flow circular: you had to already know something was wrong to grant the agent access to find out. We moved the incident to fire on page load, so green is what it actually is on a real on call shift. An alert is firing, and nobody has triaged it yet. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent asks for permission on its own. Nothing in a prompt tells it to. It works out that it can't read logs, notices that request_escalation exists, and argues its case with the actual numbers off the console. The first time that happened unprompted was the moment the project felt real. We got real unmounting working, not a workaround. Tools genuinely leave the browser's registry when severity drops, and the page proves it by showing the browser's own getTools() count next to its own. That took finding a spec change most tutorials online still haven't caught up with. The deny path works as cleanly as the approve path. When you refuse a rollback, the agent doesn't retry or argue. It reports that the console's approval gate denied it, states that the service is still failing, and stops. A human saying no is a first-class outcome rather than an error to route around. And it holds. A destructive tool call sat frozen for over a minute waiting on a click, in a real browser, without the agent timing out or losing the thread. Last one is smaller but we're glad we did it: the whole thing is one HTML file with no build step. You can read the entire tool lifecycle in a single scroll, which felt like the right shape for something arguing that permissions should be legible. What we learned That the tool surface is a security boundary, not a menu. Recent research on WebMCP tool surface poisoning (arXiv:2606.06387) shows agents can be hijacked by tools injected or reframed mid session. A tool that was never registered cannot be poisoned. Scoping registration to a human controlled state is a real mitigation, not just tidy UX. That the agent will find the escalation path on its own if the tool descriptions are right. Nothing in a prompt told it to ask for yellow. It worked that out from the fact that request_escalation existed and query_logs did not. And that you should test the browser instead of trusting the docs. Two of our central design decisions were wrong until a 60 line probe page corrected them. What's next for Nightwatch Real backends behind the same lifecycle. The tool definitions would not change, only what each function calls. Per service scoping, so an engineer can grant rollback for one service without arming it across the estate. And a signed audit export, since the timelin

title: Clearance
pitch: Your agent shops. You set the rules.
about_excerpt: Your agent shops. You set the rules. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenAI killed Instant Checkout in March 2026 after a Walmart test showed ~3x worse conversion: people do not trust an agent to spend their money without guardrails. Forrester (Apr 2026) found ~75% of US/UK/CA adults uncomfortable letting agents complete purchases even WITH spending limits. The missing piece was never a smarter agent - it was visible governance living where the shopping happens. The W3C WebMCP spec even names this gap (Section 6.3.2.3 'Ambiguous Finalization') and lists it as unsolved in 6.3.2.4. Clearance is a working answer. What it does Clearance is an agent-native storefront. Your AI agent can search, compare, and build a cart - but a server-side rules engine gates every purchase against limits YOU set on the page: a monthly envelope, a per-purchase cap, an approval threshold, category whitelists, and a merchant blocklist. Over the cap, the agent's checkout call PAUSES and an in-page approval card appears showing exactly which rule fired and why the agent chose this item. Approve and it executes; reject and it stops. Every action lands in a SHA-256 hash-chained receipt ledger, and any purchase can be undone within 5 minutes - the 'escape hatch' Consumer Reports says every agentic-commerce provider must build under UETA 10(b). How we built it TanStack Start (React 19) + Tailwind v4 + PGlite (server-side embedded Postgres) for the store, rules engine, and ledger. The agent surface is the native WebMCP API: 8 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool, with readOnly/untrustedContent/humanInTheLoop annotations. checkout_purchase uses requestUserInteraction to pause for human approval; @mcp-b/global polyfills the same tools into any browser when native WebMCP is absent. One shared rules engine governs both human clicks and agent calls - there is no separate, weaker 'agent lane'. Challenges we ran into Designing approval UX that prevents both false approvals and alert fatigue: auto-execute inside the envelope silently (no nagging), gate only over the cap, and add a hold-to-confirm for >$200 purchases (Nielsen Norman Group guidance on rubber-stamping). A rubber-stamp guard watches the approve-rate and warns if you approve everything and reverse nothing. Making the ledger tamper-evident with a live /api/verify endpoint was straightforward but was the differentiator judges noticed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The end-to-end loop is real: agent calls checkout over WebMCP, the page pauses, a human approves on the card, the receipt is written to a hash chain, and the human can undo within the window. We also nailed the spec a head-of-time: humanInTheLoopHint and untrustedContentHint predate their own proposal, mapping to webmcp issue #198 and Chrome's agent-content guidance. What we learned Governance has to be first-class UI, not a backend API. Stripe's Machine Payments Protocol already has our exact rule types - but ships them as a backend API nobody wraps in a consumer surface. The merchant page is the right place for the human-agent contract because that is where the spend actually happens. What's next Deploy to Netlify, add multi-agent shared ledgers, and richer declarative form-tools for the approval step. Longer term: let merchants recognize a governed-agent session and surface the consumer's own rules, closing the loop between shopper intent and checkout. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

title: PixlPal
pitch: Imagine having an AI agent that uses Photoshop with you. PixlPal lets anyone edit photos. Just describe the changes you want in plain English.
about_excerpt: Imagine having an AI agent that uses Photoshop with you. PixlPal lets anyone edit photos. Just describe the changes you want in plain English. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The Problem with diffusion models AI image editing is getting popular because it allows people without any experience in using image editing software to create beautiful edits of their photos. However, the problem with AI image editing approaches right now is that they regenerate the photo . This approach is prone to mistakes such as the image generation model adding or removing certain details, or introducing diffusion noise. And since it "edits" by regenerating the whole photo, it leaves little control for the user to tweak certain image editing parameters themselves. It is not a true edit . PixlPal's Approach PixlPal believes that AI should instead use deterministic tools (like in photoshop) to truly edit the images directly. So I created a custom Rust engine that exposes tools/APIs for an AI agent orchestrator to edit photos. The coolest part: I added a segmentation model that agents can call so it can select specific objects to apply specific transformations to as well. Think of it like watching an AI agent use Photoshop or Lightroom while you watch and tweak, instead of having it one-shot regenerate the whole image. People and Agents working together PixlPal's approach also creates a better user experience because the user has more control over the editing process. With image gen models, this was impossible: they need to regenerate the image as a whole. It is not a "true" edit. But with PixlPal, users can tweak edits directly if they want. AI Agents and People working together. How we implemented WebMCP, and what it brings I already had a custom-built Rust engine to do image/pixel transformations set up, as well as tool definitions exposed to my built-in AI agent. For this challenge, it was just a matter of bridging those tools to WebMCP. WebMCP turned out to be a great complementary approach to the built-in agent. Users can now effectively "Bring Your Own Agent" (BYOA) to PixlPal, and their agents might have better specific context of their tastes and what kind of photos they like. Or if they're just more comfortable using their own agent, WebMCP allows users to use their own agent. Challenges we ran into Usually people want to apply changes only to specific objects instead of the whole image (think of the lasso tool). Without that capability, PixlPal was just a filter-applier rather than a true agentic image editor. At first, I thought this would mean needing to get an AI agent to use a lasso tool (very hard). Eventually, I realized I can just add an Image Segmentation Model as a tool-call for the agent. So the agent does a natural-language prompt to the segmentation model i.e. "select the red snack bag", and the segmentation model returns the exact pixels of the red snack bag, and then the agent can apply pixel transformations specifically to those pixels. Accomplishments that we're proud of Figuring out how to make AI agents select/segment specific objects easily. Creating a working product that lets anyone edits their photos. No background in professional editing needed. What we learned Human UI (clicking buttons, moving around cursors, drag and drop) are quite clunky for AI agents to interact with. In contrast, I think of WebMCP as like a UI for agents. WebMCP allows agents to easily navigate and use web apps and websites. What's next for PixlPal Image Segmentation Model is currently run client-side via WebGPU. This makes edits where PixlPal needs to segment a specific object slow unless the user has a GPU. In the future, I would like to host and run the segmentation model in the cloud. title: Spot
pitch: Your workout, spotted by an agent that can't drop the bar.
about_excerpt: Your workout, spotted by an agent that can't drop the bar. Like Comment Story Updates Spot is a workout tracker where a person and an AI agent work on the same live session, in the same browser tab. Most AI fitness apps just talk at you. They write you a plan and leave. Spot lets an agent actually execute that plan, and work on the session with you. Tell you when to progress, and when to ease off. The app you use at the gym, and the tools the agent uses, hit the same data. All your lifting history, preferences, and personal context can factor into your lifts. Spot makes the plan, you log the sets. Live at https://spot.mootoo.co — no login. Source under AGPL-3.0 at https://github.com/moolikethecow/webmcp-workout . Why this use case fits WebMCP A workout is a living document that changes every ninety seconds while you're in the middle of it. A chat model can't hold that state: it remembers what you said, not what you did. The tracker holds the truth but can't reason with you. WebMCP puts the agent inside the page that owns the truth. Tools register on document.modelContext from the page you're actually looking at, run in your own browser session, and read and write the exact session the logger renders. No API keys, no sync, no drift. How it creates a better user experience You train. You tap sets done. Then you say "my shoulder's bugging me and I've got 30 minutes, keep what I've done, work around the shoulder, hit whatever's freshest" — and the remaining exercises change while the sets you finished stay exactly as you logged them. The replacements weren't hallucinated: the app filtered a 1,318-movement catalog by your stated constraint and your equipment, and the agent picked from that pool. Ask why the next incline press session says 80 lb and the answer cites your last six sessions and the double-progression rule that produced it. Ask it to log a set and it won't invent the numbers — it asks what you actually lifted. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Restructure a workout mid-session without losing what's been done. Every write carries the session revision; a stale edit is rejected with current state and the agent re-reads. State a training constraint once and have it enforced everywhere — search, drafts and live edits all pass through one eligibility function over a precomputed biomechanical demand profile for every exercise in the catalog. Choose today's work from per-muscle readiness derived from your own history, not generic advice. Get progression answers that are auditable: explicit policy in, next target out, rule quoted. Say "I'm in a hotel gym, dumbbells and a smith machine only" and have the catalog narrow to the room you're standing in. A gym never recorded before is created from the description. Let an agent stage a claim about your body without being able to assert it. The training-constraint tool is a form: the agent fills it, the call stays pending, and it completes when you press Add. The human is better at feeling how a set went and calling an audible. The agent is better at querying six weeks of history, reconciling constraints with readiness, and doing the arithmetic. The page is where they meet. How WebMCP is implemented Both halves of the API are used, and the split between them is the design. Sixteen page-scoped tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool by a React hook on mount and unregistered through an AbortController on navigation: get_training_context , get_active_workout , edit_active_workout , log_active_sets , search_exercises , get_muscle_readiness , get_training_constraints , set_training_constraint , draft_workout , edit_workout_draft , start_workout , get_exercise_progress , get_workout_history , get_training_plan , list_gyms , switch_gym . Each execute performs a same-origin fetch to the app's own API routes, which call the same library functions the UI uses, then invalidates the page's data so the logger refetches. Mutations pass expected_revision and return the new revision. Read tools carry readOnlyHint . Descriptions carry the invariants: completed sets preserved, warm-ups are not working volume, substitutions come from the eligible pool only, constraints are hard limits, no diagnosis. get_training_context returns the collaboration rules so an agent has a one-call orientation. The tool list is page-scoped because a tool list is a prompt: edit_active_workout and log_active_sets aren't offered where there's no live session. One declarative tool, registered by markup. report_training_constraint is a <form> on the dashboard carrying toolname and tooldescription . There's no registerTool call for it — Chrome reads the controls and derives the schema: required becomes JSON Schema required , a <select> becomes an enum carrying its option labels. The reason to use a form is what it does to timing. Chrome fills the fields and then waits. The call doesn't resolve until the form is actually submitted, so an agent can put shoulder_joint / limiting / left shoulder on screen but a person commits it. SubmitEvent exposes agentInvoked and respondWith() , so one handler serves both callers. ChatGPT's built-in browser implements a subset of WebMCP with no declarative API, so a <form toolname> isn't a site tool there. Rather than lose that beat in the client judges are told to use, the page treats the form as the definition and the declarative API as one way to publish it : where the browser hasn't published the form, the same report_training_constraint is registered in code, and its execute fills the same form and waits for the person's press. Chrome's indefinite wait is the one thing registerTool can't reproduce, so after twenty seconds the call resolves with awaiting_confirmation and the values stay on screen for the press. One name, one form, one submit handler, three callers. That gives the app an honest line: what the agent may do alone is registered in code; what needs a hand on the button is a form. Reading, searching, drafting and re-prescribing work not yet done are the first kind. Asserting a limit on your own body is the second. And because it's a real form, a browser with no WebMCP gets an ordinary constraint editor. Every visitor gets an isolated Postgres schema seeded with a fictional athlete's six weeks of training, so judges can mutate freely and reset from Settings. Inspiration I already had a workout tracker I'd built for myself. What I didn't have was any way for an agent to actually use it. When I injured my shoulder, there was no way to change my workouts on the fly, or update my progressions. Every AI fitness tool I tried would happily write me a program and then have no idea what I did in the gym, and couldn't adapt. I wanted to close the loop. Building the app with WebMCP now means that Spot can plan my workouts, monitor my lifts inside the workout with me, look at my results, adjust my plans, and frankly, just handle my workouts. How I built it Next.js 15 and React 19 over Postgres, with every query written as SQL through Drizzle rather than an ORM abstraction. Each visitor gets their own Postgres schema, provisioned on first request and pinned per connection, so the app stays single-tenant code and all the isolation lives in one file. The training engine is deterministic (constraint eligibility, readiness and progression are pure functions over logged sets) and covered by around 1,400 tests, which is what made it safe to let an agent write to a live session at all. What I learned A tool description is a prompt, and so is the tool list. Page-scoping which tools exist changed agent behaviour more than any wording change I made. The bigger lesson: a tool's success message can lie. Three of mine reported work they had not done. Search claimed to apply an equipment filter it never ran, eligibility counts were taken over a sample but presented as the whole catalog, and a constraint that excluded nothing said it had excluded things. All three passed their tests. They surfaced only by driving the deployed app and reading what the tool actually said, rather than checking that it returned ok. Challenges ChatGPT's WebMCP is a subset with no getTools and no declarative forms, so the form tool would not exist at all in the client judges are told to use. The page now detects that and registers a code-defined stand-in that fills the same form and still waits for a human to press the button. Chrome cancels a pending declarative call if the form is reset, which meant an agent-invoked submit had to leave the values on screen rather than clearing them. Where it comes from Spot is the open agent surface of a larger health ecosystem app I built. The logger and the deterministic training engine were extracted from it; the WebMCP layer, per-visitor workspaces and the demo athlete were built for this challenge. docs/PRIOR_WORK.md in the repo draws the exact line, with commit timestamps. title: Spatialize
pitch: The floor plan that talks back.
about_excerpt: The floor plan that talks back. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Blind and low-vision visitors rehearse a route before entering an unfamiliar building, because getting it wrong means a wasted trip or being stranded. The data they need usually exists — as a flat PDF nobody can ask questions of. And it rots, because updating it means a human opening an app and filling in a form. I had already built the part that makes a plan answerable: upload a floor plan, a vision model proposes rooms, doors and a route graph, and a deterministic topology validator decides whether it ships. What that version couldn't do was let the person standing at the door change it, or let their own assistant ask it anything. That's the gap WebMCP closes, and it's a strange one: the answer a disabled visitor needs is not on the page. There is no screen anywhere that says "can I get from the north entrance to the quiet room without stairs, through doorways at least 760 mm wide?" That answer has to be computed from the building's geometry, in the venue's own session, at the moment somebody asks. A DOM-scraping agent can't find it, because it was never rendered. What it does Spatialize publishes a venue's floor plan to any agent in your browser as fourteen WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . With them, a person and their agent can do six things that were difficult or impossible before: Ask a building a question it couldn't answer. find_step_free_route runs Dijkstra over the validated route graph. Google Maps knows whether a building has an accessible entrance; it doesn't know the topology inside. The route is computed, never estimated. Hear why , not just no . When no step-free route exists, the tool re-runs against the unrestricted graph and names the exact door that blocks it, with its clear width — instead of returning nothing. Check a route against one specific body. check_route_clearance takes the narrowest doorway that person can pass, in millimetres, and answers CLEAR, BLOCKED or UNKNOWN — saying unknown rather than clear whenever a doorway on the route is low-confidence or disputed, and saying how old the data is. CHI 2025 (N=190) found scooter users judge 46% of barriers impassable against 28% for cane users, so a single accessible-yes/no bit is wrong for somebody by construction. The tools give the measurement and leave the threshold to the person, because the threshold is theirs. Fix the building's data by talking, and be refused when wrong. Four propose_* tools file what a visitor found on the ground. Every one runs through the same topology validator that guards the rest of the app. An impossible change comes back with the exact rule and field path, so the agent self-corrects — where a DOM-scraping agent would have gotten a silent success and left a corrupted building behind. Disagree with the building, on the record. A venue can decline a report. It cannot delete one. Declined reports stay as disputed claims and list_disputed_claims tells the next agent both sides — because in the 2024 Euan's Guide survey (n=6,665), 77% of disabled respondents found venue-published access information misleading. The venue is the least reliable source on its own accessibility, so it doesn't get the last word. Rehearse a closure before it happens. simulate_closure answers which destinations lose step-free access if a lift goes out of use, and changes nothing. It's the question an access manager faces before every works notice, and no button on any venue site does it. Nothing an agent says goes live. Every write is a proposal: gated in the browser for fast feedback, re-applied and re-validated on the server from a five-field mutation, then decided by a human. You can also just talk to it — gpt-5.6-luna runs a function-calling loop over the same tools, and a spoken "mark the gallery door as not accessible" files a proposal through the same review ledger, with the spoken sentence kept as its provenance. Why this has to live in the browser rather than behind an API: when my agent reports a step, the proposal card lands in the review queue on the screen I'm looking at , the 3D view moves to the door it means, and when the venue declines it, the dispute is visible to me and to the next visitor's agent in the same window. The venue's validator, the venue's record and the person's own eyes are in one tab. The economics are the reason to bother. Detailed venue accessibility data is sold today by human surveyors — AccessAble covers about 70,000 venues at 30–60 minutes of surveyor time each; standalone audits run £3,000–£6,000. That model is labour-bound, which is why it covers 70,000 venues and not 15 million. WebMCP turns the update into a sentence spoken at the door, and because the validator refuses incoherent edits before a human ever sees one, quality goes up rather than down. A demo venue loads itself for every visitor, in its own isolated server-side run, so you can try all of this with no upload, no login and no setup. How I built it Tools are registered directly on document.modelContext — no wrapper library — tied to an AbortController , and they're a function of page state, not a static list : the four propose_* tools are only published when there's a venue record to propose against, because a proposal with nowhere to be kept would be a lie. Every change fires toolchange so an idle agent learns the surface moved. Results come back in canonical MCP content form. Reads carry readOnlyHint ; anything carrying visitor-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . The scene contract is written twice on purpose — Zod in the browser, Pydantic on the server — so no unvalidated geometry crosses the wire in either direction. The browser's gate is fast feedback; the server is the boundary. A proposal is five fields, never a scene: the backend applies it to its own copy of the venue, re-validates, and computes the accessibility impact from that. So a "rename this room" cannot also widen a door. I built against Chrome's published guidance, and it reshaped the surface. Write tools were originally named report_* , which implied they changed things — they queue proposals, so all four became propose_* . And propose_landmark originally demanded metre coordinates, which made models invent numbers; it now takes a room's name and computes the centroid. A test asserts that no tool in the surface accepts an x or z parameter. Front end is React 19 + Three.js; backend is FastAPI; scene versions, review ledgers and provenance live in Backblaze B2 with SHA-256 manifests. The frontend is on Vercel, the API on Render. Challenges I ran into Trusting the browser was a vulnerability, and a review proved it. The first version of the review ledger accepted a candidate scene built by the client. A "rename this room" proposal could therefore smuggle in a widened door and clear the review issues, and the description the venue reviewer approved would say nothing about it. The server now applies the mutation itself and re-validates; a test asserts the installed scene differs from the base only where the mutation says. A one-second race that only a real browser could find. All my unit tests passed, so I wrote a script that drives the tools through Chrome's own WebMCP surface. It scored 8/13. The store was hydrating from the server by replacing local state about a second after the tools went live, so an agent that acted in that second had its proposal wiped mid-flight. Hydration merges now. Chrome changed the host API underneath me, mid-project. Running that same script against the deployed app scored 2/13. Chrome had auto-updated 151 → 152, which removed navigator.modelContextTesting and folded the host surface onto document.modelContext : getTools() in place of listTools() , and executeTool() taking the RegisteredTool object rather than a tool name. The page itself needed no change — the tools registered and ran correctly the whole time — but my harness did, and it now runs on 149 through 152. Building on an origin trial means the ground moves. Auditing myself against Chrome's guides found three real defects. I checked the surface against all 181 checkable rules across the five WebMCP guides, including the newer tool-security and agent-security pages: propose_doorway filled an unmeasured doorway with a 0.9 m default and stamped the evidence as a human observation — laundering my own placeholder into the venue's record as a visitor's measurement. Width and step-free status are now optional; an unmeasured width is evidenced as derived below the confidence floor, so a clearance check answers UNKNOWN rather than CLEAR, and the reviewer's card says "width not measured" beside what they approve. minimum_clear_width_mm: "760mm" parsed to null, which meant "no width given", which meant no doorway was ever compared against it — so the tool could answer CLEAR to a wheelchair user whose chair had never been checked. Unreadable values are now refused, naming the expected format. The 1.5K per-result budget he
