title: Ingram Sheets
pitch: A spreadsheet whose engine runs in your browser and publishes twelve tools to whichever agent is driving the tab. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets.
about_excerpt: A spreadsheet whose engine runs in your browser and publishes twelve tools to whichever agent is driving the tab. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Ingram Sheets is a spreadsheet whose calculation engine runs in the browser. It publishes its operations to whichever agent is driving the tab: read a range, write a block, extend a pattern, format, restructure, undo, point at a cell. ChatGPT supplies the model; we supply the sheet and hold no inference key. Why it needs WebMCP The engine is IronCalc compiled to WebAssembly, holding the live workbook in memory. There is no server-side copy of the sheet you are looking at: nothing that could recalculate it remotely, no endpoint that knows where your cursor is. An agent outside the tab has nothing to call. Spreadsheets for models, not models for spreadsheets The engine keeps every intermediate result at a stable address, so the model writes D17 instead of recopying a value it can transcribe wrong. It owns the dependency graph, so the model declares one local relation at a time and the engine keeps the global result consistent. And every write returns the cells whose computed values changed, recalculation ripple included. That return value is the tool contract: the model is corrected at each edit rather than at the end of a script, and it can skip the read that would otherwise confirm what it just did. Working alongside it Person and agent are in the same document at the same time. The agent's writes recalculate on screen, its focus moves across the grid in its own colour, and it can highlight a range and attach a note. Edit a cell while it works and your change is attached to its next tool result, so it re-plans against the current sheet. A code interpreter cannot do this. Its state ends with the session and its output is not editable. In a workbook every intermediate value sits next to the formula that produced it, and whoever knows the discount rate is wrong fixes the cell. How it is built Twelve tools, generated from the Zod schemas that also drive the built-in chat agent, so the two surfaces cannot drift. Every write goes through one controller, so an outside agent gets the same cursor and highlight behaviour as the built-in one, and its edits ride the same compare-and-swap save as a keystroke. Reads are marked readOnlyHint so the host can run them unattended. The two that return cell contents are marked untrustedContentHint : a cell can hold any text, including text shaped like an instruction, and the agent is told up front that what comes back is data. Results are returned as plain text rather than MCP content blocks, because the host serializes whatever a tool returns and the wrapper reaches the model as JSON noise around the grid. Prior work and hackathon work Ingram Sheets is a pre-existing project. WEBMCP.md in the repository separates what shipped before the submission period from what was built during it, with the commit history. Trying it Open https://sheets.ingram.tech/try in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser, on GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. No sign-in. The panel on the right logs every tool call with its result.  Inspiration

 What it does

title: Shipmail WebMCP
pitch: Your browser agent can handle email setup. Shipmail shows each call, and you press Send.
about_excerpt: Your browser agent can handle email setup. Shipmail shows each call, and you press Send. Like Comment Story Updates A completed tool call in the Browser agent activity log. Pause removes the signed-in tools until you resume. The Browser agent button stays in the header until you need it. Why WebMCP fits Shipmail Setting up business email means bouncing between Shipmail and DNS: add a domain, copy the records, wait, create a mailbox, and send a test. Shipmail already has the details. WebMCP lets a browser agent use the tools on the page you have open, so you don't have to copy values into a chat or keep a checklist on the side. What you can do with it On Inbox, your agent can read what's on screen, check recent mail, or open a draft. On Domains, it can check setup, return the exact MX, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records, test propagation, and create a mailbox. Shipmail changes the tools with the page. Each call leaves a timestamped receipt in the Browser agent popover. Press Pause and the signed-in tools disappear from discovery. Press Resume and Shipmail registers them again. Shipmail keeps sensitive or irreversible actions out of WebMCP. The agent cannot send, delete, or forward email, change billing, or read credentials. Mailbox passwords stay on the server. Preparing an email opens the usual composer, where you review it and press Send. How we built it Shipmail registers tools with document.modelContext . We kept navigator.modelContext as a temporary fallback for older prototype builds. Each call goes through the same authentication and permissions as the rest of Shipmail. Tool annotations say whether a call reads or changes data. Mail and DNS results from outside Shipmail are marked as untrusted. Pause aborts the current registration. Resume makes a new controller and registers the tools for the page again. shipmail.to is enrolled in Chrome's WebMCP origin trial. It serves Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) . What we added for the challenge Shipmail already had four public WebMCP tools. We added eight signed-in tools for setup, domains, DNS, mailboxes, drafts, recent mail, and the inbox on screen. We also built the activity popover, receipts, and Pause/Resume control. The browser API changed during the build, so we moved the code and types to document.modelContext , isolated the legacy fallback, and updated the tests. What we tested We used Chrome's #enable-webmcp-testing flag and the official inspector on the live Inbox. The inspector found the tools, ran shipmail_get_inbox_view , and Shipmail logged the completed call. Pause removed the account tools. Resume brought them back. Next We want the agent to carry DNS values between Shipmail and your DNS provider, then help when a record won't verify. title: grid-search
pitch: A local-first word-association game where humans and multiple agents play cooperatively and competitively to decode the key first.
about_excerpt: A local-first word-association game where humans and multiple agents play cooperatively and competitively to decode the key first. Like Comment Story Updates Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Grid Search makes WebMCP part of the game itself, rather than adding an AI assistant beside it. The website owns the rules, roles, private information, current match state, and legal actions; the agent brings reasoning, language, and knowledge of the human it is playing with. That division lets each side contribute what it knows best. The get_rules tool also shows how a website can distribute a small, current skill/context file at the moment it is needed. A non-technical player does not have to find, install, update, or manage an agent skill or copy a long prompt. Opening the game gives every compatible agent the same authoritative instructions, and a hint in the HTML tells agents to call /get_rules before doing anything else. Grid Search explores several useful WebMCP tool types in one small experience: a skill/context tool, an identity tool, a read tool, and validated write tools. How it creates a better user experience The player opens one website and can invite one or more agents to join the lobby—there is no model picker, API key, bot integration, or prompt setup. Agents register for a team and role, learn the rules from the page, read only the state they are allowed to see, and take their turns through clear game actions. The human and agents compete or cooperate on one authoritative board with shared scores, turn indicators, and game history. That board is synchronized across tabs. Separate agent threads and sub-agents cannot share one browser tab, so each can open Grid Search in its own tab—including headless or non-persistent tabs—and still participate in the same match when they share the same browser profile and origin storage. A versioned snapshot in same-origin localStorage , browser storage events, and polling keep those independently controlled tabs aligned. The tools are designed to keep play moving with fewer calls. Every successful clue, guess, or end-turn write returns fresh authorized game state, including the next active player, legal actions, remaining guesses, scores, and turn number. An agent can immediately tell whether it may act again or should wait, reducing redundant state reads, tokens, and delays between turns. Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before One person can now turn a browser game into a shared surface for several independent agents. Using the sub-agent pattern, up to three agents can join as distinct players alongside the human, cooperate on one team, or compete against each other on the same board. Each registration receives an opaque, web-app-generated token that identifies that agent and scopes every later read or action to its seat. The token determines which role-filtered version of the board the agent may receive and which actions it may take on its turn. Re-registering with the same player name rotates the old token. These tokens are local capability credentials for the match, not internet user accounts. WebMCP also makes games with asymmetric information practical. The clue-giver must see the answer key while the guesser must not. Grid Search does not merely hide secret assignments with CSS: unrevealed alignments are omitted from the guesser’s role-filtered state before the WebMCP response is created. When the human is the guesser, that same filtered projection renders the board, so those assignments never enter the card DOM. A hold-to-reveal control protects the human clue-giver’s key on a shared screen and removes it again as soon as the control is released, preventing an agent from casually discovering the key while inspecting the normal page. Each participant receives the information its role permits while still playing on one shared surface. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP Grid Search is a static TypeScript and Vite application with no backend. It feature-detects document.modelContext and registers six imperative tools with a name, description, strict JSON input schema, and asynchronous execute handler: get_rules , register , get_state , submit_clue , make_guess , and end_turn . get_rules serves the game’s skill/context file directly from the website, so its instructions stay versioned with the experience. A browser-owned GameController is authoritative for both human UI actions and WebMCP actions in each tab. register assigns an available seat and returns a cryptographically generated opaque token. Every player tool validates that token, resolves its team and role, checks turn legality, and produces a role-filtered response. Before reading or mutating, each controller synchronizes from the versioned snapshot in localStorage ; successful writes persist the next snapshot, refresh the human board, and return the caller’s updated authorized state. Same-origin tabs receive storage events and also poll as a fallback, allowing separately controlled agents to share one match without sharing one tab.  Inspiration 

 WebMCP is a genuine leap forward for agentic web apps, a page can expose a real tool ( transfer_funds , export_customers , get_session_token ) and any AI agent gets a standard way to call it via document.modelContext.executeTool . But that also means the moment a site adopts WebMCP, an agent gets the same reach a logged-in human has with no confirmation dialog, no audit trail, and no idea whether the tool it's calling is safe to call. Browsers ship extensions that block ads and trackers; nothing exists yet that treats an agent's tool calls the same way. We wanted to find out what that missing layer should actually look like and build both halves of the problem to prove it: a real WebMCP app with genuinely risky tools, and the guard that makes calling them safe. 

 What it does 

 We built two things: 

 
 A demo WebMCP business app , built purely to give Surf something real and risky to protect — five tools across the risk spectrum: get_balance (read), export_customers (data-egress), get_session_token (credential), transfer_funds (destructive write), and add_payee (account-takeover risk), registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() like any real WebMCP site would. 
 Surf , a Chrome MV3 extension that works on any page exposing WebMCP tools — not just our demo. It injects into every page at document_start ( matches: ["<all_urls>"] ) and sits between every agent and every tool that page exposes:

 
 Blocks explicitly blocklisted tools outright, by name, regardless of what the page's own annotations claim. 
 Holds any tool call that isn't provably safe for an in-page human approval prompt, Approve/Deny buttons rendered directly on the page before it's allowed to run. 
 Masks sensitive data in tool results before it reaches the caller: PII (SSNs, credit cards, emails, IBANs), secrets (API keys, JWTs, bearer tokens), and any field whose name alone looks sensitive. 
 Records every call agent-driven or manual in a live, cross-tab audit trail any page can subscribe to in real time. 
 
 

 The demo app exists to let judges see Surf actually doing something — you can watch it hold transfer_funds for approval, block add_payee outright, and mask a token out of get_session_token 's response but the protection itself is site-agnostic and needs zero cooperation from the page it's protecting. 

 How we built it 

 The core trick is where and how we intercept. The guard ( guard/mcp-guard.ts ) runs in the page's own MAIN JS world from document_start — before any page script runs and polls cheaply for modelContext to appear (since a polyfill or native implementation may define it moments later), then wraps executeTool in place rather than using Object.defineProperty . That matters: a global monkey-patch risks breaking other scripts touching the same built-in, and it wouldn't even help against a native implementation that never defines the property through page-visible calls anyway. Wrapping the method in place works retroactively regardless of how or when modelContext showed up, because callers invoke mc.executeTool(...) at call time rather than caching a reference. 

 Holding a call for approval means the guard has to pause mid-call: it await s a decision, posting an APPROVAL_REQUEST into the page via postMessage , picked up by an isolated-world content script bridge that renders a shadow-DOM prompt directly on the page (isolated from the page's own render cycle) and posts the decision back. A 45s timeout, enforced on both ends, auto-denies so a call can never hang forever. 

 The live audit feed uses externally_connectable so a trusted page can chrome.runtime.connect() straight into the extension and get pushed every entry as it happens, across every tab not just the one it's running in. 

 DLP rules and masking logic were adapted from Surf's own production DLP engine, so tool results get classified the same way real user data already is elsewhere in the product. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 MV3 service worker lifetime. Background service workers terminate after ~30s idle, which silently closes the audit-feed port — naively treating that as "extension not installed" produces a false flip where a real connection looks like it vanished. We fixed it with a client-side heartbeat (any message resets the idle timer) plus automatic reconnection, only reporting "not installed" after several consecutive failures. 
 Injecting UI without fighting the page. The approval prompt has to render reliably on top of arbitrary pages — including ones running their own React/Vue render loops — without a layout fight. Rendering it from the isolated-world bridge as an anchored shadow-DOM element, rather than trying to inject it from the MAIN-world guard, solved this cleanly. 
 Safe-by-default without full annotation coverage. Most real tools won't bother annotating readOnlyHint / destructiveHint , so strict mode needed a sane fallback — a name heuristic ( get_ / list_ / search_ reads as safe) that we know isn't a real safety analysis, which is exactly why the explicit blocklist exists as the actual zero-trust override. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting protection to work transparently and generally — no page changes required, no cooperation needed from the site, working on any WebMCP-enabled page rather than just our own demo — while still being retrofittable to a modelContext that shows up late. 

 What we learned 

 How much of "agent safety" is really a timing and trust problem, not a policy problem, the hard part wasn't deciding what to block, it was guaranteeing we're in position to intercept before an agent (or the page) ever gets a live reference to executeTool , and staying resilient to a background execution model (MV3 service workers) that wasn't designed with this kind of always-on interception in mind. 

 What's next 

 Real safety-classification instead of name heuristics, broader cross-origin iframe coverage for the inspector, and since a Chrome extension only protects regular Chrome exploring what the same policy engine looks like at the browser or network layer for agents that bring their own embedded Chromium.

title: Labmate
pitch: An AI lab where your tutor watches the experiment, not the chat. The agent proposes evidence, the learner stays in control — bidirectional tutoring on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An AI lab where your tutor watches the experiment, not the chat. The agent proposes evidence, the learner stays in control — bidirectional tutoring on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration When we entered the WebMCP Challenge, our honest goal was to check what we could do with it. The showcase examples were mostly agents filling shopping carts and forms — useful, but one-directional: the agent acts, the page obeys. Meanwhile, every AI tutor we knew worked beside an educational tool, never inside it. The learner plays with a simulation, then manually types what happened into a chat; the model reasons from a stale summary and, worst of all, happily does the thinking the student was supposed to do. That combination suggested a question: what if the tutor lived inside the lab page itself — reading the same live bench, proposing evidence, but structurally unable to take over the scientific method? A tutor that is bidirectional: the agent sees what the learner actually did, and the learner sees and approves everything the agent actually proposes. LabMate is our answer. What it does LabMate is a 15-minute high-school physics inquiry around one LED circuit, following the scientific method: Predict → Design → Evidence → Reflect . The learner states a prediction ("if resistance decreases, the LED gets brighter because current increases") and locks it. The hypothesis and the final conclusion are learner-owned : visible to the agent, writable by no tool. Through WebMCP, the agent sees the exact live bench — voltages, saved trials, the current stage, model limits, and the page's revision number. It proposes one fair experiment at a time. The proposal appears as a preview card and touches nothing until the learner approves, edits, or rejects it. The demo's climax is a confound challenge: the learner changes the voltage from 5 V to 9 V after the agent last looked. The agent's now-outdated proposal is rejected atomically ( stale_revision ), because it was written against a world it never observed. The agent re-inspects, spots the second variable, and proposes a revised trial that restores a valid controlled comparison. Once a controlled pair exists, the page compares trials and reports the valid pairs. The learner — not the agent — answers four reflection prompts (what changed, what stayed constant, what the measurements show, whether the prediction was supported) and locks the conclusion. Under the hood, the simulation is a conceptual teaching model: $I = V/R$, $P = V \times I$, LED brightness bands keyed to current, and six trial slots — of which the agent may fill at most four, so one slot is always reserved for the learner. Every accepted mutation increments a shared revision and records a Human/Agent receipt, so the collaboration is auditable. And when document.modelContext is unavailable, the status chip flips to LAB READY and the whole lab still works in a regular browser. How we built it The app is a static front end: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, Tailwind CSS with shadcn-derived controls. No database, no login, no OpenAI API calls, and deliberately no custom chat surface. Everything — human clicks and agent tool calls — flows through one revision-safe command layer: gates → validation → revision + 1 → a single atomic state update → a receipt. The agent's three Site tools are thin views over those same commands: inspect_experiment() — the only read-only tool; returns the full experiment snapshot. propose_trial(...) — the approval gate; creates a visible preview card, not evidence. compare_trials(...) — surfaces controlled pairs. Two discipline points we refused to compromise on: every tool schema rejects extra fields ( additionalProperties: false ), and actor is never accepted from the model — the registration adapter pins it to agent . Failures are structured codes ( hypothesis_required , approval_required , student_slot_reserved , stale_revision , trial_limit_reached …), never prose, so the agent can actually replan from them. For quality: 26 Vitest unit/contract tests and 3 Playwright flows, including a document.modelContext shim that lets us test the full agent loop headlessly — plus a live run in ChatGPT's desktop browser. typecheck , test , test:e2e , build , and lint are all green. Challenges we ran into Trust by construction. The hardest question wasn't "how does the agent help" but "how do we guarantee it can't write the conclusion?" Our answer is structural: learner-owned fields exist in the page state but in no tool schema. There is nothing for the model to call. Two authors, one page. Human and agent mutate the same state concurrently. Optimistic concurrency ( expected_revision ) makes stale writes fail atomically — but making that rejection legible , so the agent understands "the world changed, look again," took real schema and prompt design. A deterministic demo with a probabilistic actor. Our centerpiece moment depends on the model doing the right thing on stage. We shaped the tools (one-proposal-at-a-time, structured errors) and the demo prompts so the inspect → propose → human-intervenes → stale-rejection → replan loop happens reliably. Testing without ChatGPT. CI can't drive the desktop app, so we mirrored document.modelContext in a Playwright shim and contract-tested the adapter against it. Honest scope. The simulation is a conceptual teaching model: overloaded is a teaching warning above 20 mA, not a real component rating, and forward voltage, tolerance, and temperature are intentionally omitted. The page always says so. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop runs live in ChatGPT's built-in browser: agent proposes → learner approves → human changes the world → stale proposal rejected → agent re-plans → learner concludes, with a receipt for every step. The agent is useful because it is constrained: one proposal at a time, a trial quota that always leaves the learner a slot, and zero silent writes. The lab never depends on the agent: in a plain browser, the pedagogy stays intact. The quality gate is green end-to-end: 26 unit/contract tests, 3 e2e flows, typecheck, build, lint. What we learned Treating the page as the source of truth turns tool design into contract design . Structured error codes beat chat prose for agent replanning. Human–agent experience is mostly a state machine: who may write what, when, and what happens when the world changes under the agent. Getting that machine right is the product. Strictness is what makes trust possible: additionalProperties: false and a pinned actor are the difference between learner control as an aspiration and as an invariant. "The agent may only propose" felt restrictive at first — it turned out to be the feature. It kept the experiments fair and kept the student thinking. What's next for LabMate More missions on the same Predict → Design → Evidence → Reflect skeleton — optics, kinematics, reaction rates — with teacher-authored content. A classroom view so teachers can see receipts, common confounds, and where students get stuck. Extracting the pattern : learner-owned fields, approval gates, revision-safe commands, and agent quotas generalize beyond this lab, and we want to package them for other "human-owned page, agent coach" sites built on WebMCP. title: ReuseRoute
pitch: An agent-native circular economy assistant that finds the best next life for unwanted items through repair, reuse, parts recovery, or recycling.
about_excerpt: An agent-native circular economy assistant that finds the best next life for unwanted items through repair, reuse, parts recovery, or recycling. Like Comment Story Updates ReuseRoute Let your AI agent find the best next life for anything you no longer need. Inspiration: Getting rid of an item is deceptively complicated. A cracked laptop might be repairable, refurbishable, useful for parts, or finally ready for material recovery. A chair could be donated if pickup exists. Damaged clothing might still be repairable or useful for fibre recovery. The web has plenty of information about these options, but the user journey is fragmented. People often have to open several pages, interpret different acceptance rules, compare conditions, and then figure out what to prepare before a handoff. The easiest option can become the trash bin simply because the better option takes too much research. We wanted to explore a different kind of open web: one where circular-economy services do not just publish pages for humans to read, but also expose clear, structured actions that a user's agent can call on the person's behalf. What it does: ReuseRoute is a human-first web app with an agent-native WebMCP layer. A person describes an unwanted item, its condition, their transport constraint, and what matters most. A browser agent can then: find eligible repair, reuse, salvage and recycling routes, compare the strongest options using structured fields, select one option and open its details on the page, prepare a visible handoff checklist, save the selected route locally, pre-fill a visible handoff request for the person to review. The last step is intentionally human-confirmed. The declarative WebMCP form does not auto-submit. The agent can prepare the task, but the person makes the commitment. All organizations and service data in the hackathon demo are fictional, so the app never presents invented availability or eligibility as real-world guidance. How we built it: ReuseRoute is a dependency-free static web app built with semantic HTML, responsive CSS and vanilla JavaScript. The WebMCP implementation uses both APIs: Imperative WebMCP: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) defines structured search, comparison, selection and saved-state tools using JSON Schema. Dynamic tool lifecycle: after a route is selected, ReuseRoute registers route-specific prepare_selected_handoff and save_selected_route tools. An AbortController removes the old contextual tools when the selection changes. Declarative WebMCP: the handoff form uses toolname, tooldescription and toolparamdescription attributes so an agent can fill the real visible form. Shared state: every agent action updates the same interface the human sees — result cards, details dialog, checklist, saved indicator and activity log. Progressive enhancement: the complete manual experience still works when WebMCP is unavailable. The demo uses local browser storage for saved routes and confirmed demo handoff requests. There is no backend and no network write operation. Challenges we ran into: The main design challenge was resisting the temptation to expose one giant "do everything" tool. WebMCP is more useful when the tool surface reflects the product's real task boundaries. We split the journey into discovery, comparison and selection, then made the tool set state-aware. A handoff-preparation action should not exist before a route has been chosen, so those tools are registered only in the relevant context. A second challenge was deciding where the agent should stop. Preparing a handoff request is useful automation; silently submitting one is a different level of commitment. The declarative form became our human checkpoint: the agent can populate it, the browser makes that visible, and the person confirms. Finally, we wanted the demo to be trustworthy. Instead of pretending fictional services were real, every program and impact signal is clearly labeled as demo data. What we learned: The biggest lesson was that agent-friendly design is not the same as adding chat to a website. WebMCP works best when the website itself becomes legible as a set of intentional capabilities. We learned to think about: the user's goal before individual tool calls, initial application state, the smallest useful tool boundaries, when tools should appear or disappear, which outputs should visibly update the UI, and where a human confirmation is more appropriate than autonomous execution. What's next: A production version could let real repair cafés, charities, retailers and municipal reuse programs expose their own WebMCP tools. A user's agent could then discover and orchestrate those capabilities across the open web without relying on fragile DOM scraping. The long-term idea is simple: when someone is finished with an object, the web should make its next useful life easier than throwing it away. title: Agent Hands Task Board
pitch: An agentic set of hands for users who cannot reliably drag cards or complete dense forms.
about_excerpt: An agentic set of hands for users who cannot reliably drag cards or complete dense forms. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Hands - Kanban for Accessibility Agent Hands — Focus Relay for WebMCP Inspiration Many everyday web tasks still depend on dense controls, precise pointer input, and repeatedly locating the same item after switching attention to an agent. That creates friction for everyone and can make conventional task boards especially difficult for people using keyboards, switch control, eye gaze, or other assistive input. We asked a simple question: what if a person could establish context with the input that works for them, then safely tell an agent to act on this ? What it does Agent Hands is an accessibility-first task board that demonstrates the Focus Relay pattern. A person reaches a card with ordinary keyboard navigation or another input method. The page preserves that deliberate focus as a visible agent target. The person can then ask an agent to update “this” card without restating its title or manipulating a crowded editing interface. The core action, update_current_card , can move the card, change the assignee and priority, and set a due date in one validated, atomic WebMCP call. The board immediately shows an accessible before/after receipt. One Undo reverses the whole intent, while conflict-safe checks refuse to overwrite newer human changes. Why WebMCP is the right fit A typical backend API can update a card by ID, but it does not know which card a person just reached in the live page. Focus Relay uses WebMCP to connect ephemeral, human-established page context to structured agent actions. That makes collaboration direct without scraping the DOM, copying card names into chat, or asking people to repeat navigation work. People and agents can now work in the same interface: people set intent through focus; agents handle the multi-field manipulation; the page makes the result, history, and recovery visible to both. How we built it The project is a React, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed on Vercel. Board state, focus persistence, atomic intent mutations, bounded history, and conflict-safe Undo live in a Zustand store. The page registers twelve schema-validated WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a compatibility fallback using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill . The interface is keyboard-operable, has visible focus treatment, and provides a polite ARIA activity log for tool receipts. The verification suite covers the complete Focus Relay journey, atomic updates and Undo, stale targets, human/agent races, keyboard-only flows, accessibility scans, reflow, offline behavior, reloads, and tool-registration stability. Challenges we ran into The hard part was preserving human control while still making the agent useful. We needed the target to persist when focus moved from the page to agent chat, while also avoiding stale or ambiguous changes. The result is a narrow, explicit handoff: human focus establishes context, structured tools make changes, and an intent-level receipt plus conflict-safe Undo keeps the person in control. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it augments a working human interface rather than replacing it. The strongest agent actions are not generic click automation: they are small, validated operations grounded in shared page context and paired with feedback that people can see, understand, and reverse. title: TERRA — Voice-Driven Earth Engine
pitch: A shared 3D Earth that people and browser agents can explore together through six typed WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A shared 3D Earth that people and browser agents can explore together through six typed WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Climate systems are difficult to understand from articles and static charts alone. TERRA explores a more direct interface: ask a question, let a browser agent change the shared Earth scene through WebMCP, and inspect the same evidence together. What it does TERRA is an interactive 3D Earth for exploring climate evidence. A person can drag and zoom the globe, choose a region, scientific layer, IPCC scenario, year, and presentation style. A WebMCP-capable browser agent can operate those same controls through six typed tools. The current experience connects: NASA Blue Marble day imagery, Black Marble night lights, and a moving cloud shell OSCAR-derived open ocean-current streamlines NOAA OISST v2.1 observed sea-surface temperature NSIDC Sea Ice Index observed September 2025 extent IPCC AR6 global temperature and sea-level assessment ranges Short, interruptible Arctic–AMOC and global sea-level stories Why WebMCP This is not a chatbot placed beside a globe. The website exposes its real controls with document.modelContext.registerTool . The agent can read the scene, fly to named regions, change an evidence layer, set a scenario and year, change the rendering style, or play a guided story without guessing DOM coordinates. Every write requires the current revision. Stale writes are rejected with revision_conflict . Human controls and agent tools mutate the same visible browser state, and a human action interrupts an active agent story. Human and agent collaboration The agent can compose several precise scene changes from a natural-language question. The person keeps direct control: they can rotate and zoom the globe, interrupt the sequence, compare sources, and choose how the evidence is presented. Both sides see the same camera, data layer, year, sources, and uncertainty labels. How we built it TERRA uses Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Three.js, Vinext, and ChatGPT Sites. The page registers six imperative WebMCP tools: earth_read_scene earth_focus_region earth_set_layer earth_set_scenario earth_set_render_style earth_play_story The Earth renderer uses locally bundled NASA imagery. Ocean-current paths were generated from the July 2014 mean of six OSCAR five-day composites obtained from the public NOAA CoastWatch mirror. The temperature texture is an August 2026 mean of 30 available daily NOAA OISST preliminary fields. Missing SST cells remain transparent. The sea-ice geometry is based on the NSIDC September 2025 extent mask. Scientific boundary TERRA is an exploratory, reduced-order visualization. It does not run a global climate model, predict weather, or map local flooding. The fixed day/night lighting is presentation lighting, not the current solar position. Future sea-ice contraction is marked as illustrative rather than presented as a geographic forecast. Challenges The hardest work was maintaining scientific honesty while still creating a cinematic experience. We separated observed textures, assessed global ranges, reduced-order interpolation, and illustrative future geometry in both the interface and narration. We also corrected longitude alignment, story interruption, scenario-dependent AMOC values, and reduced-motion behavior through an adversarial audit. Accomplishments A working public 3D Earth that both a person and a browser agent can control Six narrow, discoverable WebMCP tools with optimistic locking Visible provenance and uncertainty boundaries Photographic Earth rendering with data-derived scientific overlays English and Japanese interfaces A public MIT-licensed repository with reproducible data-generation scripts What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it lets an agent conduct a living interface rather than imitate clicks. The protocol also makes responsibility clearer: the site defines the available actions and data boundaries, while the person can see, interrupt, and redirect every shared state change. Testing Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to read the scene, focus on Japan, show ocean currents, then move to the Arctic and display sea ice in 2100. The final Arctic state should be labelled illustrative. You can also drag the globe and use the zoom controls directly. title: SeqCraft
pitch: A browser-native DNA engineering workspace where AI agents use WebMCP to analyze, edit, validate, and automate real molecular biology workflows.
about_excerpt: A browser-native DNA engineering workspace where AI agents use WebMCP to analyze, edit, validate, and automate real molecular biology workflows. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration SeqCraft began when I kept facing a problem while using DNA tools. I could ask an AI about a plasmid cloning strategy, primers or restriction sites. Get a helpful answer.. When I wanted the AI to work with the actual sequence I had to copy data between the chat and various biology tools again. The AI could think about biology. It had no real link to the workspace where the biology was happening. WebMCP made me rethink that. Of giving an agent generic UI controls I wanted SeqCraft to reveal the real molecular biology operations of the app. What it does SeqCraft is a browser-based DNA engineering workspace where the user and the agent share the biological state. It supports: linear and circular DNA views annotations and feature navigation GenBank and FASTA import/export direct sequence import from NCBI, ENA. Supported Addgene records restriction analysis and digest simulation Golden Gate workflows and sequence domestication primer analysis and PCR simulation CRISPR target analysis document comparison and history Opentrons protocol generation SeqCraft exposes these capabilities through WebMCP as domain-level tools. So an agent can import pBR322 from NCBI go to beta‑lactamase find a cloning conflict stage a mutation check the resulting sequence design a PCR assay or work across many DNA documents. For sequence‑changing operations the agent does not edit the DNA quietly. SeqCraft stages the mutation against the document revision and sequence hash shows the biological consequences and waits for human approval. How we built it SeqCraft is written in TypeScript. Runs in the browser. The UI and WebMCP tools use the underlying domain logic so the agent works with the same documents, annotations, revisions and history as the user. Scientific operations are exposed as WebMCP tools instead of generic browser actions. For example the agent can ask SeqCraft to analyse restriction sites show a feature compare documents or stage a sequence edit directly. External sequence records from NCBI, ENA and supported Addgene sources go through the import pipeline as uploaded GenBank and FASTA files, preserving topology, annotations and provenance. The workspace also tracks sequence revisions and hashes so analysis results and mutation proposals stay tied to the state they were calculated from. Challenges we ran into The part was not registering WebMCP tools. It was making a stateful scientific application reliable enough for an external agent to operate. Some of the problems we ran into were: document state after mutations circular DNA coordinate edge cases reverse‑strand handling imported GenBank annotations behaving differently from built‑in demo data keeping UI state and WebMCP state synchronized inconsistent restriction‑enzyme behaviour across different workflows making mutation proposals safe across document revisions returning useful errors so an agent can recover instead of getting stuck Testing with real NCBI sequences exposed several bugs that would have been easy to miss with only hand‑made examples. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part I'm most proud of is that SeqCraft can handle a complete workflow without the user specifying which tools to call. In one test I gave the agent pBR322 and eGFP with a goal and a few constraints. The agent: evaluated cloning strategies rejected BsaI because it conflicted with the ampicillin‑resistance gene selected a BamHI–SalI strategy preserved the replication origin and ampicillin resistance disrupted tetracycline resistance for screening built and annotated the recombinant construct designed a colony‑PCR assay generated an Opentrons PCR protocol exported the final GenBank file and pointed out that fluorescence should not be assumed because the insert did not include a dedicated bacterial promoter or RBS Another part I am proud of is the human‑review boundary. The agent can. Prepare a sequence mutation but SeqCraft keeps the final sequence‑changing action under explicit human control. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that WebMCP becomes more useful when an application exposes its domain instead of mirroring its interface. For SeqCraft the useful operations are not: “click this button” or “open this panel” They are: “analyse this sequence” “show this feature” “compare these constructs” “stage this mutation” Once the application exposes those primitives the agent can choose and combine them based on the user’s goal. We also learned that real external data matters. Testing with GenBank records from NCBI revealed edge cases that clean demo sequences never exposed. What's next for SeqCraft The next step is making SeqCraft beyond the hackathon workflow. I want to improve: larger and more complex construct handling annotation and feature libraries more cloning and assembly strategies stronger primer and CRISPR analysis better interoperability, with existing biology formats and tools more lab‑automation workflows collaboration and reproducible project sharing I also want to keep improving the WebMCP surface so agents can handle longer scientific workflows while staying grounded in the exact document state they are operating on. The long‑term goal is simple: make SeqCraft a browser‑native molecular biology workspace that both humans and agents can use together. title: ClaimDesk | Agent-Native Lost Property Recovery
pitch: ClaimDesk turns airline lost-and-found into an agent-led investigation, using WebMCP to search, match, and verify lost property while keeping humans in control of recovery.
about_excerpt: ClaimDesk turns airline lost-and-found into an agent-led investigation, using WebMCP to search, match, and verify lost property while keeping humans in control of recovery. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The idea came from a very simple situation — you lose something while travelling. Suppose I leave my backpack somewhere after a flight. First question itself is confusing: did I leave it inside the aircraft or somewhere at the airport? Then I have to figure out whether to contact the airline or airport, find the correct lost-and-found page, fill forms and keep checking for updates. I thought, why can't I simply say: "I lost my black backpack on my Mumbai to Delhi flight. I'm not sure where I left it. Please help me find it." And let an AI agent handle the investigation. That's how ClaimDesk started. What I built ClaimDesk is a lost-property portal for AeroOne, a fictional airline I created for this project. It works like a normal website where passengers can report and track lost items. But using WebMCP, the same website also exposes its recovery capabilities as tools that an AI agent can use. In my demo, I tell ChatGPT that I lost a black backpack on flight AO-123. From that one request, the agent creates a claim, checks the flight, searches found inventory and compares possible matches. I intentionally added multiple similar backpacks. One is from the wrong flight, one is a partial match at the airport, and one is a strong match from the aircraft. So the agent actually has to investigate instead of simply getting one perfect search result. Ownership and human control Finding a black backpack doesn't automatically mean it belongs to me. For this, I added private ownership evidence. The correct backpack has an identifying detail which is not shown publicly and is also not given to the agent. ChatGPT has to ask me for something only the owner would know. I tell it there was a small red keychain inside , and ClaimDesk verifies this against the private record on the server. Even after ownership is verified, the agent cannot release the item automatically. It can prepare the recovery, but I have to explicitly approve the final release. This rule is enforced by ClaimDesk itself, not just through instructions given to the AI. How I used WebMCP I didn't want to build another chatbot inside the website. ClaimDesk remains a normal web application. I used WebMCP to expose capabilities like creating claims, searching inventory, comparing matches, verifying ownership and preparing recovery directly to the agent. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same application state and business logic. So when ChatGPT investigates a claim, I can see the same claim getting updated on the ClaimDesk website. Challenges and learnings One challenge was deciding what the agent should control and what the application should control. I finally kept it simple: the agent can decide how to investigate, but ClaimDesk decides what is allowed. Another challenge was making the demo realistic. Having only one perfect matching item was too easy, so I added wrong and partial matches and made ownership verification a separate step. The biggest thing I learned from this project is that an agent-friendly website doesn't need to become an AI chatbot. With WebMCP, the website can continue working normally for humans while also exposing meaningful capabilities to agents. With ClaimDesk, instead of understanding the complete lost-and-found process, the passenger can simply explain what happened and let the agent take it from there. about_excerpt:
Transformando desabafos em conexões humanas. O Real Me usa IA e WebMCP para ajudar pessoas a encontrar, com privacidade e consentimento, quem viveu experiências semelhantes.

 Inspiration 

 Many people go through loneliness, life changes, relationship problems, professional uncertainty, grief, anxiety, or other difficult experiences without having someone they feel comfortable talking to. Real Me • DeepMatch was created around a simple idea: sometimes the person who can understand you best is someone who has already lived through something similar. 

 Instead of building another social network based on followers, likes, popularity, or public exposure, Real Me focuses on experiences. Users can share what they are going through and the platform can help identify people with similar experiences, always putting privacy, safety, and consent at the center of the interaction. 

 What it does 

 Real Me • DeepMatch is a web platform designed to transform personal experiences into meaningful human connections. 

 A user can share an experience or situation. Artificial intelligence helps interpret its context and the DeepMatch system can identify compatible experiences from other users. 

 The goal is not to replace human relationships with AI. AI acts as a bridge between people. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we are extending Real Me so AI agents can discover structured tools provided by the platform and help users interact with Real Me through natural conversations. 

 How we built it 

 The existing Real Me application was created as a web application using technologies including React, Vite, Supabase, Netlify and AI-assisted development. 

 I am a non-technical founder building the project with the assistance of AI tools, particularly ChatGPT. AI has helped me transform product ideas into working software, understand technical concepts, debug problems and progressively build the platform. 

 Real Me existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the challenge, the project is being extended with WebMCP capabilities. This distinction is intentional and transparent: the existing platform provides the foundation, while the WebMCP integration is new work being developed specifically during the challenge period. 

 Our goal for the WebMCP implementation is to expose useful Real Me capabilities as structured tools that AI agents can discover and use with appropriate user consent. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges has been building a technology product without a traditional software engineering background. 

 Instead of treating that limitation as a reason not to build, I have been using AI as a development partner: learning each component, testing implementations, identifying errors and improving the product step by step. 

 The WebMCP Challenge introduces another challenge: moving from a traditional website interaction model toward an agent-native experience where AI can understand and use capabilities exposed directly by the application. 

 Privacy and consent are also fundamental challenges because Real Me deals with personal experiences. Agent actions must therefore be designed carefully so users remain in control of what is shared and what actions are performed. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Real Me evolved from an idea into a working web product. 

 The project already has the foundation for users to share experiences and for DeepMatch to explore compatibility between them. 

 Another accomplishment is demonstrating that AI-assisted development can allow a non-technical founder to move beyond prototypes and participate directly in building a real technology product. 

 For this challenge, our next milestone is making Real Me agent-accessible through WebMCP while maintaining the human-centered philosophy of the platform. 

 What we learned 

 Building Real Me has shown us that AI can do more than answer questions. It can help people create technology that previously required technical knowledge they did not have. 

 The WebMCP Challenge is also teaching us to think differently about websites. Instead of designing only for humans clicking interfaces, applications can expose structured capabilities that agents can understand and use. 

 For Real Me, this creates an interesting possibility: an AI conversation does not need to end with an AI response. With the user's permission, it can become the beginning of a meaningful human connection. 

 What's next for Real Me • DeepMatch 

 During the WebMCP Challenge, our immediate goal is to implement and test Real Me's WebMCP tools and demonstrate an end-to-end agent interaction. 

 After the challenge, we want to continue developing DeepMatch, improve privacy and safety mechanisms, expand the matching experience and explore how agent-native interfaces can make meaningful human connections easier to discover. 

 Our long-term vision is simple: 

 AI should not replace human connection. It should help people find it.

title: VerifyHere
pitch: Content Credentials make provenance conversational. With WebMCP, simply ask where content came from, how it was edited, and trace its journey from capture to creation and beyond.
about_excerpt:
Content Credentials make provenance conversational. With WebMCP, simply ask where content came from, how it was edited, and trace its journey from capture to creation and beyond.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 In the age of generative AI, seeing an image is no longer enough . 

 We increasingly want to know: 

 
 Where did this content come from? 
 Who created it? 
 Has it been edited? 
 Was AI involved? 
 Can I trace it back to the original? 
 

 Content Credentials , based on the C2PA standard, provide a powerful foundation for answering these questions by giving digital content a verifiable provenance history. 

 But there is still a usability gap. Understanding provenance often requires knowing where to look, opening specialized tools, and interpreting technical metadata. 

 So we asked: 

 
 What if understanding the history of content was as easy as asking a question? 
 

 That inspired VerifyHere — an exploration of making Content Credentials conversational with WebMCP . 

 What it does 

 VerifyHere lets you talk to the provenance of your content. 

 Instead of manually digging through metadata, you can simply ask: 

 
 "Where did this photo come from?" 

 "Has this image been edited?" 

 "What changed?" 

 "Take me back to the original." 
 

 VerifyHere uses WebMCP to connect these natural-language questions with the underlying provenance information. 

 The experience follows content across its journey: 

 Capture → Verify → Edit → Trace → Recover 

 For example, a photographer can capture an image with Content Credentials, inspect its provenance, edit it in Photoshop, and then explore how the edited asset relates to the original. 

 The goal isn't to tell people what to trust. It's to give them more context about how content came to be . 

 How we built it 

 We built VerifyHere as a web experience combining WebMCP with C2PA Content Credentials . 

 Our application exposes provenance capabilities as tools that an AI agent can discover and invoke through WebMCP. 

 This means the user doesn't need to understand C2PA manifests, cryptographic signatures, or metadata structures. 

 They can express their intent naturally: 

 
 "Tell me where this image came from." 
 

 WebMCP can then connect that request to the appropriate capability in VerifyHere, inspect the available provenance information, and return an understandable answer. 

 When an edited asset contains provenance linking it to an earlier asset, VerifyHere can also help users explore that chain and move back toward the original. 

 This turns Content Credentials from something users inspect into something they can interact with conversationally . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was provenance at capture . 

 We experimented with different mobile capture workflows and quickly discovered that real-world C2PA interoperability isn't always as straightforward as the specification makes it appear. 

 Credentials can behave differently across capture applications, exports, file transfers, editing workflows, and verification experiences. 

 That challenge actually reinforced the motivation behind VerifyHere: 

 
 Users shouldn't have to understand the implementation details of provenance technology to benefit from it. 
 

 We also thought carefully about the distinction between edited content and untrustworthy content . 

 An image being edited doesn't automatically make it misleading. Photography and creative work naturally involve editing. 

 Content provenance isn't about labeling content as "good" or "bad." It's about providing transparency and context , so people can understand what happened and make their own informed decisions. 

 What we learned 

 Our biggest learning was that Content Credentials become much more approachable when we stop thinking about provenance purely as metadata people need to inspect . 

 Instead, provenance can become context that agents can reason over . 

 WebMCP provides an exciting bridge between these two worlds. 

 The underlying provenance can remain structured, machine-readable, and cryptographically verifiable, while the user experience can become as simple as asking: 

 
 "Tell me the story behind this image." 
 

 We also learned how important durability and interoperability are. 

 Content travels everywhere — through editing tools, websites, social platforms, downloads, screenshots, and even into the physical world. Provenance becomes most useful when people can continue discovering that history wherever the content travels. 

 What's next for VerifyHere 

 We imagine VerifyHere going far beyond inspecting individual images. 

 The same conversational provenance experience could extend to: 

 
 Creative libraries 
 Published media 
 Video 
 AI-generated and AI-edited content 
 Social content 
 Physical and printed media 
 

 Imagine asking: 

 
 "Which photos in my library are original camera captures?" 
 

 or: 

 
 "Show me everything derived from this original." 
 

 or simply: 

 
 "Can I learn more about where this came from?" 
 

 Agents could help creators trace their work, understand how it has changed, discover missing provenance, find originals, and receive attribution as their content travels across the internet. 

 Our vision is simple: provenance shouldn't be something you have to hunt for. It should be as easy as asking.

about_excerpt:
The link management platform where AI agents handle geo-targeting, 
A/B testing, and bot protection — so marketers just describe what 
they want and get a production-ready tracking link in seconds.

 Link Creator: Simple and fast interface to generate new short links with custom routing parameters.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Content creators, influencers, and small business owners spend hundreds of dollars 
monthly on tools like ClickMagick, Voluum, and Linktree — just to manage links and 
track who clicks them. We wanted to build one platform that replaces all of them, 
and takes it a step further by letting AI agents do the complex marketing setup work 
on behalf of the user. 

 What it does 

 Smart Link is a link management and bio page platform with full WebMCP agent support. 

 Users can create short links, build bio landing pages, track real-time analytics 
by country and device, run A/B tests to find the best-performing URL, and protect 
their links from bot traffic automatically. 

 What makes Smart Link unique is its agent-native design. When opened in ChatGPT's 
in-app browser, the platform exposes three WebMCP tools that AI agents can use: 

 
 create_marketing_link: Creates a fully-configured tracking link in one step — 
with geo-targeting rules (route Saudi users to an Arabic page, French users to 
a French page), device routing (mobile vs desktop), UTM tracking parameters, 
A/B testing between multiple URLs, and bot protection. A task that would normally 
take a marketer 15 minutes across multiple tools now takes one sentence. 
 get_link_analytics: Retrieves total clicks, human vs bot breakdown, top countries, 
device types, and A/B test results for any link by short code. 
 shorten_url: Instantly shortens any URL without requiring an account. 
 

 How we built it 

 The platform is built with a full-stack architecture using React, Tailwind CSS, 
and Vite on the frontend, deployed on Vercel. The backend runs on Node.js with 
Express.js, MongoDB Atlas for persistence, and Redis for caching and rate limiting, 
deployed on Fly.io. We use Brevo for email campaigns and Lemon Squeezy for 
subscription billing. 

 For WebMCP, we registered the three agent tools directly in the HTML using 
document.modelContext.registerTool(). We built a dedicated public API endpoint 
that AI agents call to create links with full marketing configuration. When a 
logged-in user opens the site in ChatGPT's browser, their session token is read 
automatically so created links appear in their personal dashboard. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest technical challenge was achieving sub-150ms redirect speeds while 
simultaneously recording click analytics and running bot detection in real time. 
We solved this by caching redirect targets in Redis and processing analytics 
asynchronously in the background. 

 For WebMCP, the challenge was designing a public API that exposes advanced features 
like geo-targeting and A/B testing to AI agents, while preventing abuse through 
strict rate limiting and Google Safe Browsing URL safety checks on every request. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 Smart Link is a live production application with 41 registered users and over 
1,800 tracked clicks — built and running before this hackathon. We are proud of 
the sub-150ms redirect performance and being one of the first link management 
platforms to expose agent-native WebMCP tools, allowing marketers to set up 
complex geo-targeted, bot-protected campaigns through a single natural language 
conversation. 

 What we learned 

 We learned how to design APIs that serve both humans and AI agents — with clear 
parameter descriptions, meaningful error messages, and structured responses that 
agents can reason about. We also deepened our understanding of Redis caching 
strategies for high-traffic systems. 

 What's next for Smart Link 

 We plan to add create_bio_page and run_ab_test as new WebMCP tools, letting agents 
build full landing pages and launch experiments without touching the UI. We also 
plan to add AI-powered UTM suggestions and integrate Facebook Pixel and Google Tag 
Manager firing directly through the agent tools.

title: First Look
pitch: Turn ChatGPT research into qualified customer conversations with WebMCP tools that expose accurate information, useful assets, site checks, and the next action on one shared page.
about_excerpt: Turn ChatGPT research into qualified customer conversations with WebMCP tools that expose accurate information, useful assets, site checks, and the next action on one shared page. Like Comment Story Updates Assets via WEBMCP Inspiration More customers now begin their research in ChatGPT. On a conventional website, the agent often has to scrape the interface, interpret incomplete context, and guess what actions are available. When the customer reaches the business, they may have to start the conversation again. WebMCP offers a better model: the website can expose accurate information, useful assets, and explicit actions directly to the agent. Commerce demos show how an agent can find a product and complete checkout. This project explores the service-business journey, where the next step often requires context, evidence, qualification, and human judgment rather than simply adding an item to a cart. What it does This page creates one shared workspace for a visitor and their browser agent. Together, they can: Understand what the page offers and what it does not claim Browse real public work without invented clients or case studies Open and explain a published brief on the same screen Run a limited analysis of a public URL Review its title, description, heading, declared tools, llms.txt , and robots.txt Fill a question using the findings Submit that question for human review The page exposes twelve WebMCP tools. Eleven are imperative JavaScript tools, and ask_rafalai is a declarative form tool with toolautosubmit . The submission is real, but nothing is automatically answered or acted upon. A person reviews every message. Why WebMCP WebMCP lets the website define its capabilities instead of forcing the agent to infer them from the DOM. That produces a better customer experience because the person and the agent work with the same information, assets, actions, and visible state. The conversation can move forward instead of restarting when the customer leaves ChatGPT and reaches the business. This page is one example, not the final product. A store could expose products, inventory, recommendations, and checkout. An agency could expose services, briefs, qualification, audits, and intake. Other businesses can expose the actions that match how they actually serve customers. The commercial opportunity is straightforward: better answers, less friction, more qualified conversations, and more customers. How we built it Eleven tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool in JavaScript. The Ask form provides the twelfth tool declaratively using toolname , toolparamdescription , and toolautosubmit . The same underlying functions power both agent calls and the visible Run buttons, so the experience remains demonstrable in browsers without WebMCP enabled. The URL analysis calls GET /api/look , a Cloudflare Pages Function that fetches public HTML, /robots.txt , and /llms.txt . It rejects localhost, private networks, credentialed URLs, and unsafe redirects. It does not use paid ranking APIs. The project is hosted on Cloudflare and released in a public MIT-licensed repository. Challenges The central design challenge was creating a meaningful WebMCP experience that was not another shopping-cart demonstration. We also needed to: Keep agent actions visible to the person Separate drafting from submitting Preserve human review after submission Safely accept user-provided public URLs Avoid duplicate imperative and declarative tool registrations Demonstrate a service-business journey without inventing clients or results What we learned The difficult part of WebMCP is not registering a function. It is deciding which actions should exist, describing them clearly, and establishing the correct boundaries. WebMCP is also different from search optimization. Search helps information get discovered. WebMCP helps an agent use a website accurately once it arrives. Agent-ready websites can become a new customer-acquisition interface: a place where AI systems present reliable information, provide the right assets, and perform useful actions while people remain responsible for the work.
