title: UCE Evidence Lens
pitch: People and AI agents, alone or together, inspect the same public evidence - verifying integrity, chronology, assertions, and file matches with no work uploaded and creators keep control.
about_excerpt: People and AI agents, alone or together, inspect the same public evidence - verifying integrity, chronology, assertions, and file matches with no work uploaded and creators keep control. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Seven typed, read-only WebMCP tools discovered directly from the live production site. An agent invokes verify_uce_record and receives a structured, source-bound result—without DOM scraping. Browser checks verify schema, record identity, ES256 signature, and public transaction chronology. Chronology separates claimed dates, recorded system events, and independently retrieved public evidence. Authorship, identity, AI-use, and rights remain recorded assertions—not verified facts. A public UCE record binds the asset to its manifest hash, timestamps, source, and recorded authorship context. The verifier is itself evidenced: the production v1.0.0 site release has its own independently checkable UCE record. Overview A shared browser verifier where people and AI agents inspect the same cryptographic evidence, chronology, rights assertions, and local-file match. Problem Creators, agencies, reviewers, counsel, and journalists increasingly receive public evidence records that combine cryptographic facts with human claims. Understanding one record can require moving among a verification page, machine-readable JSON, a signature, an Arweave transaction, and the original local file. A person can miss a distinction; a general-purpose agent scraping the visible page can do worse by promoting a publisher statement or authorship claim into a verified fact. The difficult part is not merely retrieving data. It is preserving evidentiary boundaries: what this browser independently checked, what the publisher reported, what the claimant asserted, what is temporarily retryable, and what the public format does not yet support. Solution UCE Evidence Lens is a static, browser-first public record inspector. A person can load a CbyUCE verification URL, a direct Arweave manifest, pasted public JSON, or the bundled demonstration. The browser validates the record, checks its public ES256 signature, binds chronology to public Arweave block metadata, separates recorded assertions from verified results, and can compare a user-selected file by locally calculated SHA-256. The same page exposes seven read-only WebMCP tools. An agent can load, summarize, verify, inspect chronology, list assertions, inspect rights declarations, and report an already-selected local file comparison through structured operations rather than guessing from the interface. The human sees the same underlying state and wording. Why This Matters Evidence review is a strong fit for WebMCP because the workflow is structured, multi-step, and precision sensitive. Without page-defined tools, an agent has to infer controls and semantics from layout, possibly leaving out technical details or overstating a legal conclusion. With WebMCP, the site defines exactly which evidence operations are available and returns typed, source-bound results. For a reviewer, the experience changes from manually correlating several technical sources to asking one focused question while retaining a visible and easily understood inspectable record. For an agency or production team, the demonstration also shows a credible market path: a work can originate in the published Copyright by UCE Figma plugin ( the Figma plugin is now available for use), become a public UCE record, and then be inspected by both a person and an agent before delivery. This does not turn evidence into a legal verdict. It makes the evidence easier to inspect without erasing its limits. How We Used AI The product is agent-enabled without placing a model inside the trust boundary. Deterministic browser functions perform parsing, cryptography, chronology retrieval, and digest comparison. WebMCP lets an AI agent select and compose those operations, explain the structured results, and guide a person through the same evidence the interface displays. The key collaboration is intentional: the agent can inspect an already-selected digest but cannot open a file picker or access file bytes. The person controls the sensitive local input; the agent works with the resulting evidence state. How We Used Codex Codex helped scope the public/private boundary, scaffolded the TypeScript application, implemented and reviewed the seven WebMCP tools, debugged browser discovery and CORS, hardened trust and concurrency boundaries, built regression tests, ran security and dependency audits, tested responsive and live-browser behavior, prepared Cloudflare deployment, and helped me tighten the judge-facing language because I can get a bit wordy and go off on tangents...(see what I mean...). The development process repeatedly challenged optimistic claims. For example, canonical manifest recomputation remains explicitly unsupported because the public format does not define the exact hash construction. Publisher flags are recorded rather than substituted for browser checks. The result is a narrower but more defensible product. As the Copyright by UCE product grows, so will UCE Evidence Lens as an Open-Source resource helping creatives to secure their creativity. The Copyright by UCE Canva App plugin is in design review now having passed functional and technical review and the Pro Tools and Ableton plugin and extension respectively are being finalized over the next few weeks. The UCE Evidence Lens is poised to be a very useful tool for creatives and the agencies and organizations that serve them. Key Features Seven top-level, imperative WebMCP tools with strict JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint: true . Human/agent parity through shared controller operations and shared result wording. Public ES256 compact-JWS verification against a reviewed, application-owned P-256 key registry. Direct Arweave transaction, block, height, timestamp, and confirmation inspection. Consumer-oriented result states that distinguish verified, mismatch, retryable, reported, and unsupported outcomes. Recorded authorship, identity, originality, AI-use, and rights values clearly separated from verified facts. Local SHA-256 comparison without uploading the file or exposing its bytes to the agent. Bundled demo, direct Arweave, CbyUCE JSON, and pasted-JSON resilience paths. Static Cloudflare deployment with no account, backend, analytics, database, runtime secret, or production dependency. Architecture UCE Evidence Lens is a static Vite and TypeScript single-page application. Pure modules parse and verify records; a memory-only controller binds each result to its source and manifest hash; a semantic DOM renderer and the WebMCP adapter call the same controller operations. Browser Web Crypto provides SHA-256 and ECDSA P-256. WebMCP tools register before asynchronous demo loading and confirm same-origin discovery through document.modelContext.getTools() where available. Production headers opt the page into an origin-keyed agent cluster and allow same-origin tools. Remote access is restricted to validated HTTPS CbyUCE and Arweave routes, with byte, depth, and timeout limits. There are no production npm dependencies and no server function, Worker, proxy, database, or persistent application storage. Testing Instructions Open https://uceevidencelens.com/ in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the page reports: “7 read-only AI-agent tools registered and discoverable.” The bundled public UCE record loads automatically. Ask the agent to call verify_uce_record and summarize verified checks separately from recorded assertions. The result should begin with “No integrity problems found.” Ask the agent to call inspect_uce_chronology . Confirm it distinguishes the claimed creation date, system events, and the independently retrieved Arweave block. For the real Figma-origin example, load https://cbyuce.com/verify/cc7680c80721f69295dab10bb547065fd74c14de420d915df0da051ee5e0727a with load_uce_public_record , then repeat the verification and chronology calls. Optional local comparison: choose the matching public PNG in the normal interface. The browser displays its SHA-256 result; compare_local_file_to_uce_record can report that result but cannot access the file bytes or trigger selection. No login or credentials are required. If live retrieval is temporarily unavailable, reload the bundled demo or use the direct Arweave manifest URL shown in the public record. Known Limitations Independent canonical-manifest recomputation is unsupported until CbyUCE publishes a reproducible hash profile with test vectors. Direct chronology uses a public Arweave gateway rather than a trustless light client; pending or unreachable results are retryable, not mismatches. The trusted platform key registry requires a reviewed application release for rotation or revocation. Only UCE manifest schema 1.0.0, SHA-256 file digests, and ES256/P-256 compact JWS are s

title: Pitch The AI
pitch: A live Shark Tank-style pitch arena where four AI investors challenge founders in real time using WebMCP to control the experience.
about_excerpt: A live Shark Tank-style pitch arena where four AI investors challenge founders in real time using WebMCP to control the experience. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Pitch The AI actually started long before this challenge. About a year and a half ago, I became obsessed with the idea of humans and multiple AI agents working together. I built my own agents, experimented with multi-agent collaboration, and quickly learned that simply putting a bunch of autonomous agents together creates chaos. That led me to build governance software called Promethios: shared state, roles, permissions, accountability, provenance, workspaces, and governance for humans and AI working together. At one point, I built Pitch The AI (previously called Pitch Arena) as a side experience inside that world. The idea was simple and a little ridiculous: let people challenge agents in a Shark Tank-style pitch competition, compete against each other, and share the results. The system used my own agents I built and the coordination was very difficult. I love Shark Tank. I love personalities, competition, theater, and marketing, so it was one of those projects that just fit me. But my thinking about AI changed. Once OpenClaw came out, I stopped building my own agents. I wanted build a way for people to bring the AI they already use wherever they go on the web to make their AI portable. That led to months of experimenting with provider sessions, routing, companion apps, MCP servers, browser agents, desktop agents, and ways of letting different AIs participate in the same environment using MCP tools running through infrastructure I built. Then WebMCP arrived. I had thought before about putting the tools directly into the platforms I was building, but I had never really taken the plunge. When this challenge started, I realized I could bring Pitch The AI back but this time, the website itself could expose the game to a visiting AI. I also kept thinking about something I hear constantly: AI can be a great cheerleader. Sometimes too great. One AI telling you your idea is amazing isn't always very useful. So what happens if, instead, you put your idea in front of four different AI personalities whose job is to scrutinize it, challenge your assumptions, remember what you said, and make you defend your thinking under pressure? That became Pitch The AI. What it does Pitch The AI is essentially Shark Tank with AI judges. A founder enters the arena, sets an ask, chooses a difficulty level, optionally provides evidence and a founder photo the agent or agents can see, and pitches an idea to four AI investors with different personalities and priorities. Then the room comes alive. The AI can: question the founder inspect submitted evidence react to answers remember what the founder previously said change each investor's interest change the mood of the room make offers counteroffer trigger bidding wars reject a deal walk an investor out pause or advance parts of the experience deliver a final verdict The human remains part of the loop. The founder answers questions, supplies evidence, accepts or rejects offers, and influences what happens next. The use case underneath all of the theater is pitch practice, presentation practice, and pressure-testing your ideas. This is something I have struggled with myself. Explaining an idea clearly when you have unlimited time is easy. Explaining it when someone challenges your assumptions, asks for numbers, remembers what you said two minutes ago, and forces you to defend yourself is very different. Pitch The AI gives people a fun place to practice communicating clearly, quickly, and articulately under pressure while also finding the weak spots in an idea. How we built it Through WebMCP, the AI can participate in the application itself. Pitch The AI exposes semantic actions and room state that lets a visiting agent understand what is happening and take authorized actions inside the game. The webpage remains the shared environment and turns those actions into the experience the human sees: (a judge monitors descend, interest changes, music reacts, questions appear, evidence is reviewed, investors leave, offers arrive, and the game advances). I also used the project to experiment with another idea I have been working on for a while: allowing users to choose their provider. I have been building a separate private-beta browser experience, where users can connect the AI they already use and bring it into agent-ready websites. That browser contains WebMCP experiences including shared human/AI workspaces where people can work together, bring their preferred agents, connect third-party services, and audit what happened through the governance infrastructure I have been developing in Promethios. The important part for me is that users are not limited to one model provider or one kind of agent. They can bring API-based agents, browser sessions they already use, desktop agents, or CLI-based agents into the same environment. For this challenge, I connected Pitch The AI to that browser as well. Then I took the experiment one step further: instead of having one visiting AI perform all four investor personalities, I allowed different configured AI sessions to occupy different investor seats in the same Pitch The AI room. In one test, the four judges were powered independently by a ChatGPT browser session, Hermes running on a free model, a Grok browser session, and a Claude browser session. All four were participating in the same WebMCP-enabled website and shared room. That means the application does not have to be designed around one specific AI provider. The website exposes its tools, and the user can choose which AI participates. Challenges we ran into The difficult part was making the AI a reliable participant in a shared live experience. The room has to know things like: whose turn it is which question is waiting for a human answer which actions belong to the AI which actions require the human what evidence actually exists what each investor remembers whether an offer was really made whether the founder actually accepted it whether an investor is still in the room, etc I learned quickly that a convincing multi-agent experience needs authoritative application state and clear boundaries. We also had some entertaining failures during development. At one point founder responses were not making it back to the visiting agent, so the judges interpreted my silence as avoiding their questions and began walking out of my own demo. Oddly enough, that failure was also proof that the state mattered. The judges weren't simply generating disconnected dialogue. They were reacting to what they believed had actually happened in the room. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that Pitch The AI feels like a game rather than a WebMCP demonstration. The theatrics are fun, but many of them are also demonstrations of different kinds of agent interaction with a live web application. The result is something where neither the human nor the AI completely controls what happens next. I'm also proud that I was able to take an application I originally built around my own agents and turn it into an environment that other agents can enter. I also feel like it can be educational and entertaining for humans to use at the same time. That represents a much bigger change in how I think about building for AI. The funny thing is that I whipped a lot of this together at the last minute and have 100 more ideas to improve the game flow. I also realize, with webMCP, games might be one of the first real applications. They don't require the public to understand tooling to play a game. What we learned I'm increasingly interested in building the places where agents and humans can meet. WebMCP makes that idea much more practical because the intelligence can belong to the agent while the website creates the environment, tools, rules, permissions, and shared state. But while building this, I started thinking about another possibility. What if WebMCP doesn't only let an agent use an application? What if an application deliberately exposes tools that let an agent extend it for the user? Imagine visiting a WebMCP-enabled application and asking your AI: "I wish this page could do this..." Instead of waiting for the application developer to build that feature for everyone, the site could expose governed extension points that allow the user's agent to create a new workflow, interface, visualization, automation, or other capability on top of the existing application. The next time that user visits, their version of the application could now have a capability that didn't exist before something created specifically around how they wanted to use it. The site owner sets the rules. The agent isn't randomly rewriting someone else's application. title: Glyph Motion Studio for WebMCP
pitch: Direct motion in natural language. Keep every vector, keyframe, preview, and final decision under your control.
about_excerpt: Direct motion in natural language. Keep every vector, keyframe, preview, and final decision under your control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does## Overview Glyph Motion Studio is a visual GSAP editor where users direct vector composition and animation in natural language through their own WebMCP-compatible browser agents. Instead of generating arbitrary JavaScript or raw SVG, the agent works through ten typed site tools that can inspect semantic animation targets, construct scenes from bounded vector primitives, create and revise timelines, stage previews, apply approved changes, undo edits, switch scenes, and save projects locally. Glyph keeps the user in control throughout the workflow. Composition and timeline changes first appear as visible previews. Every operation is revision-checked, validated against strict schemas, reflected in the canvas and timeline, and recorded in the Agent Activity panel. The user decides whether to apply, discard, edit, undo, or save the result. The primary demonstration starts from a blank canvas. A browser agent constructs a complete radar interface from vector primitives, including concentric rings, crosshairs, a centre-pivoted sweep arm, grouped contacts, warning text, and a status indicator. It then creates and iteratively refines a coordinated detection animation. Additional showcases include a 17-step Glyph brand ident and a 24-step orbital-deployment sequence coordinating four independent SVG assets. These examples demonstrate how WebMCP lets an agent handle complex, repetitive timeline work while Glyph remains the trusted visual editor and the human remains the creative director. title: Sigmora Live Relay
pitch: Stay live while an agent builds, reviews, and verifies the launch moment with you.
about_excerpt: Stay live while an agent builds, reviews, and verifies the launch moment with you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Sigmora Live Relay Inspiration Going live is when creators most need cross-platform promotion—and when they can least afford to leave the stream to edit, rewrite, upload, and check posts. Sigmora Live Relay turns one selected live event into a reviewable 12-second vertical campaign on a shared release board. What it does The page exposes eight narrow WebMCP tools. An agent reads the visible brand and destination context, finds or declares the source live event, drafts the relay, polls generation, revises copy, queues exact destination accounts, releases the human-approved revision, and checks each destination independently. Every tool call updates the same board the creator sees. The consequential checkpoint remains human. Queue items are bound to exact account IDs and one immutable revision. The creator reviews those items in the UI and approves them there; approval is deliberately not exposed as a tool. Any revision invalidates the receipt. Release requires that receipt plus an idempotency key, and partial failure can never be reported as total success. Why WebMCP This is a strong WebMCP fit because the useful context and collaboration live on the open page: current creative state, selected destinations, approval, and receipts. Without WebMCP, an agent must infer buttons and duplicate state. With WebMCP, it uses an explicit contract while the person keeps visual control. People and agents can now share one live workspace: the agent handles multi-step coordination while the creator remains present with the audience and retains authority over publication. How we built it The challenge implementation is framework-free TypeScript built around document.modelContext.registerTool(...), closed JSON Schemas, typed result envelopes, an observable shared controller, page-scoped teardown, a strict HTTP adapter, and a deterministic local provider. The normal manual interface continues to work when WebMCP is absent. The eight tools cover context, source discovery, drafting, job polling, revision, exact destination queuing, approved release, and independent status verification. Unit and end-to-end tests exercise schemas, lifecycle cleanup, revision invalidation, idempotency, partial failure, and the manual fallback. Challenges The hardest design problem was preserving human authority without making the agent workflow brittle. We solved it with an immutable approval receipt bound to an exact revision and destination set, plus clear state transitions visible to both sides. Another challenge was truthful partial failure: each destination receives an independent receipt, so a mixed outcome stays mixed. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it is not simply a hidden automation API. The shared page should remain the source of truth, and the tool contract should expose exactly the capabilities that benefit from agent reasoning while keeping consequential consent visible and human. What's next The public reference is intentionally simulated and says so throughout the UI and tool results. Next we would connect the strict provider adapter to real publishing APIs, preserving the same approval, idempotency, readback, and partial-failure guarantees. title: LaxFinder
pitch: AI agents can search 1,331 college lacrosse programs through LaxFinder’s WebMCP tools—while the same map stays visible, synchronized, and under the student’s control.
about_excerpt: AI agents can search 1,331 college lacrosse programs through LaxFinder’s WebMCP tools—while the same map stays visible, synchronized, and under the student’s control. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP in action: ChatGPT interprets the request, LaxFinder searches its live data, and the student stays in control. LaxFinder Advisor connects natural conversation with 1,331 college lacrosse programs through ChatGPT and a live map. The problem isn’t finding information—it’s seeing the opportunities hidden across disconnected websites, lists, and searches Explore programs on one live map, then open school details to compare academics, admissions, athletics, and possible fit. Opportunity begins with discovery: ask naturally, discover real programs, explore your options, and decide your own path. Inspiration College lacrosse opportunities are scattered across NCAA, NAIA, NJCAA, MCLA, WCLA, and other pathways. I built LaxFinder to bring those opportunities together in a map-first experience where student-athletes and families can explore more than 1,300 programs. But finding the data is only part of the problem. Students increasingly use AI to help them think through decisions. I wanted to explore a different model: instead of building another chatbot that tries to know everything about college lacrosse, what if a student's AI assistant could work directly with the specialized application that already has the data, filters, map, and school details? WebMCP made that possible. What LaxFinder does with WebMCP LaxFinder exposes two deliberately narrow, read-only WebMCP tools: search_lacrosse_programs searches LaxFinder's structured program data and synchronizes the same filters, result count, markers, and map the student sees. get_program_details retrieves a specific program by stable program ID and opens LaxFinder's existing visible program-details interface. A student can ask a compatible AI assistant in everyday language: Show me women's lacrosse programs in Colorado with Health Sciences. Keep all divisions open. The agent interprets the request. LaxFinder performs the authoritative search. In the judge-accessible full hosted dataset, that request returns 7 programs , and the visible LaxFinder filters, count, and map update to match. The student can then continue exploring the live application, click map markers, inspect school details, or refine the search conversationally. The agent interprets. LaxFinder searches. The student decides. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Traditional browser automation forces an agent to infer how a site's UI works, manipulate controls, and reconstruct state from what it can see. That is especially fragile in a map-first application with interdependent filters, clusters, result counts, and program-detail views. WebMCP lets LaxFinder explicitly expose the actions an agent is allowed to take and connect those actions to the same application state the human sees. That creates a better division of responsibility: the AI assistant handles natural-language interpretation; LaxFinder remains the source of truth for program data and search behavior; the human remains inside the visible map experience and retains control of the decision. The result is not an invisible agent-only answer. It is a shared human + agent interaction with one synchronized application state. What people and agents can now do together Before this WebMCP extension, a student could either use LaxFinder manually or ask a general-purpose AI about college options separately. Those were disconnected experiences. With WebMCP, the student can express a search conversationally and have the agent call LaxFinder's specialized tools directly. The resulting filters, count, markers, map position, and program details become visible in LaxFinder, where the student can continue exploring manually. That makes AI useful without asking it to replace the application or make the decision. What was added during the WebMCP Challenge LaxFinder existed before the challenge as a map-first college lacrosse discovery application. The challenge work began after the Submission Period opened on August 25, 2026 and meaningfully extended the existing product with WebMCP. The challenge extension added: imperative WebMCP registration with document.modelContext.registerTool ; search_lacrosse_programs ; get_program_details ; a narrow bridge from tool calls into LaxFinder's existing visible filter/map/detail state; feature detection for browsers without WebMCP; strict schemas and runtime validation; bounded search results and stable program IDs; unsupported-criteria handling rather than guessing; read-only behavior and output sanitization; deterministic contract tests for registration, search, detail lookup, invalid inputs, zero/multiple results, sanitization, and visible UI synchronization; a separate frozen judge-accessible WebMCP deployment and public open-source reference repository. The repository's CHALLENGE_BUILD.md explicitly separates pre-existing LaxFinder functionality from work added for this challenge and records the validated challenge build. How it was implemented The WebMCP layer is implemented in the browser using document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool calls operate on data already loaded by LaxFinder and invoke the application's existing search and UI behavior. A successful search_lacrosse_programs call updates the visible filters, matching-program count, map markers, and map view before returning a structured response. get_program_details accepts an exact stable program ID, opens the corresponding visible detail panel, and returns sanitized program and available admissions fields. Neither tool follows external links or performs a mutation. The public repository contains the complete WebMCP/application implementation plus a small representative fixture dataset for local development and deterministic testing. The judge-accessible hosted challenge deployment uses LaxFinder's separately maintained full 1,331-program runtime dataset. No OpenAI API key is required for the WebMCP interaction. The compatible AI assistant provides conversational reasoning; LaxFinder provides the specialized tools and authoritative application state. Validation The end-to-end consumer workflow was validated through ChatGPT Work / Cloud Browser. ChatGPT discovered both LaxFinder WebMCP tools, invoked search_lacrosse_programs for women + Colorado + Health Sciences, received 7 structured matches from the full hosted dataset, and the visible LaxFinder filters, result count, and map synchronized to those results. ChatGPT then used get_program_details for Colorado Mesa University and LaxFinder opened the existing visible school details interface. That demonstrated the complete interaction: AI conversation → WebMCP tool discovery → authoritative LaxFinder search → structured response → synchronized visible human interface. Challenges and design decisions One of the most important decisions was defining what the AI should not do. If a student asks for a criterion LaxFinder does not authoritatively expose, the system should not silently substitute a proxy or invent an answer. Unsupported criteria are surfaced as limitations instead. Another challenge was preserving human visibility. Returning structured data only to the agent would have been simpler, but it would split the AI interaction from the trusted Finder experience. The WebMCP bridge instead keeps the existing map, filters, counts, and details synchronized with agent actions. What I learned WebMCP changed how I think about AI integration. LaxFinder does not need to recreate a general-purpose AI assistant. It can concentrate on what it uniquely provides: structured college lacrosse opportunity information and reliable, bounded tools for interacting with that information. Compatible AI assistants can provide the conversation and reasoning. That separation creates a more trustworthy pattern for agent-native applications: specialized sites expose authoritative capabilities, agents interpret user intent, and people stay in control of the visible experience. What's next The next direction is not to give agents broader control for its own sake. It is to expose additional useful LaxFinder capabilities only when they can remain authoritative, bounded, and visible to the student. Longer term, the same pattern could support richer opportunity information supplied and maintained by college programs themselves, allowing compatible agents to help student-athletes discover opportunities without requiring the AI to infer them from the open web. The goal remains simple: make better opportunity information easier for students and families to discover, understand, and act on. title: blockchain-agent-treasury
pitch: Agents prepare exact x402 payment terms across EVM, Solana, and Gno via WebMCP — humans keep custody and give the final wallet approval. Mainnets stay locked.
about_excerpt: Agents prepare exact x402 payment terms across EVM, Solana, and Gno via WebMCP — humans keep custody and give the final wallet approval. Mainnets stay locked. Like Comment Story Updates demo What's next for blockchain-agent-treasury Inspiration AI agents can move quickly, but payments should not require giving an agent a private key or asking it to guess through wallet UI. We built x402 Agent Treasury around a safer division of labor: the agent handles discovery and exact preparation, while the person keeps custody and makes the final signing decision. What it does The deployed app exposes seven narrow WebMCP tools directly from the page. An agent can: list five configured EVM, Solana, and Gno payment rails distinguish testnet-ready paths from independently locked mainnets prepare wallet-bound, short-lived x402 terms inspect the live Gno Pearl gateway and scheduled indexer search canonical Pearl activity open the matching human review screen retrieve one exact durable payment receipt The consequential boundary stays visible. Preparation never signs or settles. The wallet review shows network, asset, amount, recipient, payer, resource, and expiry before a person approves. How we built it The application uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript on Vercel, with Neon PostgreSQL as the authoritative challenge, payment, and audit store. The top-level page registers imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool has a strict JSON Schema, bounded output, cancellation support, and read-only or state-changing annotations. The chain-neutral payment layer supports Base Sepolia USDC through EIP-1193 and EIP-712/EIP-3009, Solana Devnet USDC through Wallet Standard and a sponsored v0 transaction, and Gno Pearl WUGNOT through Adena and TM2 RPC. Ethereum, Solana, and Gno mainnet paths remain independently fail-closed. Server-issued challenge IDs, payment IDs, expected payer, recipient, amount, asset, resource hash, expiry, and unsigned payload fingerprints are bound together. The server rechecks the terms immediately before signing and prevents replay or cross-challenge substitution. Chrome support is delivered as a progressive enhancement with explicit origin isolation and a same-origin WebMCP permissions policy. The same deployed page also works in ChatGPT's in-app browser. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was preserving human authority without reducing WebMCP to a read-only demo. The agent needed enough power to prepare useful work, but not enough power to silently change recipients, tokens, networks, or settlement endpoints. Multichain signing also differs significantly. EVM uses typed authorization, Solana uses a short-lived blockhash and signed v0 message, and Gno uses Adena-encoded transactions. We kept one agent-facing workflow while retaining chain-specific verification. Chrome's experimental implementation additionally requires the testing flag and an origin-isolated document. We added explicit Origin-Agent-Cluster and tools permissions headers and verified that all seven registrations complete in a fresh Chrome tab. Accomplishments that we're proud of a working public WebMCP deployment with seven registered tools one coherent human-agent handoff across three chain families independently locked mainnet gates durable PostgreSQL challenge and receipt records tamper, replay, policy, settlement, and WebMCP safety coverage 119 automated tests passing on the submission build What we learned Agent-native interfaces are strongest when tools expose intent and constraints, not when they merely automate clicks. For sensitive actions, a prepared object shared by the agent, server, UI, and wallet is a better collaboration primitive than an invisible autonomous action. What's next We plan to add continuously indexed Gno activity, complete recorded real-wallet testnet acceptance on every rail, and expand the same human-approved pattern to paid compute and storage workflows. title: Cliffcheck
pitch: A raise can leave you poorer from benefit cliffs. CliffCheck maps that cliff across 16 US states, and now exposes WebMCP tools so an in-browser agent can answer "should I take this promotion?"
about_excerpt: A raise can leave you poorer from benefit cliffs. CliffCheck maps that cliff across 16 US states, and now exposes WebMCP tools so an in-browser agent can answer "should I take this promotion?" Like Comment Story Updates Hero Impact and action Inspiration A raise should never leave you poorer. But for millions of US households that gethelp with food, health coverage, rent, or childcare, it happens all the time. Earn a few hundred dollars more and a benefit worth thousands can cut off. The programs are run by different agencies and none of them coordinate, so the loss is invisible until the paycheck lands. CliffCheck started as an entry in a community hackathon built around one theme: escape the permanent underclass. The benefits cliff is one of the traps that keeps people stuck, because the rational move looks like turning down a raise. That first version drew the cliff for a single state and placed third. Since then it has become a live tool with a benefit-rule engine covering 16 states, and it found an audience through people sharing their own cliff online. The WebMCP Challenge added a new angle. When someone asks an AI assistant whether to take a promotion, the assistant guesses. It has no real model of how benefits phase out as income rises. I wanted it to call the actual engine instead. What it does You enter your state, household size, current income, and which benefits you receive. CliffCheck draws your real income across every wage level from $0 to $200,000 and marks every point where earning more would leave you with less. It shows your safe target: the wage where a raise finally puts you ahead. It also writes a short, copy-paste brief you can take into a conversation with your manager. All of it runs in your browser. No account, no upload, nothing saved. Your financial details never leave your device. With WebMCP, an in-browser agent gets that same engine as four tools it can call: calculate_cliff — your real income before and after a raise, and the change get_cliff_curve — the full curve, plus the steepest drop and what causes it get_safe_exit — the lowest wage that clears your current income for good list_supported_states — the 16 states with vetted rules How the number works Your real income is not just your wage. It is your wage, plus the cash value of every benefit you receive, minus every tax you owe: real income = wage + benefits − taxes CliffCheck works that out at every wage level and draws the line. Most of the time the line goes up: earn more, keep more. A benefits cliff is where the line goes down instead. You earned more and ended up with less, because what you lost in benefits was worth more than the raise. I model each benefit as a gradual phase-out rather than a hard on/off switch, which is closer to how they actually work, so the chart shows a slope you can see coming instead of a single vertical drop. Here is the built-in example. An Ohio family of four, one earner at $44,000, offered a promotion to $70,000. At the higher wage they lose SNAP, Medicaid, and most of their childcare subsidy, they start paying for health coverage, and more of the wage goes to tax. Add it all up and the $26,000 raise leaves them about $14,600 worse off over the year. The chart shows their safe target is around $96,000, and the sharpest single step down is just after $47,000, where the childcare subsidy ends. How I built it The engine is plain TypeScript with no framework tied to it. Federal rules (SNAP, poverty guidelines, ACA premium caps, the EITC and Child Tax Credit, payroll and income tax) live in one module. Each state is a single file with its Medicaid rules, childcare subsidy schedule, housing standards, and income tax brackets. Adding a state is one file and one line. Every state ships with automated tests that check the cliff math and confirm each rule value cites a government source. There are 219 of these tests. The app is Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind, and Recharts for the chart. Most pages are static. The only server code is a contact form. The WebMCP layer is small on purpose. One file defines the four tools and their inputs. One file registers them with the browser through document.modelContext and does nothing if the browser has no WebMCP support. A small component mounts that from the app shell so the tools are available on every page. The tools run the same calculations the visible app does, with no network call, so an agent gets the same answer a person does and the privacy promise still holds. Challenges I ran into The standard is new. WebMCP is behind a Chrome origin trial and the API isstill moving. I kept our adapter thin so a spec change is a small edit, not a rewrite. CredSutra brings credit-card intelligence to AI with WebMCP—review, compare, discover news, calculate rewards & lounge benefits, and get personalized card recommendations based on your spending.

 1 2 3 



 
 About the Project 

 I’ve always wanted to build a website that brings together useful, practical information about credit cards. 

 When I started earning, choosing the right credit card was surprisingly difficult. There were limited sources of information, information was scattered across different websites, and it wasn’t always easy to figure out which card actually made sense for my spending habits. I had the idea of building something that could solve this problem, but like many side projects, I never found the time to actually build it. 

 AI changed that. 

 With the rise of AI-powered experiences, I thought: why not finally give it a shot? That idea eventually became CredSutra — a platform designed to help people understand, compare, and choose credit cards based on how they actually spend. 

 For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I took CredSutra one step further. Instead of making users navigate through pages and manually search for information, I exposed CredSutra's capabilities through WebMCP. The website currently provides six tools that an AI agent can interact with: 

 
 Card Review — get detailed information and insights about a credit card. 
 Card Comparison — compare cards and understand their differences. 
 Credit Card News — discover relevant and recent card-related updates. 
 Reward Calculator — estimate rewards based on spending. 
 Lounge Calculator — determine lounge eligibility and benefits. 
 Card Recommendation — find cards that fit specific spending criteria. 
 

 The interesting part for me was seeing how a website can evolve from being a destination that users browse into a capability that AI agents can interact with . 

 What I Learned 

 Building this project taught me that WebMCP is more than just exposing APIs. The real challenge is thinking about how an AI agent will understand and use your tools. 

 I had to think carefully about tool descriptions, inputs, outputs, and how to structure the capabilities so that an agent can make meaningful decisions instead of simply calling an endpoint. 

 It also made me rethink the traditional website experience. A user might ask an AI something like: 

 
 "I spend ₹50,000 a month on travel and dining. Which credit card would give me the best rewards?" 
 

 Instead of the user learning how CredSutra works first, an AI agent can use CredSutra's tools to find the relevant cards, calculate potential rewards, and provide an answer. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was deciding what should become a tool and what should remain part of the website experience. 

 I also had to make the tools useful independently while ensuring they could work together as part of a larger AI-driven workflow. Designing clear inputs and outputs and making the tools predictable for an agent required more thought than I initially expected. 

 And, of course, building a real product while learning and experimenting with a relatively new technology comes with plenty of iterations and debugging. 

 What's Next? 

 CredSutra is still very much a beginning. 

 There are many more features I want to add, more credit-card data to bring together, and many ways I can make the recommendations smarter and more personalized. 

 What started as an idea I had years ago but never got around to building has finally become something real — and WebMCP has given me an exciting new direction for it. 

 This is just the beginning.

title: DecisionPlay Live
pitch: A decision board an agent and a person edit together: the agent researches and scores, you override what you disagree with, and it reasons from your judgment instead of arguing with it.
about_excerpt: A decision board an agent and a person edit together: the agent researches and scores, you override what you disagree with, and it reasons from your judgment instead of arguing with it. Like Comment Story Updates Why this use case fits WebMCP A decision is not a request. It is a workspace two parties keep changing. Most agent integrations are request-shaped: you ask, the agent answers, the answer arrives as text. That shape is a poor fit for deciding anything real, because the interesting part is not the conclusion, it is the twenty small judgments underneath it, each of which a person may want to disagree with. WebMCP fits because it puts the agent's hands on the same surface the person is looking at. The agent is not describing a decision board to me in prose. It is editing the one on my screen, and I am editing it back, in the same session, with no copy-paste between us. A conventional MCP server could fetch the same search results. It could not put them on my screen, and it could not see that I moved a weight from 3 to 5 thirty seconds later. How it makes the experience better You can see the work. Options, criteria, weights, and scores appear on the board as the agent creates them, each tagged with who set it. Nothing is buried in a transcript you have to scroll back through. You can interrupt at the level of a single judgment. If the agent scored one county a 4 on unmet need and you know that is wrong, you click that cell and change it. You do not have to re-litigate the whole analysis in prose to correct one number. The evidence stays attached. Every live search the agent runs pins to the board with source, date, and link, so a claim and the thing it came from stay in the same place. You can disagree with a specific source rather than with the model's tone. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Correct an agent mid-analysis and have it actually absorb the correction. The board records who set every score. When you override a value the agent chose, that override is flagged in the state the agent reads back through get_board . The agent sees that a human overrode it there and continues from your number. The scoring tool goes further and refuses to overwrite a human-set cell at all. It returns a message telling the agent to state what it would have scored and why, and leave the decision to you. That is a deliberate stance: an agent working alongside someone should not quietly overrule them, and WebMCP is the first place I have been able to encode that as a property of the tool rather than a hope about the prompt. The result is a genuine division of labor. The agent is better at breadth, running twelve searches and drafting twelve rationales. The person is better at knowing that the third one is wrong. Before this, those two things happened in different windows. How WebMCP is implemented Seven tools registered on document.modelContext in public/index.html : Tool What it does get_board read question, options, criteria, every score with its author, the ranking, and unscored cells. readOnlyHint: true set_decision set the decision question add_option add an option, idempotent so retries are safe add_criterion add a criterion weighted 1 to 5 gather_evidence live SerpApi search (web / news / related), pinned to the board score_option score one cell with a rationale; refuses to overwrite a human explain_verdict ranking, margin, most leveraged criterion. readOnlyHint: true Registration goes through an AbortController signal, which is how WebMCP unregisters; there is no unregisterTool . Every tool carries a title as well as a name , so a client listing site tools shows a readable label. Every execute returns the MCP content shape { content: [{ type: "text", text }] } so results pass through client normalization unmodified, and receives the AbortSignal from its options argument, which gather_evidence passes into fetch so a cancelled call cancels the request. Tools are registered from the top-level document, since WebMCP does not discover tools inside iframes. The page feature-detects and degrades to a normal manual tool when no agent is present, so it is a complete product either way. gather_evidence is marked untrustedContentHint . It pulls arbitrary third-party web content into the agent's context, which is the case that hint exists for. Everything rendered from those results is HTML-escaped and outbound links carry noopener noreferrer . Score entry is an inline editor rather than window.prompt , because embedded and in-app browsers routinely suppress prompt() and that would have silently broken the override path in exactly the clients this runs in. The board is keyboard operable and the activity log is an aria-live region. Everything runs client-side except the SerpApi proxy, a zero-dependency Netlify function that keeps the API key server-side. No framework, no bundler, no lockfile. Two files. Testing instructions for judges No login required. Free and open for the full judging period. Open https://decisionplay-live.netlify.app in the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser (use GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra; Luna has WebMCP disabled), or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the pill at the top right reads "agent connected · 7 tools". Give the agent this prompt: Use the tools on this page. The decision is where a small Michigan nonprofit should place one new community health worker in 2026. Add Wayne, Genesee and Marquette County as options. Add criteria for unmet need, existing coverage, travel burden and funding, and weight them. Search for real current evidence on each county before you score anything, then score every cell and tell me where the decision actually turns. Watch the board fill in. Evidence cards appear on the right with live sources. Click any cell the agent scored and change the number. Then ask the agent "what did I just change, and does it move your recommendation?" It calls get_board , sees the override flagged as yours, and reasons from your value. Step 5 is the one worth seeing. Provenance and scope Built from scratch on September 2, 2026. No pre-existing code was carried in. It shares a name with an earlier project by the same author, decisionplay.app, and shares no code with it. The ranking is labeled MODELED and the evidence LIVE, consistently, throughout the interface. The tool does not give legal, medical, or financial advice. about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered AI agent that analyzes project decisions, compares scenarios, previews consequences, and acts with human confirmation.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 About LifeSim 

 LifeSim is an interactive project-management simulation where an AI agent helps a human make strategic decisions for a student innovation project. 

 The idea came from a simple question: what would happen if an AI agent could not only give advice, but actually understand the current state of a live simulation, compare possible decisions, preview their consequences, and then act with the user's confirmation? 

 What we built 

 LifeSim uses WebMCP to expose structured tools that allow an AI agent to interact with the simulation. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the current simulation state; 
 see tasks, team information, resources, risks, deadlines, and success probability; 
 retrieve the decisions currently available; 
 compare different strategic options; 
 preview the consequences of a decision; 
 apply a confirmed decision; 
 advance the simulation. 
 

 The core WebMCP tools include get_simulation_state and get_available_decisions . These tools return real data from the running simulation instead of relying on a static description. 

 Human-in-the-loop 

 An important part of LifeSim is keeping the human in control. 

 The AI agent can analyze the situation and recommend an action, but consequential state changes go through an explicit preview and confirmation flow. This makes the agent's actions visible and understandable instead of allowing decisions to happen silently. 

 The interface also shows Agent Activity so that users can see what the agent is doing and how successful tool calls affect the simulation. 

 What we learned 

 Building LifeSim helped us understand how WebMCP can connect an AI agent with a real interactive web application through structured tools. 

 Instead of treating an AI agent as a separate chatbot, WebMCP allows the agent to work with the application's actual state and capabilities. 

 We also learned the importance of designing clear tool interfaces and making state-changing actions observable and controllable. 

 Challenges 

 One of the main challenges was making sure that the AI agent, WebMCP tools, and simulation UI remained synchronized. 

 We tested the project through multiple demo steps and verified that the WebMCP tools returned the expected simulation data and that the project could successfully build and run. 

 We also had to work around an API quota limitation during development. Because the core WebMCP functionality is independent from that limitation, we focused on making the underlying simulation, tools, validation, and agent workflow reliable. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 LifeSim demonstrates how WebMCP can let an AI agent interact with a live web application through structured tools while keeping the human in control of consequential actions. 

 The goal is not simply to make an AI that talks about a simulation, but an AI that can understand the application's state, reason about available actions, and interact with the application through explicit, verifiable tools.

title: Fairground
pitch: A neutral ground where two people and their AI agents settle real disputes in minutes: sealed offers, a neutral mediator, and an agreement only humans can sign. Built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A neutral ground where two people and their AI agents settle real disputes in minutes: sealed offers, a neutral mediator, and an agreement only humans can sign. Built on WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The pitch in one line, with the green badge confirming this page has already handed its tools to your agent. Three one-click demos, a live docket of settlements signed so far, and the research on why people give up. How a case moves, and the idea underneath it: the tools an agent can see are the procedure it has to follow. The questions everyone asks before trusting this. Is it binding, can they see my number, what does it cost. Opening a case takes four fields. Practice mode lets you rehearse against an AI before involving anyone real. Sealed offers, round one of three. Autopilot is ready, bounded by a private floor the other side never sees. The mediator proposed $808 and both sides accepted, so the agreement gets drafted in plain language. Both humans signed, and the case is resolved. Minutes from opening the dispute, with no lawyer involved. Signatures, timestamps, and a SHA-256 seal anyone can verify later. Then we ask how fair the process felt. A real case gives the claimant one link to send. That is all it takes to bring the other side to the table. The same case from the other chair, with their own agent, their own reality check, and your evidence on record. Inspiration A client owes a freelancer $1,800 and stops replying. A lawyer costs more than the claim. Small claims court takes months. So most people give up, and research says this is the norm rather than the exception: 92% of low-income Americans' civil legal problems get no meaningful legal help, and 71% of freelancers have struggled to collect payment. Justice below a few thousand dollars is economically irrational to pursue. Yet eBay resolves about 60 million disputes a year with software , and British Columbia runs a fully online public tribunal . Structured resolution works. But it exists only inside closed platforms, and always with one shared form or one shared bot. Nobody could give each side its own advocate on neutral ground , because neither side had an advocate to bring. Now everyone browses with an agent, and WebMCP lets a website hand those agents governed tools. That is the gap we built into. What it does Fairground is a small online courthouse for everyday disputes: State your case. Tell your agent what happened. It files the claim and evidence for you, or you type it yourself. Everything also works by hand. They join by link. The other party opens your invite with their own agent , which reviews the record and gives them a private, honest reality check. Sealed offers. Each human privately sets a true limit their agent cannot cross. Up to three rounds of sealed offers follow. If the numbers overlap, the case settles instantly at the midpoint. The other side never sees your numbers, only whether the gap grew or shrank. Neutral mediation. No overlap? A mediator controlled by neither party reads the full record, including the sealed history neither side can see, and proposes a neutral settlement amount, numerically clamped between the parties' last positions. Humans sign. A plain-language agreement is drafted. No tool can sign it. Two humans read and sign, and the settlement is stamped with a cryptographic record seal anyone can verify later. Also inside: practice mode (an AI plays the other side so you can rehearse, or a judge can try the full two-party flow solo), Autopilot (both advocates run the whole procedure automatically, bounded by your limit, stopping only at your signature), a live public Docket of settlements, a fairness rating after every case, three one-click staged demos on the landing page, and a downloadable court-preparation record if a case ends without agreement, containing the claim, the response, dated evidence, your own sealed offers, the mediator's proposals, and an attestation that settlement was attempted in good faith. Walking away costs you nothing. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Our core design idea: the tool surface is the procedure. All 27 tools are registered per role and per phase . The respondent's agent has no offer tool until it files a response. Nobody can bid before their human sets a limit. There is deliberately no signing tool at all . Due process is enforced by tool availability, not by prompts. It is a multiplayer WebMCP app: two opposing agents on one neutral page. The server filters each side's view, so no tool exists that could leak your private limit to the other side, even to a prompt-injected agent. Humans stay in the loop where it matters. If an agent wants to concede beyond its human's limit, it can only raise an approval card on the human's screen. Only a human click converts it into an offer. We use both halves of the spec : the imperative API (via Chrome's official use-webmcp-tool hook) and the declarative API , where our fairness-rating form is itself the registered tool. Tools reading the opponent's words carry untrustedContentHint with fenced content, per Chrome's security guidance. Together, a person and their agent can do something neither could alone: the person brings judgment, limits, and consent; the agent brings tireless procedure, evidence handling, and negotiation; and the neutral tool surface enforces fairness between two opposing agents . That interaction pattern did not exist on the web before. How we built it Next.js on Vercel; case state machine in Upstash Redis; capability-keyed links with no accounts; OpenAI gpt-5-mini through the Vercel AI SDK for the mediator, reality checks, drafting, and the practice counterpart, all with deterministic fallbacks so the product never dead-ends on a model error; rate limiting and 35-second call timeouts throughout. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was an unusual threat model: the prompt injector is the opposing party. Their story, their evidence, their messages all flow to your agent. We answered with layered defense: untrusted-content hints, explicit content fencing, and above all structure, because the tools that could leak your numbers simply do not exist on the other side's page. Second hardest: making procedure feel effortless for agents. The answer was ending every tool result with contextual "NEXT:" guidance, so agents flow through the process without guessing. Accomplishments that we're proud of We measured it. 30 randomized disputes run end to end through the live deployment: 100% of completed cases settled, at a mean 70% of the claim, in 52 seconds each. For claims this size the real-world alternative is usually zero. We red-teamed our own courtroom. The opposing party plants a message demanding the private mandate. The agent reads it, even replies, and does not disclose. A structural sweep then executes every tool on the opponent's page and proves the number appears in zero outputs. The eval suite passes 7 of 7. Agreements that outlive the argument. Every signed settlement carries a SHA-256 record seal, verifiable by anyone holding the document. A live Docket: every settlement on the platform, including yours if you try it, feeds a public counter. What we learned Fairness can be architecture. Procedural justice research ( Tyler ) shows people accept even disappointing outcomes when the process gives them voice, neutrality, transparency, and respect. Every one of those became a feature, and we now measure ourselves against it with the post-settlement fairness score. What's next for Fairground Jurisdiction-specific filing packs built on the court-preparation record we already generate, an embeddable dispute widget for marketplaces, escalation to a human mediator for complex cases, and more languages. Try it (60 seconds) Open https://fairground-umber.vercel.app in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome 149+ with the WebMCP flag. Click a one-click demo , or just tell your agent: "A client owes me $1,800 for a logo, 75 days overdue. Open a practice case and help me settle it." Set your floor, hit Autopilot, and sign the one thing no agent can. title: AI Delegation Boundary
pitch: A WebMCP-powered system for defining, challenging, and approving where agent autonomy ends and human authority begins.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered system for defining, challenging, and approving where agent autonomy ends and human authority begins. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT works through WebMCP tools while the web app retains delegation state and human authority. The workspace guides each Human-Agent handoff while keeping the delegation boundary and approval state visible. Inspiration AI agents are increasingly able to make decisions and take action across real workflows. As their autonomy grows, a harder question follows: Where should agent authority end, and where should human authority begin? AI Delegation Boundary began as a way for us to understand WebMCP by building with it. While developing the project, we realized that WebMCP could support more than letting an Agent operate a web page. The web application could hold the current boundary, constraints, human judgments, and approval state, while the Agent reasons and acts through tools exposed by that page. That led to the core idea: Make AI delegation itself something a human and an Agent can examine, challenge, revise, and approve together. What it does AI Delegation Boundary helps a human decide what an AI Agent may do on its own. A human first defines the work being considered. The Agent then uses WebMCP tools exposed by the page to: Inspect the current delegation boundary. Propose a revision. Challenge that revision with a concrete scenario. Re-test it against Guardrails and previous human decisions. Inspect the revision history and current state. When the Agent finds a case that requires judgment, it stops and returns control to the human. The human decides whether that case should be: Agent-only Human review Not delegated That judgment becomes a regression test for future revisions. The collaboration loop is: Proposal → Challenge → Human Judgment → Re-test → Human Approval → Apply The Agent cannot approve its own revision. Only the exact revision explicitly approved by the human can be applied. How we built it AI Delegation Boundary is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP, and is deployed on GitHub Pages. The web application holds the delegation boundary, Guardrails, human judgments, revision state, approval, and applied state. WebMCP exposes five normal tools to the Agent: Inspect the delegation workspace Propose a boundary revision Challenge the current revision Review the current revision Inspect revision history After the exact current revision receives explicit human approval, an additional apply capability becomes available. There is no dedicated AI backend. The conversational Agent works directly through the WebMCP tools exposed by the page. Our architectural principle is: Conversation is the Agent; state and authority live in the web app. Review combines three different controls: Guardrails — deterministic invariants that must not be violated Known Decisions — previous human judgments preserved as regression tests Agent Challenges — concrete scenarios generated to actively challenge the current boundary Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not exposing tools to an Agent. It was designing the authority model around them. We needed to ensure that the Agent could propose and challenge changes without granting itself additional authority. We also had to make sure that: human judgments became reusable tests, a changed boundary required a fresh Agent Challenge, approval referred only to the exact state the human reviewed, and an Agent could never silently approve or expand its own authority. Another challenge was the Human-Agent handoff. We did not want users to type tool names, revision numbers, or challenge scenarios manually. The browser therefore tells the user what happens next, where the next action takes place, and provides copy-ready handoffs when control moves back to ChatGPT. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built a complete Human-Agent governance loop through WebMCP. The Agent can inspect, propose, challenge, and re-test changes to its delegation boundary, while the human retains final judgment and approval. Human judgments do not disappear after one decision. They become regression tests that constrain future revisions. We also made the Agent capability surface depend on human authority: five normal tools are available during collaboration, and the apply capability becomes available only after explicit human approval of the exact current revision. Most importantly, WebMCP is not used here simply as a remote-control layer for a website. It is part of the mechanism that separates Agent action from human authority . What we learned Building AI Delegation Boundary changed how we think about WebMCP. The interesting part is not simply that an AI Agent can operate a website. A web application can hold state, constraints, and authority while an Agent reasons and acts through that surface. This allows the collaboration itself to be designed: what the Agent may change, what it must challenge, when it must stop, what only a human may decide, and when additional capability may become available. For us, WebMCP became a way to connect Agent reasoning with a governed web surface. What's next for AI Delegation Boundary AI Delegation Boundary is a focused implementation of a broader problem we are exploring through SOLIFAN and ReadinessOps: How can organizations expand the practical use of AI Agents while deliberately retaining the judgments and authority that should remain human? Next, we want to connect this model to real organizational workflows, richer evidence, additional delegation factors, and reusable governance patterns across different Agent environments. The long-term goal is to make Agent authority something organizations can deliberately: Design → Test → Approve → Evolve Built With chatgpt github react typescript vite vitest webmcp Try it out solidfdn.github.io github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I conceived AI Delegation Boundary and built the project end to end, from the Human-Agent authority model and WebMCP architecture through implementation, testing, UX refinement, documentation, and the final demo. title: ShowOnce - WebMCP for “do what I did.”
pitch: Record a web task once, send a link. Their agent finishes it on-page via WebMCP—they approve the final step. No screen share. Safe help from anywhere.
about_excerpt: Record a web task once, send a link. Their agent finishes it on-page via WebMCP—they approve the final step. No screen share. Safe help from anywhere. Like Comment Story Updates ShowOnce WebMCP is how any site exposes capabilities. ShowOnce is what makes delegation safe — record once, hand off a portable procedure, agent executes within scope, human approves the irreversible step. WaitingRoom.gov is our stress-test UI modeled on real legacy portals (India Post PLI, NIC, PIB) — not a greenfield app. Built for the WebMCP Challenge . The problem Remote web help today relies on screenshots, phone calls, screen sharing, remote control software, or handing over a password. Screenshots lose context. Screen sharing and remote control require both people to be free at the same time and give one person full access to the other's session. Credential sharing gives up account security entirely. None of these let a second person's own agent pick up where the first person left off, on the second person's own account. What ShowOnce does A sender demonstrates a real task once, live, inside a fully interactive connected demo application called Northstar Benefits (an employee benefits portal). ShowOnce does not screen-record or ask the sender to pick steps manually: because the demo app's UI and ShowOnce both call the same shared domain command layer, every meaningful action the sender takes (selecting a plan, changing a preference, confirming an address) is automatically captured as a semantic event. Those events are compiled into a portable, sanitized procedure — intent only, no selectors, credentials, sessions, or screenshots. A recipient opens the resulting handoff link. They can act on it directly in the same live app, rendered against their own account state, or they can ask a WebMCP-capable agent (for example, ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled) to "do what [the sender] showed me." When an agent is used, it invokes real document.modelContext tools registered by ShowOnce — the exact same commands the human UI uses — so the visible, live Northstar Benefits app updates in front of the recipient as the agent works. Nothing is simulated or faked. ShowOnce compares the demonstrated procedure against the recipient's actual state and decides, deterministically, what still applies, what can be safely applied, what differs materially, and what must be left for a human to decide. For any consequential, identity-bearing action — actually submitting the renewal — an agent can get the recipient all the way to a final reviewable summary, but no further. A human must check a personal attestation checkbox and click "Confirm & submit" themselves. That single click is the only human step, and no WebMCP tool can ever perform it. How WebMCP is used Real document.modelContext.registerTool(...) registrations, made client-side once the recipient route mounts (see src/webmcp/registerTools.ts ). Strict JSON Schemas for every tool's input, with no free-form or untyped arguments. readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations so a calling agent knows which tools only read state and which tools are handling handoff-authored content. AbortController -based lifecycle: tools are registered with a scoped signal and unregister themselves cleanly when the recipient route unmounts. A single shared executeCommand() domain layer used by both the human UI and every WebMCP tool, so there is exactly one implementation of the business logic behind "select a plan" or "set paperless" — not a UI code path and a separate agent code path. A human-only, atomic final step: WebMCP tools can read state, apply safe preferences, and prepare a renewal summary, but the recipient_attestation semantic event that authorizes submission can only ever be issued by a human clicking a button in the browser — executeCommand() refuses it outright if the source is 'webmcp' .
