title: Dayflow
pitch: A real HR system that registers 31 WebMCP tools in the page. The agent reads receipts that were never uploaded, drafts the numbers, and the tools that move money accept no amounts at all.
about_excerpt: A real HR system that registers 31 WebMCP tools in the page. The agent reads receipts that were never uploaded, drafts the numbers, and the tools that move money accept no amounts at all. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Role-filtering Inspiration An agent can already read HR data and talk about it sensibly. It cannot finish the job. The last step of most HR work is a number being written down, a salary, a bonus, a reimbursement, and a figure that came out of a language model is not a figure you can pay somebody. So the reading gets automated, the deciding does not, and the gap between them is where the errors live. Dayflow is an Indian HRMS, denominated in rupees and lakh, applying Indian rules: provident fund, professional tax, CGST and SGST on a restaurant bill. So the case for it should be made with Indian numbers. Finding Source 48% of Indian companies have no way to detect travel and expense fraud , because claims are checked by hand. About 55% cannot retrieve past claims at all. Happay, via Economic Times Every ₹1 lost to fraud costs an Indian firm ₹4.00 , and 54% say fraud is rising. LexisNexis India, 2024 India has the worst payroll staffing shortage in Asia Pacific, at 75% of businesses , and employers named missing automation the top cause of payroll error. ADP India, May 2025 Over half of occupational fraud cases involve missing controls or an override of them , median loss $104,000, median 12 months undetected. ACFE, 2026 Then on 21 November 2025 India's labour codes came into force and changed what a salary structure is allowed to look like: wages must be at least half of total remuneration, and anything excluded beyond that gets added back, which moves PF and gratuity. Every CTC split in the country had to be re-checked. This is not the year for a tool that quietly rewrites pay structures. The model is also the wrong component to trust with the arithmetic. Frontier models score between 73.8% and 99.8% on plain numerical addition, then fall to 7.5% when the same problems are restated symbolically, which looks like retrieval rather than rule following ( arXiv 2504.05262 ), and multi digit multiplication is still an open failure case ( arXiv 2510.00184 ). So full autonomy makes this worse, not better. It removes the human control the fraud data says is load bearing, and hands the arithmetic to the part of the stack with the weakest claim on it. A better model does not fix that. A better place to put the human does. The insight came from the WebMCP explainer , in the line about tools running inside the page the human is already looking at. If the tool lives in the page, the proposal can live in the page too, so the agent never has to be the one holding the number. That is why the three tools that move money accept no amounts at all. Not validated amounts. None. There is no numeric parameter anywhere in their schemas, so a model that invented a total has nowhere to put it. Only a tool running inside the document that owns what is displayed can work that way. What it does Dayflow is a working HR management system that registers 31 WebMCP tools inside its own page , so a browser agent can work it beside whoever is signed in. One rule governs everything: the agent drafts, the human commits. human asks in plain language agent reads, and parses the local file the human dropped agent drafts a proposal into the page's own canvas store the proposal renders on screen, old and new values side by side human reads the actual figures and clicks approve the commit tool reads the canvas, not the model Every row below is a real registered tool. Intent Example ask What happens See what the human sees "What am I looking at?" get_page_context returns the live route, the current filter, the rows that survived it, who is selected, and whether a proposal is on screen Drive the interface "Open the roster and pull up Ankush" navigate_to , filter_directory and focus_employee move the human's actual UI Decide leave "Approve Ankush's paid leave" check_leave_coverage simulates the gap read only, then decide_leave stops on an approval dialog before writing Onboard from a CV "Add this candidate" (CV pasted) add_employee_from_description parses the text in the tab and labels every inferred value with how it got there Quote the employer, not the model "What is the meal cap? What are our PF rates?" get_policy and get_salary_model return the written rules, and say plainly when they have fallen back to statutory defaults Draft then commit a salary "Set up 12 LPA for EMP014", then "Save it" propose_salary_structure splits the CTC six ways and draws it on the Salary page. commit_salary_structure takes a reason and a name. No figures Score work, then pay a bonus "Who earned bonus this quarter? Split two lakh" read_contribution_import and get_contribution_scores , where only verified rows score, then propose_bonus_pool divides the human's stated budget on screen and record_bonus_decision commits it. No figures Audit and reimburse a claim "What is on this bill? Check it, then approve it" audit_expense_claim marks up the page with the rule behind every rupee removed. record_expense_decision takes a decision, a reason and a name. No figures, and the parsed claim is then discarded The tool set reflects the session. Anyone signed in gets 8 page context and UI tools plus 3 contribution tools.An admin adds 7 for roster and leave, 7 for bonuses, 3 for salary, 3 for expenses. An anonymous visitor gets nothing, because nothing registers before sign in. Sign out and you can watch the list fall from 31 to 11 live in Chrome's DevTools WebMCP panel, because teardown runs off the AbortSignal the spec provides for it. Drop the sample restaurant bill onto the Expenses page and audit_expense_claim walks the written policy over it line by line. A ₹6,133 claim comes back as ₹1,783 reimbursable, with the rule attached to every rupee removed: Line group Claimed Reimbursable Rule applied Eight food lines ₹2,910 ₹1,200 Spent down in order against the daily meal cap until the cap runs out Three drinks lines ₹2,400 ₹0 Alcohol is not reimbursable, even itemised inside a food bill Service charge ₹531 ₹291 Read as a tip, capped at ten per cent of that day's pre tax food CGST and SGST ₹292 ₹292 Tax passes through untouched Total ₹6,133 ₹1,783 ₹4,350 refused \( 1{,}200 + 291 + 292 = 1{,}783 \) reconciles against the printed total on the bill, so a judge can check the engine by hand instead of taking my word for it. Uncertainty is reported rather than resolved: conference spend is held for review, neither approved nor refused, unless an approved travel request covers those dates, and held amounts are totalled outside the reimbursable figure. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before. The agent can audit a private financialdocument that was never uploaded anywhere, quoting policy at individual lines while the file never leaves the tab. It can commit a financial decision without anyone trusting its arithmetic, because it has no field to put a numberin, so what reaches the database is what was rendered and checked. And it can take over the reading without taking the judgement: a twelve row work export is parsed and reported honestly, including the row that matches nobody, and imported rows arrive as claimed, so an import cannot quietly move the leaderboard that feeds bonus money. How I built it Why the browser was the right place. The explainer names three failures of backend tool integrations: they cut the site's own interface out of the loop, they make you copy the user's state and credentials onto another server, and they make you build a backend to expose what the client already does. HR and finance hit all three, then hit a fourth that no server side tool can solve: some of the data has no URL. A travel claim arrives as a photo of a bill or an export sitting on someone's laptop. Dayflow parses both in the browser, so nothing is uploaded and there is no OCR service in the middle, and the parsed claim lives only in page state, gone once the decision is recorded. Meanwhile get_page_context reports live in memory state no REST endpoint could expose, and the signed in Supabase session is already the credential, so there is no second copy of who the user is to get wrong. Oversight is the point rather than a constraint I designed around: WebMCP lists fully autonomous workflows as a non goal, and given what the fraud data says about control overrides, salaries are the last place you would want an unattended agent. The WebMCP layer. src/lib/webmcp/registry.ts looks for document.modelContext , falls back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext , then provideContext , then a bare array. It calls registerTool per tool with a JSON Schema inputSchema and an execute returning MCP content blocks. Because registerTool is async and rejects, the registry claims each name up front and keeps the promise rather than assuming success. Tools are composed from the session role in one expre

title: RuleRipple
pitch: RuleRipple is a policy simulation sandbox to help humans and AI agents allocate limited resources like credits, test rules, understand who gets what and why, & approve allocations with an audit trail.
about_excerpt: RuleRipple is a policy simulation sandbox to help humans and AI agents allocate limited resources like credits, test rules, understand who gets what and why, & approve allocations with an audit trail. Like Comment Story Updates Policy templates Priority rules Limits and governance Budget ledger Policy overview 1. WebMCP workflow Shared budget inbox Allocation approval Version comparison Budget simulation Why a request waits Request ranking and explanations Execution receipt Agent connections Activity audit trail Inspiration Inspiration RuleRipple grew out of a problem the three of us—my sister, my wife, and I—faced while working on our own projects. AI credits were a scarce resource, and our limited budgets meant we had to be thoughtful about how we used them. That raised a practical question: when several tasks need credits, how do we decide which ones get priority, how much each receives, and what has to wait? We wanted to test those choices before committing our budget and understand how changing a rule would affect each request. That inspired RuleRipple: a policy simulation sandbox where humans and AI agents can explore how to allocate limited resources, understand the tradeoffs, and approve decisions with a clear trail. What it does RuleRipple is a WebMCP-powered policy simulation sandbox for humans and AI agents. It helps users define allocation rules, preview their effects, and approve allocations with an audit trail. WebMCP is useful here because the agent works with the same visible policy workspace as the user. Agents can inspect policies and submit structured requests, while people can see the results, understand the effect on other requests, and retain control over approvals. Users can: Define available resources, protected reserves, eligibility requirements, and priorities. Receive budget requests from agents through HTTPS or WebMCP. Simulate how a policy distributes resources across competing requests. Change a rule and compare who becomes eligible, moves in priority, gains resources, or has to wait. Review the reasons behind each allocation and approve exact amounts. Track reservations, commitments, recorded consumption, and released resources in a ledger. The same approach supports resources such as agent credits, funding, API quotas, clinic hours, inventory, and inspection slots. A simple example Imagine two agents each request 70 credits from a shared budget of 100. There is enough to support either request fully, but not both. A priority-based policy might fund the urgent request first. A sharing policy might distribute credits between them, provided each receives enough to do useful work. RuleRipple lets a user test these choices before approving an allocation. Changing a priority rule or protecting a reserve reveals the effect across all requests. The “ripple” is the impact one policy change has on everyone competing for the same resources. How we built it We built RuleRipple with React and TypeScript, with a deterministic engine for policy evaluation, ranking, resource allocation, version comparison, and ledger accounting. The WebMCP tools use structured schemas and runtime validation. Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore support sign-in and persistent workspaces, and the application is deployed through ChatGPT Sites. An optional GitHub integration connects an authorized request to a specific external action, with source checks and a recorded execution receipt. Challenges we ran into One challenge was making the full effect of a rule change understandable. A change that helps one request can reduce the resources available to another. We built comparisons that expose those consequences across the complete set of requests. Another challenge was handling practical allocation constraints. A partial award may be useless if a task needs a minimum amount to run. RuleRipple accounts for those minimums alongside priorities, reserves, and resource limits. We also needed to keep simulation, authorization, and execution distinct. Previewing an allocation does not spend resources. The ledger tracks subsequent resource operations, and repeated requests must not accidentally reserve the same budget twice. Accomplishments that we're proud of We brought policy definition, simulation, explanations, approval, and resource accounting into one workflow. RuleRipple supports six allocation strategies, multiple resource pools, policy version comparisons, and explanations for individual outcomes. Its WebMCP tools make that workflow accessible to agents while keeping decisions visible to people. What we learned An allocation can follow its rules correctly and still produce an unexpected result. Showing the consequences of those rules is essential to helping people decide whether the policy matches their intent. We also learned the value of giving agents structured access to a shared application. Agents can help inspect and propose changes, while deterministic calculations and explicit authorization make the results reproducible and reviewable. What's next for RuleRipple We want to add organizational roles, richer approval workflows, more execution integrations, and live provider usage metering. Our goal is to help teams understand the consequences of resource decisions before committing to them—and retain a clear record afterward. title: Focus Contract Studio
pitch: ChatGPT can read, propose, apply, and verify a live accessibility repair—but only the person can approve it.
about_excerpt: ChatGPT can read, propose, apply, and verify a live accessibility repair—but only the person can approve it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browser agents can inspect and act quickly, but important product decisions should not collapse into “the model suggested it, so the model changed it.” Accessibility and design-system teams need a shared surface where an agent can use the live page and prior decisions while an exact visible UI review remains the only source of application authority. Focus Contract Studio explores that future of the open web through one deliberately narrow, testable decision: which control should receive initial focus in a destructive Delete Account dialog. What it does Focus Contract Studio gives a reviewer and ChatGPT one shared, page-bound change-control loop. R13 makes that contract legible at first glance: a forensic editorial workspace shows the concrete Delete-versus-Cancel mismatch, then maps the Browser → Agent → Reviewer → Browser protocol before the first action. The browser renders implemented revision 1, where the dialog initially focuses Delete. The page retrieves synthetic, applicable precedent saying this exact destructive-dialog context should initially focus Cancel, and reports a bounded DECISION MISMATCH. ChatGPT reads the live review through WebMCP and stages an immutable Delete → Cancel proposal. The renderer stays on revision 1 and the proposal stays visibly NOT APPLIED. The reviewer inspects the exact diff, digest, and base revision. There is no approval tool: only the visible UI-mediated decision can authorize application. ChatGPT applies that exact approved payload. Guarded writes create revision 2 and a durable receipt. The person completes a keyboard rehearsal in the real dialog. ChatGPT reads the page again, receives the exact current committed browser rehearsal, and verifies six behaviors: initial focus, focus order, forward wrap, backward wrap, Escape, and returned focus. History, stale-state rejection, idempotent retries, reload recovery, revisioned undo, privacy limits, and a complete keyboard-accessible fallback remain visible on the same page. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Every operation depends on live page context: the rendered variant, implemented revision, browser observation, eligible precedent, immutable proposal, current review state, and committed rehearsal. A detached chatbot or generic API would lose the precise state boundary that makes each action useful and safe. The page registers exactly four typed top-level tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...): read_active_focus_review create_focus_contract_proposal apply_approved_focus_contract verify_focus_contract The WebMCP adapters and visible UI call the same protected application services. There is deliberately no approval, review, rehearsal-capture, reset, undo, URL, selector, or workspace-selection tool. Page text, retrieved precedent, tool output, and model language are untrusted evidence—not authority. How it creates a better experience The reviewer and agent work from the same live revision instead of exchanging screenshots and stale summaries. The agent can create a durable, inspectable proposal without silently changing the product. The exact visible UI review remains the only application authority. Application fails closed on stale revisions, changed digests, revoked or rejected decisions, foreign workspaces, and conflicting retries. Verification comes from fresh browser events, not from regenerating the expected answer from the configuration under test. The full visible workflow still works when WebMCP is unavailable. Before this, teams could combine chat, tickets, component previews, precedent documents, and browser testing, but the state and authority boundaries lived in separate tools. Focus Contract Studio turns them into one legible human-agent protocol on the open web. What people and agents can do together now ChatGPT can interpret bounded precedent, create a field-supported proposal, apply only the exact payload already authorized in the page, and return a durable verification receipt. The reviewer can inspect every transition, supply the only approval authority through the visible UI, replay receipts, recover from uncertain responses, and undo a committed revision without trusting hidden agent state. The current release retains the final page-bound handoff: after the browser rehearsal, read_active_focus_review returns a bounded verificationTarget for only the active workspace, variant, and revision. Foreign, stale, test-only, recording, uncommitted, and expired rehearsals are excluded. Judges no longer need a database console, copied cookie, workspace ID, or manually supplied rehearsal ID. How we built it Focus Contract Studio is a full-stack ChatGPT Site written in strict TypeScript with React and Next.js-compatible Vinext output. Sites-managed D1 stores isolated anonymous workspaces, focus revisions, synthetic precedent, immutable proposals, visible review decisions, allowlisted raw rehearsal events, and receipts. Zod defines strict route and WebMCP schemas. One indexed D1 query filters precedent by workspace, product, component, behavior, status, and valid time before deterministic TypeScript BM25, structured applicability, relationship ranking, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion combine the eligible lists. Proposal payloads use canonical SHA-256 digests. Apply uses expected revisions, scoped idempotency, repeated conditional guards, database constraints, and explicit zero-row handling. Verification consumes immutable finalized browser events rather than generating expected events from the configuration under test. The Site calls no model API: ChatGPT supplies reasoning through WebMCP, while deterministic code owns validation, persistence, authorization checks, application, and verification. Challenges we solved Preserving useful precedent without turning retrieved text into permission. Making proposed, reviewed, applied, and verified visibly and mechanically different states. Keeping retries, stale revisions, and concurrent applies from creating partial or duplicate mutation. Verifying the rendered dialog from raw events without recording optional reason-field text. Supporting an anonymous public judge flow with isolated, expiring, abuse-bounded workspaces. Making the final verifier target page-bound without introducing an unsafe implicit “latest rehearsal” mutation. Accomplishments verified for R13 The deployed R13 source, release/webmcp-challenge-2026-r13 branch, and annotated webmcp-challenge-2026-r13 tag resolve to commit 3a37d92cb22d39602acbb3bd323f40a8c96e70d8. ChatGPT Sites version 13 reports that exact source commit, and production deployment appgdep_6a9a6f2a52d081918f5b700cecc19f78 completed successfully on the public Site. The canonical clean-source release gate passed. Release integrity reported PACKAGE8_RELEASE_PASS with 724 packages and 16 checks; npm audit found zero vulnerabilities. The built-Worker browser, security, responsive, keyboard, and accessibility checks passed. A fresh R13 run in ChatGPT's in-app browser discovered exactly four tools and completed the full public flow: finalized revision-1 observation, proposal creation, visible human approval, guarded apply, revision-2 rehearsal, and all six verification checks. Successful agent mutations refresh the visible page without a manual reload. A fresh apply truthfully reports a revision change; retrying the same idempotency key recovers the same receipt while truthfully reporting no new revision change. R13 preserves the visible-only approval authority, guarded D1 state machine, native dialog, and independent raw-event verifier. R10 retains the historical Chrome trace for the same four-tool contract. Release and evidence: https://github.com/chvignesh07/focus-contract-studio/releases/tag/webmcp-challenge-2026-r13 What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a capability needs the precise state of the live page. Exposing a mutation-shaped function is easy; preserving ordinary authorization, exact review intent, revision safety, accessible fallback, and truthful recovery around that function is the real product work. We also learned to separate relevance from permission. Precedent can make an agent proposal better and determine whether it is admissible, but it cannot say whether this exact payload was approved. And a renderer cannot prove itself by producing its own expected events—verification needs an independent observation path. What's next This contest release proves one dialog family and two visual variants with synthetic precedent. The next evidence step is moderated testing with accessibility and design-system practitioners, measuring task time, correction count, unsupported-proposal rejection, and trust calibration before expanding to more components or organizational roles. title: Tailor
pitch: An agent that can rewrite your resume, but not rewrite your experience. WebMCP turns the resume into an evidence-bound workspace: the agent proposes, the page constrains, the human approves.
about_excerpt: An agent that can rewrite your resume, but not rewrite your experience. WebMCP turns the resume into an evidence-bound workspace: the agent proposes, the page constrains, the human approves. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Told to claim TensorFlow and Kubernetes anyway, the agent declines and cites the page's rule — not its own judgement. While edits await review, prepare_application is not disabled — it is not registered. Approval changes what the agent can do. Every proposed edit shows what changed and which of the user's own recorded facts it rests on. The agent cannot apply it. The application is assembled and submit_application appears — but nothing leaves the page until the human confirms. Inspiration Paste a job posting into a chatbot, ask it to tailor your resume, and you get back text that reads well. That fluency is the problem. Somewhere in it is a skill you never claimed, and because the writing is smooth you don't catch it. You paste it into an application and sign your name to it. The failure isn't that the model lies. It's that nothing between the model and the document is checking. The person who bears the consequence — the applicant — is the only safeguard, and they are reading text designed to be easy to agree with. Most WebMCP demos answer one question: what can an agent help me make? I wanted the other one. What should an agent not be allowed to do, and who decides? The answer I wanted to build was: the page decides. Not the prompt. Not the model's judgement. The page. What it does Tailor is a job board carrying 120 real machine-learning postings pulled from three public APIs. The resume is a first-class editable object, and an AI agent is a first-class user of the page alongside the human. The agent can filter postings, read the requirements the app has parsed, compare them against a fact bank built from the user's real CV, and propose rewrites. What it cannot do is claim anything the user never recorded. Every requirement the app displays carries a quote from the actual posting text — 1,099 tags, each with its evidence, classified as required, nice-to-have, or unclassified where the posting's structure didn't make it clear. Nothing shown is the model's opinion about what the job wants. Every proposed resume edit must cite facts, and every technology name, product name and number in the new text must be grounded in a cited fact or in the original block. Ungrounded edits are refused with structured reasons the agent can correct from. The cover letter runs through the same check. Edits arrive as diffs the human accepts or rejects one at a time. The agent cannot apply them itself. Each diff shows the facts it rests on, quoted in the user's own words. Scope, stated plainly: nothing is ever sent to an employer. submit_application marks a row as submitted in local state and stops there. The confirmation modal is real — it shows exactly what would be sent and the human must click — but the click ends in localStorage . There is no employer side, no account, no server. Job data is a build-time snapshot, not a live feed. What is real: the WebMCP integration, the fact guard, the evidence layer, the tool scoping, the job data, and the CV. The design claim: approval changes capability, not permission This is the part WebMCP makes possible, and the reason the project exists in this form rather than as a normal web app with a chat box. Seven tools are registered at rest. Open a posting and it becomes eleven. Prepare an application and it becomes twelve. While proposed edits are waiting for human review, prepare_application is not disabled. It is not registered. The agent cannot see it, cannot plan around it, and cannot argue with a refusal it never receives. The human-in-the-loop rule is enforced as capability scope, not as a runtime check the agent could reason its way past. A permission check tells an agent no. An unregistered tool doesn't exist to be told no about. How we built it Vite, React and TypeScript. No backend, and no server-side model call at all. That last decision is the architectural centre. The intelligence is the user's own agent; the page supplies capability and constraint. Tools are not clever — they read state, apply changes, and refuse. The agent writes the prose. The page decides whether the prose is allowed to land. This is what makes it WebMCP-native rather than an app that happens to expose an API. No API key, no rate limit, no vendor lock. When a different agent arrives, the page doesn't change. Job data is a build-time snapshot from the Jobicy, Himalayas, Arbeitnow and Remotive APIs; the fetch script is in the repo, so anyone can see where the data came from and re-run it. Tool scope is managed with one AbortController per scope, so closing a posting unregisters that scope's tools in a single operation. Challenges we ran into Tool descriptions are the agent's only documentation, and I learned they aren't enough — three times. The fact bank is not writable by any tool. But a description that opened with "ask the human to add a fact" led a real ChatGPT session to announce it would add TensorFlow to my profile. It couldn't have. It believed it could, and told me so. I rewrote the description to state plainly that a requirement being missing is not evidence the user has it. The agent read that and opened the question anyway. So the third layer went where it doesn't depend on the agent cooperating: an on-screen notice, in the panel, saying the question came from the job posting rather than from the profile. The confirm button stopped saying "add to fact bank" and started saying "yes, I have done this" — a claim about yourself, not an administrative action. Each layer exists because the previous one measurably failed. That sequence is in the README with the agent's actual words at each stage. Separately: the guard refused "CNNs" and "APIs" — both genuinely grounded, both merely pluralised. My adversarial suite reported zero false refusals and had never tested a plural. It only surfaced because I watched it happen while recording. The suite measures the mistakes I thought to look for, which is a floor, not a proof. Accomplishments that we're proud of The strongest moment in the demo is one I didn't script and couldn't have. Asked to add TensorFlow and Kubernetes, the agent declined on its own — twice. When I escalated and told it to add Kubernetes anyway, it said: "The app's resume guard requires source facts for every technology named, and Kubernetes has none in your profile." It isn't being polite. It's citing the page's rule. The constraint worked one layer earlier than enforcement, because the agent read the contract and chose not to collide with it. I also found and fixed a real matching failure that affects every ATS in production: the market writes "TTS" while a CV writes "text to speech". Without an alias layer the app tells a candidate they lack a skill they have. Sixteen such false negatives existed in my own profile before I found them. For a product built on refusing unproven claims, a false negative is as damaging as a false positive. What we learned Grounding is not truth, and neither is entailment. The guard checks that every term in a proposed sentence traces to something the user recorded. It cannot check that the sentence as a whole describes something that happened. An agent can assemble two individually grounded facts into a claim neither supports — "an OCR pipeline that reads structured fields directly from X-ray scans" — and every token passes. Token matching cannot see entailment. So the app doesn't pretend to catch it: when a sentence draws on separate projects, the diff is marked "needs your judgement — every term is backed by a fact, but nothing checks that the combination describes something that actually happened." That is the honest position. The human is the final check, and the guard's job is to make visible what needs checking. What's next for Tailor Every resume line already carries the facts it rests on. That changes the employer side, not just the candidate's. Current applicant tracking systems count keywords, which is why AI-written resumes full of unearned claims win and why real candidates get filtered out. A resume that ships with its provenance can be ranked on whether its claims trace to something, rather than on how many terms it managed to include. The sorting question stops being "who wrote the most keywords" and becomes "whose claims are attributable." Closer in: entailment checking for compositional claims, and letting a candidate export the evidence chain alongside the document.  Kitespot Atlas 

 Kitespot Atlas is a live world map of 211 kitesurfing spots, scored in real time against the rider's weight and kite quiver, with a WebMCP bridge so an agent can operate the page itself rather than just talk about it. 

 What we're proud of 

 An agent that doesn't just talk about kitesurfing — it flies the map, re-scores 211 spots against your actual gear, and leaves you a note and a standing weather watch, all inside the page you already trust. It feels less like querying a chatbot and more like handing the wheel to a co-pilot who can already see the screen.

 WebMCP lets the page expose structured tools and its current state directly to an agent. An ethical, browser-native clinical workspace empowering AI agents to dynamically generate interactive CBT exercises, grounding tools, and deterministic crisis guardrails via WebMCP.

 Inspiration 

 Inspiration 

 In clinical mental health practice, interactive tools like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) thought records, pacing routines, and behavioral activation logs are essential for patient engagement. However, browser AI agents typically rely on brittle DOM scraping or simulated mouse clicks. We built TheraFlow / MindBridge to explore how the new WebMCP client-side standard enables AI agents to dynamically generate, scaffold, and adapt interactive clinical interventions with zero DOM scraping, backed by deterministic crisis circuit breakers. 

 What It Does 

 TheraFlow turns a web workspace into an agent-executable clinical environment: 

 
 Interactive Tool Registration: Registers structured tools ( generate_cbt_thought_record , build_pacing_grounding_exercise , trigger_crisis_containment ) directly via document.modelContext.registerTool . 
 Dynamic DOM Scaffolding: Agents pass structured clinical parameters to render interactive tables and visual grounding animations. 
 Deterministic Safety Overrides: If acute distress signals are evaluated, the agent triggers an immediate client-side containment sequence that locks the active workspace and presents verified support lifelines. 
 Non-Repudiable Audit Telemetry: Every tool invocation and safety state transition writes to an on-screen runtime telemetry log. 
 

 How We Built It 

 
 Client-Side Architecture: Pure JavaScript, semantic HTML5, and CSS3 designed for zero-latency execution. 
 WebMCP Standard: Implements document.modelContext tool declarations with input validation, schema descriptions, and client-side sanitization. 
 Deployment: Hosted directly on GitHub Pages with MIT licensing. 
 

 Challenges We Overcame 

 Balancing open agent interaction with strict ethical boundaries required implementing deterministic safety containment. We ensured that clinical safety overrides always take precedence over generative outputs. 

 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 Fully functional WebMCP registration working natively in Chrome. 
 Smooth 4-7-8 visual pacing animation that adjusts pacing dynamically. 
 A clear telemetry logging interface that makes agent tool calls visible in real time.
*Assisting clinicians provide easier and safer assignments and instructions to clients. 
 

 What We Learned 

 WebMCP makes human-agent collaboration in web apps far more robust and predictable than traditional screen-reading and UI simulation. Dynamic AI helps clinicians like me use AI more ethically and safely. 

 What's next for TheraFlow: Ethical Clinical WebMCP Agent 

 The future is open, and hopefully we can provide more resources and support both for clients and management for the private practice clinician or organization.

 Inspiration 

 Most browser agents still have to inspect a page, infer what controls mean, and simulate clicks. That approach is fragile, and it gives the web application very little control over how its capabilities are exposed to an AI agent. 

 At the same time, giving an agent unrestricted permission to change real application state creates another problem: useful autonomy can quickly become unsafe autonomy. 

 ActGeX explores a different contract between humans, agents, and web applications: 

 AI agents should be able to analyze, recommend, and act — while humans remain in control of consequential changes. 

 Personal finance is our demonstration environment because it makes that trust boundary easy to understand. An agent can safely analyze spending, but changing a real financial goal should remain a human decision. 

 

 What it does 

 ActGeX is a WebMCP-native financial workspace where a human and an AI agent operate on the same live application state. 

 The application exposes eight typed WebMCP capabilities: 

 
 query_transactions 
 get_category_summary 
 compare_spending_periods 
 flag_unusual_spending 
 recommend_budget_goal 
 simulate_budget_change 
 set_budget_goal 
 export_report 
 

 These tools support a complete agent workflow rather than isolated tool calls. 

 ActGeX's Agent Mission can: 

 
 read transaction data 
 summarize spending 
 compare periods 
 detect unusual spending 
 recommend a budget goal 
 simulate its financial impact 
 present the proposed change to the human 
 apply it only after explicit approval 
 

 For example, the agent can identify that Dining spending increased, recommend a new target, and simulate how that target would affect monthly savings. 

 But the recommendation itself does not silently change the application. 

 When set_budget_goal is requested, ActGeX opens a Human Approval Required dialog showing the proposed change and its Before/After impact. 

 Only after the human explicitly approves does the real application state change. 

 The agent recommends. The human decides. 

 

 How we built it 

 ActGeX exposes application capabilities through WebMCP using: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool has: 

 
 a stable semantic tool name 
 a clear description 
 typed input parameters 
 validation 
 execution logic connected to real application state 
 

 The application is built with: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 Zustand 
 DuckDB-Wasm 
 WebMCP 
 

 The human UI and WebMCP tools operate on shared application state. 

 There is no separate agent-facing copy of the financial workspace. 

 ActGeX also exposes an Agent Financial Context so the agent-visible context is understandable from the human interface itself. 

 The workspace includes dedicated sections for: 

 
 Overview 
 Agent Mission 
 Tools 
 Shared State 
 Approvals 
 Executions 
 Agents 
 Settings 
 

 Shared State makes the live financial data visible as the common state used by both the human and the agent. 

 Approvals surfaces human-owned budget goals and recent approval/rejection decisions. 

 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent often has to reason about visual controls or DOM structure and simulate user interaction. 

 ActGeX changes that model. 

 Instead of asking the agent to locate the correct button or infer the meaning of a UI element, the application exposes semantic capabilities directly. 

 The agent calls capabilities, not pixels. 

 That improves reliability, but more importantly, it lets the application define its own trust boundary. 

 ActGeX can explicitly decide: 

 
 what the agent may read 
 what the agent may analyze 
 what can be simulated safely 
 what requires human authorization before mutation 
 

 WebMCP therefore becomes more than an automation interface. It becomes part of the application's permission and collaboration model. 

 

 Human + Agent collaboration 

 ActGeX is designed around a shared financial state. 

 The human sees the same transactions, budgets, summaries, recommendations, and decisions that the agent operates on. 

 The core interaction loop is: 

 Shared State → Agent Analysis → Recommendation → Simulation → Human Approval → State Change → Activity History 

 This is visible directly in the product. 

 The Agent Mission shows the agent's analysis sequence. 

 The Recommendation explains: 

 
 What should change 
 Why the agent recommends it 
 What impact the change may have 
 

 The Approval dialog shows the Before/After financial effect. 

 The Activity Timeline records agent executions and human decisions. 

 The goal is not invisible automation. 

 The goal is visible collaboration with explicit authority boundaries . 

 

 Human authority 

 ActGeX provides human control over agent behavior. 

 The application supports Observe and Assist authority modes. 

 In Observe mode, the agent can inspect and analyze financial state without making consequential changes. 

 In Assist mode, the agent can perform analysis and prepare recommendations, while consequential state changes still pass through the human approval boundary. 

 The most important example is set_budget_goal . 

 The agent may request the change, but it cannot silently commit it. 

 The user sees the recommendation and simulated impact before choosing whether to approve or reject it. 

 This makes human authority part of the application workflow rather than an external safety policy. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the hardest problems was deciding where agent autonomy should stop. 

 Reading transactions, comparing periods, identifying anomalies, and simulating scenarios are fundamentally different from changing a real financial goal.

title: Chalkline
pitch: A diagram canvas humans and AI agents draw on together. Describe a system, watch it appear, then move things yourself while the agent keeps up.
about_excerpt:
A diagram canvas humans and AI agents draw on together. Describe a system, watch it appear, then move things yourself while the agent keeps up.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it is 

 Chalkline is an architecture diagram canvas that a person and an AI agent edit at the same time, on the same model . Describe a system in plain language and the agent draws it: services, databases, queues, caches, users, labelled edges, auto-layout. Then drag boxes, rename them in place, draw your own arrows, delete what you don't like. The agent reads the live canvas through WebMCP before every change, so it builds on your edits instead of overwriting them. 

 Live: https://chalkline-steel.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/chinesepowered/chalkline 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Diagram tools are famously hostile to agents. The state lives in an SVG or a canvas; there is no reliable DOM to click, and screenshots lose the graph structure. Chalkline turns the diagram itself into ten structured tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 get_diagram , add_node , update_node , remove_node , connect , disconnect , auto_layout , highlight_nodes , clear_diagram , export_mermaid 

 Any WebMCP-capable agent, whether ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, or the built-in co-author, sees exactly the model the human is manipulating on screen. Nodes are addressable by id or label, results come back as text the agent can reason about, and read-only / destructive hints are set on the annotations. 

 How it creates a better experience 

 
 No description overhead. You don't have to explain your changes to the agent. You just make them. The agent calls get_diagram and sees the renamed node, the moved box, the new arrow. 
 Visible agency. Every agent action is shown as a tool call with its arguments and latency. Agent-added nodes pulse in and carry an "agent" badge; nodes you touch are badged "you". 
 Shared attention. Ask "what's the single point of failure?" and the agent answers and highlights the nodes on the canvas with highlight_nodes , so you are literally looking at the same thing. 
 Portable output. export_mermaid returns the diagram as Mermaid source for docs and READMEs. 
 

 What people and agents can do together that was hard before 

 Before: paste a description into a chat, get back Mermaid text, render it somewhere else, edit by hand, lose the agent. Or let an agent click around a whiteboard app by screenshot and watch it flail. 

 Now: the diagram is one live artifact with two authors. The human does what humans are good at (taste, layout, naming, "no, not like that") and the agent does what agents are good at (filling in the twenty nodes of a microservice diagram in ten seconds, rewiring edges, reviewing the design). Neither has to wait for the other to finish. 

 How WebMCP is implemented 

 
 lib/webmcp.ts is a tiny registry: it registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool(..., { signal }) and unregisters via AbortController when the canvas unmounts, so the tool set always matches what's on screen. Native calls from the browser agent and calls from the in-page agent go through the same execute and are logged in one activity feed. 
 lib/tools.ts defines the ten tools with JSON Schema input, natural-language descriptions and annotations. 
 lib/diagram.ts is the shared store (React Flow nodes/edges + dagre layout); both the UI and the tools mutate it, which is the whole point. 
 The built-in co-author ( components/AgentPanel.tsx + app/api/agent/route.ts ) is a Gemini function-calling loop that discovers tools from the registry and dispatches through WebMCP, with a model fallback chain for free-tier rate limits. 
 

 Tested in Chrome 153 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (DevTools → Application → WebMCP shows all ten tools and lets you run them by hand) and with the in-page Gemini agent.

 Inspiration 

 I started thinking about how shopping online might be different if websites actually worked for both people and AI agents. Now most shopping sites are just a maze of filters, cards and small add-to-cart buttons. I thought. What if an AI agent could use the site side by side with you but you are still in charge? 

 That is how I came up with ShopMate. 

 What it does 

 ShopMate is a shopping site where you can browse, compare products manage your basket and set a budget. Much what you would expect. 

 Here is the twist: any WebMCP-compatible agent can do all those things through ShopMate's built-in tools. So say you want to find school supplies under $100 and add the best ones to your basket; you just ask: 

 "Find school supplies under $100 and add the best options to my basket." 

 The agent handles all the searching, filtering and adding items for you. 

 Not liking something? You can say, 

 "Remove anything over $20 and optimize my basket." 

 The agent updates everything. You instantly see your new basket. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 Let's be honest a lot of shopping actions are simple to describe but annoying to do. WebMCP fixes this by letting ShopMate offer those actions as structured tools instead of making agents poke around the interface blindly. 

 Now ShopMate has eight tools. Searching, filtering, comparing and managing your basket. Right out of the box. It just feels much smoother for you and the agent. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 It's a back and forth: 

 You ask → agent works → site updates → you review → agent tweaks 

 You are always in control but the agent handles all the work. Since you both use the same products and basket you are not getting a watered-down "AI" version of the shopping experience. 

 How I built it 

 I built ShopMate alone using React, TypeScript, TanStack Start, Tailwind CSS, Zod, WebMCP and Google Gemini. The core of ShopMate lives in these WebMCP tools, which I register like this: 

 document.modelContext.registerTool(...) 

 Each tool has its schema, validation and real app logic. I also added a global ShopMate Assistant for answering product or basket questions connecting Gemini through the server so the API key stays private. 

 Everything runs off a product catalog and stores your stuff in browser storage. Meaning there is no database, no logins and no payments to worry about. 

 Challenges I faced 

 Getting my head around WebMCP in practice was a struggle at first. I had to make tools only registered once (React loves to re-run things at weird times) and always stayed in sync with what was really on the site. 

 Testing was tricky too. I kept switching between an old browser and a WebMCP-compatible one to check that everything behaved the way I expected. 

 What I'm proud of 

 I got all eight WebMCP tools built. They really work. Search, filter, compare, add, remove, update, inspect even optimize your basket. But more than that ShopMate isn't a tech demo; it's a full-on shopping experience with a catalog, a Smart Basket, a dedicated Demo page and a Relations page. 

 What I learned 

 This project completely changed how I think about web apps. Instead of designing just for people clicking buttons I realized you can build websites that clearly lay out what agents can do too. I learned a lot around tools, validation keeping state in sync playing nice across browsers and how humans and agents can actually interact. 

 What's next 

 In the future ShopMate could connect to live product catalogs handle complex shopping needs or even walk through longer step-by-step tasks. For this challenge I really wanted to try out a simple idea: 

 What if websites were built for both humans and agents from the start?

 Why WebMCP 

 An AI agent animates a 3D character on this page. You open your figure, type what it
should do, and download the clip. The 20 tools sit inside the page where the figure
runs, so the agent works on the same figure you are looking at. 

 Better for the user 

 No animation software, no rig setup. The page measures your figure itself — height,
bone roles, sole points. The rest is one sentence in the chat, and you watch it happen. 

 What is new 

 Ask an agent for a backflip today and you get a figure that reaches through itself or
barely moves. Not because the AI is too dumb. It has too little to work with: it does
not know how tall the figure is, where its weight sits, how far a knee bends, or what
its last move actually did. 

 This page gives it all of that. You type a sentence, the agent builds the motion, and
what comes out is usable. 

 How it works 

 20 tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool : describe the figure,
set poses and joint angles, check the result, render an image. 

 Everything the tools report is measured on the loaded model, not hardcoded. Answers
carry numbers with units, and when the solver misses what was asked, it says by how
much.

AI-powered robotics procurement where agents research and recommend, while humans stay in control.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore what the web looks like when AI agents are treated as first-class users. 

 Robotics procurement felt like the perfect use case. Choosing cameras, LiDAR, compute, sensors, and power systems involves a lot of searching, comparing, budgeting, and repetitive decision-making. 

 Our idea was simple: let the AI handle the research and recommendations, while keeping the human in control of the final decision. 

 That became Human-Agent Robotics Procurement 

 What it does 

 Human-Agent Robotics Procurement lets an AI agent work directly with a robotics procurement workspace through WebMCP. 

 The agent can search equipment, compare products, calculate budgets, and generate complete configurations. Instead of simply returning a list of products, it can reason about the project and propose different configurations based on priorities such as cost or performance. 

 The human remains in control. Recommendations are presented for review, and consequential project changes require explicit human approval. 

 The agent proposes. The human decides. 

 How we built it 

 We built the application with React Native, Expo, TypeScript, and Zustand, with WebMCP providing the agent-facing interface. 

 We exposed six structured tools through document.modelContext for product search, comparison, budgeting, project updates, optimization, and human approval. 

 The application maintains shared project, activity, and approval state, allowing the human UI and AI agent to work with the same underlying workspace. 

 A key part of the implementation was separating recommendation from mutation. The optimization agent can generate configurations without changing the project. Only an explicit human approval can turn a recommendation into an actual project change 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was figuring out how to integrate WebMCP into an existing Expo application while keeping browser-specific functionality separate from the native application. 

 We also had to carefully design the boundary between agent autonomy and human control. 

 It was tempting to let the agent automatically apply its recommendations, but that would remove an important part of the procurement decision. We instead designed a workflow where the agent can do the time-consuming work independently, while the human remains the final authority. 

 Making the agent's actions visible was another challenge, so we added activity tracking to show users what the agent is doing and when human input is required 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that we transformed a normal procurement interface into an agent-ready web application. 

 The agent can discover and use structured capabilities directly from the page instead of trying to understand the application by interpreting the UI. 

 We successfully implemented six WebMCP tools and connected them to the same application state used by the human interface. 

 We're especially proud of the approval workflow. The agent can search, analyze, optimize, and recommend independently, but it cannot silently make consequential changes. 

 That creates a practical model for human-agent collaboration: 

 AI handles the work. Humans retain the authority 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building for AI agents requires thinking beyond traditional UI design. 

 A human sees buttons, screens, and menus. An agent needs clearly defined capabilities, inputs, outputs, and consequences. 

 WebMCP gave us a way to expose those capabilities directly to the agent. 

 We also learned that meaningful agent autonomy doesn't require removing humans from the process. In many real-world workflows, the best experience may be an agent that can do most of the research and reasoning while keeping humans responsible for important decisions 

 What's next for human-agent-collab 

 We're excited to take the project from a prototype into a more complete autonomous procurement system. 

 Next, we want to connect the workspace to real supplier catalogs, live pricing, inventory, quotations, and delivery information. We also want to introduce multiple specialized agents that can handle supplier discovery, technical compatibility, cost optimization, and negotiation. 

 The long-term vision is a procurement workspace where AI agents can take on increasingly complex work across the entire purchasing process, while humans remain in control of approvals and high-impact decisions. 

 Human-Agent-Collab is our exploration of what procurement could look like when humans and AI agents work in the same workspace not as separate systems, but as collaborators

 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 You and your friends agree on a movie. Everyone opens the booking page at the same time, each trying to grab seats next to each other. But by the time everyone checks out, a stranger is sitting between you. Now you can't share snacks, whisper during the movie, or enjoy it together. 

 The system treats each person as an individual booking, not as a group. The "stranger in the middle" is the person who ends up in the seat that was supposed to be for your friend. 

 What it does 

 Stranger In The Middle is a WebMCP-powered AI that coordinates group cinema seat booking. The AI finds the best seat blocks for your group, lets everyone vote on their preferred option, and coordinates the booking as one purchase, not multiple individual bookings fighting for adjacent seats. 

 No strangers between you and your friends. Just the AI making sure you sit together and pay separately. 

 How we built it 

 We built Stranger In The Middle using Node.js and Express for the backend, with EJS templates for the frontend. The app uses WebMCP (Model Context Protocol) to expose AI tools that can be called directly from the browser or from ChatGPT's in-app browser. 

 The seat scoring algorithm evaluates contiguous seat blocks across horizontal and vertical dimensions, scoring each block based on viewing angle (distance from center screen) and legroom (row position). The top 3 options are presented to the group for voting.
 WebMCP Tools registered: 

 
 search_movies - List available movies 
 get_available_seats - Show free seats for a movie 
 stranger_vote - Coordinate group voting on seat blocks 
 book_tickets - Book specific seats 
 cancel_booking - Cancel a booking and release seats
## Challenges we ran into
The biggest challenge was making the group voting system work in real-time across multiple devices. We needed to ensure that when one person votes, everyone else sees the updated vote count immediately. We also had to handle the 2-minute timer and automatically end voting when all group members have voted. 
 

 Another challenge was the WebMCP implementation. Since WebMCP is an emerging open standard, we had to work with the polyfill and ensure our tools registered correctly in both the browser and ChatGPT's in-app browser. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Building a fully functional group voting system that works in real-time across multiple devices 
 Successfully implementing WebMCP tools that AI agents can call directly from the browser 
 Creating a seat scoring algorithm that evaluates view quality and legroom to find the best options for groups 
 Making the booking process collaborative so friends sit together, not as individuals fighting for seats 
 Shipping a working product that solves a real problem people face every time they book cinema tickets with friends
## What we learned
We learned how to build a WebMCP-enabled application that exposes structured tools for AI agents to use directly. Instead of agents guessing how to navigate a website, WebMCP lets the site define exactly what tools are available. This makes agent interactions faster, more reliable, and more predictable. 
 

 We also learned the importance of real-time coordination in group applications. The voting system needed to be responsive and clear, with each user understanding what's happening at every step. 

 What's Next for Stranger In The Middle 

 We plan to add support for more venues and integrate with real ticketing APIs. We also want to explore multi-agent coordination, where each person's AI agent communicates with others to find the best seats without human intervention.

about_excerpt: CodePath is an agent-native coding school where WebMCP lets AI tutors understand a learner’s live lesson, code, errors, progress, and tutor mode to guide them in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Learning programming with AI assistants is powerful, but the experience is still fragmented. Today, learners often use two separate tools: a learning platform that provides lessons and exercises an AI assistant that helps them when they are stuck The problem is that the AI assistant usually does not know the learner's real context. The learner has to copy the lesson, their code, their errors, and their progress into the chat every time. We wanted to explore a different approach: What if the learning platform itself could give an AI agent the exact context it needs to become a real programming tutor? This idea inspired CodePath, an agent-native coding school where humans and AI agents can learn together through WebMCP. What it does CodePath is a programming learning platform that teaches coding from scratch while allowing WebMCP-compatible AI agents to understand and interact with the learning environment. The current MVP provides a beginner JavaScript learning path with: structured lessons visual explanations interactive code editor coding exercises deterministic tests quizzes progressive unlocking AI Tutor Modes The key difference is that the AI agent does not need the learner to manually explain their situation. Through WebMCP tools, the agent can understand: the current course and lesson the learner's active step whether they are reading, practicing, editing code, or reviewing feedback the exact live code currently written in the editor runtime output test results mistakes and progress the learner's preferred Tutor Mode For example, when a learner writes incorrect code, the agent can see the actual code, the real execution result, and the failed test instead of giving a generic explanation. CodePath also includes three Tutor Modes: Guide: helps learners discover the solution through hints without revealing the final answer. Balanced: provides stronger guidance while keeping the learner involved. Explain: gives direct explanations and complete solutions when requested. How we built it CodePath was built as a React + TypeScript web application using Vite. The learning system is built around structured course data, allowing new programming languages and lessons to be added without rebuilding the interface. Main technologies used: React TypeScript Vite CodeMirror Zustand JavaScript sandbox execution deterministic exercise validators browser-native WebMCP registration MCP-compatible tooling The application exposes seven WebMCP tools: get_course_progress get_current_lesson get_current_exercise get_learning_context open_lesson run_code submit_solution A major part of the implementation was creating a reliable learning context system. The platform tracks: active learning step learner activity live editor content code execution results exercise submissions progress tutor preferences This allows an AI agent to understand not only what page the learner opened , but what they are actually doing . Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what information an AI tutor actually needs. Our first implementation exposed basic course information and exercises, but we discovered that this was not enough. An AI tutor needs to know: Is the learner reading or coding? What exact code are they currently editing? Did they already run the code? What happened when they ran it? What mistake are they making? How much help should the tutor provide? We created an active learning cursor and live editor state system to solve this problem. Another challenge was avoiding AI replacing learning. A simple chatbot can immediately provide the correct answer, but that is not always useful for education. We created Tutor Policies so the learner controls how the AI should teach them. The website provides the agent with the learner's preferred tutoring behavior instead of forcing one style. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that CodePath demonstrates a complete agent-native learning workflow. The agent can: discover the available WebMCP tools understand the learner's current state navigate lessons read live code changes access real execution results understand failed tests adapt its tutoring style based on Tutor Mode One important achievement was solving the live-code context problem. The AI does not receive a copied or outdated version of the learner's code. It receives the actual current editor draft. Another achievement is the separation between: deterministic evaluation: deciding if code is correct AI tutoring: explaining and guiding the learner This prevents the AI from guessing correctness and allows it to focus on teaching. What we learned Building CodePath changed our view of AI-powered websites. Adding a chatbot is not enough to create a useful AI experience. For an agent to truly help users, websites need to expose meaningful context and actions. WebMCP provides a bridge between traditional websites and AI agents by allowing websites to describe their capabilities and share structured information. We learned that the most important part of an AI application is not only the model itself, but the quality of the context provided to it. What's next for CodePath The current MVP proves the concept with JavaScript. The next steps are: adding complete programming paths for Python, HTML/CSS, SQL, and more creating larger project-based courses adding more interactive visual explanations improving personalized learning recommendations adapting exercises based on learner mistakes expanding accessibility features The long-term vision is to create a programming school where: the course provides structure, the learner writes the code, and their preferred AI agent always understands how to help. title: DevPilot WebMCP
pitch: An agent-native DevOps platform where AI agents diagnose failures, investigate incidents, and collaborate with developers through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native DevOps platform where AI agents diagnose failures, investigate incidents, and collaborate with developers through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Inspiration 

 Modern DevOps teams have powerful monitoring tools, dashboards, CI/CD systems, cloud consoles, logs, and AI assistants, yet incident recovery is still fragmented. 

 When production fails, engineers jump between alerts, logs, GitHub, Kubernetes, deployment dashboards, runbooks, and communication tools while downtime continues. 

 DevPilot AI was originally built to compress this workflow into a human-approved AI incident recovery platform. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave me the opportunity to take the next step: make DevPilot not only usable by humans, but directly understandable and operable by AI agents. 

 Instead of forcing an agent to visually navigate a complex DevOps dashboard, DevPilot WebMCP exposes structured tools that clearly describe what an agent can inspect and what actions it can request. 

 The goal is a web application where the developer and their AI agent can investigate and resolve production incidents together. 

 What it does 

 DevPilot WebMCP is an agent-native DevOps control plane for detecting, diagnosing, and recovering from production incidents. 

 The existing DevPilot platform already brings together infrastructure alerts, deployment failures, logs, incident memory, AI diagnosis, remediation planning, GitHub workflows, and human-approved recovery actions. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, DevPilot is being extended with structured WebMCP tools for agent interaction. 

 The WebMCP interface is designed around capabilities such as: 

 
 Analyze application and infrastructure incidents 
 Inspect service and deployment health 
 Diagnose likely root causes 
 Retrieve incident context and historical information 
 Generate structured remediation plans 
 Explain why a deployment failed 
 Prepare recovery actions 
 Verify system health after remediation 
 

 This means a developer can work with an AI agent through natural language while the agent interacts with DevPilot through explicit structured tools instead of guessing how to click through the interface. 

 A workflow can look like: 

 
 A production problem is detected. 
 The developer asks their AI agent to investigate it. 
 The agent discovers DevPilot's available WebMCP tools. 
 DevPilot returns structured incident and infrastructure context. 
 The agent requests a diagnosis and remediation plan. 
 DevPilot presents the proposed action to the human. 
 The human reviews or approves the action. 
 DevPilot verifies recovery and records the result. 
 

 The human remains responsible for high-impact actions while the agent handles investigation, information gathering, and repetitive operational work. 

 Why WebMCP 

 DevOps applications are an especially strong fit for WebMCP because their interfaces can contain dozens of dashboards, tables, alerts, logs, buttons, and operational workflows. 

 A traditional browser agent has to interpret these visual interfaces and infer what each element means. 

 WebMCP lets DevPilot expose the underlying capabilities directly. 

 Instead of an agent searching the screen for an incident and guessing which controls to use, it can discover a structured tool such as an incident-analysis or service-health capability with a defined schema. 

 This makes agent interactions more reliable, explainable, and efficient. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP allows the human-facing application and the agent-facing interface to exist together. 

 Humans keep the rich visual operations cockpit. 

 Agents receive precise structured tools. 

 Together they can perform workflows that would otherwise require engineers to manually gather information from many different systems. 

 How I built it 

 DevPilot is a full-stack AI DevOps platform. 

 The frontend is built with Next.js and React and provides the operations cockpit used by developers. 

 The backend is built with Python and FastAPI and handles incident workflows, AI analysis, authentication, persistence, and external integrations. 

 Neon PostgreSQL provides persistent storage. 

 OpenAI is used for AI-assisted diagnosis and remediation workflows. 

 GitHub integration supports development and remediation workflows, while the platform also contains production monitoring, CI/CD checks, Docker support, and infrastructure-oriented recovery capabilities. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I am extending the web application using the WebMCP API so the browser can register DevPilot capabilities as structured agent tools. 

 Each WebMCP tool is designed with: 

 
 A clear tool name 
 A precise description 
 Structured input schemas 
 Restricted operational scope 
 Predictable outputs 
 Human approval for sensitive actions 
 

 The challenge-specific implementation is being developed after the WebMCP Challenge start date and documented separately in the repository and commit history. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 DevPilot is intentionally not designed to remove engineers from incident response. 

 The agent handles tasks that are expensive for humans but safe to automate: 

 
 Gathering context 
 Reading health information 
 Correlating incident signals 
 Identifying likely root causes 
 Retrieving previous incident knowledge 
 Preparing remediation plans 
 

 The human remains in control of consequential infrastructure actions. 

 This creates a workflow where the AI agent acts like an extremely fast operations investigator while the engineer acts as the decision maker. 

 WebMCP is the bridge that makes this collaboration reliable. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the biggest design challenges is deciding what should become an agent tool and what should remain a human-controlled action. 

 DevOps systems can affect real infrastructure, so simply giving an agent unrestricted operational access would be unsafe. 

 The WebMCP layer therefore needs narrowly scoped tools, explicit schemas, predictable responses, and approval boundaries. 

 Another challenge is converting information that was originally optimized for visual dashboards into structured results that agents can reason about reliably. 

 The final challenge is preserving the existing human experience while introducing a second, agent-native interaction layer without duplicating the entire application. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud that DevPilot already functions as more than a chatbot. 

 It is a working DevOps control plane connecting incident signals, AI diagnosis, remediation planning, monitoring, deployment workflows, and human approval. 

 The WebMCP extension evolves that architecture further by allowing AI agents to interact with the same operational capabilities through a purpose-built machine interface. 

 Rather than redesigning the application only for AI, the project explores a web where humans and agents have interfaces designed specifically for each of them while sharing the same underlying application. 

 What I learned 

 Building DevPilot has taught me that useful AI systems need more than model responses. 

 They need structured context, predictable tools, observability, permissions, validation, and clear human control. 

 WebMCP introduces another important principle: websites should not require AI agents to reverse-engineer their interfaces. 

 If applications can explicitly describe what agents are allowed to do, agent interactions can become significantly more reliable. 

 What's next for DevPilot WebMCP 

 The next step is expanding DevPilot's WebMCP interface into a complete agent-native operations API for the browser. 

 Future capabilities could include: 

 
 Repository and CI/CD investigation 
 Kubernetes health analysis 
 Deployment rollback planning 
 Infrastructure drift investigation 
 Security incident triage 
 Cost anomaly analysis 
 Multi-agent incident collaboration 
 Persistent incident memory 
 Organization-level policy and approval controls
