title: RippleTrace
pitch: RippleTrace lets agents investigate enterprise evidence and propose remediation via WebMCP, while humans retain review and approval-making change discoverable, verifiable, and safe to execute.
about_excerpt:
RippleTrace lets agents investigate enterprise evidence and propose remediation via WebMCP, while humans retain review and approval-making change discoverable, verifiable, and safe to execute.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Overview 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 The idea for RippleTrace came from my experience working at a software company. Whenever a feature, configuration change, or update was pushed to production, I watched DevOps engineers manually check multiple platforms to trace its potential consequences. 

 They had to move between deployment dashboards, monitoring tools, logs, incident systems, and other services to understand whether the change had caused something downstream to fail. The information was available, but it was fragmented across different interfaces. During a production incident, every minute spent switching platforms and reconstructing context mattered. 

 That experience inspired RippleTrace: a faster way to trace the ripple effects of a production change, understand which systems may be affected, and identify where an investigation should begin. 

 What it does 

 RippleTrace helps engineering and DevOps teams investigate the potential impact of production changes from one place. 

 A user can begin with a deployment, commit, service, or incident. RippleTrace then gathers the relevant signals, connects related events, and presents them as a single investigation trail. Instead of manually checking every platform, the user can follow the path of a change and see how it may have affected the wider system. 

 RippleTrace is designed to help answer questions such as: 

 
 What changed immediately before an issue appeared? 
 Which services or dependencies could be affected? 
 Are errors, alerts, or other events connected to the deployment? 
 What should the team investigate first? 
 What evidence can be shared with the rest of the team? 
 

 The goal is not to replace engineers’ judgment. It is to reduce the repetitive work required to collect context so engineers can spend more time understanding and resolving the actual problem. 

 How we built it 

 We built RippleTrace as a unified investigation experience for production changes. It organizes information from different engineering platforms into a consistent model of changes, services, events, and possible consequences. 

 We used WebMCP to make the product’s capabilities directly understandable to AI agents. RippleTrace exposes structured tools that describe the actions an agent can perform and the information it can retrieve. 

 This allows an AI assistant to work with explicit application capabilities instead of attempting to interpret the interface through screenshots, page text, or fragile click sequences. An agent can request relevant deployment context, examine related signals, and help the user navigate an investigation through well-defined inputs and outputs. 

 The human-facing dashboard and the WebMCP tool layer operate on the same underlying context. This means users can visually inspect the evidence while an AI assistant helps them explore it. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was connecting information from platforms that represent the same incident in very different ways. A deployment, an alert, an error, and a service may all have different identifiers and timestamps. Establishing useful relationships between them requires careful normalization and correlation. 

 Another challenge was determining how much confidence RippleTrace should place in a possible connection. Events that occur close together are not necessarily related. We therefore designed the experience to present evidence and potential relationships without claiming certainty where it does not exist. 

 Designing the WebMCP tools was also an important challenge. Each tool needed to be focused enough for an agent to use reliably while still returning enough context to support a meaningful investigation. Clear descriptions, predictable parameters, and structured responses were essential. 

 Finally, we had to keep the AI workflow transparent. Production investigations are high-stakes, so users should be able to see why something was surfaced and verify the underlying evidence themselves. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that much of incident response is not a lack of data—it is a lack of connected context. Teams already have valuable information, but it is distributed across tools that were designed for separate stages of the software lifecycle. 

 We also learned that building an agent-ready web application requires more than placing a conversational interface on top of it. An effective AI experience needs clearly defined capabilities, structured data, useful metadata, and strong boundaries. 

 WebMCP provides a practical way to expose those capabilities directly from the web application. It gives an AI agent a shared language for interacting with the product while keeping the user in control. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that RippleTrace turns a fragmented, multi-platform investigation into a more coherent workflow. 

 We created an experience that supports both people and AI agents: engineers can inspect the information visually, while agents can access the same capabilities through structured WebMCP tools. We are also proud that the product focuses on assisting human decision-making rather than hiding the investigation behind an unexplained AI answer. 

 Most importantly, RippleTrace was built around a real problem we observed in production environments—the time and effort engineers spend tracing the consequences of every change. 

 What's next for RippleTrace 

 Next, we want to expand the number of platforms and data sources that RippleTrace can connect with. We also plan to improve event correlation, service-dependency mapping, investigation timelines, and team collaboration. 

 Future versions could proactively identify unusual signals after a deployment, compare current behavior with previous releases, generate incident summaries, and recommend the most relevant next steps. We also want to add configurable policies so organizations can control which actions AI agents may perform and what information they can access. 

 Our long-term goal is for RippleTrace to become the starting point for every production investigation: one place where teams can trace a change, understand its ripple effects, and respond with confidence.

title: AuraQL — Zero-Server AI Analytics Engine
pitch: Zero-server in-browser OLAP analytics studio where AI agents execute sub-10ms SQL and manipulate live dashboard visualizations in real time via WebMCP.\n\n
about_excerpt:
Zero-server in-browser OLAP analytics studio where AI agents execute sub-10ms SQL and manipulate live dashboard visualizations in real time via WebMCP.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 🔮 Inspiration: The Broken Cloud Analytics Paradox 

 Traditional cloud business intelligence requires piping sensitive customer records, financial logs, and transaction streams to remote third-party databases. When analysts consult AI, language models frequently hallucinate arithmetic calculations on large datasets. 

 We built AuraQL to completely invert this paradigm: 

 
 Zero-Server In-Browser OLAP : The columnar database and vectorized SQL evaluator run 100% inside your client-side browser tab memory. 
 Deterministic AI Math : The AI agent writes the SQL query, but the in-browser engine evaluates aggregations (SUM, AVG, COUNT, STDDEV) in under 10 milliseconds with mathematical accuracy. 
 WebMCP Dual-Control Canvas : Both the human user and AI agent collaborate simultaneously on the same dashboard canvas via the emerging open standard document.modelContext . 
 

 

 ⚡ Why Our Use Case is a Strong Fit for WebMCP 

 Analytics dashboards are notoriously difficult for computer-vision and click-based agents: DOM selectors break, dynamic canvas elements cannot be inspected, and SVG splines are opaque to LLMs. 

 WebMCP provides the ideal interface: 

 
 Instead of brittle DOM scraping, AuraQL exposes structured analytical primitives directly to the agent. 
 The agent calls list_tables_and_schema to discover table schemas and column datatypes. 
 It evaluates relational SQL via execute_sql_query . 
 It commands the user's viewport directly via render_interactive_chart and apply_dashboard_filter . 
 

 

 🚀 How It Creates a Better User Experience 

 
 100% Client-Side Privacy : Financial data and customer churn metrics never leave the user's browser RAM. Zero cloud data storage costs, zero telemetry tracking, and zero database credentials to expose. 
 Sub-10ms Latency : Queries against columnar memory buffers execute faster than a network roundtrip to a cloud data warehouse. 
 Co-Pilot Simultaneous Vision : When you ask the agent a question like "Show quarterly revenue breakdown by region as a bar chart" , the dashboard mutates in real time before your eyes while the agent explains the business takeaways. 
 Pro Studio Interface : Dual-axis resizable grid windows, high-contrast borders (black in light mode, neon purple in dark mode), and drag-and-drop CSV/JSON ingestion. 
 

 

 🤝 What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Impossible Before 

 
 Natural Language Scenario Simulation : Humans specify hypothetical business conditions ( "What if critical churn accounts decrease 25% and MRR increases 15%?" ). The agent calls simulate_forecast_scenario to execute in-memory adjustments and render baseline vs. projected variance charts immediately. 
 Instant Statistical Anomaly Isolation : The agent uses detect_anomalies to calculate Z-scores ($|Z| \ge 1.85$) and Interquartile Ranges (IQR) directly in browser memory, isolating revenue spikes or margin compression without needing Python or external Jupyter notebooks. 
 True Cross-Platform Agent Access : The exact same WebMCP tools are available inside:

 
 ChatGPT’s native in-app browser ( document.modelContext ) 
 Desktop ChatGPT & Claude Desktop via Server-Sent Events ( /sse ) 
 OpenAI Codex CLI over Stdio JSON-RPC 2.0 
 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Implemented WebMCP 

 AuraQL implements the official W3C WebMCP specification: 

 
 Native Browser Standard : Inspects document.modelContext on mount and registers 6 analytical tools: 

 
 list_tables_and_schema (Schema & metadata discovery) 
 execute_sql_query (Columnar SQL aggregations) 
 render_interactive_chart (Viewport visualization mutation) 
 apply_dashboard_filter (Cohort isolation) 
 simulate_forecast_scenario (What-if financial modeling) 
 detect_anomalies (Statistical anomaly detection) 
 
 Universal Polyfill & Bridge : 

 
 If running in standard Chrome or without native browser flags, AuraQL binds a spec-compliant fallback to document.modelContext and window.modelContext . 
 An external Node.js WebMCP bridge deployed on Render ( scripts/mcp-bridge.mjs ) synchronizes with the active browser tab via Server-Sent Events ( /api/bridge/events ) with 25-second keepalive heartbeats, allowing desktop clients (Codex CLI, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT Desktop) to steer the live web app remotely.

 WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) 
 TypeScript & React 
 In-Memory Columnar OLAP Engine 
 Vite & Tailwind CSS 
 Node.js MCP Bridge (SSE + Stdio) 
 Vercel (Frontend Hosting) 
 Render (WebMCP Server Hosting)

title: EasyTax - Your convenient tax WebMCP
pitch: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission.
about_excerpt: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates The Problem Filing an annual individual tax return (1770 S) under Indonesia's centralized Coretax system creates a learning curve for salaried workers. Translating personal life events into rigid government tax classifications creates a high burden and confusion across generations. Knowing your salary or family situation is different from knowing which tax field or classification it belongs in. While the system offers spreadsheet bulk uploads to bypass manual entry, they frequently fail due to minor error, forcing users back to rework manual entry or exposing them to server timeouts during peak traffic. Independent sentiment analysis of over 53,000 digital conversations during the early rollout Coretax system revealed that 39% of user sentiment was negative, driven by procedural confusion and system navigation (Source: Journal UII / 2025 ). Despite these points, the submission is massive. By late April 2026, over 13 million annual tax returns were filed following the activation of nearly 12.9 million individual accounts (Source: Tempo.co ). The Solution: Human-Agent Collaboration via WebMCP This project demonstrates how WebMCP can turn a complex tax administration portal into a collaborative interface. Rather than hiding the form's complexity or forcing users to navigate hidden form logic, the browser exposes section-level tools directly to the assistant, keeping the detailed form visible to ensure user review control capability. The Workflow Conversational Extraction: The assistant conducts a plain-language interview to extract necessary tax facts such as salary, deductions, and family status without requiring users to memorize form codes or tax classifications. They can use their own ways to describe their condition and an AI assistant will translate it. For example, when a user says, “My employer was PT Nusantara Digital, gross salary 180 million for the year, 6 million in pay deductions,” WebMCP translates it into: “Records the employment slip, derives net income, recomputes the tax.” Deterministic State Updates: As facts are confirmed, the assistant invokes section-level WebMCP tools (such as updating taxpayer profiles, recording employment, or adding cash and assets). The website itself handles all validation, calculation, and conditional branching, deriving fields like PTKP (e.g., K/1) and recomputing the tax balance automatically. Manual Submission: Final review, resolution of data conflicts, declaration, and submission remain strictly manual. No tool can execute a final filing, and the assistant explicitly states this if asked. title: Wayfinder
pitch: An agent-native trip planner where people, browser agents, and a live map stay in sync.
about_excerpt: An agent-native trip planner where people, browser agents, and a live map stay in sync. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a trip is naturally collaborative, but most trip tools treat an AI agent as a separate interface. I wanted to explore what becomes possible when a person, their browser agent, and the app itself can all work from the same live plan and map. What it does Wayfinder turns a rough idea—like “a rainy Sunday in Porto with kids”—into a map-ready trip plan. It asks focused follow-up questions about timing, companions, budget, interests, and accessibility, then finds relevant places and keeps the conversation, plan, itinerary, and live map in sync. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can start or resume a trip, answer the guided interview using the visitor’s preferences, update the plan, ask Wayfinder’s place specialist questions, read the itinerary, and move the map—without scraping the UI. How I built it Wayfinder is built with Laravel, Vue, Inertia.js, and WebMCP. The Laravel assistant guides trip discovery, saves structured plans, geocodes named places with Nominatim, and searches OpenStreetMap data through Overpass. Vue manages the interactive conversation and map experience. I implemented 18 WebMCP tools: two safe guest-only navigation tools and 16 authenticated trip, chat, itinerary, and map tools. Tools are registered reactively according to the visitor’s login state and current trip phase, so agents only see capabilities that are relevant and safe at that moment. Challenges I ran into The core challenge was making WebMCP useful in a genuinely stateful product. A trip planner has many moving parts: the active discovery question, saved preferences, conversation history, selected trip, itinerary, and map viewport. I needed browser-agent actions to remain synchronized with the person’s visible experience. I also needed to avoid exposing overly broad tools or handling credentials through agent tools. My solution was phase-aware, typed tools that reuse the visitor’s existing session and return structured results. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built a complete trip-planning experience rather than a WebMCP proof of concept. A person can begin planning manually, let an agent continue from the same state, refine the plan, and see changes immediately on the live map. I am especially proud of the tool design: WebMCP is integrated into the product journey, not bolted on. Tools appear and disappear as the experience changes, with read-only actions marked appropriately and guest tools limited to opening authentication UI. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools represent meaningful product actions and current context—not just a remote-control layer for UI buttons. I also learned that agent collaboration needs clear boundaries. Typed tools, phase-aware availability, and explicit read/write distinctions make the experience more reliable for agents while keeping people in control. What's next for Wayfinder Next, I want to deepen the planning experience with richer itinerary editing, better preference memory, collaborative planning for groups, and more local discovery sources. I also want to explore more agent-native flows: letting a visitor’s agent compare options, coordinate constraints across a group, and proactively suggest refinements while Wayfinder remains the specialist for trip context, places, and the live map. title: GraphContract
pitch: Design agent behavior together—before it becomes code.
about_excerpt: Design agent behavior together—before it becomes code. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Agent workflows are usually reviewed after they have already become code, prompts, and framework-specific configuration. At that point, important decisions such as branching, tool use, approval gates, parallel work, retries, and failure paths are scattered across files and difficult to understand as one system. I built GraphContract because I wanted humans and coding agents to agree on agent behavior before implementation—not debug that agreement afterward. What it does GraphContract is a human-governed planning layer for agent systems. It gives a person and a coding agent a shared visual canvas where they can design, review, revise, and freeze an agent workflow as a structured contract. A user can start from a blank canvas or a reusable workflow pattern. A coding agent reads the currently accepted graph through WebMCP and proposes a structured revision. GraphContract renders that candidate separately, shows what was added, changed, or removed, and keeps the accepted graph locked until the human decides what happens next. The human can inspect the proposal, request changes, approve it, or reject it. Once the contract is accepted, GraphContract derives deterministic branch scenarios, lets the user inspect each route on the canvas, freezes the reviewed contract, and exports implementation handoff artifacts. The canvas supports typed Start, Task, Agent, Tool, Human, Merge, End, and Subgraph structures; normal, conditional, command, fallback, bounded-loop, and dynamic Send ×N routing; human-in-the-loop gates; sensitive-effect policies; deterministic scenarios; and a read-only runtime projection. How WebMCP powers the collaboration GraphContract deliberately exposes exactly three browser-native WebMCP tools: get_graph reads the accepted contract, its revision identity, validation state, and outstanding human feedback. propose_graph_changes submits typed operations against a known revision and produces a review-only candidate. get_branch_scenarios reads the deterministic paths derived from the accepted graph. The small tool surface is intentional. The agent can inspect and propose, but it cannot approve, reject, freeze, unfreeze, answer human gates, control runtime execution, or download artifacts. Those actions remain visible and human-owned in the interface. This is where WebMCP adds real value. A graph has stable identities, topology, validation rules, revisions, and authority boundaries. Asking an agent to infer those from screenshots or cursor coordinates would be fragile. WebMCP lets the agent work with the graph as structured data while the website remains the source of truth and the place where consequential decisions are made. How I built it The application is built with React, TypeScript, React Flow, Zustand, and Zod. React Flow powers the canvas, Zustand manages the local workspace and proposal lifecycle, and Zod enforces schema and migration boundaries. The public application is deployed on Netlify with a custom domain. I also created a portable GraphContract skill published from the website. A browser-capable coding agent can discover the skill, learn the inspect → propose → review → revise → freeze → handoff lifecycle, and then use the three WebMCP tools consistently. Codex helped throughout the project: researching real agent patterns, shaping the domain model, implementing the canvas and proposal workflow, debugging browser behavior, and building the test library. I used Vitest and Testing Library for domain and component contracts, plus Playwright journeys that exercise the real page-registered WebMCP tools in a cold browser. Challenges I faced The hardest part was not drawing nodes. It was keeping the experience truthful under human–agent collaboration. I needed one accepted graph and a separate proposal candidate; atomic validation without silently repairing agent input; deterministic scenarios that remain bounded around loops and dynamic parallelism; and runtime observations that never become editable design truth. I also had to keep the interface understandable while representing nested subgraphs, human gates, Merge reducers, Send ×N workers, and multiple routing modes. Accomplishments I am proud of A complete human–agent planning lifecycle instead of a single tool-call demo. Structured proposals that never mutate accepted state before human approval. Clear visual diffs with request-changes, approval, and rejection flows. First-class human approval gates, sensitive effects, conditional routing, fallback paths, bounded loops, nested structures, Send ×N, and Merge. Deterministic scenario review and downloadable graph, scenario, and Python path-test handoffs. A reusable agent skill and a deliberately narrow WebMCP authority boundary. What I learned The best human–agent interfaces do not simply maximize agent authority. They make authority legible. WebMCP is especially powerful when it exposes the smallest structured surface an agent needs while leaving validation, review, and consequential actions visible to the person. I also learned that a visual graph can be more than documentation. With stable identities, typed edges, revision checks, scenarios, and explicit approval state, it can become a negotiated contract between human intent and agent implementation. What's next Next I want to generate framework-specific implementations from frozen contracts, add repository-linked contract diffs in CI, accept trusted runtime events so live execution can be highlighted against the frozen graph, and expand the library with more source-backed agent patterns. title: MC Beats
pitch: Think OP-1 but to jam live (with agents).
about_excerpt: Think OP-1 but to jam live (with agents). Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration MC Beats began as an investigation into human-agent interaction. As a musician, one of the most interesting forms of interaction I experience is playing music with other people. When I perform with someone, I am always listening, reacting, and looking for small cues that help me understand what they are doing. I wanted to explore what that relationship could look like with an AI agent. Could I build an instrument where I could play with an agent, respond to its ideas, and let it respond to mine? What it does MC Beats is a browser-based live synthesizer and two-deck performance tool. I can play drums, bass, chords, and lead; record loops; shape each sound; and move between two four-bar decks. At the same time, a WebMCP agent can read the musical state, follow what I am playing, prepare new material, arrange patterns, schedule transfers, and perform solos. This lets me play while the agent works in the background, then respond when it brings a new idea into the performance. Everything runs on one shared musical clock. The agent queues its actions to beats and bars, so its changes fit the timing of the music. The interface shows what is on each deck, what is playing, and what the agent is doing, which helps me understand the performance at a glance. Every sound is generated in the browser using oscillators, filters, envelopes, effects, and procedural noise. There are no recorded samples or backend music services. How I built it I built MC Beats in three main stages. I started with the synthesizer. I set myself the challenge of generating every sound from basic waveforms, such as sine and saw waves, along with random noise. It took a couple of days to get the synth sounding good. I spent much of that time adjusting the values for each instrument until the drums, bass, chords, and lead sounded the way I wanted. Next, I designed the interface. I first sketched it by hand, drawing some inspiration from instruments such as the OP-1. I wanted it to feel like a physical music tool while still making sense as a web app. I then gave it my own visual style, with two decks, clear instrument colours, playable controls, and a compact layout. The third stage was the WebMCP integration. I connected the interface and synthesizer to tools that let an agent understand the current performance and take musical actions. This was the point when the separate parts came together and began to feel like one instrument. Challenges The hardest problem was timing. Agents work across two conflicting time scales. Once an agent makes a tool call, the action can happen almost instantly. However, listening to the music, processing the available information, and deciding what to do can take longer than it takes me to reach the next bar. In my first implementation, the agent queued every action at an exact musical time. Calls sometimes failed because they were formatted incorrectly. Other calls arrived after their requested time had already passed. Each failure meant another tool call, more thinking, and another delay in the music. I worked on this from both sides. I built higher-level WebMCP tools that give the agent more context and let it complete useful musical tasks in fewer calls. I also gave it clearer information about the current bar and the earliest safe time for its next action. One experiment was to tell the agent how many tokens it could use during each bar, encouraging it to make faster decisions. I also let the agent schedule actions across several bars. A single tool call can prepare a phrase, arrange a deck, or plan a transfer that unfolds over time. This helps the agent’s actions fit the pace of a live performance. The second challenge was communication. When I play with other musicians, I use eye contact, movement, and other small signals to understand what they are about to do. Those cues do not naturally exist when I play with an agent. I tried to recreate some of that awareness through the interface. My actions and the agent’s actions use a similar visual language. A control bar shows what the agent is doing, and the deck displays let me see the current state of the music. In the other direction, WebMCP tools give the agent structured information about the key, transport, deck contents, and what I have recently played. What I learned Building MC Beats taught me how much good collaboration depends on timing and shared information. Giving an agent control is easy compared with helping it understand when to act, what I am doing, and how to show me what it plans to do. I found that an agent works best as a musical partner when it can listen, prepare ideas in the background, enter at a useful moment, and leave enough space for me to respond. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. about_excerpt:
Let your Agent use Busan through WebMCP. You set the intent, the Agent acts, and you stay in control.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 🌊 HELLOBUSAN: The WebMCP Agent Governance Platform 

 
 💡 Core Question: "What if a city becomes machine-readable for AI agents, while humans retain absolute control?" 

 🚀 3 Key Breakthroughs: 

 
 🌐 WebMCP City OS: Replaces unstable DOM scraping with 10 explicit WebMCP Tool schemas. 
 🔐 Agent Wallet: Granular permission boundaries (Read: ALLOW / Book: ASK / Pay: DENY). 
 ⚡ Empirical Proof: 84% faster execution & 0% DOM parsing failures. 
 
 

 Inspiration 

 AI agents are becoming capable of reasoning, planning, and taking actions on behalf of people. But most websites are still designed only for humans. 

 I asked a simple question: 

 What if a real city could become usable by AI agents, without taking control away from people? 

 This question led me to HELLOBUSAN. 

 I chose Busan as my real-world testbed because a single human goal can require many different services: discovering places, checking events, comparing restaurants, calculating routes, managing time, estimating costs, and eventually making reservations. 

 Normally, people have to move between many websites and applications to complete these tasks. 

 I wanted to explore a different model: 

 The human expresses the goal. 

 The Agent handles the complexity. 

 WebMCP connects the Agent to real web capabilities. 

 The human remains in control of consequential actions. 

 HELLOBUSAN is therefore not just another AI travel planner. 

 It is an experiment in designing a new relationship between Humans, Agents, and Cities. 

 What it does 

 HELLOBUSAN allows a person to describe what they want to accomplish in natural language. 

 For example: 

 
 “Plan a six-hour rainy-day trip in Busan for my family within a ₩50,000 budget.” 
 

 Instead of manually searching multiple services, the Agent can use WebMCP tools to discover information and coordinate actions. 

 The Agent can: 

 
 Search places, restaurants, and events 
 Retrieve detailed information 
 Check relevant conditions such as weather 
 Calculate routes and travel time 
 Estimate and optimize the budget 
 Build and update an itinerary 
 Coordinate multiple services around one user goal 
 

 The key difference is that HELLOBUSAN does not treat autonomy as unlimited permission. 

 I designed an Agent Permission Model: 
 Search ALLOW
Compare ALLOW
Route ALLOW
Schedule ALLOW
Reservation ASK
Payment DENY

 
 How I built it 

 HELLOBUSAN is designed as a WebMCP-based agentic interface with a Cloudflare-native backend. 

 Instead of requiring an Agent to interpret a website only through visual elements, HELLOBUSAN exposes structured capabilities through WebMCP tools. 

 My tool architecture includes capabilities such as: 

 
 search_places 
 search_restaurants 
 search_events 
 get_place_details 
 get_weather 
 calculate_route 
 estimate_cost 
 get_itinerary 
 update_itinerary 
 request_reservation 
 

 Each capability has a defined purpose and structured input/output schema. 

 I separated read operations, reversible actions, and consequential actions so that the Agent's level of autonomy can be controlled. 

 The application architecture uses: 

 
 React and TypeScript for the user interface 
 WebMCP for Agent-facing web capabilities 
 Cloudflare Workers for application logic and API routing 
 Cloudflare D1 for persistent application data 
 Cloudflare Durable Objects for stateful trip sessions and coordination 
 REST APIs and structured JSON data for service integration 
 

 A key design decision was to make permissions a system-level boundary rather than merely a visual setting. 

 The interface may show that payment is disabled, but the backend must also enforce that restriction. 

 I also designed an Agent Activity Log so that users can understand what the Agent is doing instead of experiencing an invisible autonomous process. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest challenge was not generating an itinerary. 

 It was deciding where autonomy should stop. 

 Giving an Agent more capabilities is technically attractive, but greater capability also creates greater responsibility. 

 I identified three different levels of action: 

 
 READ: The Agent can retrieve and understand information. 
 ACT: The Agent can perform reversible actions such as organizing an itinerary. 
 COMMIT: The Agent performs a consequential action that may affect the user. 
 

 The third category requires human approval. 

 This became particularly important when designing reservations and payments. 

 I deliberately avoided the assumption that: 

 
 “The user asked for a trip, therefore the Agent can do anything necessary to complete it.” 
 

 Instead, the system distinguishes between intent and authority. 

 A user's intention to “plan a trip” does not automatically grant permission to spend money or make an irreversible commitment. 

 Another challenge was making WebMCP meaningful rather than decorative. 

 I did not want to build a conventional travel application and simply add a WebMCP label. 

 The Agent interaction itself had to depend on structured capabilities. 

 I therefore designed the product around a comparison between conventional web interaction and WebMCP-based interaction, focusing on task steps, tool usage, errors, completion, and human approvals. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 My biggest accomplishment is that HELLOBUSAN turned WebMCP from a technical capability into a visible user experience. 

 The user does not need to understand WebMCP. 

 They simply express a goal. 

 Behind the interface, the Agent discovers available capabilities, calls structured tools, reasons over the results, updates the itinerary, and stops when human authorization is required. 

 I am especially proud of the Agent Wallet concept. 

 Instead of treating an Agent as either “fully autonomous” or “not autonomous,” I give the user granular control over what the Agent can do. 

 I am also proud of the Agent Activity / Black Box experience. 

 Users can see: 

 
 What the Agent is doing 
 Which tool it is using 
 What information it found 
 What it changed 
 Which permission it used 
 Where human approval is required 
 

 This makes autonomy visible. 

 Most importantly, the prototype demonstrates a different philosophy of agentic computing: 

 
 The goal is not to maximize what the Agent can do.
The goal is to maximize what the Agent can safely do on behalf of a human. 
 

 What I learned 

 The biggest lesson was that the hardest problem in agentic systems is not capability. 

 It is control. 

 An Agent that can only answer questions is limited. 

 An Agent that can take actions is useful. 

 But an Agent that can take consequential actions without clearly defined authority creates a trust problem. 

 WebMCP made me think beyond the question: 

 
 “How can an Agent use the web?” 
 

 I began asking: 

 
 “How should the web communicate its capabilities and boundaries to an Agent?” 
 

 And then: 

 
 “How should a human control those capabilities?” 
 

 This led me to a new mental model: 

 Intent → Capability → Action → Approval 

 I also learned that the best Agent experience should not hide autonomy. 

 It should make autonomy understandable. 

 The user should know when the Agent is thinking, what it is doing, what it is allowed to do, and when a decision belongs to them. 

 This changed HELLOBUSAN from a travel application into an experiment in Human-Agent Interaction Design. 

 What's next for HELLOBUSAN 

 Busan is only the beginning. 

 My next step is to expand HELLOBUSAN from a travel planner into an Agent-ready city interface. 

 Restaurants, museums, cultural venues, hotels, transportation providers, local businesses, and public services could expose structured capabilities that Agents can discover and use. 

 Instead of every Agent learning how to navigate every website independently, the web could increasingly provide explicit, machine-readable capabilities. 

 This could enable a future where a person does not need to understand which website or application to use. 

 They simply express an intent: 

 
 “I need to spend Saturday in Busan with my family.” 
 

 The Agent coordinates the available city services within the permissions defined by the person. 

 My long-term vision is not: 

 
 “AI control

 Inspiration 

 I wanted to see if i could replicate the same realtime collaboration experience that Iron Man and Jarvis have in the movies. 

 What it does 

 This is a infinite shooter game where the goal is to get the highest score by killing enemies, and getting your suit upgraded by earning credits and having you ai copilot decide when the best time to get upgrades and what upgrades to get are based on the realtime game state. 

 How we built it 

 I used WebMCP and Codex to build out all the assets, I used chatgpt sites for the hosting. I gave the agent a lot of webmcp tools to interact with the game, and a initial prompt that allows it to run in a loop until the player dies in the game. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I wanted to make the game use voice dictation for the experience, but it was really lacking because when clicking outside the browser the interaction in the game would stop and you would need to click back the browser. It made it so the experience was not that smooth. I decided to solve it wby making the agent always operate in a loop as long as the player is still alive, and giving the user the option to request the agent for upgrades, but the agent can still reason about it and either accept or deny the request. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am really proud of how the overall game feels, It is the first game that i have made that I actually have fun playing. I also really like the vibe that i gave the game, really comic like, and keeping the playability really simple. At first i wanted like full control with keyboard arrows for movement, but it overcomplicated the game, and keeping it simple with just the spacebar control made immediate sense after i tried it. I am also proud of how real the game can feel at times when you need the help of your ai copilot and it gives you that sense of urgency, as you wait for it to react and hopefully reasoning the correct outcome for you. 

 What we learned 

 I learned that the webmcp protocol is really powerful, but still has some features that would make the protocol even better, like adding a Agents.md for the site that immediately tells the agent about the site. I got over this by just giving the agent a long prompt about the website. I also learned that keeping the tools as much client side as possible is the best way to use webmcp because in teh case of chatgpt sites i would sometimes get rate limited and the ai would stop playing the game 

 What's next for Armored Ascent 

 After the challenge i am planning on soft launching it on twitter, and depending on its success i would love to add more enemies to the game, give the agent more tools, maybe give the players the ability to have their own builds as the webmcp allows to have dynamic tools depending on state, so you could imagine people choosing their own powerups, or even leveling up to unlock new powerups. I feel it could be a cool game that is a first of its kind Human to AI collaboration. I love that in the game you can go far alone, but you go further with your AI.

title: ANAI The Operating Layer for WebMCP
pitch: ANAI is an AI agent that discovers and executes real WebMCP tools to automate infrastructure safely, stopping at consequential actions until a human approves.
about_excerpt: ANAI is an AI agent that discovers and executes real WebMCP tools to automate infrastructure safely, stopping at consequential actions until a human approves. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The Problem AI agents are getting very good at reasoning about what users should do. But there is a gap between telling someone how to operate a web application and actually operating that application . For infrastructure workflows, that gap matters. An agent might be able to recommend a compute service, compare prices, configure an environment, and validate it — but traditionally, the final interaction still depends on clicking through the application's UI or building a separate integration. We wanted to explore a different model: What if the web application itself could expose its capabilities directly to an AI agent? That's where ANAI comes in. What We Built ANAI is an operating layer for WebMCP-enabled web applications. Forge is a simulated cloud infrastructure workspace that exposes its capabilities as WebMCP tools. ANAI discovers those tools through the browser's model context and uses them to operate the application. A user can simply provide a requirement such as: "I need an AI backend under $50/month. Don't touch production." ANAI turns that outcome into an operational plan. It can then: Discover available infrastructure services Retrieve service details and pricing Compare possible services Calculate the resulting cost Create a development environment Configure the selected services Validate the configuration For our golden demo, ANAI produces a four-service development environment costing $42.02/month . But there is an important boundary. ANAI does not autonomously cross consequential actions. When deployment requires human approval, it stops at a confirmation gate and clearly shows what will happen, the environment, and the estimated cost. Only after the user clicks Confirm deployment does the simulated deployment proceed. Production remains unchanged throughout the workflow. Why WebMCP? The important part of this project is that ANAI isn't controlling Forge by pretending to understand its UI. Forge exposes actual capabilities as WebMCP tools. ANAI discovers those capabilities through the browser and invokes them through the WebMCP API. The results of those calls become evidence for the next steps in the plan. The flow is: User requirement → ANAI → WebMCP discovery → real tool execution → Forge state → validation → human approval → result This creates a much more explicit boundary between an agent and a web application. The application defines what the agent can do. The agent doesn't invent capabilities that aren't exposed. Safety by Design We deliberately designed the demo around constrained autonomy. ANAI can automatically perform lower-risk, reversible development operations, but consequential deployment actions remain behind a human confirmation boundary. We also enforce development-only behavior in the demo. ANAI never receives a production target, and production state remains isolated and unchanged. The confirmation gate is not just visual. The underlying deployment action is blocked until explicit human approval. We also tested failure scenarios, low-budget requirements, unsupported requests, retries, and repeated deployment calls to verify that the safety boundary and idempotency behavior remain intact. How We Built It The project is a Next.js application with a deterministic client-side infrastructure runtime. The Forge surface exposes 10 WebMCP tools , including service discovery, service details, comparison, pricing, cost estimation, project creation, configuration, validation, deployment, and platform inspection. ANAI has a deterministic requirement parser and planner. The planner uses the requirement to determine the objective, budget constraint, development environment, and production constraint. Every agent action goes through the registered WebMCP tool interface: getTools() → discover capabilities → executeTool(RegisteredTool, JSON.stringify(args)) We also built a second independent WebMCP surface called Repo , which exposes five development-repository capabilities: create_repository get_repository configure_repository set_environment validate_repository Repo has its own state, types, registration layer, and contract verification, demonstrating that the approach is not tied specifically to Forge. What We Learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent that can actually operate a web application is very different from building a chatbot that describes what should happen. The WebMCP contract becomes an important part of the system design. We had to think carefully about: What capabilities should the application expose? What arguments should each tool accept? Which actions are safe to automate? Where should human approval be required? How should tool results become evidence for subsequent planning? How do we prevent production state from leaking into an isolated development workflow? How do we make the agent's activity observable without fabricating reasoning? We also learned that refusing an unsupported request is often better than improvising a plan. ANAI deliberately uses deterministic requirement matching and refuses scenarios it cannot safely support. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was preserving a clean separation between agent reasoning, application capabilities, and human authorization . It would have been easy to create a scripted demo that simply moved through predetermined UI states. Instead, we verified that the workflow uses the actual registered WebMCP tools and that the UI reflects the resulting application state. We also tested the WebMCP contracts independently, including tool names, descriptions, schemas, argument formats, failure handling, retries, and isolation between Forge and Repo. The final system has 61 automated tests across 19 suites , along with linting, TypeScript checks, production builds, and Chrome-based end-to-end verification. The Result ANAI demonstrates a simple idea: A web application can expose its capabilities to an AI agent without giving the agent unlimited control. The application defines the tools. ANAI discovers and operates them. The application enforces the boundaries. And the human remains in control when the action becomes consequential. That's the direction we wanted to explore with WebMCP.  Inspiration 

 I didn't want to build a niche tool used by only a few people; I wanted to build something that helps everyone reclaim their time. The browser is where we spend most of our digital lives, yet it often feels chaotic and disconnected from our AI tools. 

 I was inspired to build Cognito not just as a chatbot, but as a true Browser Agent . My goal was to create a companion that lives in the side panel, understands your context, and handles the tedious tasks like organizing tabs, summarizing videos, or connecting to your notes so that you can focus on the "wins." 

 What it does 

 Cognito is an agentic Chrome extension that lives in your side panel. It transforms how you browse by: 

 
 Organizing Chaos: Automatically grouping and organizing messy tabs by topic. 
 Deep Research: Using Tavily to browse the live web, synthesizing answers from multiple sources (with citations). 
 /research (in the chat input ): triggers the Agentic Research mode. This uses your actual browser to autonomously open tabs, read pages, and navigate to find deep answers (simulating a human researcher). 
 Contextual RAG: Letting you "chat" with any webpage, PDF, or YouTube video. 
 Browser Automation: Performing multi-step tasks like navigating to Gmail, composing emails, and clicking buttons. 
 MCP Integration: Connecting to external data sources (like Notion) and website-specific tools via the Model Context Protocol. 
 

 Installation & Setup 

 
 Download: Download the production build linked in this submission (or clone the GitHub repo to build from source). 
 Install: Go to chrome://extensions , toggle Developer Mode (top right), click Load unpacked , and select the downloaded folder. 
 API Configuration: 

 
 Gemini: After onboarding, click the three-dot menu in the extension → AI Provider Setup . Note: The Gemini API method is tested and recommended (Vertex setup is currently experimental). A paid tier key is suggested to avoid rate limits/latency, though free keys will work with potential retries. 
 Tavily & Supermemory: Simply open Settings and scroll down to input these keys. 
 
 

 How to Access & Use 

 Entry Points: 

 
 Extension Icon: Simply click the Cognito icon in your Chrome toolbar (the easiest way to open the side panel). 
 Floating Button: Click the "Ask AI" button that appears on pages after installation. 
 Omnibox (Address Bar): Type ai followed by a space to send a message directly from the address bar. 
 Keyboard Shortcut: Set a custom shortcut via chrome://extensions/shortcuts for instant access. 
 

 Testing WebMCP: 
You can test the WebMCP integration at https://codewarnab.in/ . 

 
 If the WebMCP tools do not appear immediately in the tools menu, please perform a hard refresh . 
 Note: Currently, this displays tools built by the website owner. I am working on a future feature where users can inject WebMCP tools into any website using a user-script mechanism. 
 

 Troubleshooting: 
If you run into issues, you can view common solutions in the three-dot menu within the extension. 

 Features: 

 
 Slash Commands: Type /write to open the Writer interface or /ask for quick queries. 
 Summarization: Select any text on a webpage to see a "Summary" tooltip. 
 Rewrite: Select text, right-click, and choose "Rewrite" from the context menu. (Fun fact: It can rewrite any content on the page, not just input fields!) 
 

 How I built it 

 I built Cognito as a Chrome Extension using the Side Panel API to keep it non-intrusive. 

 
 Frontend: React & TypeScript. 
 Intelligence: Powered by Gemini for reasoning and Tavily for live search. 
 Connectivity: Implemented the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to bridge the browser with web MCP server and remote servers. 
 Privacy-First Architecture: Everything happens on your client device. Requests are sent directly from your browser to the Gemini API endpoint. No user data is sent to my servers , ensuring your browsing history and personal data remain private. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Building a truly "agentic" workflow in a browser is tricky. Managing the context window when a user has 20 tabs open was a significant engineering hurdle. We also faced hurdles in ensuring the automated actions were reliable across different website layouts. 

 What I learned 

 Early Standards Adoption is Hard But Worth It. 
MCP was supposed to be standardized, but I discovered it's still in the early stages. Many services need special invitations and have inconsistent implementations. However, being an early adopter gave me a competitive advantage and helped me understand how to contribute to the ecosystem's development. 

 What's next for Cognito 

 I view this hackathon submission as just the beginning. To make Cognito a daily driver, I plan to implement: 

 
 Multi-Model Support: While currently optimized for Gemini, I will soon add support for all major model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) to give users full choice. 
 WebMCP Injection: Enabling users to inject WebMCP tools into any website using a user-script feature, allowing the agent to interact with sites that don't natively support MCP. 
 The "Unblockable" Agent (Debugger Support): To handle websites that block standard script execution, I plan to leverage the Chrome Debugger API . This will allow Cognito to interact with the browser at a lower level, ensuring it can click, type, and navigate even on restrictive websites. 
 Voice Support: Adding full voice interaction so users can speak commands naturally instead of typing, making the experience even more accessible. 
 Action Approval Mechanism: For sensitive tasks, I'm adding a "human-in-the-loop" system. Cognito will ask for explicit permission before taking actions like sending emails or making payments. 
 Enhanced Security & Prompt Injection Prevention: As the agent gains autonomy, security is paramount. I am developing a multi-layered defense system to ensure external web content cannot manipulate the agent. 
 Integration with More Services: Expanding the MCP ecosystem to include business tools like Slack, Microsoft Teams, and Salesforce.

 About the Project 

 ClientOps was inspired by a common problem for freelancers
 and small agencies: client work is scattered across task
 lists, email, spreadsheets, invoices, and notes. This
 makes it easy to miss follow-ups, lose track of delivery
 work, or delay billing. 

 I built ClientOps as an agent-native client-work command
 center. It brings projects, tasks, invoice drafts, and
 follow-ups into one workspace that both humans and AI
 agents can use. Through WebMCP, an agent can retrieve a
 workspace briefing, create work items, update task status,
 and prepare invoice or follow-up drafts. 

 The app was built with a lightweight HTML, CSS, and
 JavaScript frontend, Supabase REST persistence, and Vercel
 deployment. WebMCP tools are registered with
 document.modelContext.registerTool() and include
 structured JSON schemas so agents can interact with the
 app reliably. 

 A core design principle is human approval. Agents can
 prepare an invoice or message, but they cannot send it or
 charge a client automatically. This keeps automation
 useful without giving it unsafe control over financial or
 external actions. 

 While building the project, I learned how to design AI-
 facing tool schemas, expose browser actions through
 WebMCP, persist frontend state to a hosted database, and
 create safe human-in-the-loop workflows. 

 The main challenges were working with an evolving WebMCP
 API, supporting browsers where WebMCP is unavailable, and
 deciding which actions should be automated versus approved
 by a person. I addressed these with feature detection,
 fallback behavior, explicit read-only annotations,
 structured outputs, and draft-only financial workflows. 

 ClientOps demonstrates how websites can become reliable
 working environments for both people and agents—not just
 interfaces that an AI has to interpret visually.

about_excerpt: LinkUp helps people recover after a flood, fire, or earthquake and more. Tell us what happened and agent turns it into a simple Situation Map for housing, power, documents Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration After a flood or fire, people often have to explain what happened over and over again—to the county, the utility company, housing programs, and different relief organizations. When your home is already damaged, even figuring out which form to start with can be overwhelming. The problem isn't always that nobody wants to help. It's that the help is spread across different websites, forms, and systems that don't really talk to each other. We started wondering: what if an agent could handle some of that coordination for you, without making decisions on your behalf? That is what made WebMCP interesting to us. A website can expose specific tools to an agent while still controlling exactly what the agent is allowed to do. The agent can take care of repetitive work, while the resident stays in control of what gets shared, approved, or submitted. What it does 2030MCP LinkUp is designed for the days after a flood, fire, earthquake, storm, or other disaster. Instead of entering the same information into multiple systems, you explain what happened once. LinkUp turns that into a simple Situation Map showing what it understood, what information is still missing, and which services may be relevant. For example, the system may identify that you need temporary housing, utility support, replacement documents, or disaster relief. The agent can then read provider requirements, organize the information you already provided, and prepare the next step for you. The important part is that it does not make the final decision. It cannot decide whether your story is true, approve your case, or submit something on your behalf without your review. You see what the agent plans to do first and choose whether to continue. How we built it We built LinkUp with Next.js App Router, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The WebMCP layer is built around document.modelContext.registerTool. Instead of registering every tool all the time, LinkUp rebuilds the available tool registry from the current signed case state. That means a tool only becomes available when the user has reached the right step and given the required consent. We also enforce the same boundaries on the server. Route handlers validate signed session data including the user's role, disaster scenario, and origin. We use strict Zod schemas, state version checks, idempotency keys, packet hashes, expiring grants, and rate limits to prevent replay, tampering, or unintended submissions. Every action that changes the case is also recorded in a server-side audit log. For the disaster flows, we created separate provider fixtures for floods, fires, earthquakes, and storms. The provider policy version is selected before evidence is collected, so changing the incident later cannot silently change the rules applied to the case. Testing was a major part of the project. We currently have 108 Vitest tests covering the WebMCP contract, dynamic tool registration and removal, replay prevention, tamper rejection, and session integrity. We also run strict TypeScript checks and GitHub Actions with pinned revisions. Most importantly, we tested the real WebMCP flow in a browser using the native document.modelContext interface. We verified that the send tool appears only after consent and disappears again after it has been used. For Chrome testing, the project also includes a Chrome 149+ path using chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. To keep the demo easy to run, the entire resident session survives serverless cold starts without requiring a database. Case state is stored in signed, Brotli-compressed cookie chunks with strict size limits. We also test the deployed version with npm run test:golden to make sure a fresh incognito session can complete the full flow from beginning to end. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making "the human is in control" something the system actually enforces. At first, it is tempting to put instructions in the tool description and say that the agent should ask before doing something important. But that still depends on the model following the instruction. We wanted the restriction to exist at the system level instead. So we moved permissions into the tool registry itself. A consequential tool does not exist until the user has explicitly given consent. After a one-time action is used, the tool removes itself from the registry. That gave us something we could actually test: not just whether the agent behaved correctly, but whether the tool was available at all. Another challenge was writing tool descriptions for an agent rather than for a person. We added clear authority boundaries such as CONSEQUENTIAL, ONE USE, explicit fields that prevent the agent from implying provider approval, and untrustedContentHint for information that comes from free-text user stories. Another challenge was keeping a complete resident session working across serverless instances without a database while still staying inside browser cookie limits. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that LinkUp actually works as a deployed product, rather than being just a mockup of an agent workflow. The WebMCP registry changes live as the resident moves through the process. A one-use send tool appears after consent, can be used once, and then disappears. We also built a read-only audit interface so another agent can inspect what happened without being able to change the case. And instead of using one generic disaster demo, we built separate provider contracts for floods, fires, earthquakes, and storms so the workflow behaves differently depending on the situation. What we learned If a tool should not be available yet, the safest option is not to register it at all. We also learned that tool descriptions matter much more than we expected. They are not just documentation for developers; they are part of the interface the model uses to understand its authority and responsibilities. Clear descriptions made the agent much more likely to ask for review instead of acting as if it had approval from a provider. WebMCP also showed us a different way to think about agent safety. Instead of putting every restriction inside a chat prompt, some of the rules can be enforced directly by the website and its tool lifecycle. What's next for 2030MCP LinkUp First, a server-issued human-presence challenge so consequential actions can verify that a real resident is still present. Second, an encrypted case database for longer-term recovery cases and larger documents. Third, real provider integrations for housing agencies, utilities, local government, and relief organizations. The WebMCP contracts are already structured so providers could publish their own requirement and submission tools. The county, housing, and utility portals in our demo are examples of how those provider-owned integrations could work. The long-term goal is simple: people should not have to rebuild the same disaster story for every organization they need help from. They should explain what happened once, review what gets shared, and stay in control of the process.  Inspiration 

 There is a groundswell of interest within Canada for buying Canadian products from fellow Canadians right now. 

 What it does 

 Enables Canadian consumers to search and browse categorized products from Canadian retailers who use the Shopify platform, and highlights products which are made in Canada. 

 How we built it 

 Shopify recently allowed access to the global product catalog, allowing us to structure queries to surface items specific to our special interests. This site leverages that to pull in products shipped from Canadian stores, to Canadian buyers, and tags them if they mention that they are made in Canada. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Query limits; needing multiple queries to tag items as mentioning "made in Canada" as well as the French equivalents; using local data structures to temporarily store query results for sorting and filtering while staying within the guidelines for Shopify's global catalog usage. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 It really is a showcase of the scope and variety of great things that Canadians contribute to the world. Other sites have had merchants trickle onto them by signing up for listings, while this one immediately surfaces thousands of Canadian creations. 

 What we learned 

 The Shopify global catalog is a rich source of product information, supporting niche sites and special-interest groups; there are endless possibilities! For the past year, analyzing Shopify Collective as a way to accomplish this seemed like a full-time job of contract negotiations and convincing Canadian merchants to join Collective as a supplier. This is a far better route to quickly surface all things Canadian from Shopify's vast range of stores. 

 What's next for Buy Canadian from the Shopify Global Catalog 

 If it is accepted into the Promoted Placements dev preview program, there will be a source of revenue for paid hosting (currently "hobby" plan on Vercel) and a properly branded standalone domain name. :) 
Features: additional filtering on category pages by subcategories, and additional query filters for Canadian stores which ship to other countries beyond Canada (allowing folks outside of Canada who want to support Canadian merchants a way to find items which will ship to their country).

title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. With Web and CP, the agent in ChatGPT's browser writes and directs them with you on the real product. The page is open in ChatGPT's built-in browser, the full studio, and on the right, the agent rail reports that the site tools are registered. The first request goes in. The agent reads the authoring guide and writes the script. This wait is sped up. The script lands through load script and the camera comes on. The stage plays it right away. A heading, three bullets, and a code block typed out on the stage. Next, a choice step. Edit message adds three options and picks the developer one.
