title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: No Upload MCP
pitch: Let an agent read your documents. Without ever uploading them.
about_excerpt: Let an agent read your documents. Without ever uploading them. Like Comment Story Updates App Home Page App being controlled by codex - Finance App being controlled by codex - Diet plan review App being controlled by codex - Diet plan Inspiration At home I use excels to make my savings plan and at work I am the Agent Emperor. I dread coming into my financial planning tools and I wanted to supercharge it. When I saw WebMCP, I actually got interested. I am a passionate programmer and read through the spec, I immediately wanted to build something to absorb the concepts. Thats why I build this tool. I would really want to be involved in defining the spec for WebMCP, not sure if I am allowed to or if I can participate? Am Beggingggggg.... begggingggg yoouuuu ohhh uuuuu... Why is the usecase a strong fit for WebMCP Getting an agent to help with a sensitive document normally means uploading the whole thing. With No Upload MCP users submit their confidential docs to the JS runtime in the browser, which deterministically parses PDF using text extraction - (for eg - bank statements) or in case of a pdf image uses OCR. This happens locally using user's CPU and browser, NO UPLOADs!!! Tadaa! Then the user can review extracted records, control what the agent may process, approve mappings, generate charts, and create editable financial or dietary plans without uploading their documents to an application server. The agents via webmcp get access only to the required info and they supercharge it with generative context, on which human and agents can cross collaborate. Earlier I could do all the above things, but I had to do searches separately , do a lot of copy paste and boring context switching. But now its quite immersive. I get everything done in one tab in one context. Best part it runs in the browser for free. I get the best of both worlds - my privacy in my hands with a zero trust and all the capabilities of the agents. Challenges I ran into Convincing my wife to let me build this on a Saturday night On a serious note, the documentation I felt was quite sparse. I wanted to try out scenarios where: The page could hook to the agent once an async flow was done, this seems to be not possible. Setting up certain guardrails for the agent and instructions. Maybe i didn't understand the spec well. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I don't need to use excel anymore. I can finally use AI without the concern of my private data leaving my machine! What I learned Loads about web MCP and I love the concept. I am already brimming with so many ideas for this! Thanks thanks thanks for running this hackathon. I already feel like a winner by building this use case for myself. ---------x-----------(below this line generated by AI reviewed by human)------------ WebMCP: What It Improves & Enables ✨ User Experience Enhancements Visual Transparency: Delegate tasks in plain language and watch every consequence update instantly in the UI. Explicit Merchant Rules: Converts raw descriptions (e.g., "amzn mktp" ➔ Amazon ➔ Groceries ) into bulk-applicable rules rather than silent, row-by-row guesses. Instant Rejections: Dismiss incorrect agent assumptions with a single click instead of an argument. Strict "Propose, Don't Commit" Architecture: Mappings, ranges, and plans sit in a pending UI state with a visible source link. Nothing becomes durable just by looking plausible. 🤝 Advanced Human-Agent Collaboration Real-Time Financial Planning: The agent drafts budget reductions (e.g., saving $50,000 for a car) from your actual spend. Drag a slider, type "keep my gym membership," and evaluate feasibility instantly. Synchronous UI State: The agent reads the exact value under your cursor—not a turn from five minutes ago—because the UI mirrors inputs before writing to disk. Interactive Health Reviews: Plot lab analytes against printed reference ranges, inject cited standards where data is missing, manually remove allergens from a drafted food plan, and have the agent re-verify the edited text before final publication. 🚫 Why Chat & Automation Fail Chat interfaces force you to manually re-upload files or describe UI changes by hand. Browser automation scrapes raw DOM objects and hopes they don't break. Neither features a native contract for consent, provenance, or safe, staged execution. WebMCP Architecture & Implementation 🛠️ Central Registry & Tool Dispatch Centralized Management: Handled via src/core/mcp/registry.ts . Schema Conversion: Converts typed internal tool specs into JSON input schemas. Model Registration: Passes generated schemas directly to modelContext.registerTool . Audited Execution: Routes every execute command through a secure dispatcher. Detailed Logging: Records arguments, results, and duration for the in-page log. 🔄 Dynamic Tool Lifecycle Baseline State: Eight core tools remain permanently registered. Plugin Selection: Activating a plugin registers 17 finance tools or 12 labs tools. Cleanup Mechanism: Retires inactive tools using their AbortController signal. Schema Refresh: Automatically updates document-shaped schemas after data ingest. 📡 Resilient Host Discovery Target Detection: Scans window , document , and navigator for modelContext . Continuous Polling: Searches indefinitely since hosts can inject context long after load. Session Longevity: Ensures hour-long persistent sessions never miss a late injection. 🛡️ Five-Tier Authority Model Every tool declares a strict authority tier. This tier is explicitly built into the tool description provided to the model, acting as a public promise rather than simple internal bookkeeping: Read : Standard data retrieval. Attention : Modifies only the visible screen. Consent : Restricts data return until a policy and grant check passes. Staged : Proposes actions but commits no permanent changes. Memory : Accesses page-owned durable state. title: Fenoa
pitch: Fenoa is a social platform for short fiction where creators publish stories and communities remix them into new branches, with humans, AI, and WebMCP agents working on the same living story state.
about_excerpt: Fenoa is a social platform for short fiction where creators publish stories and communities remix them into new branches, with humans, AI, and WebMCP agents working on the same living story state. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Fenoa started from a simple idea I kept coming back to: What if a story did not have only one continuation? A creator could write the setup, publish it, and someone else could take the same characters in a completely different direction. Maybe one person continues the story normally. Another changes one decision. Someone else introduces a new character. Another person takes Episode 2 and turns it into a completely different branch. That sounded much more interesting to me than treating a story like one fixed document. Most writing tools are still built around a fairly linear workflow. You write something, edit it, and eventually publish the final version. Even with AI, the interaction is usually still "ask for some text, copy the text, edit the text." I wanted Fenoa to feel more like a living network of short fiction. A creator can publish a short story or mini-drama, and the community can keep branching it into new versions without destroying the original. While building that, another problem became obvious. Once stories start branching, continuity gets difficult very quickly. Who knows which secret? Which characters trust each other? What rules are still true? Did something already happen in another episode? What did the original creator say should never change? That is why Fenoa also keeps structured story state underneath the writing. The reader mostly sees the story. But underneath it, Fenoa understands the characters, relationships, facts, rules, constraints, episodes, and branch history. That structure also turned out to be a very natural fit for WebMCP. What it does Fenoa is a social platform for short fiction and remixable stories. Creators can build a fictional setup, turn it into a short story or mini-drama, publish it, and let other people create their own branches from it. The simplest way to think about it is: Create a story → publish it → remix it → branch it again. A Fenoa world can contain: a premise genre and tone characters relationships important facts secrets rules story constraints locations a story spark A creator can write all of this manually. There is also a built-in Creative Partner that can help develop the idea. For example, a creator can start with a rough concept and ask the Creative Partner to help build characters, motivations, relationships, tensions, and rules. The important part is that the AI output does not stay trapped inside a chat message. When the creator chooses to apply it, Fenoa turns the useful parts into real structured story data that can still be edited manually. Creators can also generate artwork for their story and publish it. Once published, another person can start a remix. A remix is a new branch of the story. It inherits the original context, but it can develop in its own direction. For example: continue the original story change an important event introduce a new character switch point of view create a darker or funnier version turn one moment into a larger mini-series remix an existing remix The original story is never overwritten. Each branch keeps its own creative direction, episodes, branch-specific characters, rules, constraints, and lineage. Short stories and mini-dramas I did not want Fenoa to become a long-form novel editor. The format is intentionally closer to short fiction and episodic mini-dramas. A branch can contain a small sequence of episodes, each focused on one clear development in the story. That makes remixing much more approachable. Someone does not need to read a 100,000-word novel before contributing something. They can understand the setup, read a few short episodes, and take the story somewhere new. I think this also fits the way people already consume creative content online. Shorter stories are easier to discover, easier to share, and much easier to remix. The Creative Partner Fenoa has a built-in Creative Partner for both world creation and remix development. It is meant to feel more like a collaborator than an automatic "write everything for me" button. A creator can ask it to: suggest possibilities challenge an idea connect existing story elements resolve continuity problems build structured story content For example, during the demo I start with a fairly simple comedy idea. The Creative Partner helps turn that into actual characters, motivations, relationships, world rules, and story material. Later, inside a remix, it can also help create episodes around a new direction. The creator can then open those episodes and change them manually. That combination was important to me. AI can move the story forward, but the human never loses control of the work. Remix Studio Remix Studio is where a branch becomes its own story. It brings together three things: The episodes being written The Creative Partner The current story context The story context matters because a remix is not just another blank prompt. It inherits information from the story it came from. That can include: characters relationships facts story rules constraints branch-specific changes episode history A creator can also add decisions that should remain true inside the branch. For example, a character might not be allowed to know a certain secret yet, or a specific fact may need to remain true throughout the story. Those decisions become part of the branch state instead of living only inside someone's memory or prompt history. Why WebMCP matters in Fenoa This is probably the part of the project I found most interesting technically. Fenoa already had a structured representation of the story. WebMCP gave me a way to expose that meaning directly to browser agents. Without something like WebMCP, an agent interacting with a creative app would often have to inspect the page, understand the UI, find the correct buttons, and infer what the visible text means. That is possible, but it is a very indirect way of working with the product. In Fenoa, the page can expose semantic tools instead. The current WebMCP tools are: Tool What it does get_branch_state Reads the current remix and its story state get_episode Reads one episode together with its version and relevant constraints update_episode Updates an existing episode move_episode Changes episode order add_branch_character Adds a character specifically to the current remix set_story_constraint Adds a constraint that the story should respect update_branch_rule Adds, changes, or removes a branch-specific rule Publishing is intentionally not exposed as an agent action. That remains a human decision. A shared story state The part I cared about most was making sure WebMCP was not a completely separate automation layer. Fenoa has three different ways a story can change: the human editor the built-in Creative Partner a WebMCP client All three work on the same underlying story state. For example, a person can edit Episode 1 manually and add a story constraint. A WebMCP client can then read the branch and see that latest state. It can read Episode 2, including its current version and relevant constraints. It can then update Episode 2. The Remix Studio reflects the change because the WebMCP action is modifying the same real branch that the human is working on. There is no separate copy of the story created just for the agent. That was one of the main architectural goals of the project. How we built it Fenoa is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Firebase is used for: authentication Firestore realtime data Cloud Storage production hosting Firestore realtime listeners are especially useful inside Remix Studio because changes can appear without requiring the user to manually reload the story. The Creative Partner uses OpenAI's Responses API. I use structured outputs and validation before applying AI-generated changes. I did not want the model to have direct freedom to write arbitrary data into Firestore. The AI suggests or builds structured changes, and those changes still go through Fenoa's normal domain logic. World artwork is generated separately with Gemini and stored in Cloud Storage. For native WebMCP, the tools are registered directly on the page with: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) There is no separate MCP server acting as a substitute for WebMCP. The tools are part of the browser experience itself. Architecture decisions One decision I made early was that WebMCP should not get a privileged shortcut directly into the database. The human interface and WebMCP actions both use the same application/domain operations. That means validation still applies regardless of whether the change came from a human or an agent. title: Teachback
pitch: Turn one handled case into a reusable WebMCP playbook—drafted by an agent, bounded and applied by people.
about_excerpt: Turn one handled case into a reusable WebMCP playbook—drafted by an agent, bounded and applied by people. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A person sets the reusable boundary by comparing source and proposal, then tightening the permitted arrival time. Human approval gates the commit. Only the exact approved run can be applied, with expiry, digest, version, and replay checks. The agent drafts; the website keeps control. A WebMCP-capable agent turns the record into reusable operations and wording. Recorded work becomes structured evidence. Teachback preserves saved operations, exact diffs, and evidence IDs—not clicks. Preparation is not execution. WebMCP returns exact proposed changes while the reservation remains unchanged. The website refuses work outside the published boundary and returns the compensation case to a person. Teachback is a WebMCP app that converts one handled case into a reusable, approval-first workflow, so agents can suggest actions while humans keep control of execution. What Teachback does Teachback explores a practical question: how can a team reuse an experienced person's response without treating one successful case as unlimited permission? The demo uses synthetic hotel reservations. A staff member handles Aiko's late arrival in the normal website and saves four operations: the arrival update, a meal box, a guest message, and a shift handoff. Teachback records semantic commands, exact before-and-after values, and evidence IDs—not click coordinates. A WebMCP-capable agent reads that record and authors its own playbook draft. It must identify supported operations, replace Aiko's name and time with permitted case fields, preserve the recorded wording, and propose an arrival boundary. The website checks the proposal against the actual evidence. A person then compares source and reusable wording, tightens the cutoff, and publishes the reviewed version. Publication is deliberately not a WebMCP tool. For Emma, the agent reads the published version and current case data, then asks Teachback to prepare a run. The website evaluates deterministic safeguards and produces the exact diff. Nothing changes until a person reviews that proposal and selects Approve and apply in the website. The agent can read the committed result afterward, but it has no approval or application tool. When the same playbook is tried on Noah's compensation request, the website returns PLAYBOOK_NOT_APPLICABLE and sends the case back to a person. Why WebMCP is the right interface The difficult part is not clicking hotel fields. It is turning concrete work into a proposed reusable structure, then carrying that structure into a new case without blurring who decides. A generic page reader sees labels and pixels; WebMCP exposes the concepts that matter: demonstrations, evidence-backed drafts, published versions, cases, and prepared runs. This creates a clean division of responsibility: the person demonstrates work, edits boundaries, publishes, and applies; the agent interprets the recording, drafts reusable wording, and prepares a case-specific proposal; the website validates evidence, enforces fixed safeguards, calculates exact changes, and refuses work outside the published boundary. The result is an explicit handoff between interpretation and authorization. An agent can help with the genuinely ambiguous part—drafting from evidence—without receiving a generic mutation API or the authority to approve its own output. How WebMCP is implemented The TypeScript/React application registers seven typed tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(): teachback_get_demonstration teachback_create_draft teachback_update_draft teachback_list_playbooks teachback_list_cases teachback_prepare_run teachback_get_run Tool input is schema-checked and size-limited. Draft steps must cite recorded evidence, reproduce the final saved operations, and parameterize source-specific names, dates, IDs, and times. Published playbooks are immutable versions. Preparing a run binds it to the case version and published-content digest. Human approval is bound to the exact run digest, expires after five minutes, and can be used once. Request IDs make mutating WebMCP calls idempotent, while compact receipts and session limits prevent unbounded browser storage growth. The audit trail separates Human, Agent, and Website decisions. Prototype scope Teachback is a client-side prototype with eight synthetic reservations and four supported operation types. It demonstrates recording, proposal validation, human publication, exact-diff approval, deterministic refusal, and audit semantics. It is not connected to a real hotel system and does not claim production authentication, authorization, multi-user storage, arbitrary browser automation, or autonomous batch execution. title: HowToPC
pitch: An agent-native PC configurator where people and AI build the same PC together without sacrificing compatibility or trust.
about_excerpt: An agent-native PC configurator where people and AI build the same PC together without sacrificing compatibility or trust. Like 1 Comment Story Updates HowToPC logo High-End Gaming PC RTX 4060 starter build Inspiration Building a PC looks like shopping. In reality, it is a constraint problem. A CPU determines which motherboard sockets are valid. A motherboard determines memory type, expansion capacity, and storage resources. A GPU needs enough power, the right connections, and enough physical clearance. A cooler needs the correct socket and enough room inside the case. One component can quietly invalidate several others. Our starting question was simple: What if an AI could help build a PC without becoming the authority on whether the hardware actually works together? Most AI assistants sit outside the configurator. They can recommend parts, describe what buttons to click, or attempt to understand a page through browser automation. That creates an awkward divide: Traditional AI assistant HowToPC with WebMCP Reads or scrapes the interface Reads structured application state Guesses what actions are possible Uses explicitly registered tools Maintains its own idea of the build Shares the real builder session Can suggest incompatible changes Mutations pass deterministic checks Needs UI automation Calls semantic application capabilities WebMCP gave us a different model. Instead of teaching the agent how to operate HowToPC, we made HowToPC itself explain what it can do . The result is a configurator where the human and the agent can alternate control of the same build while deterministic application logic remains the final authority. The AI proposes. HowToPC verifies. The person stays in control. What it does HowToPC is an agent-native PC configurator that combines a traditional hardware builder with structured WebMCP capabilities. A person can browse a large sourced component catalog, assemble a computer, inspect compatibility, monitor motherboard resources, and visualize the configuration through a parametric Digital Twin. At the same time, an AI agent can work with that exact same configuration. For people HowToPC provides: 26,415 sourced hardware products CPU, motherboard, memory, GPU, storage, PSU, case, cooler, fan, and networking categories searchable catalog filters and compatibility-aware discovery RTX 4060 Gaming PC and High-End Gaming PC starter templates deterministic compatibility checks DIMM, M.2, SATA, PCIe, and other resource accounting GPU length and CPU cooler clearance checks modeled component collision detection a real-scale parametric Digital Twin explicit UNKNOWN states when reliable geometry or topology is unavailable For agents The same page exposes 10 structured WebMCP tools : WebMCP tool Capability builder_get_state Read the current PC configuration catalog_search Search the sourced hardware catalog catalog_inspect_product Inspect structured component specifications builder_add_product Add a component builder_remove_product Remove a component builder_replace_product Replace an installed component builder_compatibility_report Request deterministic compatibility diagnostics builder_resource_usage Inspect consumed and available hardware resources builder_geometry_diagnostics Inspect physical clearances and modeled collisions builder_find_compatible Search for hardware compatible with the current build The important part is not simply the number of tools. It is that they operate on the same canonical builder session used by the visible interface . If a person changes a component, the agent immediately sees it. If the agent replaces a component, the person immediately sees it. There is no hidden "AI version" of the PC configuration and no synchronization layer trying to keep two builds aligned. Compatibility remains deterministic The language model does not decide whether two components are compatible. For example, if an agent attempts to install an Intel LGA1700 motherboard into a build containing an AMD AM5 CPU, the mutation is rejected by HowToPC's transaction and compatibility logic. CPU socket does not match motherboard. That same protection applies whether the requested change came from a person or an agent. Unknown is not compatible. When HowToPC does not have enough evidence to verify something, it reports that limitation rather than fabricating confidence. How we built it HowToPC is a TypeScript monorepo built around a separation between product data, engineering rules, application state, geometry, and agent capabilities. Architecture ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Human UI │ │ Parts / Build / Twin │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Canonical Builder │ │ Session │ └──────────┬────────────┘ │ ┌────────────┼─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Compatibility Resources Geometry Engine Accounting Engine ▲ ▲ ▲ └────────────┼─────────────┘ │ ┌──────────┴────────────┐ │ WebMCP Tools │ │ AI agent actions │ └───────────────────────┘ Both interfaces converge on the same state and the same validation logic. Sourced hardware catalog We normalize a pinned snapshot of BuildCores OpenDB into deterministic product records. The public catalog contains: Source Products Normalized BuildCores products 26,408 Curated sourced references 7 Total public catalog 26,415 Catalog searching, facets, compatibility filtering, and pagination happen against the full data set rather than a small demo fixture. Deterministic compatibility Compatibility is handled outside the language model. The rules cover areas including: CPU and motherboard sockets memory generation motherboard and case form factors CPU cooler socket support GPU and case clearance motherboard resource consumption installed quantities PSU and component requirements compatibility-aware builder transactions An agent can request a change, but it cannot bypass these rules. Parametric Digital Twin We also built a geometry layer that converts known hardware dimensions into a real-scale parametric preview. The system can reason about values such as: GPU length CPU cooler height Case internal limits Modeled component volumes Component collisions Mount topology We deliberately avoid presenting the Twin as manufacturer CAD. If exact mounting geometry is not sourced, the application says so. That makes the model less visually magical, but much more trustworthy. WebMCP bridge The WebMCP implementation registers tools through the browser's native model context surface. Conceptually: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "builder_find_compatible", description: "Find products compatible with the current PC build", // structured input schema // deterministic application handler }); The important architectural decision was to reuse existing application services . We did not create separate AI-only compatibility rules, a separate agent catalog, or a parallel builder state. Engineering confidence The project currently has: 53 test files / 182 automated tests Coverage includes: catalog ingestion normalization catalog searching compatibility rules quantity transactions resource accounting geometry collision detection starter templates API routes canonical builder sessions WebMCP registration WebMCP tool behavior The starter templates also have regression gates requiring them to remain both deterministically compatible and free from modeled component collisions . Challenges we ran into 1. Deciding where AI reasoning should stop The easiest implementation would have been a tool like: change_my_pc_build(prompt) That would also have been the least interesting architecture. It would make the language model responsible for interpreting hardware constraints and deciding whether its own proposed changes were valid. We wanted a stronger boundary. The model can decide what it wants to try . HowToPC decides whether the requested transaction is allowed . That separation became one of the most important design principles in the project. 2. Working with incomplete real-world hardware data Real hardware catalogs are messy. Some components have detailed measurements. Others omit dimensions, connector topology, mounting coordinates, or other fields required for exact mechanical reasoning. We had a choice: invent reasonable-looking values make uncertainty visible We chose the second option. For example, if exact PCIe slot topology is unavailable, the Digital Twin can use a standardized parametric position for visualization while separately reporting that the exact topology is unknown. Similarly, if an AIO cooler has known radiator dimensions but no reliable case mounting coordinates, we do not invent a radiator location. Missing data is treated as information, not an invitation to hallucinate. 3. Making the Digital Twin honest and useful A visually convincing 3D scene can create false confidence very quickly. title: PrepWise Lite
pitch: Smart pantry tracking and recipe management web application that helps you keep track, manage and generate your inventory, shopping lists, and recipes with a privacy first approach.
about_excerpt: Smart pantry tracking and recipe management web application that helps you keep track, manage and generate your inventory, shopping lists, and recipes with a privacy first approach. Like Comment Story Updates Using Chat GPT MacOS Desktop app for testing, Chat GPT is reasoning through and doing tool calls. Confirmation modal for user after Chat GPT did its work Recipe view that shows the new recipes from Chat GPT The first expanded recipe from Chat GPT The second expanded recipe from Chat GPT Inspiration My wife asks if we have ...breadcrumbs, After checking all four obvious spots I said no, later after she returns with freshly purchased groceries she finds the breadcrumbs in another spot that I didn't think to check. This was not a "we need an app" problem so much as "nobody knew what we had in our pantry and kitchen", and it is exactly the kind of question an AI assistant should be able to answer instantly, if it could ever actually see the pantry. I started building PrepWise Lite earlier this month on my free time as a local-only, privacy first pantry tracker with zero backend by design. when the WebMCP challenge landed, it was the first time there was a legitimate way to let an agent read that data without breaking the one promise the app makes: nothing leaves your device unless you say so, What it does PrepWise Lite tracks a pantry, a cookbook, and food allergies, entirely in the browser's localStorage, no accounts, no backend, no network calls once loaded. Beyond the usual inventory/recipe/shopping-list/expiration features, it now exposes 13 WebMCP tools so an agent open in the same tab can: summarize the pantry and shopping list, find what's expiring soonest, check what's missing (and by how much) from a recipe to help ground a substitution suggestion, rank recipes for weekly planning by what rescues an expiring ingredient, batch several recipes' timing so an agent can sequence them across limited stovetop/oven/air-fryer capacity, check a recipe against a recorded allergy, propose new inventory from a fridge photo, and write up a whole recipe with per-step timers, propose new inventory from a fridge photo, and write up a whole recipe with per-step timers. Every write is staged as a preview the user must confirm, never applied automatically and that preview is a refining pass rather than a yes/no gate: a quantity the model misread off a photo gets corrected in place, and any row dropped, before anything lands. How PrepWise was built Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no bundler, no runtime dependency. The CSP is connect-src 'none', so the app is structurally incapable of making a network call. "assets/js/webmcp.js" registers each tool via "document.modelContext.registerTool();" handlers run in the page next to the same state object the UI already renders from, so exposing a tool is a local function call, not a new attack surface. The governing rule: reads are answered directly, writes are staged. Every write tool builds a backup-shaped payload and routes it through the exact "validateBackup()" to "sanitizeBackup()" then to "import-preview" gate a hand-edited backup file would go through. An agent gets no shortcut a hostile file wouldn't get. The whole feature is off by default; registering nothing until the user intentionally ticks one Settings checkbox. Challenges I ran into Real agents find real bugs static tests miss. An early run against a live agent returned every recipe with a blank method the step text lived in content, and the code read .text. The existing test only asserted "Ingredients:" appeared, so it passed on a recipe with an empty method. Fixed, and the test now checks for actual step text. Keeping "an assistant can propose, never apply" airtight under UI tampering. It's not enough to hide the "replace everything" radio button for agent-sourced imports the confirm handler independently re-checks the source of the import regardless of what the (hide-able, script-editable) radio says. Resisting the urge to fake domain expertise. A few tool ideas we considered such as calculating food-safety timelines during a power outage, flagging "nutritional gaps," reverse-engineering a spice blend, would have required PrepWise to invent plausible-sounding heuristics from a bare item name, with zero temperature, storage-location, or nutrition data behind them. For a food-safety context, a confidently wrong heuristic is a real harm, not just a bug. We scoped those down to "PrepWise hands over the real data it has; the agent's own food/nutrition knowledge does the actual reasoning" instead. Testing an API that doesn't exist yet in a test browser. WebMCP is a moving W3C Community Group draft behind a Chrome flag; Playwright's bundled Chromium doesn't support it at all. Lots of trial and error. Making the preview editable without turning the sanitizer into decoration. The whole point of staging a write is that nothing reaches the pantry unchecked, so adding form fields to that screen is exactly where a safety property quietly dies. The rule we settled on: an edit is still input. Edits land on the staged payload, and the confirm handler re-runs the same sanitizer over all of it before applying — nothing is trusted for having been in the page. The item's name deliberately stayed read-only, because changing it changes whether the merge sees a duplicate, so the row would have to re-decide between "will add" and "already in your pantry" as you type. Accomplishments that I am proud of Added a full agent-facing tool surface without loosening the CSP by one character, connect-src 'none' on day one is still connect-src 'none' today. Every single write path, file import, sample data, or an agent's proposal goes through the identical "validate/sanitize/preview/confirm" gate. There is no separate, quieter door for a model to walk through. Allergy severity is never disclosed to an agent, matching exactly what Settings promises a human user and it's pinned by a test that stages a real conflict and asserts the severity string never appears in the output. 13 tools, off by default, verified against a real agent in real Chrome. The human-in-the-loop gate is a refining pass, not a rubber stamp. A vision model miscounts what it cannot see like six oranges in the photo is eight in the bag once the buried ones are counted. So an agent's proposed rows carry an editable quantity and unit and an Add tick: correct what it misread, drop what you don't want, then confirm, which is more efficient than throwing all the work away and doing a new call. What I learned The right mental model for handing an agent access to a personal-data app isn't "sandbox what it can see" it's "answer freely, stage everything that changes something" which turned out to generalize cleanly across a dozen tools built weeks apart. A local-first architecture, which we'd built for privacy reasons that had nothing to do with AI, turned out to be exactly what makes an app trustworthy to hand to an agent: there's no server in the loop to leak to in the first place. The most valuable thing a tool can do for a model is supply ground truth the model has no other way to get such as what's actually on your shelf, what's actually about to expire, and then get out of the way not try to out-reason the model on things it already knows better such as food chemistry, nutrition, spice profiles. "Approve or reject" is the wrong shape for a human-in-the-loop gate when the model's mistake is small and numeric. Forcing a binary choice on a proposal that is 90% right means the user either accepts a number they know is wrong or discards work that was mostly correct, and the first of those is what actually happens. Letting them fix it in place is better UX and a stronger safety argument: the human stops being a rubber stamp and becomes the one who ultimately decides and approves the unit and value. What's next for PrepWise Lite More refining, and more agentic testing to try and catch anything a real agentic conversation surfaces that a test suite wouldn't. Beyond that: the two other ideas from the original design such as starting a timer, and switching views are still unbuilt, and a couple of the scoped-down ideas from this new round of edits like an honest "storage-location-aware version of the outage/storm tools" would need a deliberate data model addition rather than another heuristic, worth designing and iterating on it properly rather than rushing in under deadline pressure. title: GenScape WebMCP
pitch: A persistent creative run that people and browser agents can inspect, pause, resume, and move into Canvas together.
about_excerpt: A persistent creative run that people and browser agents can inspect, pause, resume, and move into Canvas together. Like Comment Story Updates Creative work is not a single prompt. It moves through intent clarification, skill selection, model routing, asynchronous generation, review, and revision. Screen-driven agents are brittle in this environment: they can click the wrong model, lose a long-running job, repeat a paid request, or expose internal execution prompts. We wanted people and browser agents to share the same visible, recoverable workflow while the human keeps control of consequential creative choices. What it does The page registers six WebMCP tools for the current authenticated user: discover professional skills by workspace; start one real Agent, image, video, or audio run; read bounded public run status and result asset IDs; answer a pending Human-in-the-Loop question and resume the same run; list recent Canvas projects; create a visible Canvas project and return its stable URL. Mutating calls appear in the normal GenScape interface. Status recovery reuses the original run identity instead of silently creating another paid request. Tool results exclude system prompts, planning prompts, optimized execution prompts, provider channel IDs, credentials, routing diagnostics, and hidden model reasoning. How we built it We added a dependency-injected WebMCP layer on top of GenScape's existing authenticated client APIs. The imperative tools use document.modelContext.registerTool() , JSON Schema inputs, WebMCP annotations, one registration AbortSignal , and per-invocation cancellation signals. A React bridge owns registration for the signed-in page identity. Persistent Agent Run IDs connect start, status, Human-in-the-Loop answer, and resumed status. The Apache-2.0 public repository contains the competition adapter, clean standalone reference runtime, tests, and documentation. The existing VOZEB-PRO-derived GenScape host predates the challenge and remains under its existing BUSL/proprietary boundary; it is not copied or relicensed in the competition repository. The hosted demonstration integrates the new adapter with that existing host. The standalone runtime is explicitly a schema and lifecycle fixture and does not claim to generate paid AI media. Challenges The hardest boundary was returning enough state for an agent to make progress without leaking internal planning content. Long-running creation also required stable run identities, idempotent request identities, explicit Human-in-the-Loop state, and cancellation that stops pending browser requests without pretending an already accepted upstream task never happened. Accomplishments Six discoverable tools backed by the same visible workflows as the human UI. A complete start -> status -> answer -> status loop on one persistent run. Canvas creation with a stable URL. Registration removal on logout or page-owner change. Invocation cancellation forwarded through AbortSignal . Public result shaping with tests proving internal fields stay isolated. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools map to durable domain actions rather than UI controls. A reliable creative tool returns stable identities and visible state transitions, while the page remains the review and control surface. Browser-native tools are also a useful privacy boundary: the agent receives the public workflow state it needs, not the host's internal execution context. What's next Add tools scoped to the active Canvas selection, browser-mediated confirmation before high-cost generations, standardized output schemas when the proposal stabilizes, and progress notifications for long-running media work. title: OVERTURN
pitch: Health insurers deny 1 in 5 claims and almost no one fights back. Overturn pairs you with an agent that builds the appeal through WebMCP tools — and waits for your OK to file.
about_excerpt: Health insurers deny 1 in 5 claims and almost no one fights back. Overturn pairs you with an agent that builds the appeal through WebMCP tools — and waits for your OK to file. Like Comment Story Updates landing page with the problem stats parsed case file, 160-day deadline, evidence checklist after approval, confirmation and payer timeline in the console use this one first: the agent paused mid-tool with the drafted letter, strength score 78/Strong, and the "Approve & file / Decline" card Inspiration Health insurers deny about 1 in 5 in-network claims, and fewer than 1% of patients ever appeal — even though a large share of appeals that get filed succeed. The fight isn't hard because it's complicated; it's hard because it's tedious : decode the denial codes, find the payer's medical policy, match your facts to its criteria, cite guidelines, compute the deadline, draft the letter, file on time. That tedium is exactly what an agent should do. The judgment, the consent, and the signature are exactly what a human must do. The WebMCP Challenge asked for an app that gets meaningfully better when people and agents use it together — an appeals office is that, almost literally: two workers, one case file, a clear division of labor. What it does Paste a denial letter into Overturn (it stays in your browser — nothing is uploaded). The agent then works through 13 WebMCP tools: it parses the letter into a structured case, decodes the claim-adjustment codes, finds the payer medical policy that justified the denial, checks each coverage criterion against the record, attaches citable guideline evidence, computes the filing deadline by plan type, drafts a full appeal letter, and scores its strength with a factor-by-factor breakdown. Then the part the product exists for: when the agent calls submit_appeal , the tool pauses and an approval card appears. Nothing is filed until the human clicks Approve & file . After filing, human and agent watch the payer timeline together. No WebMCP available? A built-in "Run demo agent" walks the identical tool implementations — including the approval pause — so anyone can see the loop. How we built it A zero-dependency, zero-build static page (GitHub Pages), with a strict separation between pure logic and the WebMCP layer: js/tools.js registers 13 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) , each returning MCP-style { content: [{ type: "text" }] } envelopes with isError on failure. Following Chrome's WebMCP security guidance: annotations.readOnlyHint on every state-preserving tool, annotations.untrustedContentHint on every tool whose output embeds the (untrusted) denial letter, and Chrome's design budgets — ≤500-char tool descriptions, ≤150-char parameter descriptions, ~1.4K-char outputs. Tool descriptions teach workflow ("Call draft_appeal_letter first — the human must be able to read what will be filed"). The human's UI and the agent's tools are two surfaces over one shared pipeline : the app's own buttons call the same tool implementations with actor: "human" , so the console shows exactly who did what. The approval gate is a tool promise that only resolves when the human clicks — defense in depth on top of whatever the agent's host requires — with a 3-minute timeout that declines by default. Pure pipeline logic (parsing, criteria matching, deadline math, drafting, scoring) is unit-tested in Node: 25 assertions, all passing. Challenges we ran into Consent inside a tool call. submit_appeal has to stop mid-execution and wait for a human. We resolved it by parking the tool's promise on an approval card in the UI — which raised real questions (what if nobody answers? default-deny after a timeout) that most apps never have to think about. Parsing adversarial prose without a server. Extracting payer, claim, codes, and plan type from a letter using only regex and keyword rules — including a negation guard so "no red flags" doesn't count as evidence for red flags. The 1.5K output budget forced us to design tool results as agent-oriented summaries with pointers ("the full letter is in the human's editor") instead of dumping state. A delightful DST off-by-one: computing "days left to file" across a time-change boundary needs calendar arithmetic, not millisecond diffs. A unit test caught it. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop works end-to-end: paste → agent legwork → human edit → approval → confirmation and payer timeline — verified in a real browser against the deployed site. The approval moment is genuinely good product design, not a checkbox: the agent can do everything except the one step that matters, alone. Graceful degradation: feature-detecting document.modelContext means the app is fully usable everywhere, and the demo agent gives judges without WebMCP the exact same story. What we learned Tool descriptions are prompts. Writing them as workflow guidance (what to call next, what to do when data is missing) mattered more than any schema detail. Annotations are a design language. Marking untrusted content and read-only tools forced us to think about trust boundaries the way a security reviewer would. Output budgets are a feature. Constraining tool results made the agent interface better — small, pointed results with pointers beat dumps. Building for two users at once (human + agent) makes the product simpler, not more complex, when the state is genuinely shared. What's next for OVERTURN Real-world ingestion: PDF/photo import of denial letters and EOBs (still on-device). A payer-connector layer so submit_appeal can target real portals behind explicit per-payer consent, plus certified-mail and fax fallbacks. Multi-appeal dashboard with deadline tracking across a household's claims, and an exportable audit log of every agent action for regulators and advocates. Delegated review: let a family member or patient advocate be the approval authority. Keep contributing to the WebMCP conversation: this project is a strong argument for app-level consent gates as a standard annotation. title: Alun Agent Desk
pitch: A human–agent cultural intelligence workspace that turns traceable AI-and-music evidence into policy-ready briefs without hiding uncertainty or replacing judgment.

A human–agent cultural intelligence workspace that turns traceable AI-and-music evidence into policy-ready briefs without hiding uncertainty or replacing judgment.

 What's next for Alun Agent Desk 

 Inspiration 

 AI policy discussions often move faster than cultural institutions can verify evidence, preserve uncertainty, or include artists in decisions. Alun Agent Desk explores a simple question: what if an agent could work directly with a trusted cultural evidence surface while human judgment remained visible and accountable? 

 What it does 

 Alun Agent Desk is a shared human-agent workspace for AI-and-music developments. A person can browse source-linked records and see their evidence status, geography, implications, and uncertainty. A WebMCP-capable agent can use four structured tools to search developments, inspect a record, compare jurisdictions, and prepare an audience-specific cultural brief. 

 Every tool call changes the same visible interface. The person can see which evidence the agent selected, review the resulting brief, and verify the original sources. The app does not silently turn events, consultations, or platform policies into settled law. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer meaning from page layout or conduct an unrelated web search. With WebMCP, Alun exposes a bounded, traceable evidence model directly to the agent. This makes the interaction faster and more reliable while preserving provenance and uncertainty for the human reviewer. 

 The key collaboration is: the agent finds and structures evidence; people retain interpretation, legitimacy, and decision authority. 

 How it was built 

 The application is a responsive React and TypeScript site hosted on ChatGPT Sites. It registers four tools through document.modelContext.registerTool: search_developments, inspect_development, compare_developments, and prepare_cultural_brief. Tool results update React state so agent actions and the human review surface remain synchronized. 

 The evidence set is deliberately small and source-linked. Search supports geography, status, and thematic filters, including explicit reporting when requested regional evidence is missing. 

 Challenges and learning 

 The main design challenge was preventing a polished brief from appearing more authoritative than its sources. The interface therefore keeps source URLs, evidence status, jurisdiction, and uncertainty visible. Testing also exposed a hidden audience filter that made tool results diverge from the visible list; it was removed so the agent and person now share the same result set. 

 What is next 

 The prototype can expand into the Alun Situation Room as a public cultural-technology evidence layer. Future work would add carefully reviewed records and institutional workflows without turning the tool into an automated policy authority.

title: Briefly
pitch: Briefly lets content teams research trends, bring in business context, and co-write briefs with an AI agent that sees and acts on the same app state.
about_excerpt:
Briefly lets content teams research trends, bring in business context, and co-write briefs with an AI agent that sees and acts on the same app state.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Turn a rising trend into a structured, on-brand content brief ready for review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give agents your audience, brand voice, offerings, and claim guardrails to guide every brief. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Explore trend signals, growth charts, and sample content to find your next angle. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Review the draft and approve it when it’s ready—AI assists, you decide. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Turn a rising trend into a structured, on-brand content brief ready for review. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give agents your audience, brand voice, offerings, and claim guardrails to guide every brief. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Explore trend signals, growth charts, and sample content to find your next angle. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Review the draft and approve it when it’s ready—AI assists, you decide. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Selecting a trend and offering makes the relevant tools available for agents to compose and save a brief. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 A trending keyword is easy to find. A useful content brief is harder. You need
the source material, the right audience, the product you actually want to sell,
and a clear list of what the business can and cannot claim. 

 We kept thinking about the annoying part of this workflow: why do we still copy
a trend from one dashboard, open the product notes somewhere else, explain all
of it again in a chat, then copy the answer back into a document? Every move
loses a little context. 

 So we built Briefly around one idea. What if the agent works in the same
workspace as the person, understands what they are looking at right now, and
writes the result back into the actual workflow? 

 What it does 

 Briefly puts trend discovery, business context, content briefs, a calendar, and
performance examples in one browser workspace. 

 The flow is simple. A person opens a trend, reads its source material, and
chooses a business offering. Once both are selected, the agent can read the
full context and write a draft into the brief library. The person can inspect
the draft, create their own version in the composer, change its workflow
status, or schedule it on the local calendar. 

 This is where WebMCP matters. Briefly does not give the agent one giant static
list of tools. Its tool surface changes with the interface. Open a trend and
the detail tools appear. Open the business-profile editor and the editing tools
appear. Select both a trend and an offering and get_brief_context ,
 generate_brief , and save_brief become available. Remove either selection
and those tools disappear again. 

 There are 37 tool definitions in the app, but they are not exposed all at once.
The point is not the number. The point is that the right tool appears when the
person and the agent have enough context to use it. 

 The current prototype uses seeded trend and performance data. It does not fetch
live social metrics, prove engagement growth, or publish anything to a social
platform. A "published" status in Briefly is local planning state, not a real
network post. Saved briefs can be inspected and moved through the workflow,
but their content cannot yet be edited in place from the library. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. We kept the runtime
small: React + React DOM are the only runtime packages. Browser-local stores
hold the briefs, business profile, watchlist, calendar, and tool traces. 

 WebMCP tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool . Their
lifecycle follows the same React route and selection state that controls the
interface. The human controls and agent tools call the same store functions, so
when the agent navigates or saves a draft, the person sees it happen on screen. 

 We also built a local console bridge that exposes the same schemas and executor
functions in browsers without native WebMCP support. It is useful for
development and inspection, but we do not treat bridge access as proof of a
native WebMCP flow. 

 Two optional Vercel endpoints use Gemini for trend analysis and draft
generation. The core agent flow does not depend on them. A connected agent can
read the context, write the brief itself, and save the draft through
 save_brief . 

 The interface uses CSS custom properties with warm off-white surfaces and
oxidized-iron accents. We added committed checks for tool contracts, surface
changes, important UI states, and the production build. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was not registering a tool. It was deciding when that tool
should exist. 

 A static catalog looked complete, but in practice it gave the agent actions
that could not succeed yet. Briefly had to track the route, the open trend, the
selected offering, and whether an editor was open. That is what made the tool
surface feel connected to the product instead of attached on top of it. 

 Host compatibility was another real problem. Some WebMCP hosts support tool
registration but do not provide the event-listener methods the inspector first
expected. We changed the inspector so native registration stays intact while
its discovery view can fall back to the local registry. 

 We also had to be strict about what this prototype proves. Seeded metrics are
not customer results. Local workflow state is not social publishing. The
optional deployed model endpoints still need repair and a full retest, and
some captured cover images still need documented permission or replacement.
Hiding those limitations would make the demo sound stronger, but the product
less trustworthy. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that the demo is not just a chat response beside a dashboard. The
agent can navigate the same workspace, read the selected context, and leave a
real draft inside the library for the person to review. 

 The app now has 37 state-dependent tool definitions across eight tested surface
states. It covers discovery, business context, brief creation, scheduling,
performance, and the trace log. Human controls and agent calls share the same
stores, so the two paths do not quietly create different versions of the app. 

 We are also proud of the less visible work. generate_brief returns an unsaved
draft. save_brief always creates a draft. Tool calls receive trace IDs, and
the agent can inspect the same trace log shown to the person. The tool-contract
suite currently passes 51 checks, including invalid inputs, refusal paths,
idempotent operations, and recovery actions. 

 What we learned 

 More tools do not automatically make a better agent experience. Sometimes the
best tool is the one that stays hidden until the context is ready. 

 We learned that human and agent parity also goes both ways. If the person can
add something to a watchlist, stop a video, correct a calendar entry, or inspect
a failed action, the agent needs a safe way to do that too. Creation alone is
not enough. The agent needs to read, undo, and recover. 

 We also learned to separate saving from deciding. save_brief creates a draft,
but another tool can still move its local status forward. That means Briefly is
not a human-only approval system yet. Being precise about that distinction is
important, especially in a demo where a local "published" label can easily be
mistaken for a real post. 

 What's next for Briefly 

 First, we want to replace the seeded trend data with a transparent source of
real data and test whether Briefly actually saves time for content teams. 

 Second, we want to add authentication, shared persistence, and proper review
permissions so a team can see who changed a brief and who approved it. 

 Third, we need to finish the unglamorous but necessary work: repair and retest
the deployed Gemini endpoints, resolve or replace the cover images with missing
permissions, and test the full workflow across more native WebMCP hosts. 

 The bigger goal is still the same. We want the agent to understand the work
that is already happening on screen, help at the right moment, and leave
something useful behind when the conversation ends.

title: Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos
pitch: A shared, traceable olfactory workspace where people and agents reason over the same live 3D Atlas.
about_excerpt: A shared, traceable olfactory workspace where people and agents reason over the same live 3D Atlas. Like 1 Comment Story Updates ChatGPT using Olfaria's five WebMCP tools beside the authenticated Crystal Neural Atlas. Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos showing traceable olfemes and graph relationships in the live 3D workspace. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Olfaria Crystal Atlas Neural Erdos Inspiration Smell is difficult to search and explain. Sensory language is ambiguous, formulation problems are contextual, and the evidence behind a recommendation is hard to keep visible. The existing Olfaria Crystal Neural Atlas made those relationships explorable for a person, but an agent still had to guess how to operate a dense 3D interface. WebMCP provided the missing contract between structured reasoning and shared visual context. What it does A perfumer can describe a problem in natural language while an agent uses five typed Olfaria tools: search_olfemas maps language to bounded corpus results. get_relations reads recorded relationships and uncertainty. compare_olfemas separates shared attributes from differences. find_path traces a reproducible route through existing graph edges. focus_nodes makes the relevant evidence visible in the live Atlas without modifying the corpus. The person remains in control of the visual exploration. The agent handles precise retrieval and traversal, then points back to the same olfemes on screen. Corpus evidence stays separate from formulation interpretation. Why WebMCP Conventional browser automation would have to infer meaning from canvas graphics, controls and transient UI state. Olfaria instead declares exactly what an agent may do, with bounded JSON schemas and explicit side-effect semantics. The agent does not scrape the 3D interface or receive unrestricted application internals. It calls narrow tools that reuse the Atlas's deterministic graph service and existing visual controller. This makes the interaction faster and more reliable, but the larger improvement is epistemic: a recommendation can remain visibly connected to its source concepts, stored relations and uncertainty. Human-agent experience Before WebMCP, a person could explore the Atlas and an agent could discuss fragrance concepts, but their contexts were separate. With WebMCP they collaborate in one loop: the person supplies intent, the agent retrieves structured evidence, the Atlas visualizes the exact nodes, and the person evaluates the result. The visual state becomes a shared working memory rather than a screenshot to interpret. How it was built The existing Crystal Neural Atlas remains the only product renderer. A narrow window.OlfariaAtlasApi bridge exposes visual focus without leaking internal state. The page registers five tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. Four read-only tools call bounded deterministic graph operations. focus_nodes delegates to the Atlas controller and changes only the current browser view. The corpus loader validates the dataset, constructs immutable indexes and records a SHA-256 digest for reproducibility. Authentication protects the production Atlas, APIs and WebMCP registration with signed, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict browser sessions. The public repository documents the implementation and includes the WebMCP adapter, service design and approved media, while local test packages, proprietary corpus data, production account hashes and session keys remain outside Git. Challenges Preserving the existing 3D renderer instead of creating a parallel agent-only experience. Defining tool outputs that distinguish stored evidence from deterministic technical inference. Keeping graph traversal bounded over 5,000 olfemes and 12,560 relationships. Making a session-protected WebMCP app deploy safely under a subpath. Publishing implementation context without releasing proprietary corpus data or credentials. Accomplishments Five stable, typed WebMCP tools with clear side-effect annotations. A real human-agent fragrance workflow that keeps evidence visible in the Atlas. Deterministic corpus operations with bounded inputs and traceable outputs. Graceful degradation when WebMCP is unavailable. A sanitized public implementation record without local test data or production secrets. A production login boundary that does not place credentials in the repository. What we learned Agent-native design is not the same as automating more clicks. The most useful interface was a small semantic contract aligned with the application's real domain boundaries. Visual actions and scientific reads also need different trust semantics: focusing a node is reversible browser state, while corpus claims must remain immutable and traceable. What's next Version the WebMCP contract independently from corpus releases. Add audit identifiers to every result so a judge or researcher can trace it to a specific corpus build. Add controlled multi-user workspaces without weakening session isolation. Extend evidence visualization while preserving the distinction between recorded and derived relationships. Challenge-period extension The Crystal Neural Atlas and corpus existed before the challenge. Between August 25 and September 3, 2026, the project was meaningfully extended with the WebMCP bridge, five typed tools, deterministic service endpoints, visual focus controller, English human-agent workflow, production authentication and subpath-safe deployment. The public repository preserves the implementation record and includes a dedicated development-history document. title: NatureX Seller Copilot
pitch: A WebMCP-powered copilot that helps live sellers manage customer claims, inventory, orders and restocks while they stay focused on the broadcast.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered copilot that helps live sellers manage customer claims, inventory, orders and restocks while they stay focused on the broadcast.
