 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 NatureX Seller Copilot comes from a problem I deal with in real life. 

 I sell products through live streams. During a live sale, I need to present the product, talk to viewers, read comments, notice who wants to buy, remember the product and price, keep track of stock, and manage orders at the same time. 

 In my current workflow, when someone comments a product code or says “aldım” — Turkish for “I’ll take it” — I may write the username, product and price down manually so I do not lose the order. 

 It works, but during a busy live stream it becomes very easy for the seller to lose focus or miss something. 

 That is where the idea for NatureX came from. 

 When I discovered WebMCP, I started wondering: instead of asking AI to replace the seller, what if the application could give an AI agent clear tools to help with the operational work while the seller stays focused on the live audience? 

 That became NatureX Seller Copilot. 

 What it does 

 NatureX Seller Copilot is a live-commerce control dashboard designed to be used by both a human seller and an AI agent. 

 The seller can use the normal interface, while WebMCP exposes structured tools that allow an AI agent to understand and assist with the live-selling workflow. 

 The prototype focuses on tasks such as: 

 
 checking the current live-sale state 
 reviewing pending customer claims 
 managing order decisions 
 checking inventory 
 identifying low-stock products 
 viewing sales information 
 handling products that are temporarily out of stock but expected to be restocked 
 

 The main idea is simple: the seller keeps selling, while the copilot helps manage what is happening behind the scenes. 

 How we built it 

 I am building the challenge project as a separate web prototype based on the real workflow behind NatureX. 

 The important design decision is that the visual dashboard and the WebMCP tools should not have two different sets of business rules. 

 Whether the seller acts through the interface or explicitly authorizes a WebMCP-assisted stock reservation, both paths go through the same underlying application logic. 

 WebMCP gives the agent explicit tools instead of forcing it to guess which buttons to click on the screen. 

 The tool set is intentionally small and focused on real live-commerce operations such as session state, customer claims, stock, order resolution, sales information, and incoming-stock context. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One challenge is deciding what the AI should be allowed to do and what should remain under human control. 

 Live commerce moves quickly, but an automated decision can still affect a real customer and real inventory. Because of that, I do not want the AI to simply “do everything.” 

 Another challenge is inventory. 

 For example, during a live sale a product can reach zero stock even though more units are arriving the next day. In my real workflow, automatically cancelling every order in that situation would not always be the right decision. 

 The system therefore needs to understand the difference between a product that is truly unavailable and one that is temporarily waiting for restock. 

 A third challenge is designing WebMCP tools that are useful without creating too many overlapping tools that confuse the agent. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What I like most about this project is that it did not start as an AI demo. 

 The problem existed before the hackathon. 

 I already wanted to build NatureX because managing live sales manually creates a lot of repetitive work while the seller is trying to stay engaged with viewers. 

 WebMCP gave me a new way to think about that problem. 

 Instead of building a separate chatbot beside the application, I can make the application itself understandable and usable by an AI agent. 

 I am also proud of the human + agent approach: the seller is still in control, but does not have to handle every small operational task alone. 

 What we learned 

 Before this challenge I was not familiar with WebMCP. 

 The biggest thing I learned is that making an application useful to an AI agent is not only about adding AI to the interface. 

 The application needs clear actions, clear data, predictable business rules and carefully designed tools. 

 I also learned that sometimes the best role for AI is not to replace the user. 

 In this project, AI is more useful as a second pair of hands for the seller. 

 That idea is something I can use far beyond this challenge. 

 What's next for NatureX Seller Copilot 

 This hackathon project is a small prototype of a much larger idea. 

 My long-term vision for NatureX includes live-stream management, comments, customer orders, inventory, payments, shipping preparation, label printing and sales analytics in one system. 

 I would like to explore how the same WebMCP approach could eventually make those parts agent-accessible as well. 

 The end goal is not an autonomous store. 

 It is a live-commerce workspace where the human seller can concentrate on people, products and the broadcast while software and AI quietly handle more of the repetitive operational work.

title: Lattice
pitch: A better way to review architecture with your agents.
about_excerpt: A better way to review architecture with your agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am a designer and engineer, so naturally, I love whiteboarding ideas. Especially today, as the implementation of software can be abstracted more than ever, I find it both necessary and enjoyable to diagram architectures before I build my ideas with agents. However, the revision loop has lately felt more drawn out that it needs to. I tried a bunch of whiteboarding apps before landing on the excellent tldraw , but as advanced as it is, it's still tedious to use it in conversation with an agent about a given diagram. I often turn to Computer Use, which relies on the slow process of screenshots and imprecise whiteboarding editing, and the alternative is building a custom API with an unnecessary amount of complexity just to allow and agent and I to collaborate on a whiteboard. WebMCP seemed like an excellent fit to make this workflow more efficient. What it does Lattice is an infinite canvas that functions similarly to tldraw, which it's built on, but specialized for reviewing architecture diagrams with your agents. It exposes WebMCP tools to view, create, and edit diagrams, so you can ask it to explain code concepts in an instant. Where Lattice really excels, though, is in its comment tool. Just like Figma, you can easily mark up any node or area on the board, and the agent connected to Lattice is able to understand exactly what you annotated without any screenshots or even any semantic references in your comments. How I built it Each Lattice board is stored in the browser via localStorage, so it persists with no accounts or exports needed. The underlying architecture is stored as a semantic graph, where every node, edge, and comment has metadata labeling exactly what and where it is (ID, type, label, connection, position). This is what allows the connected agent to make targeted edits without screenshots and without editing unrelated parts of the board. Challenges I ran into While dogfooding the first version of this app, I found myself constantly telling the agent, "I added a few comments, check them." It became a bit tedious, so I thought this back-and-forth could be improved with a simple keyword, like "Lattice." A skill was a perfect fit here, so I wrote a lightweight one that explains what the user is trying to do when they say "/lattice create" or just "/lattice" (to edit). Accomplishments that I'm proud of Lattice is not just a demo for me. I've started using it every day in the Codex in-app browser, and it truly has made me more productive, allowing me to understand concepts better and churn out higher quality code more efficiently. What I learned Before this challenge, I hadn't heard of WebMCP, so I learned all about how it works and where it works best (hoping more companies begin integrating it into their apps!). I also learned how to maximize an agent's capabilities not by necessarily giving it more tools, but rather by improving its existing set of tools through more narrow typing, better tool descriptions, and more. What's next for Lattice I plan on sharing this app with a few friends to see if/how it fits into their workflows. I suspect that many of them use whiteboards for more than just diagramming architecture, and the great part about Lattice today is its simplicity and its foundation (tldraw) that can be expanded in countless ways to support more use cases. Along with potentially expanding its feature set, I hope to find more ways to integrate it into my own workflow, like I did when I made the Lattice skill. I can imagine that instructing the agent to automatically create new diagrams when relevant would be useful, and I could even see some sort of cross-board context coming in handy as I work on one project across multiple Codex threads. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: LightningPricePilot
pitch: Agentic Price Discovery and Negotiation - LightningPricePilot is a WebMCP-enabled laptop marketplace.
about_excerpt: Agentic Price Discovery and Negotiation - LightningPricePilot is a WebMCP-enabled laptop marketplace. Like Comment Story Updates App Landing Page Shopper Page Merchant Page Shopper joining buying group after ChatGPT negotiated a group price for the laptop Shopper placing order after ChatGPT negotiated a good price for the laptop Two-sided bargain loop diagram Architecture diagram Actors diagram Use case diagram Inspiration The app's idea was inspired by my recent coffee brewing kettle buying experience. It wasn't a great experience trying to find a reasonable price after spending a couple of hours checking on Amazon and coffee equipment websites, only to realize the bargain price kettle I want in Amazon has target delivery date next year 2027 on the very final order payment page. My intent is to get it as soon as possible. Hence, it inspired me to create LightningPricePilot - a Two-sided Intent Market so that shopper can better communicate their intent to the merchant. What it does LightningPricePilot is a two-sided intent marketplace where shoppers and merchants use AI agents to discover fairer laptop prices. Instead of scraping product cards, a shopper’s agent uses structured WebMCP tools to search laptops, compare new and refurbished prices, negotiate within merchant-defined guardrails, join group buys, subscribe to target-price bargains, receive notifications, and prepare a mock checkout. On the other side, a merchant’s agent can analyze aggregate demand, review offer activity, adjust private pricing policies, and publish limited bargains to matching shoppers. The experience keeps people in control: commitments, policy changes, bargain publication, and checkout require visible human approval. Merchant price floors remain private, shopper targets are shown only in aggregate, and the demo never collects payment or personal information. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Product discovery and pricing depend on live website state: condition-specific inventory, current and group-buy prices, group progress, active bargains, offer expiry, and merchant pricing policies. These details are difficult for an agent to understand reliably by reading page text or clicking through filters. WebMCP turns that state into precise, discoverable actions. On the shopper page, an agent can search the laptop catalogue, compare condition, group, and bargain price paths, request a rule-bound offer, join a group buy, save a target-price subscription, read bargain notifications, and prepare a mock checkout. On the merchant page, a different agent can review aggregate demand and offer activity, update private pricing guardrails, and publish or close limited bargains. Each page registers only the tools appropriate to its role, with the room code already bound to every call. Both roles use the same validated room backend, so a shopper action can change aggregate demand and a merchant action can create a qualifying shopper notification without exposing the merchant’s private floor through the shopper tool surface. This transforms the storefront from a static catalogue into a structured negotiation space for people, shopper agents, and merchant agents. How it creates a better user experience The shopper describes the outcome once: “Find me a lightweight laptop under $900. Excellent refurbished condition is acceptable. Compare every available price path and negotiate toward $800 if sensible.” The agent can then present understandable options instead of another long list of products: Buy at the current price for the selected condition Join a group buy and show how many more commitments would unlock its next discount Use an active, inventory-limited merchant bargain Request a ten-minute offer or transparent counteroffer within the merchant’s private guardrails Save the product, acceptable condition, and target price for a future bargain Every price path states why it is available, whether it is currently unlocked, and what the shopper must do next. Offers include their rationale and expiry. Joining a group, saving a subscription, and placing the fictional mock order pause for visible human approval. The shopper no longer needs to repeatedly search the catalogue, compare product conditions, monitor group progress, or refresh the page looking for a relevant bargain. Matching merchant bargains create persisted in-app notifications, while server-sent events update the open room live. Merchants gain a complementary experience: they can see group commitments, subscriber counts, average target prices, and offer volume; tune the private floor and discount limits; and publish limited bargains that are matched against saved shopper intent. They do this without receiving a list of individual shopper budgets. Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before People remain responsible for the important trade-offs: Which laptop condition is acceptable What target price is worthwhile Whether to join a non-binding group buy Whether to save buying intent in the room Whether to complete a fictional checkout On the merchant side, whether to change pricing policy or publish or close a bargain Agents handle the structured, repetitive work: Search products by need, use case, condition, and budget Compare current condition, unlocked group, and active bargain prices Request an accepted offer or explain a policy-bound counteroffer Retrieve relevant bargain notifications Summarize aggregate demand and recent offer outcomes Turn a demand signal into a proposed limited bargain For example, the merchant agent can see that a product has five group commitments, three bargain subscribers, an aggregate average target, and recent offer activity. It can propose a price, condition, inventory allocation, expiry, and shopper-facing message. The merchant reviews the action before publication; matching subscribers then receive an in-app notification that the shopper agent can retrieve and explain. This creates something that was previously difficult: asynchronous negotiation around durable buyer intent . A shopper can save a condition and target price, leave the original search, and return to a persisted notification after a merchant publishes a qualifying bargain. Demand is used to unlock lower group prices and guide shared bargains—not to secretly calculate a different price for each shopper. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP LightningPricePilot implements two role-specific WebMCP surfaces with document.modelContext.registerTool . The shopper page registers seven tools: search_products — find up to five laptops by plain-language query, use case, condition, or maximum budget get_price_options — compare the current condition price, group-buy path, and any active bargain for one laptop request_offer — create a non-binding ten-minute accepted offer or counteroffer within merchant guardrails join_group_buy — record the shopper’s non-binding group commitment and unlock a tier when its threshold is reached subscribe_bargains — save a product, acceptable condition, and target price in the demo room get_notifications — retrieve persisted bargain notifications, treating merchant-authored messages as untrusted content prepare_mock_checkout — place a human-approved fictional order from a valid offer and decrement demo inventory The merchant page registers five tools: get_demand_summary — return group commitments, subscriber counts, aggregate average targets, and offer counts get_offer_activity — return recent accepted, countered, expired, and checked-out offers set_pricing_policy — update the private floor, maximum instant discount, and five- and ten-buyer discounts publish_bargain — publish a condition-specific, inventory-limited, expiring bargain and notify matching subscribers close_bargain — stop an active bargain while preserving its notification and audit history Each tool posts its role, action, and structured input to the room action API. The server validates the room, role-specific action allowlist, and input schema before running shared domain logic against the room’s persisted state. The deterministic pricing service enforces condition inventory, merchant floors, instant-discount limits, five- and ten-buyer group tiers, bargain inventory, and expiry. How we built it We built LightningPricePilot with Next.js 16, React, and TypeScript. The shopper and merchant pages register 12 role-specific tools using document.modelContext.registerTool: seven shopper tools and five merchant tools. The app intentionally contains no embedded model or OpenAI API key—the intelligence comes from the WebMCP-capable browser agent. Every tool calls a shared, validated room API backed by Zod schemas and deterministic pricing logic. That pricing engine handles condition-based inventory, private merchant floors, instant-discount limits, group-buy tiers, expiring offers, and inventory-limited bargains. title: ONE TRIP WIN
pitch: Pack smart. Move once. A shared 3D workspace where people and AI agents plan, optimize, and validate a moving-truck load together.
about_excerpt: Pack smart. Move once. A shared 3D workspace where people and AI agents plan, optimize, and validate a moving-truck load together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have moved more times than I care to count, and I have helped enough friends move that I have become the guy with the truck . That title sounds useful until moving day arrives and everyone suddenly expects you to solve a three-dimensional furniture puzzle while carrying a sofa. Moving trucks have a special law of physics: every couch gets larger the moment it reaches the driveway, every fragile box ends up underneath a box of books, and the phrase “we can make it fit” usually means “we are about to make a second trip.” A visual load planner like ONE TRIP WIN would have saved a lot of scratched furniture, wasted truck space, and conversations that began with, “Turn it the other way,” and ended with everyone silently blaming the sectional. What it does ONE TRIP WIN is a shared 3D moving plan. You place it. AI works around it. A person enters confirmed dimensions and handling rules, drags cargo into position, and locks the choices they want to keep. An AI agent reads the same plan through WebMCP and packs around those locks. The guided demo starts with three of 18 sample items loaded and one overlap. Unpacked miniatures wait beside the truck on wide screens; the full inventory wraps into rows below. The agent arranges the load in the 12-foot demo truck, favoring front-wall compaction and supported stacks, with an animated transition into the planned positions. The default packed load uses about 82% of the floor, 52% of the bounding-box volume, and 838 lb of the illustrative 900 lb payload allowance. The person moves the first-night bag and selects Keep here , then adds a last-minute ottoman. The agent adapts the arrangement while preserving that exact locked placement. The person reviews the results and provides the final approval. The interface has fitted 3D and top views, direct drag-and-drop, rotation and height controls, Undo, and clickable issue highlights. The results show actual loaded-item counts, overlaps, unsupported items, payload, and volume. Changed cargo flashes blue, and a shared activity trail explains who changed what. How we built it The app uses React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, and Tailwind CSS, with Vinext and Cloudflare Workers through ChatGPT Sites. Six tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool: get_moving_load reads inventory, dimensions, handling, locks, placements, and checks. place_moving_item repositions unlocked cargo. remove_moving_item returns unlocked cargo to inventory. auto_arrange_moving_load packs around human-locked placements. set_moving_truck_size selects a 12-, 16-, or 26-foot demo truck. validate_moving_load reports placement issues and affected item IDs. Human controls and agent tools use one synchronous store. The agent sees human changes immediately. It cannot unlock an item, invent its measurements, or approve the plan. Undo restores the previous arrangement and requires fresh human review. Packing uses a bounded deterministic heuristic with physical dimensions, permitted horizontal rotations, payload, collision checks, full-footprint support, and cumulative bearing limits. Items that cannot be placed remain in inventory with reasons. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making collaboration visible in the same 3D workspace. A person's locked placement has to survive every editing path: direct agent moves, removal, repacking, and truck changes. A supported stack also needs its supporting base preserved. We had to represent height and support, because a moving truck is a volume, not a very expensive floor mat. We also replaced a general load score with measured results so people can understand what passed, what needs attention, and which item caused it. Accomplishments that we're proud of Six discoverable WebMCP tools operating on the same plan as the person Human-owned locks that the agent works around Direct drag-and-drop with valid and invalid placement previews Undo that preserves the need for human approval Readable 3D and top views with camera reset Measured checks with clickable cargo highlights A guided move that tracks actual agent calls and human edits A complete collaboration flow with a human-only final approval control What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when the agent is not operating somewhere behind the curtain. It becomes useful when the person and the AI can see, change, and validate the same state together. Turning a stressful real-world task into a puzzle makes the solution easier to understand—and considerably more fun than arguing with a sofa in a driveway. Try the guided move Open the live app in a browser with WebMCP support and choose Try the guided move . Ask the agent to read and pack the inventory. Drag the first-night bag, select Keep here , and add the sample ottoman. Then ask: Repack around my locked items, include the new item, and validate the result. Do not approve it for me. Review the checks and approve the plan yourself. Manual entry, packing, locks, Undo, and the guided demonstration require no API key or login. Photos are optional local visual references in the hosted demo. Dimensions and weight are always entered and confirmed by the person. The optional local AI identification integration is disabled on hosted builds. Truck specifications and sample measurements are illustrative. These are planning checks, not a transport-safety certification. There is no door-clearance or loading/unloading-path check, and the packing heuristic does not prove an optimal arrangement. What's next for ONE TRIP WIN Saved household inventories, shared moving plans, a durable allowance for hosted photo identification, and stronger packing optimization could extend the experience. The goal remains fewer avoidable second trips and a clearer plan before anyone starts carrying the sofa. title: Dwa na Jeden — Wedding Dance AI Coach

about_excerpt:
Real-time web trainer for Poland's iconic wedding dance (Szuraniec / 2-on-1). Powered by WebMCP, Web Audio & Web Vibration API to teach footwork with AI agents.

 Dwa na Jeden — Real-time Wedding Dance Coach Interface 
 
 1 2 



 
 Dwa na Jeden — Autonomous Wedding Dance AI Coach 💃🕺 

 💡 Inspiration: From Static Chatbots to Active Physical Coaches 

 Every weekend around the world, wedding guests freeze in panic when invited to the dance floor. Traditional ballroom courses are slow and intimidating, while standard AI chatbots (like ChatGPT) can only give abstract text advice that fails to build physical muscle memory. 

 We asked: What if an AI Agent could actually step onto the dance floor with you as an active, real-time dance instructor? 

 Powered by the Model Context Protocol (WebMCP), Dwa na Jeden transforms the open web into an interactive, agent-driven dance studio. The AI agent doesn't just "talk" about dancing—it acts as an Autonomous Pilot , reading the exact millisecond methodology, inspecting real-time state, and dynamically orchestrating training sessions. 

 

 🤖 The WebMCP Paradigm: Knowledge, State & Action 

 Unlike standard chatbots that guess dance steps, an AI agent connected to Dwa na Jeden via WebMCP gains native programmatic control over the trainer. We implemented a complete 10-tool WebMCP suite (P1 Milestone) that moves beyond simple data retrieval into full application piloting: 

 
 Pedagogical Knowledge ( get_step_instructions , get_wedding_songs , recommend_song_by_bpm ): The agent retrieves structured JSON breakdowns for the 4-phase syncopation ("Raz, Dwa, Trzy, I"), sub-beat timings, and biomechanical rules (soft knees, low-friction sliding). 
 Real-Time State Inspection ( get_training_state ): The agent doesn't fly blind. It inspects the live session to see which foot is bearing weight, the active step phase, and playback status in real time. 
 Autonomous Orchestration (Action Tools): We exposed direct control tools like set_song , set_tempo , set_practice_mode , and start_practice . An agent can receive a prompt like "I'm a beginner, set me up and start" , and autonomously chain multiple tools to configure the UI and launch the YouTube engine with zero human UI clicks. 
 

 

 🎙️ Hybrid Voice AI Coach: Hands-Free Mastery 

 To ensure a true dance floor experience, we built a Real-Time Voice AI Coach directly in the browser. It bridges natural language commands into the same WebMCP TrainerBridge actions used by the AI agent. Whether using a laptop or a smartphone, the system understands "Start" , "Slow down" , "Baby steps" , or "Włącz Szaloną" with zero perceptible delay. 

 🛑 The Technical Challenge: The Mobile Audio Focus Battle 

 One of our biggest technical hurdles was the Hardware Audio Focus conflict on mobile devices. Standard continuous speech recognition on Android/iOS treats the microphone as a high-priority "call," causing embedded media (YouTube) to stutter, compress audio (Hardware Audio Ducking), or stop entirely. 

 The Solution: We engineered an Adaptive Audio Focus architecture: 

 
 Desktop: Full Continuous Hands-Free mode (mic stays open for the whole session). 
 Mobile: Discrete Adaptive Listening (Push-to-Talk) with immediate Hardware Audio Release. 
 

 By explicitly managing the hardware audio release and implementing a focus-switching buffer, we guaranteed 100% smooth, stutter-free 60fps video playback on smartphones —a critical requirement for maintaining rhythm during practice. 

 

 ⚡ Core Features 

 
 Interactive SVG Footwork Engine: Digital dance floor animating mirrored foot trajectories and weight distribution. 
 Haptic Pocket Metronome: Pairs Web Audio sync with the Web Vibration API for eyes-free blind practice. 
 Two-Way Video Synchronizer: Real-time tempo scaling (0.5× to 1.25×) synchronized with authentic YouTube party tracks. 
 Bilingual i18n Support: Full Polish and English localization for a global wedding audience. 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 
 Frontend: Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion. 
 Integration: WebMCP (Native in-browser registration + /.well-known/mcp.json discovery). 
 Audio/Voice: Web Speech API, Web Audio API, YouTube IFrame API. 
 Quality & Testing: Verified 100/100 Google Lighthouse score (LCP < 600ms) with 8/8 automated Vitest unit tests passing in CI/CD. 
 Lead Architect & Methodology: Adam Gierczak. Built in synergy with AI assistants as a testament to modern agentic workflows. 
 

 

 🚀 What's Next 

 
 Computer Vision Pose Verification: Using WebRTC to verify knee flexion and foot contact in real-time. 
 Universal Partner Dance Protocol: Expanding the WebMCP tool schema to support Salsa, Bachata, and Kizomba timing. 
 Multi-Agent Coaching: Enabling "Lead" and "Follow" agents to coordinate couples training via WebMCP. 
 

 🌐 Live Demo: https://dwanajeden.netlify.app/

title: BeatScope Director
pitch: An in-browser WebMCP music workspace where AI agents can inspect timing, find visual moments, compare sections, and control playback using BeatScope’s deterministic local audio analysis.
about_excerpt: An in-browser WebMCP music workspace where AI agents can inspect timing, find visual moments, compare sections, and control playback using BeatScope’s deterministic local audio analysis. Like Comment Story Updates GIF WebMCP Director focusing and comparing measured visual ranges inside the BeatScope player. Inspiration BeatScope started from a simple problem: music visualizations often look impressive, but the timing logic behind them is usually locked inside one demo. I wanted to turn musical timing into reusable, deterministic data that could drive different visual systems — and also be understood by coding agents. The WebMCP Challenge made it possible to take that idea one step further: instead of making an agent inspect the DOM or guess how the player works, BeatScope can expose its musical state directly as structured browser tools. What it does BeatScope Director adds an in-browser WebMCP collaboration layer to BeatScope. An AI agent can inspect the loaded track, query timing and energy at any moment, read bounded musical events, find visually interesting ranges, compare sections, focus the timeline, control playback, and create loops — all inside the same player the user is watching. It currently exposes eight WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() , including: get_project_context get_state_at_time get_events find_visual_moments compare_ranges focus_range control_playback set_loop_range The agent does not receive the source audio. It works from BeatScope's already-computed analysis, while the user's normal local upload and playback workflow remains unchanged. How I built it I kept BeatScope's existing architecture and analysis pipeline intact and added WebMCP as a separate browser integration layer. Both the existing stdio MCP server and the new WebMCP Director read the same Rhythm IR and deterministic runtime, so they describe the same track with the same semantics; only the transport and lifecycle are different. The WebMCP layer is split into schemas, queries, actions, responses, and registration lifecycle code. Read-only tools are explicitly separated from tools that modify the page. Agent actions are visible in the UI and can be reversed by the user. I also built a reproducible WebMCP demo with rights-safe synthesized audio, browser smoke tests, snapshots, benchmarks, and CI coverage. Challenges The hardest part was keeping the agent useful without letting it invent musical meaning. BeatScope deliberately reports measurable facts such as beats, transients, frequency-band energy, and neutral structural repetition. It does not pretend that an onset is a kick or snare, or that a repeated section must be a verse or chorus. Another challenge was browser control. Playback actions have to respect autoplay restrictions, variable-tempo timing, cancellation, page lifecycle, and user ownership of the final state. I also wanted WebMCP to fail gracefully: if document.modelContext is unavailable, BeatScope still behaves like the normal player instead of breaking. What I learned WebMCP works best when it is not just a wrapper around buttons. The most useful tools expose the application's actual domain model. In BeatScope, that means giving the agent direct access to deterministic rhythm, structure, energy, and playback state instead of forcing it to reconstruct those concepts from the interface. I also learned that human-agent collaboration feels much safer when agent actions are visible, bounded, and reversible. The user still owns the player; WebMCP simply gives the agent a structured way to participate. title: Lemma
pitch: Lemma is an IDE for human–AI mathematical reasoning. Explore, challenge, and branch solutions without losing the thread—while humans stay in control
about_excerpt: Lemma is an IDE for human–AI mathematical reasoning. Explore, challenge, and branch solutions without losing the thread—while humans stay in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hi, my name is Bernabé, and this is my project, Lemma . Over the past year, I’ve heard stories and read news about researchers—and even students—using AI to discover new proofs or make progress on long-standing mathematical problems, including some of the famous Erdős problems. This is exciting and optimistic, but it also introduces a new challenge: as AI helps produce an increasing number of proofs, conjectures, and solutions, how will humans connect them into a coherent development of mathematics and science? And, perhaps more importantly, what role will researchers play in that process? Terence Tao recently published an insightful article exploring this topic , in case you want to go down that rabbit hole. This is a complex question that the scientific community will need to address together. I don’t pretend to have the answer, but as a software engineer, I wanted to contribute through something I know how to build. I had seen applications that use AI agents to solve mathematical problems and produce LaTeX documents. However, the result can quickly become a collection of messy, disconnected information—something similar to spaghetti code in software development. Mathematical reasoning rarely follows a single, linear path. Researchers explore different strategies, reconsider assumptions, return to earlier decisions, and abandon dead ends. In a traditional AI conversation, that structure is easily lost, especially as the context grows. That is why I created Lemma. What it does Lemma is an IDE-like collaborative workspace where humans and AI agents work on mathematical reasoning together. Engineers, mathematicians, physicists, students, and anyone working with mathematics can use Lemma to define objectives, provide context, explore strategies, and develop solutions as structured reasoning graphs. Instead of treating a solution as one long document or conversation, Lemma organizes it into objectives, strategies, branches, and individual reasoning steps. Users can interrupt the process at any moment, correct an agent, introduce a new idea, return to an earlier step, or create an alternative branch without overwriting the original path. The core workflow is interrupt, branch, continue : a human changes the direction of a solution, and the agent reads the updated state through WebMCP and continues from there. WebMCP is fundamental to this experience. Humans interact through a visual workspace, while agents can directly read and update the same structured reasoning graph. Both operate on the same source of truth, using the interface that works best for each of them. Ultimately, Lemma is my approach to keeping humans in the loop—combining human creativity, context, and judgment with the speed and capabilities of AI to pursue mathematical goals together. How we built it Lemma is built as a TypeScript monorepo using pnpm workspaces . The frontend uses React 19, Vite, strict TypeScript, React Router, XYFlow, and Dagre . XYFlow and Dagre power the visual reasoning canvas, where strategies, branches, dependencies, and mathematical steps are displayed as an interactive graph. Mathematical content is written in Markdown with embedded TeX and rendered using react-markdown, remark-math, and KaTeX . The backend is built with Supabase , using: Supabase Auth for authentication. PostgreSQL for the persisted reasoning graph. Row Level Security to protect each workspace. Realtime to keep the interface synchronized after changes. Storage for context files and supporting material. Edge Functions for the authenticated API and embedding pipeline. pgvector and full-text search for semantic step retrieval. The reasoning graph is the source of truth. Entities such as workspaces, objectives, strategies, branches, steps, assumptions, sources, decisions, and results are stored as structured relational data instead of being inferred from a Markdown document. The frontend, API, and WebMCP layer share the same Zod schemas , helping ensure that humans and agents interact with the same validated contracts. At the top-level page, Lemma registers 22 WebMCP tools . These allow agents to inspect the workspace, create and update objectives, develop strategies, add steps and dependencies, create branches, mark assumptions or dead ends, compare branches, request human decisions, search previous reasoning, and generate a clean solution. All agent mutations use the same authenticated application services as the visual interface. When an agent changes the graph, the result is immediately reflected and highlighted in the workspace. The web client is hosted on Vercel , while Supabase provides the database and backend services. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was developing a clear mental model for structuring mathematical problems. Mathematical reasoning is not simply a document, a chat, or a linear list of steps. I had to think carefully about which entities should participate in the process, how they should relate to one another, and how to preserve alternative paths without losing the history of the original reasoning. Designing the interface was another major challenge. A reasoning graph can contain objectives, strategies, branches, steps, dependencies, assumptions, and results, so presenting all that information in a way that remains comfortable to navigate and understand was difficult. I am happy with the current direction, but the interface could still be improved significantly as the conceptual model evolves and more people test it. Accomplishments that we're proud of I’m proud of having built a working prototype in record time that already allows mathematical problems to be explored in a visual and organized way. There is still plenty of room to improve the problem-solving process, but one moment made me especially proud. A friend of mine who is studying mathematics tested Lemma and told me that he loved how easy it was to work with AI agents through the application. That feedback made the idea feel real. It showed me that Lemma was not only an interesting technical experiment, but that its visual and structured approach could genuinely make AI-assisted mathematical reasoning easier to follow. What we learned The most important thing I learned was how people mentally approach mathematical problems. Although I enjoy mathematics, it is still a hobby for me. Building an application intended to help people who are significantly better at mathematics than I am was challenging at first. It forced me to think beyond the final answer and focus on the actual reasoning process: how ideas are introduced, how assumptions affect later conclusions, how different strategies emerge, and why returning to an earlier decision is such an important part of solving difficult problems. I also learned that building effective tools for AI collaboration is not only about giving agents more capabilities. It is equally important to make their work inspectable, editable, and easy for humans to redirect. What's next for Lemma The next step is to improve Lemma’s conceptual model and introduce additional entities that support other types of mathematical work. For example, Lemma could also be used as a learning environment, with dedicated explanation nodes that help users understand why a particular step works—not just what the next step is. There are many other possible workflows that could be built on top of the same reasoning graph. I would also like to integrate tools based on Lean , allowing agents and researchers to translate results into formal proofs and mechanically verify whether a conclusion is correct. This could create a valuable bridge between exploratory mathematical reasoning and formally verified results. Another feature I would love to create is a collaborative mode. Researchers could publish their work so that others could explore it, contribute new ideas or branches, and use previous research as a source of reference and context. In the long term, Lemma could become more than a workspace for solving individual problems: it could become a shared, connected environment for developing, verifying, and communicating mathematical knowledge alongside AI. title: Bandmate-WebMCP
pitch: Bandmate is a WebMCP musical sequencer, where you jam away on your instrument, and the agent arranges it all in one tab while the loop keeps playing, with creative collaboration happening in realtime.
about_excerpt: Bandmate is a WebMCP musical sequencer, where you jam away on your instrument, and the agent arranges it all in one tab while the loop keeps playing, with creative collaboration happening in realtime. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Four bars of melody and no idea what goes under it. Asking ChatGPT yields MIDI text to convert, import and audition five minutes later, and the model never heard your take. WebMCP suggested a third thing: the agent sits in the tab with the sequencer, reads your notes as structure, and writes into the bar you are still hearing. What it does Bandmate is a four-track loop sequencer (drums, bass, chords, lead; 4 bars, 64 steps) exposing 16 WebMCP tools. Play a riff on the piano or your computer keys; ask "what goes under this?"; the agent calls suggest_chords then add_chords, and teal notes cascade into the grid while the loop keeps playing. It adds bass and drums in three styles, and can play you two arrangements before committing one. Record live and its writers are unregistered until you stop. Export a Standard MIDI File into any DAW. Why WebMCP fits this use case Shared state beats generated text. The agent needs what you just played, what you just muted, and which bar you are looking at. All three live in the page's store; get_session serialises them in under 700 characters. The human must stay in the loop. Harmony is taste. audition is a tool whose execute() awaits a click; the agent's turn pauses until a human has listened. Capabilities should track the mode. While you record, writers are dangerous; during an audition they would corrupt the preview. Tool groups are disposed via AbortController and the browser fires toolchange, so the agent's tool list is truthful at every moment. No backend. One static site works in ChatGPT desktop, Chrome with the flag, or with a bring-your-own-key agent. How it improves the experience for people Five minutes per iteration becomes eight seconds. You never leave the grid or convert a file; every agent write is teal beside your amber notes and undoable in one click. The agent reacts to what you did by hand ("muted bass 5s ago"), and when it cannot decide it plays A and B instead of guessing. Students see why a chord works: numerals, names, borrowed and altered chords, a why per suggestion. What humans and agents can accomplish together that was previously impossible The agent hears your playing as structure, not audio, so it can answer "what goes under what I just played?" and drop the answer into the bar you are still hearing. A DAW has no ear for theory; a music generator has no room for you. And because the agent cannot hear, it asks your ears: it plays two options in your tab and waits for you to pick. How I built it Vite + vanilla TypeScript, Tone.js 15, no server. Registration. Each tool is a typed defineTool({name, description, inputSchema, annotations, execute}) registered via document.modelContext.registerTool(descriptor, {signal}). That is the only surface ChatGPT's browser and Chrome 152 expose; navigator.modelContext is probed only as a fallback for other builds. Tool groups and toolchange. Five ToolGroups (readers, writers, dialog, transport, recording), each with one AbortController. Recording or auditioning disposes the writers; leaving re-registers them. Abort unregisters natively, the browser emits toolchange, and the header pill shows idle 15 / recording 8 / auditioning 7. Annotations. Readers carry readOnlyHint. Exactly one tool, clear_track, carries consequentialHint: it is the only whole-track wipe, and it also asks the human first. untrustedContentHint appears nowhere, because no Bandmate content originates from a third party. Schema hygiene. Every schema is type:'object', additionalProperties:false, explicit required, enums for closed sets, numeric bounds, a description on every property. An Ajv strict test compiles all of them and enforces name ≤ 30, description ≤ 350, parameter ≤ 120. Bounded results. get_session ≤ 700 chars, get_track ≤ 1,500, everything else clipped with truncated:true. Notes use a compact b1: 1@1 3@5 5@9 degree format; drum lanes are 16-char velocity-class strings. Every result ends with hint or next. Audition as an awaiting tool. Each option is a full variant Session swapped into the store's transient layer at the next step; the engine tick reads store.current(), so previews are audible without rebuilds. Keep commits one undoable agent mutation; the promise resolves with chosen, listened, undo_id. On timeout it returns awaiting_human and the card stays open. Honours AbortSignal. Attribution and undo. Note.by / DrumHit.by are set by store.apply() from the caller's meta. Undo is a linear stack of deep-cloned snapshots (cap 50) tagged with author and label; the undo tool refuses when the top entry is human. Writers that would remove human notes call store.dryRun() then askHuman(). One clock. A single 64-step Tone.Sequence reads store.current() every 16th; no Parts, no rebuilds. Recording quantises keydown times to the nearest 16th and writes by:'human' live. Export. Pure SMF type-1 writer (PPQ 480, swing baked, drums on channel 10). The tool sets the Download button's href and spotlights it; the click is the human's. Challenges document.modelContext hands back inputSchema as a JSON string and executeTool takes one, which shaped the built-in agent and the Playwright harness. Keeping a promise pending inside execute() for up to 60 s and defining what happens after a host timeout (card stays; late click applies). Making agent writes audible on the next 16th without glitches. Autoplay: an agent transport play before any gesture must return muted_until_user_taps and spotlight Play. Accomplishments Sixteen tools that plain sentences route to across 12 eval cases; an audition whose promise waits for a human ear; a mode-driven tool list the browser reports truthfully; zero backend. What I learned Tool descriptions are UX: verb-first, one "use when", one constraint, and "returns undo_id" changed which tool the model picked more than schema tweaks did. Hinted results turn three calls into a conversation. Once every cell knows who wrote it, undo, confirmation and "what did I just do?" fall out for free. What's next WebMIDI input, more styles and time signatures, a per-bar "why this chord" explainer, auditions of fills and voicings, all as more tools on the same store. Play keys (a w s e d f …), press Stop; back to 15. Ask Export this as MIDI, click the highlighted Download button, open the file in any DAW. Chrome: DevTools → Application → WebMCP lists the registered tools with annotations (15 idle, 8 recording); ?debug=1 opens the inspector. Repo: pnpm test. title: Attic
pitch: Attic is AI web-app that brings a family closer: the place your house keeps its memories, so everyone, and the AI agents they bring, can read and add to them.
about_excerpt: Attic is AI web-app that brings a family closer: the place your house keeps its memories, so everyone, and the AI agents they bring, can read and add to them. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to build an AI tool my whole family would use together, every day. Something that connects every person in the household to one living memory and brings the family closer. Every home has one person who knows everything. The furnace filter size. The plumber who charges fairly. Where the water shutoff is. And, for the 53 million Americans caring for someone they love, who is taking Mom to cardiology on Thursday. When that person is busy, traveling, or gone, the household goes blind. Household knowledge leaks away because capture friction kills every tool built for it. The moment passes before anyone opens an app in the basement to type "check the anode rod in three years." Caregiver figure: National Alliance for Caregiving and AARP, "Caregiving in the U.S. 2020" (53.0 million adults, May 2020). What it does Attic is a living memory for one home, drawn as a cutaway house at dusk. Every lamp is one thing the house knows, glowing in the room it belongs to. A house is a private link you hand to your family. Everyone enters with the link alone. The people your family looks after live there too. The care circle holds Mom's appointments, her meds and refills, the rides still waiting to be claimed, and a journal siblings write to each other. Every family member's AI agent can read and write all of it through 17 WebMCP tools the house page publishes itself. Anyone in the house sees each change land as it happens, with a receipt they can press Undo on. How we built it The house is one hand-drawn SVG cutaway in React and Vite. Rooms, lamps, people, and the cat all sit on the same layout model, so a new memory knows which room it belongs in. Behind it is a Cloudflare Worker with one Durable Object per house. The object owns the state, applies every change as an op, stores the inverse op alongside it, keeps a 200-entry receipt log, and broadcasts to everyone connected over WebSockets. Every tool travels the same op channel as the buttons on the page. An agent's write lights a lamp in the right room on everybody's screen and leaves a receipt any family member can undo. Challenges we ran into Undo that survives other people. Working out how to reverse a change after the fact is guesswork. So every op stores its own inverse at the moment it is applied. Undo is a tool too. An agent can take back its own mistake by receipt id, and your sister can undo what your agent did from her phone in another state. Cloudflare answered before the Worker did. not_found_handling: "single-page-application" was serving index.html for API paths because the asset router sees navigations first. /api/* has to be named explicitly in run_worker_first . Making an agent's work legible. An agent quietly editing your family's records is unsettling. Every change lights the room it belongs to, writes a receipt with a name and a time, and stays undoable by anyone in the house. Accomplishments that we're proud of * An AI tool that connect people and agents, in two way network * A test suite that drives every tool and guards the spec. tests/webmcp-tools.test.mjs polyfills document.modelContext and calls all 17 house tools, both landing tools, and all three declarative forms. It also asserts that every annotation key is a member WebMCP defines. An invented hint fails the build. A two-browser test that proves the whole claim. One browser drives an agent, the other is a family member's screen. The suite watches the change cross the wire and watches the other person undo it. A demo a judge can run in any browser. The Agent tab runs the real execute() functions behind a button, so the entire tool surface is testable today, including on a phone. What we learned WebMCP changes what a page is for. The web was built for eyes and a pointer. Software reaching it has always worked from the outside: scrapers, separate servers, issued keys. WebMCP turns that around. The page itself offers what it can do, inside the user's own browser session, behind the security and permissions the site already enforces. The site stays in charge of its own rules. One codebase serves the person and the agent at once, with the agent surface designed in from the first line. I believe this is where web development goes: sites built for two audiences, with the second one treated as first class. Build the tool surface as a peer of the UI. Every tool goes through the same op channel as the buttons on the page. remember does what the add-memory panel does. claim_care_task does what the Claim button does. Once that was true, the design questions answered themselves: if a family member can do it, an agent can do it, and everyone in the house watches it happen. Tool names and descriptions are the interface. A model reads whats_coming_up , search_house_memory , claim_care_task , and undo_last_action the way a person reads menu labels. The names that work are verbs a family already says out loud. whos_here earns its place because an agent should know who else is in the house before it acts on their behalf. Returning both a receipt id and a record id from every write is what makes chained flows work: search, claim by id, then journal about it. The annotations are a vocabulary, and it rewards reading the dictionary. WebMCP defines three hints: readOnlyHint , untrustedContentHint , and consequentialHint . destructiveHint and idempotentHint belong to MCP's separate server-side set. A conformant browser keeps the members WebMCP defines and silently discards the rest. Attic declares readOnlyHint on all 17 tools and sets it true on the seven that only read. untrustedContentHint goes on the twelve whose output can carry text another family member wrote. consequentialHint goes on the two an agent should confirm first. Attic ships the three WebMCP defines. Check the annotations in a browser, beyond the spec alone. I registered a probe tool in Chrome 152 under the origin trial with six annotation keys and read it back with document.modelContext.getTools() . Two survive today: readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint . consequentialHint appears in the published dictionary but remains unimplemented, so it is dropped in conversion. Attic keeps it anyway. It is the correct member, and it starts working the day Chrome ships it. The same caution sits in the descriptions of forget and add_medication , which is the channel a model reads right now. That check takes five minutes and belongs in any WebMCP project. What's next for Attic I want Attic to become a real product. This submission is a hackathon build. The problem behind it is a solution, and it is the one I want to work on. The next step is putting OpenAI's newest models behind the house. An agent that holds a whole household in view can surface the refill that slipped and the appointment two siblings both booked. It can catch the pattern in a care journal that shows up only across months. Mostly I want Attic to be the answer when someone asks what these tools are actually for. Keeping a family close through a hard year is a real use for AI, and it is the one I care about. 1. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The thing that kills household memory is capture friction. An agent is the only thing that removes it. You say "gutters cleaned by ClearFlow, about $180" in passing to the agent you are already talking to. remember files it, dated, in the yard, with a reminder for next autumn. The knowledge gets captured at the moment it exists, which is the only moment it is ever free. Retrieval is just as agent-shaped. A year later you are in a hardware store and ask "what size filter does the furnace take?" Your sister, in another state, asks her agent "who is covering Mom this week?" Both of you want the answer where you already are, in the conversation you are in. A household memory needs structured tools. The data is small, highly structured, deeply personal, and it changes constantly from several directions at once. Attic hands agents 17 imperative tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool inside a house, and 2 more on the landing page so an agent can create or open one for you. All use JSON Schema inputs and annotations from the WebMCP ToolAnnotations dictionary, plus 3 declarative <form toolname> tools. 2. How it creates a better user experience Handing an agent write access to a family's shared memory is only tolerable if the family can see and reverse what it did. Every mutating tool call lands on the page as a receipt : who did it, through which tool, in plain language, with an Undo button any family member can press. The Durable Object stores an inverse op with every change, so undo is exact. Undo is a tool too ( undo_last_action ), so an agent can take back its own mistake by receipt id. title: PantryPilot
pitch: Meal planning a human and an AI agent do together, live through real WebMCP tools, not clicks.
about_excerpt: Meal planning a human and an AI agent do together, live through real WebMCP tools, not clicks. Like Comment Story Updates PantryPilot High-Level Architecture PantryPilot Low-Level Architecture Diagram banner Inspiration Most "AI meal planning" demos are a chatbot that describes a plan in a text box - you still have to go copy the ingredients into a shopping list app yourself. WebMCP flips that: instead of an agent guessing at button selectors or a chat window narrating what you should do, a page can expose its actual capabilities as tools an agent calls directly. Meal planning turned out to be a good fit to prove that out. It's a genuinely tedious, recurring chore with real constraints - dietary restrictions, a grocery budget, food already sitting in the fridge about to go bad - the kind of multi-step, stateful task that's tedious for a human to do by hand and awkward for a chatbot to do by description, but a natural fit for an agent that can actually read and write app state. What it does PantryPilot is a meal planner and shopping list. A household sets dietary preferences (vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free, or a free-form avoid-list), tracks what's in the pantry (including expiry dates), and optionally sets a weekly grocery budget. From there: Search and rank a 16-recipe catalog by pantry match ("what can I make with what I already have"), by what's about to expire, by cost, by prep time, or by calories/protein. Plan a single day, or hand the whole week to plan-week , which fills every empty day under whatever constraints you give it - tags, max prep time, a calorie/protein ceiling, the remaining budget, and a "use up what's expiring" priority - while never overriding an active dietary restriction and never repeating a recipe in the same week. Get a shopping list generated automatically from the plan, aggregated across recipes and offset by what's already in the pantry. See a per-day and weekly nutrition summary. See exactly what happened and who did it - every action is logged and tagged human or agent - and undo the most recent change with one click, by either party. All of that is exposed as 19 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so a human using the page and an agent acting on it are working in the same live session, not two separate experiences. How we built it Plain JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no build step - the whole app is static files. The core design decision was a single shared domain module, js/actions.js , that owns every mutation (planning a recipe, updating the pantry, regenerating the shopping list, undo). Both the human-facing UI and every WebMCP tool's execute() call the exact same functions in that module, tagged with who's calling ( "human" or "agent" ), so there's no separate, more-powerful "agent path" that could drift out of sync with what a human can do. State lives in a small reactive store backed by localStorage ; the UI and the tool layer both subscribe to its change event, so a change from either side re-renders the page immediately. Since this session's sandbox had no WebMCP-capable browser to test against, we built an in-page "Agent Console" that drives the identical document.modelContext tool handlers through a plain form (pick a tool, edit the JSON arguments, run it) - the same code path a real agent would hit, just reachable without the Chrome 149 origin trial or ChatGPT's browser. It became a first-class part of the app rather than a throwaway test harness, since it also lets anyone verify every tool works without installing anything. We also wrote a node:test suite (32 tests) against js/actions.js directly, covering dietary-conflict enforcement, shopping-list aggregation, budget math, and the undo system, and ran full Playwright end-to-end passes over every tab and every tool before each push. Challenges we ran into No native WebMCP runtime to test against. We couldn't rely on trying it in a real agent client during development, so correctness had to come from the domain layer itself (validation, tests, the Agent Console) - the tool registration is thin by design, and almost all of the actual logic lives in code we could run and test directly. Keeping the agent from being more powerful than a human. It would have been easy to write a fast "agent path" that skips validation for convenience. Instead every tool routes through the same functions the UI uses, which meant designing actions.js first as a proper API, not as UI glue. Undo without duplicating history. A single logical action like "add a recipe to Monday" cascades into a second internal update (the shopping list regenerating). A naive undo implementation would push a separate history entry for that cascade and undo the wrong thing. Snapshots are taken immediately before the actual mutating store.update() call inside each action, and the shopping-list regeneration that happens as a side effect of another action is marked silent and skipped by the snapshot - so one user-facing action is always exactly one undo step, verified with a dedicated test. Shopping-list aggregation. Merging ingredient quantities across multiple recipes, scaling by servings, subtracting whatever's already in the pantry, and preserving which items are already checked off across a regeneration all had to work together without double-counting or losing state. Accomplishments that we're proud of 19 WebMCP tools that are genuinely load-bearing - plan-week does real constraint-based selection (dietary safety, no repeats, budget, expiry priority), not a lookup table dressed up as a tool. An architecture where an agent provably can't do anything a human couldn't do by clicking around, because they're the same code. A working undo system - a real implementation of the reversibility idea in WebMCP's own security guidance, not just a line in the description. 32 passing unit tests plus a full Playwright pass over every tab and every tool, run before every push. Zero backend, zero build step, deployable to Netlify, Vercel, or Cloudflare Pages in minutes. What we learned WebMCP's imperative API is small on purpose - registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) is most of it - which pushes the real design work down into the domain logic underneath, where it belongs. Tools that compose ( plan-week reusing search-recipes 's own ranking logic) produce much better agent behavior than a flat pile of unrelated CRUD tools would. Trust in a page an agent can write to has to be built into the architecture - one shared code path, validation at the domain layer, and reversibility - not asserted after the fact in a description. What's next for PantryPilot Testing against a real WebMCP origin trial browser and ChatGPT's browser once broadly available, beyond the in-page Agent Console. Redo (undo is currently one level deep, with no way back). Recipe ratings/favorites and multi-week history ("plan like last week"). A substitution tool that suggests a swap when an ingredient is missing or newly avoided. Optional lightweight sync so a plan isn't tied to one browser's localStorage . Exploring WebMCP's declarative API and cross-origin exposedTo , e.g. a grocery-delivery origin reading the shopping list directly. title: House Design Tool
pitch: A 3D home designer that allows humans and agents to collaborate on a proejct. WebMCP gives agents 21 tools on the live house design, while a shared rulebook keeps every wall and walkway legal.
about_excerpt: A 3D home designer that allows humans and agents to collaborate on a proejct. WebMCP gives agents 21 tools on the live house design, while a shared rulebook keeps every wall and walkway legal. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every AI design tool today works like a vending machine: you describe what you want in a chat box, and a finished result drops out. That's backwards for spatial work. Nobody designs a home by describing it. They nudge a wall, stand in the kitchen, drag the sofa two feet, and look . We wanted the agent in the room with you, not on the other side of a chat log. WebMCP made that possible: if the page itself exposes its live state as tools, the human and the agent can finally work on the same object at the same time. What it does WebMCP Home Design is a 3D floorplan editor that registers 21 tools on document.modelContext . A human picks a shell (floors, then a template per floor), reshapes rooms, and furnishes by dragging, rotating, and resizing, while an agent in the browser reads the same live design and edits it through tools: placing furniture, moving walls, cutting doors, batching twenty edits in one call, even proposing three alternative layouts that ghost over the plan for the human to compare and apply. A simplified residential constraint engine (13 rules: door widths, bedroom egress, kitchen aisles, toilet clearances, furniture facing walls) referees both parties identically: every edit returns what changed and what it broke. Designs autosave locally, export as JSON, and travel as share links with the whole compressed design in the URL fragment. No server, no accounts. How we built it TypeScript end to end. The domain layer models rooms, shared walls, openings, and furniture in plan inches, with pure operations (clone in, result out) that both the UI and the agent tools call: one rulebook, two doors in. React Three Fiber renders the scene: procedural canvas-painted textures with bump and roughness maps, parametric furniture built from primitives (a resized sofa grows a third cushion), dollhouse-cut walls overhead and full walls in a street-view-style walkthrough. Zustand holds per-floor state with undo history; Zod schemas define tool inputs and compile to the JSON Schemas agents see. Everything is generated in code, with no model files and no fetched assets, so the app works fully offline. Challenges we ran into The hardest problems were about shared control. Coincident walls desynchronized until we rebuilt the model around one wall per partition. Agent calls serialize at roughly a second each in the browser, which pushed us to design apply_edits for single-round-trip furnishing. Grid snapping silently moved agent placements until every operation learned to echo where things actually landed. And a long tail of 3D truths: coplanar surfaces z-fight into flicker, room polygons run along wall centerlines so furniture sank 3 inches into walls, and an agent with no orientation guidance will happily face a wardrobe into a wall, which became both a smarter placement default and a new validation rule. Accomplishments that we're proud of The loop genuinely works both ways. An agent can validate a plan, fix a too-narrow door, furnish a bedroom, and then walk the human through the result with the camera; a human can drag a sofa and the agent's next get_layout reflects it. We're proud that refusals are as useful as successes (every rejected edit explains what would break and suggests a fix the grid can actually produce) and that 267 tests pin the whole thing down, from constraint rules to camera math to the persistence format. What we learned Tools-on-the-page is a different discipline from tools-on-a-server. The agent needs what a colleague needs: honest echoes of what actually happened, actionable refusals, bounds included in summaries so it doesn't ask twice, and documentation precise enough to reason about (our rotation docs went from "0 faces the bottom" to a full compass after watching agents guess wrong). We also learned that the referee matters more than either player: the constraint engine is what turns two editors sharing one document from chaos into collaboration. What's next for House Design Tool Furniture variants: extending propose_variants beyond wall moves so an agent can ghost three complete room arrangements, pre-validated, for the human to pick from. Stacked multi-floor 3D with stairs and alignment rules. Real collaboration transport (two humans plus an agent on one design). And a richer catalog with materials, lighting fixtures, and cost estimates, so the conversation can become "make it nicer for under $3,000."
